verdict.summary: IsIdentityConsumingSwitch dereferences the result of graph.GetNode(tensor_id.node()) without a NULL check. tensor_id.node() comes from ParseTensorName over the node's attacker-controlled input string in a serialized graph, and nothing in this code ensures the referenced node exists. When the input names a nonexistent node, GetNode returns its failure sentinel (nullptr) and IsSwitch(*input_node) dereferences it, crashing the process that consumes the untrusted model — a cross-trust-boundary denial of service.

evidence.snippet:
NodeDef* input_node = graph.GetNode(tensor_id.node());
    return IsSwitch(*input_node);
evidence.reason: The lookup graph.GetNode(tensor_id.node()) can return nullptr when the attacker-supplied input string (parsed at line 5 into tensor_id) names a node absent from the attacker-supplied graph; the result is dereferenced at IsSwitch(*input_node) with no NULL check on any path. Trigger: an Identity node with input "ghost:0" in a GraphDef containing no node named "ghost" — IsTensorIdControlling passes (non-control input), GetNode misses, and the null pointer is dereferenced, crashing the process loading the untrusted model.

assumptions: MutableGraphView::GetNode is a name-keyed lookup that returns a null pointer when the name is not present in the graph; this is the documented lookup semantics relied on per the callee boundary rule.
IsSwitch reads fields of the passed NodeDef (a predicate over the node), so binding *input_node from a null pointer results in a read through null at the call site.
The GraphDef/NodeDef content originates from serialized model state, treated as untrusted per the data-origin impact model; no deployment context was used to reach or demote the finding.
limitations: ParseTensorName's behavior on fully malformed strings (e.g., no colon, empty name) is not shown; the trigger was instantiated with a well-formed name referencing a nonexistent node, so this does not affect the verdict.

Whether callers of IsIdentityConsumingSwitch revalidate graph consistency before calling was not observable; per the guard-anchoring rule this cannot demote the finding since the defect is the unchecked dereference in this code.

verdict.summary: This predicate function checks every attacker-derived value it consumes before its sinks: the repeated-field access node.input(0) is guarded by 'node.input_size() > 0' in the same short-circuited condition, and the pointer returned by graph.GetNode(tensor_id.node()) on an attacker-chosen name is guarded by 'if (input_node == nullptr) { return false; }' before the sole dereference at IsSwitch(*input_node). Both guards lie on every path to their sinks in execution order and were edge-tested at boundary values (empty input list, missing node name, nullptr). The parsed TensorId is used only as a classifier argument and a name-string lookup key, which are not memory, index, size, or injection sinks in this code. No instantiated vulnerability exists in the given code.

assumptions: graph.GetNode(name) is a name-keyed lookup that returns nullptr when no node matches, and returns a valid NodeDef* otherwise; its nullptr failure sentinel is the only relevant behavior and it is tested before use.

ParseTensorName, IsIdentity, IsIdentityNSingleInput, IsTensorIdControlling, and IsSwitch are not shown; their behavior was treated as characterizable classifier/lookup/parse helpers. The argument passed to ParseTensorName is an arbitrary string, which is in-domain for any parse function, so no out-of-domain argument crosses a callee boundary at any call site in this code.

NodeDef content (op type, input strings, input count) is treated as attacker-data per the data-origin model; despite this, every such value reaching a sink in this code is guarded by a quoted statement.
limitations: Candidate dismissed as speculative: a potential crash or malformed TensorId inside the not-shown ParseTensorName callee on a malformed input string such as 'a:x' or 'a:'. The impact chain breaks inside callee code not given, and this code passes only an in-domain string argument, so per the callee boundary rule the defect, if any, is not in this code.

The security effect of returning false on the early-exit paths (non-Identity node, control input, missing node) depends on how callers of IsIdentityConsumingSwitch use the boolean; no caller is shown, so no fail-open or authorization consequence can be instantiated here.

verdict.summary: All memory-safety sinks in this function are guarded: the only pointer dereference (*iter->second) is preceded on every path by the quoted find/end check, no sizes, copies, or format strings are consumed, and stored pointers cannot dangle because the const a1 container is never mutated. The one real logic defect is that a duplicate name in a1 silently overwrites the map entry (DCHECK is debug-only and does not reject on the release path), so the function can return true for containers of different sizes; however, that trigger contradicts this code's own documented uniqueness contract quoted in the DCHECK message, and the security consequence depends entirely on an unseen caller's use of the returned bool, so the impact is not instantiated in this code.

assumptions: The behavior of the not-shown callee AttrDefEqual is assumed to be a pure equality predicate; only its boolean result is consumed here.
Whether callers pass attacker-controlled OpDef data (e.g., parsed protobuf) is not shown; parameters were treated as attacker-data per the data-origin model, which did not change the outcome.
limitations: Duplicate-name equality defect: if a1 contains two AttrDefs with the same name, the statement a1_set[def.name()] = &def; overwrites the first, so an a2 containing a single matching entry yields an empty map and the function returns true for unequal inputs. Not confirmed because (a) the trigger violates the precondition this code itself documents and asserts via DCHECK(... << "AttrDef names must be unique, but '" << def.name() << "' appears more than once"), and (b) the security impact depends on how a caller not shown uses the returned bool.

std::unordered_map keyed by attacker-controlled strings could in principle permit hash-flooding amplification, but no statement in this code produces that condition and it depends on the standard library's hash implementation; speculative.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. All writes to the ioctl capability struct are bounded by quotable guards: labellen is the min-clamp of sizeof(cap->card) and sizeof(dev->card_label), bus_info uses sizeof(cap->bus_info) with a literal format, and memset uses sizeof(cap->reserved). The two residual candidates, an out-of-bounds termination scan if dev->card_label were unterminated, and a NULL dereference of dev or video_get_drvdata(dev->vdev), depend on state values and pointer producers that this code never assigns, so their triggers are unsourced and speculative per the analysis rules.

assumptions: v4l2loopback_getdevice(file) returns a valid non-NULL device and dev->vdev is registered with drvdata set; these producers are outside the given code and no statement here checks them.
dev->card_label is a fixed-size array whose termination is established outside this code; no assignment to it exists in the given code.
The V4L2 core invokes this handler with a kernel-side cap buffer; cap is only written here, never read before assignment.

Struct field widths (cap->card, dev->card_label, cap->bus_info, cap->reserved) come from header definitions not present in the given code; the min-clamp and sizeof-based bounds are correct for any widths.
limitations: Potential out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) in the %s termination scan of snprintf(cap->card, labellen, "%s", dev->card_label) if dev->card_label fills its array without a NUL terminator; the trigger (unterminated card_label) is UNSOURCED in this code, and the disclosed output is truncated to labellen bytes, so no out-of-bounds data is copied out.

Potential NULL dereference (CWE-476) at ((struct v4l2loopback_private *)video_get_drvdata(dev->vdev))->device_nr and at dev->vdev->device_caps if dev or the drvdata is NULL; no producer of NULL exists in this code.
Capability flags (announce_all_caps, ready_for_capture, ready_for_output) are consumed but never assigned here; their integrity is assumed from driver state set elsewhere.

verdict.summary: The Compute op validates its key input (NumElements == 1 enforced by quoted OP_REQUIRES guards on the only path to use), iterates values within a loop-bounded, in-domain access, and checks every callee status with OP_REQUIRES_OK. The one genuinely unvalidated input, indices_tensor, is passed directly to the not-shown StagingMap::put with no validation of any form in this code; whether that constitutes a memory-safety defect depends entirely on the not-shown callee's handling of the indices, so the impact chain cannot be instantiated from the given code. The potential NULL use of map depends on an unprovable GetStagingMap failure mode.

Potential NULL dereference of map at map->put or core::ScopedUnref scope(map) requires GetStagingMap to return OK while leaving map NULL; no producer of this state is shown, making the trigger unsourced.

verdict.summary: recalc_intercepts merges L1-guest-supplied nested intercepts into the active VMCB. All array accesses are bounded by the same named constant (for (i = 0; i < MAX_INTERCEPT; i++)), guest-controlled data (g->int_ctl, g->intercepts) reaches only a branch condition and an in-range OR-merge, and no injection, allocation, format, path, or lifetime sink exists. No trigger precondition for a defect could be instantiated from statements in this code.

The consequence (additional VMEXITs and their reflection to L1) is consumed entirely by exit-handling code not given, so the impact chain is not characterizable from this code; recorded as a semantic observation, not a finding.

Any validation of the L1 vmcb12 control image before it reaches svm->nested.ctl happens in code not shown; if such validation is absent, the defect would be at that intake point, not in this merge function.

verdict.summary: ReadPSDChannelPixels advances the pointer p over the attacker-supplied decompressed channel buffer by packet_size bytes for each of image->columns iterations with no bound tied to the actual buffer size — the function does not even receive the buffer length — causing an out-of-bounds heap read (and disclosure of adjacent heap memory into the decoded image via SetPSDPixel/SyncAuthenticPixels) whenever the PSD file's channel data is shorter than columns*packet_size.

verdict.summary: BiasAndClamp never validates the relationship between bias_size and array_size. The only related statement is a debug-only TFLITE_DCHECK_EQ on divisibility, which is a no-op in release builds and in any case does not check bias_size <= array_size. The loops write bias_size elements per block into an array_size-element buffer, so any caller-supplied pair where bias_size does not evenly divide array_size, or bias_size > array_size > 0, produces out-of-bounds writes on array_data. In the NEON path the loop terminates on array_ptr != array_end_ptr while stepping by bias_size, so a non-divisible pair makes the pointer skip past the end and write unboundedly beyond the buffer.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values: bias_size and array_size are int parameters of a non-static function with no quotable caller-side validation; they directly control loop bounds, pointer stride, and the write range into array_data.

Out-of-bounds write sink (non-NEON path). The write index array_offset + i is bounded only by bias_size multiples; nothing ties it below array_size. Simulated trigger: bias_size=3, array_size=4 (line 4 rejects only 0; the DCHECK at line 10 is unquotable/debug-only). Second outer iteration (array_offset=3) writes array_data[4] and array_data[5], past the 4-element buffer; with bias_size=8, array_size=4 the first iteration already writes indices 4-7 out of bounds.

Out-of-bounds write sink (NEON path). Loop termination uses pointer inequality while stepping by unvalidated bias_size: when array_size % bias_size != 0 the pointer steps past array_end_ptr and never compares equal, so the stores at vst1q_f32(array_ptr + i, ...) and array_ptr[i] continue at addresses unboundedly beyond the array_size-element buffer. A negative array_size also makes array_end_ptr < array_ptr with the same unbounded forward writes.

assumptions: TFLITE_DCHECK_EQ at line 10 has no definition in the given code; per TensorFlow convention DCHECK macros compile to no-ops in release (NDEBUG) builds, so it provides no enforcement for this analysis and cannot serve as a guard.

The caller of BiasAndClamp is not shown; per the data-origin rules the parameters bias_size, array_size, and the buffers are treated as attacker-data, and 'the caller should have validated the sizes' is not a quotable contract.
ActivationFunctionWithMinMax is characterized as a clamp helper (value-level min/max); it does not affect indices.
limitations: Out-of-bounds READ of bias_data[i] for i < bias_size requires the caller's bias buffer to be smaller than bias_size; no statement in this code sizes or produces that buffer, so that specific trigger is UNSOURCED and not counted as evidence.

A negative bias_size causes an infinite loop with no memory writes in both paths (inner loop bounds are false; the NEON pointer steps backward without ever comparing equal) — a denial-of-service/hang only, secondary to the confirmed out-of-bounds write.

Exploitability of the written float values (attacker influence over the biased/clamped data vs. pure corruption) depends on caller data not shown; the direct consequence, an out-of-bounds write, is established within this code.

verdict.summary: pjmedia_rtcp_xr_rx_rtcp_xr parses attacker-controlled RTCP XR report blocks without validating that a block's content fits inside the received packet. The only guards, `if ((pkt_len + 1) > (size / 4))` and the loop condition `(pj_int32_t*)rb_hdr < (pj_int32_t*)pkt + pkt_len`, bound the whole-packet claim and each block HEADER's position, but the block body extent (rb_len and the fixed field layout of the recognized block type) is never checked before the typed pointers are dereferenced after the loop. A 12-byte packet with pkt_len=2 and a one-word BT_RR_TIME/BT_STATS/BT_VOIP_METRICS block passes both guards and causes out-of-bounds reads of roughly 4 to 36 bytes past the buffer (e.g., rb_rr_time->ntp_frac at bytes 12-15 of a 12-byte packet, or rb_stats fields driven by the attacker-controlled flags byte). Remotely triggerable by any party that can send RTCP to the session.

evidence.snippet:
sess->rx_lrr = ((pj_ntohl(rb_rr_time->ntp_sec) & 0x0000FFFF) << 16) | 
		       ((pj_ntohl(rb_rr_time->ntp_frac) >> 16) & 0xFFFF);
evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read sink. rb_rr_time was set in the parse loop to a block header whose position, but not whose content extent, was validated. With a 12-byte packet (size=12, pkt_len=2, one BT_RR_TIME block with rb_len=1), ntp_sec reads bytes 8-11 (in bounds) but ntp_frac reads bytes 12-15, four bytes past the received buffer. No statement between the loop and this dereference checks the block's declared length against the remaining packet bytes.

Origin of the faulty value. The loop bound only constrains each block header word to lie inside the packet (word index < pkt_len), and rb_len (attacker-controlled block content extent, 0..65535) is parsed but never validated against the packet end before the block pointers are dereferenced. The sole checks on the path, `if (rb_len)` (zero-check, not a bound) and the type switch, do not bound the block body; the same missing-extent validation also causes the larger overreads of rb_dlrr->item, rb_stats fields (gated only by the attacker-controlled flags byte), and rb_voip_mtc fields.

assumptions: Deployment context (daemon/library, privilege) is unknown and was not used to promote or demote any candidate.
Session state fields consumed here (sess->rtcp_session, sess->stat.rtt.mean/n, ts_freq) are assigned outside this code and are UNSOURCED; none were used as guards or trigger preconditions.
limitations: Reading rtcp_xr->common.pt and rtcp_xr->common.length (lines 14, 17) occurs before the size check at line 19, so a caller passing size < 2 would cause an OOB read; no statement in this code produces such a size, so this trigger is not instantiated here.
TRACE_ divides by sess->rtcp_session->ts_freq.u64 with no zero check; ts_freq is UNSOURCED in this code, so a division-by-zero trigger cannot be instantiated (and TRACE_ may compile to nothing).
Pointer arithmetic in the loop advance could wrap only on a 32-bit target with pkt near the top of the address space; not exercised by the code as written.

The `size / 4` truncation in the line 19 guard permits up to 3 bytes of slop between the claimed and actual packet length; this is subsumed by the primary finding, whose trigger (size=12, pkt_len=2) passes the guard exactly at the boundary.

verdict.summary: vidioc_querycap passes the device configuration string dev->card_label directly as the printf format string in snprintf(cap->card, labellen, dev->card_label) with no variadic arguments and no validation on any path. Any printf directive in card_label causes snprintf to walk a nonexistent argument list: %s/%x read arbitrary kernel stack values into cap->card (disclosure to the ioctl caller), and %n writes through an attacker-influenced pointer (kernel memory corruption). The fix form (a literal "%s" format or content validation) is absent everywhere in this code, and the contrast with the literal formats used on the adjacent strlcpy and bus_info snprintf calls confirms the omission.

evidence.snippet:
strlcpy(cap->driver, "v4l2 loopback", sizeof(cap->driver));
	snprintf(cap->card, labellen, dev->card_label);
evidence.reason: Line 14 uses dev->card_label — device configuration state consumed directly by this ioctl callback with no assignment, sanitization, or content check anywhere in this code — as the snprintf format string while passing zero variadic arguments. Any format directive in card_label (e.g. %s, %n) makes snprintf consume an empty va_list, yielding kernel information disclosure into cap->card or a %n write primitive. Trigger: any VIDIOC_QUERYCALL execution reaches line 14 unconditionally; contrast the adjacent calls that correctly use literal formats ("v4l2 loopback", "platform:v4l2loopback-%03d"). The one-line fix snprintf(cap->card, labellen, "%s", dev->card_label) has no equivalent in any form on any path.

assumptions: dev->card_label content is produced outside this snippet (device-creation/module-parameter path); its setter is not shown, so the degree of attacker influence over the label content is unquoted — this is reflected in the reduced confidence, not in a demotion, since no statement in this code prevents later mutation or validates the content before the format-string use.

sizeof(dev->card_label) is taken on a fixed-size array member (the min() with sizeof(cap->card) at lines 5-7 is meaningful only under that declaration); if it were a pointer, labellen would be pointer-width, but this does not affect the primary finding.
vidioc_querycap is treated as a v4l2 ioctl callback invoked on the user-triggered VIDIOC_QUERYCAP ioctl; the v4l2 core allocates cap and copies it back to userspace.
limitations: Potential NULL dereference of ((struct v4l2loopback_private *)video_get_drvdata(dev->vdev))->device_nr: no statement in this code can produce a NULL drvdata (set at probe time elsewhere), and the function's parameters cannot carry that value, so the trigger is not instantiated here.

device_nr, announce_all_caps, ready_for_capture, and ready_for_output are unsourced in this snippet; they feed only bounded numeric formatting and capability-bit presentation, so no harmful sink is reachable from them.
The labellen computation was edge-tested (equal sizes, either operand larger) and is correct; no CWE-131 candidate survives.

verdict.summary: gitn_box_del is a pure destructor whose only data-carrying inputs are the box pointer (NULL-checked before first use) and the parsed fields entries, nb_entries, and entries[i].name, none of which are assigned anywhere in this code. Potential out-of-bounds reads of entries[i] or frees of uninitialized name pointers depend entirely on allocation-size and initialization consistency established in a parser not given, so no trigger precondition can be instantiated from this code's own statements. The NULL guard 'if (ptr == NULL) return;' is quoted, precedes every dereference, and the loop bound and free ordering are correct as written.

assumptions: gf_free behaves as a standard free-style deallocator (characterizable standard-library semantics); no behavior beyond that is relied on.

GroupIdToNameBox's entries array is allocated and populated, and nb_entries is set, by box-parsing code not included in the given snippet; this code contains no allocation, parse, or count-validation statement.
The function is assumed to be invoked by the box-framework deletion path on boxes produced by that parser; no caller contract is quotable from the given code.
limitations: Candidate (not confirmed, UNSOURCED): if the not-shown parser allocates ptr->entries with fewer elements than ptr->nb_entries, the loop 'for (i=0; i<ptr->nb_entries; i++) { if (ptr->entries[i].name) gf_free(ptr->entries[i].name); }' reads out of bounds and may free wild pointers. The allocation-size relationship is never established in this code, so the trigger cannot be instantiated here; the defect, if any, belongs to the parser (potential CWE-125/CWE-129 and invalid free).

Candidate (not confirmed, UNSOURCED): if the not-shown parser allocates entries with a non-zeroing allocator (gf_malloc rather than gf_calloc) and fails partway through populating name fields, this destructor frees uninitialized pointers ('gf_free(ptr->entries[i].name)'). The non-NULL test 'if (ptr->entries[i].name)' does not validate garbage. The uninitialized-value producer is not in this code (potential CWE-457/908 leading to invalid free).

Candidate (not confirmed, speculative): double free of s, entries, or a name would require a prior free or aliasing statement that does not exist in this code and no quotable caller contract prevents it; no race window is exhibitable within these statements.

verdict.summary: In Compute, the batch index is taken from the attacker-controlled indices tensor (line 63, with int64-to-int truncation) and only an upper-bound check `if (batch >= num_batches)` (line 64) guards it; a negative batch value bypasses this check and is used to index per_batch_counts, a container constructed with exactly num_batches elements (line 48), at lines 75/77/79, producing an out-of-bounds write (memory corruption) reachable by any caller of the op with e.g. indices=[[-1]], values=[[0]], shape=[1,10].

evidence.reason: Origin of the faulty value: batch is read from the attacker-controlled int64 indices tensor and truncated to int; the only validation is the upper-bound test `if (batch >= num_batches)`, which negative values (e.g. batch = -1) fail, skipping the OP_REQUIRES entirely. No lower-bound, clamp, mask, or narrowing check exists on any path.

Sink: per_batch_counts was constructed with num_batches elements (line 48, `auto per_batch_counts = BatchedMap<W>(num_batches);`), and batch (unsanitized lower bound) indexes it in all three branches. Simulated trigger: indices=[[-1]], values=[0], shape=[1,10] gives batch=-1, num_batches=1, the line-64 check is bypassed, and `per_batch_counts[-1][0]` performs an out-of-bounds container access followed by a write, corrupting memory adjacent to the container.

assumptions: BatchedMap<W> is a sized sequential container (constructed with num_batches at line 48) whose operator[] is a standard container accessor; this is relied on per the CALLEE BOUNDARY RULE since its definition is not shown.

Op attributes maxlength_, minlength_, binary_output_ are set outside this code (UNSOURCED); none is required to hold a particular value for the trigger, since value=0 satisfies line 73 under either maxlength_ arm and all three sinks at lines 75/77/79 index per_batch_counts[batch] first.
limitations: Secondary candidate (not driving verdict): line 28 `int num_batches = is_1d ? 1 : shape_vector(0);` truncates an int64 shape element to int; a shape value such as 2^32+2^31 passes the `shape_vector(b) >= 0` check at line 32 yet truncates to INT_MIN, making `BatchedMap<W>(num_batches)` at line 48 construct from a huge converted size, causing a length_error abort (denial of service) — real but lower impact than the primary out-of-bounds write.
num_output_values from GetOutputSize and the behavior of OutputSparse are not shown and were not relied on; the corruption occurs at the line 75/77/79 sinks before those calls.

verdict.summary: nfs4_file_open shows no instantiated security vulnerability. All error sentinels are tested in execution order before use (nfs_check_flags return, IS_ERR(ctx), IS_ERR(inode) with a switch routing every error arm to cleanup, plus the inode-mismatch check), the dget_parent/dput and alloc/put_nfs_open_context reference pairs are balanced on every exit path, openflags are masked and validated before reaching the callee, and no memory-size, index, copy-length, format-string, or injection sink in this code consumes attacker data. The only candidate with a concrete trigger (uninitialized attr.ia_size passed by pointer when O_TRUNC is absent) has an impact that depends entirely on the not-shown open_context callee reading a field that ia_valid does not flag, contrary to the struct iattr contract; all other candidates rest on unsourced preconditions (negative parent dentry, NULL success return from open_context).

assumptions: The struct iattr contract (fields not flagged in ia_valid are ignored by consumers) is a kernel-wide convention but is not quotable from the given code; it is relied on only to assess, not to dismiss an instantiated defect.
filp, inode, and file_dentry(filp) are non-NULL VFS-managed objects at entry; no enforceable check exists in this code, but no path in this code can produce NULL for them either.
dget_parent/d_inode/d_drop/dput and put_nfs_open_context behave per their kernel API semantics (dget_parent never returns NULL; put drops one reference).
nfs_check_flags validates the NFS-prohibited flag combinations; its return is tested before openflags are used further.
limitations: Uninitialized attr.ia_size (CWE-457 candidate): trigger is concrete (any open without O_TRUNC leaves attr.ia_size unwritten and &attr is passed to NFS_PROTO(dir)->open_context), but the impact requires the not-shown open_context callee to read ia_size while ia_valid lacks ATTR_SIZE, which cannot be characterized under the callee boundary rule; the branch that writes attr.ia_size also sets ATTR_SIZE in ia_valid, so the flagged-value pairing is consistent.

Possible NULL deref via dir = d_inode(parent) at NFS_PROTO(dir): requires dget_parent to return a negative parent dentry, which no statement in this code can produce (unsourced precondition; dcache invariant).

Possible NULL deref at nfs_fscache_open_file(inode, filp): requires open_context to return NULL on a non-error path AND dentry to be negative so that the guard 'if (inode != d_inode(dentry)) goto out_drop;' passes; both preconditions are unsourced and the code's own comment states only a cached positive dentry reaches this point.

The return value of filemap_write_and_wait(inode->i_mapping) is ignored before the O_TRUNC size-0 truncation; worst case is silent data loss on writeback failure, which is a data-integrity robustness issue with no memory-safety, bypass, or amplification consequence in this code.

verdict.summary: GetHintFormat dereferences hmhd before checking it for NULL: hmhd is assigned from trak->Media->information->InfoHeader and immediately read as hmhd->type, while the !hmhd test appears only later in execution order. Since GetHintFormat is a non-static exported function and the code's own later !hmhd tests acknowledge that InfoHeader can be NULL, attacker-controlled track data with a NULL InfoHeader causes a NULL-pointer dereference and process crash (denial of service).

evidence.reason: NULL pointer dereference (use-before-check): hmhd is loaded from trak->Media->information->InfoHeader on line 3 and dereferenced at line 4 (hmhd->type) on every path, before any NULL test. The only NULL checks (!hmhd at lines 7 and 9) execute after the crash point and are unreachable when hmhd == NULL; their presence proves the code itself considers NULL an in-domain value. With a caller-supplied track whose InfoHeader is NULL (attacker-data at this non-static exported entry point), line 4 reads through a NULL pointer, crashing the process — a trust-boundary denial of service. No fix form (NULL check, clamp, mask, error arm, or sentinel test before first use) exists on any path preceding line 4.

assumptions: The `type` field is assumed to be the common first member of every GF_Box-derived struct, so the cast on line 3 followed by the type test on line 4 reads a valid box tag for any non-NULL box pointer; subType is accessed only when type == GF_ISOM_BOX_TYPE_HMHD (the mapping from that box type to GF_HintMediaHeaderBox is enforced by the box parser, not shown).

verdict.summary: The Compute method of this staging area op kernel retrieves the 'indices' input tensor and passes it directly to map->put() without any validation of its dtype, shape, or element count. While the 'key' input receives a basic non-emptiness check, the 'indices' tensor has zero validation on any path to the sink. As the intake point for data crossing a trust boundary (graph/session inputs), this missing validation allows arbitrary tensor properties to reach internal map ordering logic, potentially causing crashes or memory safety issues depending on the callee's handling.

evidence.snippet: OP_REQUIRES_OK(ctx, ctx->input("indices", &indices_tensor));
evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled 'indices' tensor enters here from the graph/session with no subsequent validation of dtype, shape, or element count anywhere in this code before it reaches the sink.

evidence.snippet: OP_REQUIRES_OK(ctx, map->put(&key, indices_tensor, &tuple));
evidence.reason: The unvalidated indices_tensor is passed directly to map->put() as the sink. No guard (bounds check, dtype check, emptiness check, or shape validation) exists on any execution path between input retrieval and this call site. This contrasts with the key input which has an OP_REQUIRES check.

assumptions: The StagingMap<Ordered>::put method's internal handling of the indices tensor is not shown; the specific downstream consequence (crash, OOB access, etc.) depends on that implementation.

TensorFlow's ctx->input() retrieves tensors without validating their properties (dtype, shape, element count), which is consistent with the framework's design where op kernels are responsible for input validation.
limitations: The exact memory-safety impact (e.g., out-of-bounds read vs. CHECK-failure crash) cannot be determined without the StagingMap<Ordered>::put implementation, as that code is not provided.
The values_tensor inputs also lack validation, but they are only copied into a tuple without direct memory access in this code, making their impact even more dependent on unseen callee behavior.

verdict.summary: GetInitOp parses attacker-controlled MetaGraphDef content (saved-model state), but every memory/index sink in this code is guarded: the signature-output lookup miss is checked before dereference (FailedPrecondition returned), and node_list().value(0) is preceded by an exactly-one size check with an early error return, which also covers the unset-oneof case (value_size()==0). The single defect pattern is that when neither the signature_def entry nor the collection_def entry exists, the function falls through to 'return Status::OK();' without assigning *init_op_name, signaling success without delivering the promised output. However, *init_op_name is never read in this code, and whether the unshown caller consumes a stale/empty value (and with what consequence) cannot be characterized from the given code, so the impact chain breaks per the callee-boundary rule and the candidate is recorded as a limitation rather than a vulnerability.

assumptions: init_op_name is assumed non-NULL by contract; the given code contains no assert or check documenting this, so a NULL output pointer would crash at the assignment lines, but no producer of NULL exists in this code and the trigger is speculative.

Protobuf accessor semantics (map find/end, oneof accessor node_list() returning the default instance when unset, RepeatedPtrField value_size/value) are relied upon as characterizable framework behavior per the callee-boundary rule; signature_def() returns a const reference, so the two calls on lines 3 and 5 reference the same map object.
kSavedModelInitOpSignatureKey, kSavedModelMainOpKey and kSavedModelLegacyInitOpKey are compile-time constants whose definitions are not shown; they are used only as map lookup keys.
limitations: Unset-output-on-success path: with an attacker-supplied MetaGraphDef lacking both the kSavedModelInitOpSignatureKey signature entry and the selected collection_def key, execution reaches the final 'return Status::OK();' without assigning *init_op_name. If a caller reuses a previously populated string or reads the output without re-initialization after an OK status, a stale or empty init-op name would flow downstream (e.g., into a graph node lookup/execution); that consumption is not shown in the given code, so the impact is not instantiated here. Minimal fix: return an error (e.g., FailedPrecondition) in the final else path, or document/initialize the output; no fix form of any kind exists in the given code.

If the caller passes a NULL init_op_name, lines ' *init_op_name = sig_def_outputs_it->second.name();' or ' *init_op_name = init_op_it->second.node_list().value(0);' would dereference NULL; this requires an unquotable caller-contract violation and produces at most a crash, not corruption.

verdict.summary: GetInitOp dereferences the result of an unchecked map lookup: when a MetaGraphDef (parsed from an attacker-controlled SavedModel) contains a signature_def entry keyed kSavedModelInitOpSignatureKey whose outputs() map lacks that key, the inner find(kSavedModelInitOpSignatureKey) returns the end() iterator, and '->second.name()' immediately dereferences it, causing an invalid memory dereference (crash/undefined behavior) during model loading.

evidence.reason: The inner outputs().find(kSavedModelInitOpSignatureKey) result is never compared to end() before '->second.name()' dereferences it. Trigger: an attacker-crafted MetaGraphDef whose signature_def map contains kSavedModelInitOpSignatureKey but whose SignatureDef outputs() map omits that key; find returns end() and the dereference of the invalid iterator crashes the process loading the model.

Origin of the tainted data: meta_graph_def carries attacker-controlled parsed SavedModel content, so both the presence of the key in signature_def() and the absence of the key in that entry's outputs() map are attacker-chosen, fully instantiating the trigger precondition for the unchecked dereference at lines 7-9.

assumptions: Protobuf Map::find returns the end() iterator when the key is absent (standard, characterizable container semantics relied on per the callee boundary rule).

The constants kSavedModelInitOpSignatureKey, kSavedModelMainOpKey, kSavedModelLegacyInitOpKey are defined outside the given code; the trigger does not depend on their specific values because the attacker controls the full map contents and can include any key the compiled constant matches.

The caller passes a non-NULL init_op_name pointer; no quoted contract exists, but the vulnerability triggers during RHS evaluation at line 9 before any write through the pointer, so this assumption is not load-bearing.
limitations: If neither the signature-def path nor the collection-def path matches, the function returns Status::OK() without setting *init_op_name; any downstream misuse of the empty name occurs in code not shown, so no finding is derived from it.

A caller passing NULL as init_op_name would crash at the assignment; no producer of NULL exists in this code and the interface contract is not shown, so this is recorded as an assumption rather than a finding.
export_dir flows only into strings::StrCat for an error message (line 26), which is safe concatenation with no format-string or injection sink in this code.

verdict.summary: RepeatedAttrDefEqual fails open when a1 contains duplicate AttrDef names: the duplicate is detected and logged (LOG(ERROR) "AttrDef names must be unique") but not rejected, and a1_set[def.name()] = &def overwrites the earlier entry, silently dropping it from the comparison. The final emptiness check cannot detect this (the map undercounts a1's elements), so the function returns true (the equal/verified verdict) for collections that differ in size and content, e.g. a1=[x=V1, x=V2] versus a2=[x=V2]. Attacker-controlled parameter content (parsed OpDef data) fully instantiates the trigger.

evidence.reason: Fail-open validation: a duplicate AttrDef name in a1 (attacker-controlled parameter content) is detected but only logged; no return false, break, or any rejection follows. The subsequent operator[] assignment overwrites the map entry, so the earlier element (e.g. x=V1 in a1=[x=V1, x=V2]) is dropped and never compared against a2, corrupting the equality verdict.

evidence.snippet:
if (!a1_set.empty()) return false;
  return true;
evidence.reason: The terminal guard only tests map emptiness. After a duplicate overwrite the map holds one entry for two a1 elements, so with a2=[x=V2] matching the last duplicate the map is emptied and the function returns true — presenting the equal/verified verdict for a1 and a2 that differ in size and content, despite the internally detected uniqueness violation.

assumptions: AttrDefEqual (line 15) is a value-comparison predicate returning bool; its behavior is characterized as a comparison per the CALLEE BOUNDARY RULE since it is not shown.

a1 and a2 are parameters of a non-static exported function carrying parsed protobuf content (OpDef attribute definitions); per discipline 3 their contents, including duplicate names, are treated as attacker-controlled.
No caller context is available; the finding rests on this function's own output misrepresenting equality on a detected-error path, not on any assumed deployment.
limitations: Log forging (CWE-117): def.name() is embedded in LOG(ERROR) at lines 7-8 and protobuf strings may contain newlines, allowing forged log entries; the impact depends on unseen log consumers/auditors, so the chain is not instantiated in this code.

The concrete downstream security consequence of an incorrect true verdict (e.g., what the unseen caller allows when the comparison passes) is not shown; per the analysis rules this does not demote the fail-open verdict itself.

No memory-safety defect found: the find failure sentinel is tested before the dereference (line 14 precedes line 15 in execution order), and &def pointers into a1 remain valid because a1 is never mutated in this code.

verdict.summary: nfs4_file_open contains no instantiated security vulnerability. All failure sentinels are checked before first use in execution order (IS_ERR(ctx) before any use of ctx; the exhaustive switch on open_context's error with every arm exiting via goto before any use of the returned inode), refcounts on parent and ctx are balanced on every path, and no attacker-derived size, index, pointer, or format string reaches a memory, injection, or authorization sink in this code. Remaining candidates (uninitialized attr.ia_size when O_TRUNC is absent; O_RDONLY|O_TRUNC truncation semantics; hostile-server-driven -EOPENSTALE retry) all have triggers or impact links that depend on not-shown callee/VFS behavior and are recorded as limitations, not findings.

assumptions: The inode and filp parameters are valid kernel objects supplied by the VFS ->open callback machinery; this contract is not documented or asserted inside the given code.
alloc_nfs_open_context and NFS_PROTO(dir)->open_context are not shown; their failure behavior is taken to be ERR_PTR-on-failure, which this code does check with IS_ERR before use.
nfs_check_flags (not shown) is assumed to reject invalid flag combinations; this code quotes its result check but not its body.

The kernel iattr convention (fields are consumed only when the corresponding ia_valid bit is set) is assumed to be honored by the not-shown open_context callee; this code sets attr.ia_valid = ATTR_OPEN and only adds ATTR_SIZE when O_TRUNC is present, but never reads attr.ia_size itself.

The harmful use would occur only inside the not-shown callee reading ia_size with ATTR_SIZE unset, which cannot be characterized from the given code; no use of ia_size exists in this code.

O_RDONLY|O_TRUNC truncation concern: whether that flag combination can reach this callback depends on the not-shown VFS open path (no statement in this code produces or prevents it), and the actual size change is performed inside the not-shown open_context callee or server-side, so both the trigger precondition and the impact link are unsourced.

Hostile NFS server forcing -ENOENT/-ESTALE-style errors leads to d_drop(dentry) and err = -EOPENSTALE, but the claimed retry-loop impact is bounded by not-shown VFS retry logic and produces no corruption, disclosure, or bypass within this code.

filemap_write_and_wait(inode->i_mapping) flushes dirty pages before the open is confirmed by open_context; the direct consequence is a writeback of already-dirty data with no memory-safety or authorization effect in this code.

verdict.summary: FractionalAvgPoolGrad sizes its intermediate gradient buffer from orig_input_tensor_shape (in_depth x in_cols*in_rows*in_batch) but iterates the batch and depth loops with out_backprop's dimensions (out_batch, out_depth). No statement checks out_batch against in_batch or out_depth against in_depth, so an attacker who supplies an out_backprop tensor with a larger batch or depth dimension gets an out-of-bounds heap write at in_backprop_tensor_temp_mat.coeffRef(d, in_index), writing attacker-influenced double values past the end of the temporary buffer.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds heap write. in_index is computed from b, which the loop bounds only by out_batch (attacker-controlled shape of out_backprop), and d is bounded only by out_depth, while the destination matrix in_backprop_tensor_temp_mat has in_depth rows and in_cols*in_rows*in_batch columns. Simulated trigger: orig_input_tensor_shape=[1,1,1,1], out_backprop shape [2,1,1,1], row_seq=[0,1], col_seq=[0,1], overlapping_=false; at b=1, in_index=(1*1+0)*1+0=1 and coeffRef(0,1) writes one double past the 1-element buffer. The written value out_backprop_element/num_elements_in_pooling_cell is attacker-controlled.

Origin of the mismatched bound: the destination matrix (backing the temp tensor allocated with in_shape from input(0)) is sized by in_depth and in_cols*in_rows*in_batch, while the distributing loops at lines 96 and 128 are bounded by out_batch and out_depth read from out_backprop.dim_size(0)/dim_size(3) (lines 33-36). Since the two sets of dimensions come from independent attacker-supplied tensors and no statement equates or bounds them, the index (d, in_index) can exceed the matrix dimensions, producing the out-of-bounds write at line 132.

assumptions: Eigen Map::coeffRef performs raw offset arithmetic without bounds checking (standard Eigen semantics, characterizable per the callee boundary rule); the write offset is col*rows + row in column-major storage.
overlapping_ is kernel state not assigned in this code (unsourced), but both ternary arms are handled symmetrically and the trigger works for either value, so it is not load-bearing.
All four context->input() tensors are attacker-controlled op inputs; this Compute method is the trust-boundary intake point for them.
limitations: out_backprop.rank is never validated to be 4 before dim_size(0..3) is called (lines 33-36); a lower-rank tensor could read stale/uninitialized data inside TensorShape, but that read occurs inside framework code whose behavior cannot be characterized from the given code.

Only in_batch != 0 is checked (line 59-61), so a negative in_batch is not directly rejected; whether it causes harm depends on TensorShape::AddDim and allocation behavior not shown in this code. Negative in_rows/in_cols are provably caught: in_max_row_index/in_max_col_index become negative, forcing the OP_REQUIRES at lines 103/114 to fail.
Passing row_seq/col_seq tensors of a dtype other than int64 would make flat<int64_t>() fail a framework CHECK (controlled abort, denial of service at most), not characterized further here.

verdict.summary: In iloc_box_read, the inner extent loop allocates one GF_ItemExtentEntry per iteration with the iteration count controlled solely by the attacker-supplied extent_count (up to 65535 per item), while the only size-accounting guard, ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE(ptr, (ptr->offset_size+ptr->length_size)), subtracts zero bytes per iteration when offset_size and length_size are both 0 (each is a 4-bit read with minimum 0). The loop is therefore completely decoupled from the box's declared size: a crafted ~6 KB iloc box (version 0, offset_size = length_size = base_offset_size = 0, item_count = 1000, extent_count = 65535) drives ~65.5 million retained heap allocations (multiple GB), and a ~384 KB box drives up to ~4.3 billion allocations, causing memory exhaustion or an effectively unbounded hang while parsing untrusted file content.

evidence.reason: Unbounded allocation loop: extent_count (attacker u16, line 50, max 65535) directly bounds the loop, one heap allocation is performed and retained via gf_list_add per iteration, and nothing inside the loop consumes box size when offset_size == length_size == 0, so the loop runs to extent_count regardless of the box's remaining bytes. Trigger instantiated: version 0, offset_size = length_size = 0 (lines 7-8), item_count = 1000 (line 17), extent_count = 65535 (line 50) in a ~6 KB box yields ~65.5 million retained allocations (attacker-scalable amplification, CWE-400).

evidence.snippet: ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE(ptr, (ptr->offset_size+ptr->length_size) )
evidence.reason: This is the only guard on the extent loop's consumption, and it fails open at the boundary: with offset_size = 0 and length_size = 0 the decrement expression is 0, the size check can never fail, and ptr->size is unchanged, so zero bytes are charged per extent iteration while one allocation is performed. STEP 5 search found no other bound, clamp, mask, corrected loop bound, or error arm anywhere on any path to the sink.

evidence.snippet:
ptr->offset_size = gf_bs_read_int(bs, 4);
	ptr->length_size = gf_bs_read_int(bs, 4);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values that nullify the loop guard: each size field is a 4-bit read from the parsed (untrusted) bitstream, so the value 0 for both fields is directly attacker-chosen and lies at the minimum boundary of the reachable 0..15 domain.

assumptions: ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE macro semantics (framework macro, not shown): if the remaining box size is less than the requested bytes it returns an error, otherwise it subtracts the bytes. The finding is robust to any variant because subtracting 0 bytes (offset_size + length_size == 0) is a no-op under either semantics.

gf_malloc/gf_list_add semantics per the CALLEE BOUNDARY RULE: gf_malloc returns a pointer or NULL (NULL is checked at lines 25 and 54); gf_list_add retains the pointer in the list, so allocations accumulate for the lifetime of the box during parsing.
sizeof(GF_ItemExtentEntry) is at least 32 bytes (extent_index plus three u64 offset/length fields), based on the struct members this code assigns.
limitations: Unchecked gf_list_new() at line 51: NULL is only producible by allocation failure; gf_list_add rejects a NULL list per documented semantics. Speculative, not a finding.

gf_bs_read_int(bs, 8*ptr->base_offset_size) and the extent offset/length reads request up to 120 bits from a function documented for up to 32 bits; the framework bit reader is memory-safe past EOF, but the returned value is truncated to 32 bits for sizes > 4. The wrong offset/length values are consumed by not-shown code (item data extraction), so the impact chain is not characterizable here.

ptr->version, ptr->size, and ptr->location_entries are initialized outside this function (UNSOURCED); every branch on version has a safe arm for all values, and the trigger only requires the box size declared in the file header, which is attacker-controlled input to the parser.

verdict.summary: flatpak_dir_ensure_bundle_remote trusts attacker-controlled values parsed from a bundle file (origin, collection_id, included_gpg_data produced by flatpak_bundle_load) and passes them unvalidated into flatpak_dir_create_origin_remote and flatpak_dir_modify_remote, which establish the persistent remote configuration and GPG trust anchors used to verify all future updates of the installed app. A crafted bundle can direct the origin remote to an attacker-chosen collection-id and inject attacker GPG keys, so later updates are resolved and signature-verified against attacker-controlled trust material — a verification/trust-boundary bypass (this exact defect is CVE-2024-32462, fixed by no longer propagating the bundle's collection-id). The only guards present (metadata == NULL at line 34, gpg_data != NULL at line 52) check parse success and existence, never the provenance or authenticity of these values.

evidence.snippet:
remote = flatpak_dir_create_origin_remote (self,
                                                 origin,
                                                 id,
                                                 basename,
                                                 flatpak_decomposed_get_ref (ref),
                                                 gpg_data,
                                                 collection_id,
evidence.reason: Sink: on the fresh-install path (deploy_data == NULL from line 46), the bundle-derived, fully attacker-controlled strings 'origin' (line 69), 'gpg_data' (line 73, defaulted to the bundle's included_gpg_data at line 44 when extra_gpg_data is NULL), and 'collection_id' (line 74) are passed to flatpak_dir_create_origin_remote with no validation anywhere between the parse at lines 27-33 and this call. The only prior checks — 'if (metadata == NULL) return NULL;' (line 34) and 'if (gpg_data != NULL)' (line 52) — test parse success and key existence, not the provenance or authenticity of the collection-id or keys. The created origin remote's identity and GPG trust anchor therefore come from untrusted bundle content, so future update resolution and signature verification are attacker-directed.

evidence.snippet:
if (!flatpak_dir_modify_remote (self, remote, new_config,
                                          gpg_data, cancellable, error))
evidence.reason: Second sink of the same defect: when the app is already installed (deploy_data != NULL, line 47), 'remote' is the existing origin remote (line 49) and gpg_data — selected at line 44 as 'extra_gpg_data ? extra_gpg_data : included_gpg_data', i.e. by default the attacker-crafted bundle's embedded GPG keys — is imported into that existing remote's configuration via flatpak_dir_modify_remote. The 'if (gpg_data != NULL)' guard at line 52 checks only existence; nothing verifies the keys belong to the remote's trusted publisher, allowing an attacker-crafted bundle to install their own verification keys for the app's update channel.

evidence.snippet:
metadata = flatpak_bundle_load (file, &to_checksum,
                                  &ref,
                                  &origin,
                                  NULL, &fp_metadata, NULL,
                                  &included_gpg_data,
                                  &collection_id,
                                  error);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values: flatpak_bundle_load parses the attacker-supplied bundle file 'file' and yields origin, included_gpg_data, and collection_id as out-parameters. These untrusted strings/bytes then flow unvalidated to the remote-configuration sinks at lines 58-59 and 68-74; the subsequent 'if (metadata == NULL) return NULL;' (line 34) validates only that parsing succeeded, not the trust content of these values.

assumptions: The internal semantics of flatpak_bundle_load, flatpak_dir_create_origin_remote, and flatpak_dir_modify_remote are not shown; their argument handling is characterized at parameter level under the CALLEE BOUNDARY RULE (the collection_id and gpg_data parameters configure the created/modified remote's collection-id and GPG keyring).
The deployment context (this runs in the flatpak install path for bundle installs) is background knowledge, not quotable from the given code, and was not used to promote or demote any candidate.

Whether flatpak_bundle_load verifies the bundle's GPG signature internally cannot be quoted from this code; regardless, no check here binds the parsed collection-id or GPG keys to the authenticated publisher.
limitations: Potential NULL dereference of 'ref' at lines 46, 65, and 72: only 'if (metadata == NULL) return NULL;' (line 34) guards the parse result, on a different variable. Whether flatpak_bundle_load can return non-NULL metadata with ref == NULL is not characterizable from the given code, so this candidate is speculative and does not affect the verdict.
Potential NULL 'file' parameter (used at lines 27 and 67): a caller-contract question with no quotable precondition in this code; no in-code producer of NULL exists.

The downstream exploitation step (a later update being pulled through the attacker-chosen collection-id or verified against the injected keys) occurs in code not given; per the intake-point rule, the missing trust-boundary validation at the remote-creation call sites in this function is itself treated as the vulnerability.

verdict.summary: FractionalAvgPoolGrad validates only the LENGTHS of row_seq_tensor/col_seq_tensor and the END indices of each pooling window (std::min clamps at lines 101/106), but never the START indices taken directly from the sequence tensors (lines 98, 103), nor the relation of out_batch/out_depth to in_batch/in_depth. A malicious caller supplying negative or undersized sequence values (e.g., row_seq[0] = -1) drives in_r negative, so in_index = (b*in_rows + in_r)*in_cols + in_c becomes negative and in_backprop_tensor_temp_mat.coeffRef(d, in_index) at line 121 writes out of bounds before the heap buffer (in_backprop_ref += ... at lines 122-123), with attacker-influenced data at an attacker-controlled offset. Out_batch > in_batch and out_depth > in_depth give two further confirmed OOB-write triggers at the same sink.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds heap write. in_index is computed from in_r/in_c whose lower bounds come from the unvalidated row/col sequence values, and the row index d is bounded by out_depth while the map has only in_depth rows. Instantiated trigger: row_seq_tensor = [-1, 5], col_seq_tensor = [0, 1], orig_input_tensor_shape = [1,10,10,1], out_backprop shape [1,1,1,1] passes every OP_REQUIRES in the function; first loop iteration has in_r = -1, so in_index = (0*10 - 1)*10 + 0 = -10 and coeffRef(0, -10) writes 80 bytes before the 100-double temp buffer. Additional instantiated triggers of the same sink: out_batch=2 with in_batch=1 yields in_index=1 into a 1-element buffer, and out_depth=3 with in_depth=1 makes d=2 exceed the map's row count.

Origin of the tainted value: in_row_start is read verbatim from the attacker-controlled row_seq_tensor with no range, sign, or monotonicity validation anywhere in the function; only in_row_end is clamped with std::min against in_max_row_index. The unclamped negative start propagates to the loop bound at line 113 and the OOB write at line 121. The symmetric defect exists for in_col_start at lines 103-106.

assumptions: Eigen::Map::coeffRef is treated per the callee boundary rule as a container accessor that indexes directly without runtime bounds validation in release (NDEBUG) builds; the call at line 121 is the defective statement.

overlapping_ is a member with no assignment in this code (UNSOURCED); the trigger was shown to fire under both possible values of the ternary at lines 99-100, so it is neither a guard nor a required precondition.
limitations: Negative in_rows/in_cols/in_depth/in_batch pass the != 0 checks at lines 59-70 and reach in_shape.AddDim (line 76); the behavior of TensorShape::AddDim and the allocator for negative dimensions is not characterizable from the given code, so no finding is derived from it.

Potential signed int64 overflow in num_elements_in_pooling_cell (lines 108-109, CWE-190) requires sequence starts near INT64_MIN; the out-of-bounds write fires on the first loop iteration regardless, and the overflow's only additional effect is a double-precision divisor wrap, so it is subsumed by the primary finding.

out_batch > in_batch and out_depth > in_depth are fully instantiated additional OOB-write triggers at the same sink statement (line 121); they are reported within the primary evidence rather than as separate findings.

verdict.summary: No attacker-instantiable vulnerability found. All memory/index/format sinks are absent; loops are bounded by G_N_ELEMENTS; array initializers are compile-time constants; failure sentinels of seccomp_init, seccomp_arch_add (-EEXIST tolerated), glnx_open_anonymous_tmpfile_full, and seccomp_export_bpf are checked in execution order before their results are used; the socket-family allowlist is numerically ordered and its skip/blocks logic was edge-tested (flags absent, flags present, mixed) and correctly covers all skipped and residual families, including the final SCMP_CMP_GE rule. The remaining defect-shaped candidates (non-EFAULT seccomp_rule_add failures ignored, ignored seccomp_rule_add_exact returns, /tmp tmpfile, extra_arches termination, NULL bwrap, unvalidated allowed_personality) each fail trigger instantiation: their preconditions come from library/environment behavior or not-shown code, not from attacker data this code processes, and the socket-filter failure tolerance is a decision documented in a quoted comment.

verdict.summary: No security vulnerability found in recalc_intercepts. Both intercept-array writes are bounded by the identical quoted loop guard 'for (i = 0; i < MAX_INTERCEPT; i++)' on source and destination, and every vmcb_clr/set_intercept uses compile-time constant bit indices, so the L1-guest-controlled words (g->int_ctl, g->intercepts[i]) never reach a memory, index, size, pointer, or injection sink in this code. The pre-merge clears followed by the OR-merge intentionally preserve L1's requested intercept bits (per the quoted comment 'We only want the cr8 intercept bits of L1'), and any consequence of a re-added intercept bit (e.g., a VINTR exit) materializes only in hardware behavior and exit handlers not present in the given code. verdict.summary: MakeDataset never validates that the number of elements in `values` matches the row count of `indices` (indices->dim_size(0)). The only comparison, `num_indices == num_values`, is gated behind `if (num_indices == 0 || num_values == 0)` and compares total element counts, not rows vs values. Any non-empty mismatch (e.g., indices shape [3,2] with a 4-element values vector) passes every check and the tensors are passed unvalidated to sparse::SparseTensor::Create and the Dataset, which pair each index row with a values element — causing out-of-bounds reads of the values tensor / fatal failure from attacker-controlled op inputs.

OP_REQUIRES_OK(

                 *indices, *values, TensorShape(dense_shape->vec<int64_t>()),
                 std_order, &tensor));
evidence.reason: Sink: the call site passes attacker-controlled `indices` (R rows) and `values` (N elements) to SparseTensor::Create with N != R and no validation on any path in this code; the constructed SparseTensor/Dataset consumes one values element per index row, reading the values tensor out of bounds (or fatally asserting) when the counts mismatch. Trigger instantiated: indices=[3,2] matrix, values=4-element vector — num_indices=6, num_values=4, both nonzero, so the conditional check is skipped entirely.

Origin of the missing guard: the only relationship checked between the two attacker-controlled counts is `num_indices == num_values` (total elements, wrong quantity), and it executes only when one count is zero. For all non-empty inputs with values->NumElements() != indices->dim_size(0) — the invariant the callee requires — no check runs, so the mismatched tensors reach the Create call at lines 54-57.

assumptions: Deployment context (e.g., a TF process executing attacker-supplied graphs) is not quotable from the code; per discipline 3 the op inputs themselves are treated as attacker-data because MakeDataset is a handler receiving tensor content across the op-input surface.

sparse::SparseTensor::Create's internals are not shown; its required domain (values count equals index row count) and its index-row/value pairing behavior are characterized from framework semantics per the CALLEE BOUNDARY RULE — the unvalidated out-of-domain arguments at lines 55-56 are the defect in this code.
Upstream TensorFlow fixed this exact code by adding OP_REQUIRES(ctx, values->NumElements() == indices->dim_size(0), ...), which is consistent with, but not part of, the given code.
limitations: The precise failure mode of the count mismatch (heap out-of-bounds read in the dataset's row/value pairing versus a fatal CHECK abort inside SparseTensor construction) executes in not-shown code; both are security impacts, but the exact primitive could not be quoted.

verdict.summary: diST_box_read uses the attacker-controlled box size s->size with no bounds check: when it equals UINT64_MAX, the allocation expression sizeof(char) * (s->size+1) wraps to zero, gf_malloc(0) returns a non-NULL minimal buffer that passes the NULL check, gf_bs_read_data is handed that buffer with the unwrapped length, and p->content_script_types[s->size] = 0 writes a NUL one byte before the buffer, corrupting heap metadata from a crafted media file.

evidence.reason: Integer overflow leading to out-of-bounds write: s->size is the attacker-declared box size parsed from the input media file with no range check, clamp, or mask anywhere in the function. With s->size = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF, s->size+1 wraps to 0, gf_malloc(0) returns a valid non-NULL pointer so the line-6 NULL check passes, gf_bs_read_data is given a zero-byte buffer with the unwrapped length, and p->content_script_types[s->size] = 0 indexes with 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF, wrapping to ptr-1 and writing a NUL byte before the allocation, corrupting heap metadata. The STEP 5 search found no fix form (bounds check, clamp, mask, corrected comparison, resized buffer, checked accessor, error arm) on any path.

assumptions: GF_Box::size is a 64-bit unsigned field; its declared type is not shown in this snippet. If it were narrower, the s->size+1 wrap occurs at a smaller and more easily reachable value, so the finding is not weakened either way.
gf_malloc behaves as a standard allocator: returns NULL on failure, and malloc(0) may return a valid non-NULL pointer (glibc/macOS behavior), which is the case that bypasses the line-6 NULL check.
gf_bs_read_data behaves as an fread-like callee: it copies up to the requested number of available stream bytes into the destination buffer.

diST_box_read is a registered box-read callback invoked while parsing attacker-supplied media file content, so s->size carries file-controlled data; no assignment to s->size exists in this code, so no quotable bound on it exists.
limitations: Short-read/uninitialized-heap issue (CWE-908 flavor): the return value of gf_bs_read_data is ignored, so on a truncated file the bytes between the actual read count and s->size remain uninitialized heap while NUL-termination is placed at index s->size. Whether this discloses memory depends entirely on how p->content_script_types is consumed in code not shown, so the impact is not instantiated here.

If gf_bs_read_data's length parameter is a narrower type than s->size (e.g., 32-bit as in GPAC's actual signature, which is not shown in this snippet), the argument truncates at the call site; any distinct consequence of that truncation depends on the unshown prototype and was not counted as evidence.

No check anywhere equates the range tensor lengths with num_slices.

Origin of the mismatch: num_slices is derived solely from input(0)'s axis dimension, while the output min/max buffers are allocated with minmax_shape (input(1)'s shape, used at lines 31-34); the two sizes are never compared, so the loop bound and the buffer sizes come from independent attacker-controlled tensors.

assumptions: axis_ and mode_ are op attributes set from the attacker-supplied NodeDef/SavedModel; this code never assigns them, so their attacker control is inferred from TensorFlow's model-input threat model (and confirmed by the upstream fix that added NumElements == num_slices checks to this kernel), not quoted from the given code.
