verdict.summary: The Ragel-generated request parser is memory-safe within its quoted precondition off <= len: every byte read (*p) is preceded in execution order by an explicit p == pe check (entry check for case 1, per-state 'if ( ++p == pe ) goto _test_eofN;' for all other case bodies), all callback arguments are in-buffer (pointer, length) pairs, and body_start/header_done arithmetic stays within [buffer, pe] at the boundary where the terminating LF is the last byte. The only memory-safety path (off > len making p > pe so no pe check ever fires) requires the caller to violate the code's own quoted contract 'assert(off <= len && "offset past end of buffer");'. A real robustness gap exists in that case 19 accepts any byte except CR in header values, so bare LF and NUL bytes are delivered to the http_field callback; any request-smuggling impact depends on the not-shown callback consumer and intermediaries, so it is recorded as a limitation, not a confirmed vulnerability.

assumptions: buffer points to a writable allocation of at least len bytes; this code contains no statement asserting or checking buffer non-NULL or the allocation size (only the commented-out '/* assert(*pe == '\0' ...) */' exists).

The parser struct fields not assigned in this code (initial cs, nread base value, mark, field_start, field_len, and all callback function pointers) are initialized by not-shown init/new code and are UNSOURCED; in particular the http_field/http_version/request_uri callback targets cannot be characterized here.

Assertions are active (NDEBUG not defined). With NDEBUG, the only guard for 'p = buffer+off; pe = buffer+len;' vanishes: off > len then yields p > pe, every 'if ( ++p == pe )' test is permanently false, and the machine walks out of bounds without any terminating check.

The companion assert 'assert((size_t) (pe - p) == len - off ...)' is arithmetically always true (both sides wrap to the identical value even when off > len) and therefore provides no independent validation of off.
limitations: Out-of-bounds read walk via off > len: trigger requires the caller to violate the quoted contract 'assert(off <= len && "offset past end of buffer");' (and/or a NDEBUG build removing it); no statement in this code produces off > len, so the trigger is not instantiated here.

Header values accept arbitrary bytes except CR: 'case 19: if ( (*p) == 13 ) goto tr29; goto st19;' lets bare LF and NUL bytes be consumed into the value passed to 'parser->http_field(parser, PTR_TO(field_start), parser->field_len, PTR_TO(mark), LEN(mark, p));'. This is a desync/request-smuggling precursor, but the impact chain breaks at the not-shown callback consumer and any front-end proxy, per the CALLEE BOUNDARY RULE it cannot be promoted to a finding.
'snake_upcase_char((char *)p);' casts away const and mutates the caller's buffer in place (header-name upcasing); a crash on read-only buffer memory has no attacker-reachable producer in this code.

The post-parse asserts 'assert(parser->mark < len)' and 'assert(parser->field_start < len)' can abort the process on a len == 0 invocation if the init-set fields are 0; that base value is UNSOURCED and the len == 0 invocation depends on unshown caller behavior.

The switch on 'cs' has no default arm; an out-of-range cs (from a corrupted parser struct, producer not shown) falls through to '_test_eof2: cs = 2;' and silently rewrites the state, but causes no memory access in this code.

verdict.summary: No fully instantiated vulnerability in the given code. The Ragel-generated state machine maintains p <= pe at every (*p) access on every path via the entry guard 'if ( p == pe ) goto _test_eof;' and the per-state 'if ( ++p == pe ) goto _test_eofN;' pattern; all internal marks (mark, field_start, query_start, field_len) are assigned before use within the resume chain. The only bound on the 'off' parameter is 'assert(off <= len && "offset past end of buffer")', which this code itself asserts as a documented caller contract, and no in-code data flow produces 'off'. Remaining risks are contract/assumption questions: assert-only validation (no-ops under NDEBUG), resume-with-different-buffer semantics, and unshown macros (MARK/LEN/PTR_TO), callbacks, and parser initialization.

assumptions: MARK, LEN, PTR_TO macros, snake_upcase_char, puma_parser_has_error, the parser callbacks, and the puma_parser struct layout/initialization are referenced but not defined in the given code; standard Puma semantics were assumed where noted.
The function is treated as an intake point for untrusted HTTP bytes (buffer, len are attacker-data); off is a caller-contract argument per the code's own assert.
NDEBUG may compile out all assert statements; the analysis treats asserts as documented contracts per the quoted statements, while noting they provide no runtime enforcement in release builds.
limitations: C1 (speculative): a caller passing off > len would cause unbounded out-of-bounds reads past the buffer (since '++p == pe' can never match once p starts beyond pe); the trigger requires violating the code's own asserted precondition 'assert(off <= len && "offset past end of buffer")', so it is contract-speculative, with the caveat that this assert is removed under NDEBUG.

C3 (speculative): parser->mark/field_start/query_start persist as absolute offsets across calls; resuming with a different or shorter buffer, or with off < mark, could make PTR_TO/LEN leave the buffer when passed to the request_method/http_field/etc. callbacks — impact chain breaks at unshown macros and uncharacterizable callbacks and requires unshown caller behavior.

C4 (UNSOURCED): an invalid parser->cs (e.g., uninitialized parser) falls through 'switch ( cs )' into '_test_eof2: cs = 2; goto _test_eof;', silently coercing local cs to 2; whether it is persisted depends on unshown puma_parser_has_error, and the initial cs value is set by an init function not in the given code.

C5 (UNSOURCED): the trailing postcondition asserts (e.g., 'assert(parser->mark < len ...)') are debug-only aborts and their inputs (initial mark/field_start/body_start/nread) come from unshown initialization; worst case is a debug-build assertion abort, not a release-build security effect.

All writes use fixed offsets and constant sizes. No candidate defect could be triggered with fully sourced preconditions: the remaining concerns (attribute-length enforcement, lookup NULL behavior, refcount overflow, locking) depend on unshown code and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: nft_verdict_policy is not defined in the given code; its length/type constraints on NFTA_VERDICT_CODE (NLA_U32), NFTA_VERDICT_CHAIN and NFTA_VERDICT_CHAIN_ID are assumed to enforce payload sizes, so the 4-byte read in nla_get_be32 is assumed bounded.

The trigger precondition (policy admitting a short attribute) is UNSOURCED and could not be instantiated.

Potential NULL dereference: IS_ERR(chain) does not catch NULL, and nft_is_base_chain(chain) dereferences chain; no producer of NULL exists in the given code (lookups are expected to return ERR_PTR), so the trigger is speculative.

verdict.summary: bgp_capability_msg_parse performs a fixed-size memcpy of sizeof(struct capability) bytes from the attacker-controlled BGP capability message while only validating 3 header bytes (pnt + 3 > end), so a remote peer sending a capability message whose remaining bytes are exactly 3 causes the memcpy to read past the end of the message buffer, a heap out-of-bounds read that can crash the BGP daemon and leak adjacent heap bytes into the parsed capability struct.

evidence.snippet:
/* Fetch structure to the byte stream.  */
      memcpy (&cap, pnt + 1, sizeof (struct capability));
evidence.reason: Heap out-of-bounds read: the copy length is the fixed sizeof(struct capability) (>= 5 bytes by this code's own member usage of cap.code, cap.length, cap.mpc.afi via ntohs, cap.mpc.safi), but the only prior bound is the 3-byte header check at line 16, guaranteeing just 2 readable bytes at pnt + 1. With a peer-controlled message where end - pnt == 3, the memcpy reads sizeof(struct capability) - 2 bytes past end = pnt + length, past the message buffer.

evidence.snippet:
/* We need at least action, capability code and capability length. */
      if (pnt + 3 > end)
evidence.reason: The only bounds check executed before the memcpy; it admits end - pnt == 3 (rejects only pnt + 3 > end), leaving only 2 in-bounds bytes at pnt + 1, which is insufficient for the fixed sizeof(struct capability) copy at line 26. The later check pnt + (cap.length + 3) > end runs after the memcpy and bounds the declared length, not the copy.

assumptions: The definition of struct capability is not included in the given code; its minimum size (> 3 bytes) is inferred from this code's own usage: cap.code and cap.length map to the first two copied bytes and cap.mpc.afi is a 16-bit member (passed to ntohs) with cap.mpc.safi following, so sizeof(struct capability) >= 5.

The capability message buffer is allocated by the caller (not shown) so that end = pnt + length marks the end of the attacker's message extent; reading past end is therefore past the data this code was given.
sizeof(struct capability) is assumed not to exceed the allocator's mapping behavior; the overread distance is bounded by sizeof(struct capability) - 2 bytes.
limitations: Infinite loop candidate: 'continue' in the PEER_FLAG_OVERRIDE_CAPABILITY branch skips 'pnt += cap.length + 3;', so if a configured peer has that flag set and an attacker sends a CAPABILITY_MESSAGE containing an MP capability code, pnt never advances and the while loop spins forever (CWE-835/CWE-400). The triggering precondition peer->flags containing PEER_FLAG_OVERRIDE_CAPABILITY is UNSOURCED in this code (no assignment to peer->flags exists here), so this candidate is speculative and does not drive the verdict.

If cap.code == CAPABILITY_CODE_MP but cap.length < 4, afi/safi are parsed from bytes beyond the declared capability; within the packet this is only a logic misparse (the enum-pinning check quoted in STEP 2 prevents out-of-range array indexing), and past end it is subsumed by the confirmed primary out-of-bounds read.

verdict.summary: The search operator's bounds handling is correct: 'if (size > r_size(op1)) { make_false(op); return 0; }' rejects oversized patterns before any indexing, 'if (size == 0) goto found;' prevents dereferencing an empty pattern, and the do-while loop only tests positions base..base+N-size, so every read (including memcmp of 'size' bytes) and every produced substring descriptor (match at ptr with rsize size, post at ptr+size with rsize N-k-size, pre with rsize k) terminates exactly at base+N. The no-match exit's unsigned wrap of 'count' is never read afterward. Residual candidates (the op[-3]/op[-1] stack slot addressing relative to the unshown push(2) macro, and the backward empty-pattern non-partitioned result) have triggers or impacts that depend on code not given and produce no out-of-bounds access in this code; they are recorded as limitations, not findings.

assumptions: push(2) is a Ghostscript framework macro (base/oper.h) whose expansion is not in the given code; per Ghostscript convention it verifies stack room against ostop, adjusts osp, and rebases the local 'op', so 'op[-1]', 'op[-3]' and 'make_true(op)' address the pushed result slots and op1's original slot. This cannot be quoted from the given code.
The interpreter guarantees the operator is invoked with its declared operands present, so 'op1 = op - 1' is a valid in-stack slot; no statement in this code enforces it.
check_read_type(*op1/op, t_string) enforces t_string type and read access before value.bytes is used; the macro body is not shown.
Operand string descriptors' value.bytes/r_size pairs are maintained in-bounds by the interpreter's string operators; this code assumes but does not verify them beyond the type checks.
r_size and tas.rsize have the same width, so 'op->tas.rsize = size' cannot truncate.
limitations: Candidate (a): if push(2) did NOT rebase 'op', 'op[-3].value.bytes = ptr + size;' and the adjacent rsize writes would target slots below the operands (potentially below the stack base when the stack holds only the two operands). The trigger precondition 'push does not rebind op' is UNSOURCED (macro text not given), and under that reading 'make_true(op)' would also overwrite the just-written match, contradicting the code's own comments; the candidate is therefore speculative, not a finding.

Candidate (c): for backward search with an empty pattern, 'if (size == 0) goto found;' executes before 'if (!forward) ptr += count;', yielding pre rsize = N (whole string) overlapping the empty match at base. All descriptors remain inside [base, base+N]; any harm would occur in unshown PostScript consumer code, and reachability of forward == false (no caller shown) is UNSOURCED.
Candidate (b): on a push(2) stackoverflow, 'op' already holds a match descriptor; that slot remains a valid, in-bounds readable string, so the error path leaves no corrupted state.
Candidate (e): the 'while (count--);' no-match exit leaves count = UINT_MAX, but the subsequent 'make_false(op); return 0;' never reads count, so the wrap is harmless.

verdict.summary: pcx_write_rle dereferences *from (line 14) after advancing from += step (line 13) without first checking from against end. The only bound test, 'from == end', is the right operand of '||' and is evaluated after the read, and it also omits the from > end overshoot case. On the final iteration of every normal invocation from lands exactly on end, so the condition 'data != *from' reads one byte past the end of the buffer (heap out-of-bounds read; can fault at an allocation boundary). The fix requires reordering to test from >= end before the dereference; no guard, clamp, mask, or error arm exists on any path in this code.

evidence.snippet:
from += step;
        if (data != *from || from == end) {
evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). Line 13 advances 'from' by 'step' so it can reach or pass 'end', and line 14 dereferences '*from' as the left operand of '||', evaluated before the 'from == end' check. Instantiated trigger: buffer buf[1], from = &buf[0], end = &buf[1], step = 1; loop enters (from < end), data = buf[0], from += 1 makes from == end, then 'data != *from' reads *end, one byte past the buffer. The code's own statements define end as exclusive ('while (from < end)' and the correctly ordered 'while ((from < end) && (*from == data))'), so this read is always out of bounds on the final iteration; with step > 1 an unaligned (end - from) % step additionally overshoots to end + step - 1. No bounds check, clamp, mask, or error arm exists between the increment and the dereference.

assumptions: No documented or asserted contract for the parameters from, end, and step exists in the given code; they are treated as caller-supplied data, and the OOB trigger requires no special values beyond a non-empty buffer and a positive stride.
'end' is an exclusive upper bound; this is established by the code's own statements (while (from < end); while ((from < end) && (*from == data))) rather than assumed from the interface.
The allocation extent of the underlying buffer is not shown; whether the OOB read faults or reads silently depends on placement, but the read past 'end' itself is fully instantiated in this code.
limitations: Degenerate stride (step <= 0): with step == 0, 'from += step' never advances and the loops at lines 10 and 20 never terminate (hang); with step < 0, 'from' moves backward, causing reads before the buffer and a potential division by a negative/zero step at line 29. No statement in this code produces or constrains 'step', and the real caller (which computes the stride from pixel depth) is not shown, so these are recorded as caller-dependent and are not the basis of the verdict.

In the simulated from == end cases, the out-of-bounds byte influences only the branch taken, and both branches emit identical output bytes (just 'data', or '0xc1 data' when data >= 0xc0), so no direct information disclosure into the PCX output stream was demonstrated; the security impact is the out-of-bounds read itself and a potential fault at an allocation or page boundary.

verdict.summary: update_topline() consumes only editor state (window/buffer/option fields) and contains no direct memory, indexing, copy, format, or injection sink. All loop bounds are guarded by quoted break statements verified in execution order (lnum >= curbuf->b_ml.ml_line_count || n >= halfheight; lnum <= 0 || line_count > curwin->w_height + 1; loff.lnum < curwin->w_botline), all callee arguments are constants or in-domain line numbers, and the temporarily mutated *so_ptr is restored on every path after the mutation (no return exists between *so_ptr = mouse_dragging - 1 and *so_ptr = save_so). The remaining arithmetic issues (long-to-int truncation at n = curwin->w_topline + *so_ptr - curwin->w_cursor.lnum, potential signed overflow in topline/botline + *so_ptr expressions) have UNSOURCED preconditions (p_so/mouse_dragging are never assigned in this code) and their only consequence in this code is selecting between scroll routines in unshown callees, so no security impact is instantiated in the given code.

assumptions: screen_valid, check_cursor_lnum, check_cursor_moved, check_top_offset, hasAnyFolding, hasFolding, diff_check_fill, scrolljump_value, scroll_cursor_top/bot/halfway, validate_botline, botline_forw are not shown; their behavior is uncharacterizable and was not relied on.
curwin, curbuf, p_so, mouse_dragging and their fields are produced by code outside the given snippet; per the UNSOURCED rule they were used neither as trigger preconditions nor as guards.
'scrolloff' (p_so / w_p_so) is presumed to be capped elsewhere in the editor; no cap is quotable in the given code, so no bound was assumed.
limitations: Integer truncation at n = curwin->w_topline + *so_ptr - curwin->w_cursor.lnum (long expression assigned to int n) and potential signed overflow in curwin->w_topline + *so_ptr / curwin->w_botline - *so_ptr: trigger requires *so_ptr around 2^31 or LONG_MAX, but p_so and mouse_dragging have no assignment in this code (UNSOURCED), and even when granted the value only selects between scroll_cursor_halfway and scroll_cursor_top in unshown callees; no memory-safety consequence in this code.

Potential non-termination of the while (loff.lnum < curwin->w_botline ...) loop if botline_forw(&loff) fails to advance loff.lnum and n never reaches *so_ptr; botline_forw is not shown and not characterizable, so the hang cannot be instantiated from the given code.

If a caller elsewhere permits 'scrolloff' values at the 2^31 scale, the truncation above could cause a wrong scrolling decision; any resulting defect would live in the unshown scroll routines, not in this function.

verdict.summary: Analysis of ipf_extract_frags_from_batch reveals a correctly structured packet batch dispatcher. The function iterates over network packets, identifies IP fragments, and delegates fragment processing to purpose-built handlers with proper mutex protection for shared state. No demonstrable security vulnerability was identified in the given code: mutex usage is correct (lock before ipf_handle_frag, unlock after, no bypass path), the fragment identification logic uses proper short-circuit evaluation to avoid calling wrong-protocol validators, and packet forwarding to fragment-handling functions is within their designed input domain. Potential issues (signed/unsigned index mismatch, validation outside lock, missing return type) all have unsourced preconditions and cannot be instantiated from this code alone.

assumptions: The DP_PACKET_BATCH_REFILL_FOR_EACH macro correctly iterates over batch packets and handles consumed vs. refilled packets; its implementation is not shown
The dp_packet_batch_refill function correctly places a packet back into the batch at the given index; implementation not shown
The ipf_is_valid_v4_frag and ipf_is_valid_v6_frag functions only inspect the packet's IP header and do not read mutable ipf state that requires the ipf_lock; implementation not shown
The ipf_handle_frag function takes ownership of the packet only when returning non-zero, and does not free or modify the packet when returning zero; implementation not shown
The return type (likely void) was present in the original source but not included in the extracted snippet
The batch size (pb_cnt) is bounded by the network stack's burst size (NETDEV_MAX_BURST, typically 32), preventing signed/unsigned issues with int pb_idx
limitations: Race condition between unlocked validation (ipf_is_valid_v4_frag/ipf_is_valid_v6_frag) and locked handling (ipf_handle_frag) could not be confirmed because the validation functions' implementations are not shown; if they read mutable ipf configuration state, a narrow TOCTOU window exists but requires simultaneous admin configuration change to trigger

Signed/unsigned comparison between pb_idx (int) and pb_cnt (size_t) could cause unexpected behavior if batch size exceeds INT_MAX, but no statement in this code can produce such a large batch, and realistic network stacks bound batches to ~32 packets
The missing return type declaration is likely a code extraction artifact; in actual OVS source this function is declared void

The actual security-sensitive logic (IP header parsing, fragment reassembly, list management) resides in ipf_handle_frag, ipf_is_valid_v4_frag, and ipf_is_valid_v6_frag which are not shown; any vulnerabilities in packet parsing would be in those functions

verdict.summary: In bgp_capability_msg_parse, the two `continue` statements taken for an MP capability (the invalid-afi/safi arm at line 66 and the override-capability arm at line 59) skip the loop's only pointer advance `pnt += hdr->length + 3;` (line 102). A malicious BGP peer that sends a dynamic-capability message containing an MP capability with an invalid AFI/SAFI re-enters `while (pnt < end)` with unchanged pnt forever, wedging the daemon in an infinite loop at 100% CPU (remote denial of service from a single small message).

evidence.reason: This `continue` (and the one at line 59) exits the loop body without executing the only cursor advance `pnt += hdr->length + 3;` at line 102. Since pnt and end are unchanged and every guard (lines 17, 27-28, 41) is deterministic on the same bytes, the loop re-parses the same capability forever. Trigger: peer sends a capability with action=SET, code=CAPABILITY_CODE_MP, length=4, and invalid afi/safi (e.g., afi=0, safi=0xFF); bgp_afi_safi_valid_indices fails, the continue fires, and the function never returns — attacker-controlled infinite loop / unbounded CPU consumption.

evidence.snippet:
afi = ntohs (mpc.afi);
	  safi = mpc.safi;
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values driving the trigger: afi and safi are parsed directly from the peer-supplied capability bytes (copied into mpc by the memcpy at line 49). Attacker-chosen invalid values here cause bgp_afi_safi_valid_indices to fail at line 61, whose error arm continues without advancing pnt, producing the infinite loop.

assumptions: pnt/length are the body and size of a received BGP dynamic-capability message, so their contents are attacker-controlled; this is inferred from the parser signature, error handling (bgp_notify_send to the peer), and the absence of any quotable caller contract in the given code.

struct capability_header is a 2-byte overlay (code, length as single bytes), so hdr->length is at most 255 and the normal-path advance is at least 3; the struct definitions are not included in the given code.

bgp_afi_safi_valid_indices is an index-validation predicate that returns false for at least some attacker-chosen afi/safi (its failure arm at lines 62-66 exists in this code for exactly that case) and returns true only for values in range of peer->afc_recv/afc_nego, which is what guards the array indexing at lines 79-94.
limitations: memcpy at line 49 copies sizeof(struct capability_mp_data) bytes while the guard at line 41 only guarantees hdr->length (attacker-controlled, can be 0) bytes remain; with pnt+3 == end up to sizeof(mpc) bytes are read past `end`. Whether this crosses the underlying stream allocation is not shown, and the overread bytes only reach afi/safi, which are validated at line 61 before any use — impact not instantiated, recorded as a latent out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

The continue at line 59 (PEER_FLAG_OVERRIDE_CAPABILITY set) also skips the advance and yields the same infinite loop for any MP capability, but the flag is operator configuration set outside this code (UNSOURCED precondition); the primary trigger at line 66 does not depend on it.
zlog_debug at lines 64-65 passes afi and safi with no matching format specifiers; extra printf arguments are ignored, so this is cosmetic only.
peer->flags, peer->afc, and peer->bgp are assigned outside this code; they are only read here, and no finding depends on their values.

Remaining candidates rest on unshown code (nft_verdict_policy attribute-length enforcement, caller-side use-count unwinding on error paths, desc->flags set by callers) and could not be instantiated with sourced preconditions, so no vulnerability is confirmed in this code.

nft_chain_lookup and nft_chain_lookup_byid return a valid chain pointer or an ERR_PTR failure sentinel and never NULL; their bodies are not shown.
Callers of this static function pass a valid nft_data output buffer and a valid nft_data_desc; no assert or documented contract for this is quotable from the given code.
Execution context (transaction/batch mutexing of nftables commit paths) is not shown; concurrency behavior of chain->use++ is assumed to be managed by unshown locking.

C3: chain->use++ balance on caller error paths (rule/element init abort, nft_verdict_uninit) depends on caller code not given; no use-count imbalance is provable within this function.

C6: desc->flags is read but never assigned in this code (UNSOURCED); the NFT_DATA_DESC_SETELEM binding-chain check's effectiveness depends on callers setting it, and the harmful use of a binding chain in a set element would occur in unshown set/eval code.
The deployment privilege level of the nftables subsystem (netlink reachability from unprivileged user namespaces) is not quotable from this code and was not used to promote or demote any candidate.

verdict.summary: The GBR brush loader computes the raw-data buffer size with 32-bit unsigned arithmetic: 'size = bh.width * bh.height * bh.bytes;' wraps modulo 2^32 for attacker-chosen dimensions (e.g., width=height=65537, bytes=4 yields size=524292 instead of ~17 GB), because the only guard, 'G_MAXSIZE / bh.width / bh.height / bh.bytes < 1', tests the product in 64-bit units and admits any product below 2^64. The undersized heap buffer is then passed to gimp_pixel_rgn_set_rect, which copies width*height*bytes bytes from it, producing a massive heap out-of-bounds read (crash and potential heap-content disclosure) from a small malicious brush file. Related 32-bit wraps at the pattern-path allocation '4 * bh.width * bh.height' and the case-2 conversion loop can additionally yield out-of-bounds writes with multi-gigabyte crafted files.

evidence.reason: Root cause: bh.width, bh.height and bh.bytes are 32-bit unsigned header fields, so the multiplication wraps mod 2^32 before being assigned to the 64-bit gsize 'size'. Instantiated trigger: a brush file with width=65537, height=65537, bytes=4 passes the sanitize check, wraps size to 524292, and g_malloc allocates only 524292 bytes while the image is later created at 65537x65537 RGBA, so gimp_pixel_rgn_set_rect (line 262) reads ~17 GB of pixel data from the small buffer: heap out-of-bounds read.

evidence.snippet:
gimp_pixel_rgn_set_rect (&pixel_rgn, brush_buf,
                           0, 0, bh.width, bh.height);
evidence.reason: Sink: this call site passes the undersized, attacker-derived heap buffer brush_buf together with the unwrapped dimensions bh.width x bh.height; the documented semantics of gimp_pixel_rgn_set_rect are to consume width*height*bpp bytes from the buffer, so the wrapped allocation from line 122-123 turns into a massive out-of-bounds read of heap memory.

evidence.snippet:
if ((bh.width == 0) || (bh.width > GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE) ||
      (bh.height == 0) || (bh.height > GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE) ||
      ((bh.bytes != 1) && (bh.bytes != 2) && (bh.bytes != 4) &&
       (bh.bytes != 18)) ||
      (G_MAXSIZE / bh.width / bh.height / bh.bytes < 1))
evidence.reason: The only guard on the dimensions is quoted and edge-tested: G_MAXSIZE is a 64-bit constant, so this division chain only rejects products exceeding 2^64-1. Under the quoted clamps the reachable maximum of bh.width * bh.height * bh.bytes is 262144 * 262144 * 4 = 2^38, which still wraps in the 32-bit multiply at line 122; the guard is in the wrong width domain and does not protect the allocation.

assumptions: BrushHeader and PatternHeader fields are 32-bit unsigned: inferred from 'bh.width = g_ntohl (bh.width);' (g_ntohl takes and returns guint32) and the network-byte-order decoding pattern; the struct definitions are not shown.

GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE is assumed to be 262144 (2^18), the GIMP constant; it is not shown in the given code. Any value >= 65538 for the maximum still permits the demonstrated wrap with width=height=65537 only if it exceeds 65537; the wrap is reachable for any bound above 2^16 per-dimension products exceeding 2^32.
g_malloc aborts the process on allocation failure rather than returning NULL (GLib semantics); it never returns an undersized buffer.

gimp_pixel_rgn_set_rect copies width*height*bpp bytes of pixel data from the supplied buffer into the drawable (documented GIMP API semantics), used per the callee boundary rule to characterize the out-of-bounds read.
limitations: Pattern-path out-of-bounds WRITE at lines 165/167/177 ('brush_buf = g_malloc (4 * bh.width * bh.height);' plus the loop writing brush_buf[i*4+3]): same 32-bit wrap root cause, but triggering it requires the wrapped product P = width*height (bytes=1) to exceed 2^30 so that 4*P wraps a second time, which first forces a multi-gigabyte allocation and file at line 123; recorded as a variant of the primary defect, not a separate finding.

Case-2 conversion loop (lines 190-206) can read *buf and write brush_buf[i] out of bounds when the wrapped 32-bit product exceeds 2^31 (size = 2*P wraps below 2P), but this requires a >= 2 GB allocation and input file; same root cause, heavier trigger.
Resource leaks, not memory-safety vulnerabilities: the sanitize error path at line 58 returns without close(fd), and the unsupported-depth path at line 239 leaks brush_buf and the file descriptor.
The bn_size gint truncation at line 95 was analyzed and found consistent: the allocation 'g_new (gchar, bn_size)' and the read at line 99 both use the same truncated value, so no overflow results.

verdict.summary: The GSER parser advances the cursor and subtracts lengths assuming a closing double quote was found. When the issuer or thisUpdate string is not terminated by a quote (or a doubled-quote pair ends exactly at the window end), is->bv_len / tu->bv_len equals x.bv_len, so 'x.bv_len -= len + 1' underflows and 'x.bv_val += len + 1' moves the cursor one byte past the end of the attacker-supplied input buffer. The very next statement dereferences x.bv_val[0] in the eat-spaces loop, producing an out-of-bounds heap read on any crafted attribute value (e.g. '{issuer rdnSequence:"aaa..."}' with no closing quote, or a thisUpdate of exactly 15 unquoted characters).

evidence.snippet:
x.bv_val += is->bv_len + 1;
			x.bv_len -= is->bv_len + 1;
evidence.reason: The issuer scan loop (line 65: 'for ( ; is->bv_len < x.bv_len; )') permits exit with is->bv_len == x.bv_len when no closing '"' exists, and line 73 'is->bv_len += 2;' can also produce is->bv_len == x.bv_len when a dquote pair ends exactly at the window end. With is->bv_len == x.bv_len, line 78 moves x.bv_val one byte past the input buffer (verified by simulation: for a 50-byte input ending in '}', x.bv_val becomes in->bv_val + 50, valid indices 0..49) and line 79 underflows x.bv_len to a huge value. No quote-found sentinel test exists on any path between the loop and this sink.

evidence.snippet:
x.bv_val += tu->bv_len + 1;
			x.bv_len -= tu->bv_len + 1;
evidence.reason: Identical defect on the thisUpdate path: the loop on line 107 exits with tu->bv_len == x.bv_len when no '"' is present, and the length check on line 112 ('if ( tu->bv_len < STRLENOF("YYYYmmddHHmmssZ") )') only enforces a minimum of 15 — at exactly 15 unquoted characters (e.g. thisUpdate "012345678901234 followed by '}') it passes, so line 114 advances x.bv_val one byte past the input buffer and line 115 underflows x.bv_len.

evidence.snippet: for ( ; (x.bv_val[0] == ' ') && x.bv_len; x.bv_val++, x.bv_len-- ) {
evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read sink: this is the first dereference after the cursor overrun. It evaluates x.bv_val[0] BEFORE testing x.bv_len, so with x.bv_val = in->bv_val + in->bv_len it reads one byte past the attacker-controlled input buffer on every trigger execution; because x.bv_len is underflowed (huge), a heap byte of spaces causes the loop to keep scanning out of bounds, and line 132 / line 35 then dereference OOB heap again (crash / DoS potential in the syntax-checking process).

assumptions: in->bv_val points to exactly in->bv_len valid bytes (standard berval data model); NUL termination beyond bv_len is not assumed anywhere in the analysis.

ber_len_t is unsigned per its OpenLDAP definition (not quotable from the given code); the trigger does not depend on this, since the pointer advance past the buffer end and the dereference at line 124 are instantiated regardless of the subtraction's signedness.
limitations: Returned-value heap disclosure (OOB content copied into *is via ber_dupbv_x at line 144) is NOT instantiated: every underflow path leaves x.bv_len nonzero at line 141 ('if ( x.bv_len ) return LDAP_INVALID_SYNTAX;'), so the function returns an error before *is = ni.

Unchecked allocation results (slap_sl_malloc at line 150, ber_dupbv_x at line 144) could yield a NULL ni.bv_val deref, but ni.bv_len is bounded by the input length (no attacker-scalable amplification) and allocation failure is not attacker-inducible — robustness issue, not a finding.
The read at line 70 (is->bv_val[is->bv_len+1]) was verified in-bounds: the loop condition caps is->bv_len+1 at x.bv_len, which maps to in->bv_val[in->bv_len-1] == '}' — no separate finding there.

Deployment context (whether this runs in slapd behind a network) is an assumption per discipline 3; the verdict rests solely on the attacker-data value parsed at this entry point and the quoted statements.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write in stl_remove_degenerate. Indices read from parsed STL model state (neighbors_start[].neighbor[] and .which_vertex_not[]) are used to write stl->neighbors_start[neighbor1].neighbor[(vnot1 + 1) % 3] with no bounds validation. The only check, `if(neighbor1 != -1)`, rejects solely the value -1 and does not bound the neighbor index; the `% 3` mask does not bound negative dividends (vnot1 = -2 gives (-1) % 3 = -1, and vnot1 = INT_MAX overflows vnot1 + 1 to INT_MIN, giving INT_MIN % 3 = -2). Crafted model data therefore produces an out-of-bounds heap write with attacker-influenced index and value.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink. Both indices are unvalidated attacker-model-state values: the guard `if(neighbor1 != -1)` rejects only the exact value -1 (neighbor1 = -2 or any out-of-range index passes), and the index expression (vnot1 + 1) % 3 yields -1 for vnot1 = -2 and -2 for vnot1 = -3 or for vnot1 = INT_MAX (signed overflow of vnot1 + 1 wraps to INT_MIN). Simulated trigger: facet with vertex[0]==vertex[1] (edge1=1), neighbor[1]=5, which_vertex_not[1]=-2 → writes neighbor2 at neighbors_start[5].neighbor[-1], corrupting heap memory. Same defect pattern repeats at lines 66-67 and 74.

Origin of the tainted values: neighbor1/2/3 and vnot1/2/3 are read from parsed STL model state (neighbors_start array) with no statement in this code bounding them; no range check, clamp, or normalization exists anywhere between these reads and the write sinks at lines 62-63, 66-67, and 74.

assumptions: facet_start and neighbors_start are arrays indexed by facet, and neighbor[3]/which_vertex_not[3] are fixed length-3 int arrays (so the required index domain for the % 3 expressions is {0,1,2}); inferred from usage, struct definitions not shown.

The stl model state originates from a parsed STL file (untrusted origin per discipline 3: serialized/model state); this cannot be quoted from the given code but is the only coherent origin for the consumed fields.
C semantics: % takes the sign of the dividend (C99 6.5.5), so negative vnot values produce negative indices; vnot1 + 1 at INT_MAX is signed overflow (wraps to INT_MIN on the modeled evaluation).
limitations: Unvalidated `facet` parameter (lines 14-17, 45-46, 56-59): stl->facet_start[facet] and stl->neighbors_start[facet] would read out of bounds if the caller passed an out-of-range index; no bounds check and no facet-count reference exist in this code. Neither the bound nor a violating caller is quotable here (the caller's facet derivation is not shown), so this is recorded as a limitation rather than a finding.

Line 49 `stl_update_connects_remove_1(stl, neighbor2);` executes when neighbor1 == -1 but the guard tests neighbor1 only; if neighbor2 is also -1, -1 is passed as a facet index. The callee is not shown and its behavior on -1 cannot be characterized, so the impact chain breaks per the callee boundary rule.
stl_remove_facet(stl, facet) at lines 22 and 70 is not shown; its internal handling of facet removal cannot be characterized.

The harmful model-state values (which_vertex_not <= -2, out-of-range neighbor) are produced by a neighbor-computation stage not included in the given code; per the guard-anchoring rules they are treated as attacker-data with no quotable bound, which keeps the finding valid but lowers confidence.

verdict.summary: The function is the Linux kernel BPF ring-buffer reserve routine with all its upstream guards present: a range check on the attacker-controlled size, a record-length check against the buffer size, an in-flight space check under the lock, and a modulo mask bounding the header offset. Every in-code memory write (hdr->len, hdr->pg_off) is covered on all paths in execution order. Remaining candidates (u64/u32 overflow or truncation of size-derived lengths, wrap-around record writes past the first copy of the data area, header straddling the data-area end) depend on unsourced values: the numeric bound RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ, the extent/layout of rb->data, and the initial producer_pos, none of which are assigned or characterizable in the given code, so no trigger is instantiated.

assumptions: size is treated as fully attacker-controlled (arbitrary u64) because it originates from a BPF program's call to the ringbuf reserve helper; no constraint on it is quotable in this code.

RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ, BPF_RINGBUF_HDR_SZ, and BPF_RINGBUF_BUSY_BIT are macros whose numeric values are not defined in the given code; the quoted guard 'if (unlikely(size > RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ))' bounds size, but its numeric bound cannot be verified here.

rb->mask, rb->data, rb->producer_pos, rb->consumer_pos, and rb->spinlock have no assignment in this code (only producer_pos is stored to, from input-derived values); their initialization lives in the not-shown ringbuf allocation code.
limitations: Integer-overflow/truncation candidates (wrap of size + BPF_RINGBUF_HDR_SZ, truncation of round_up result into u32 len, and the u64-to-u32 store 'hdr->len = size | BPF_RINGBUF_BUSY_BIT') are gated by the UNSOURCED value of RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ; triggering them requires that bound to be at 2^31/2^32/U64_MAX scale, which cannot be instantiated from the given code.

Wrap-around records can extend past the first (mask+1) bytes of rb->data (e.g., empty buffer, prod_pos at B-16, len = B-16 passes both quoted checks), but whether that range is out-of-bounds depends on the extent and layout of rb->data established by allocation code not shown and not characterizable; the impact chain therefore breaks and this stays a limitation, not a finding.

An 8-byte header write at offset prod_pos & rb->mask near the buffer end could exceed a (mask+1)-byte area only if producer_pos is a non-multiple of 8 (initial value UNSOURCED; this code only adds multiples of 8) or if the data-area extent is below mask+1+8 (UNSOURCED); not instantiable.
Unsigned wrap of prod_pos + len requires producer_pos near ULONG_MAX, which no statement in this code can produce from its UNSOURCED initial value.

The consumer_pos read outside the spinlock is conservative in every simulated interleaving (consumer_pos only advances, making new_prod_pos - cons_pos larger and the check stricter); the producer position is read under the lock, so no overcommit path was found.

verdict.summary: gdImageFillToBorder recurses on itself (lines 47 and 63) with no depth bound or recursion guard. Because the entry clamps only the upper bounds of x and y (lines 13-18) and never rejects or clamps y < 0, a caller-controlled negative y makes the Below branch (line 56, true for any negative y) recurse once per row, climbing from y toward 0 and through the image, so recursion depth is directly proportional to the attacker-supplied |y| (equivalently, to the attacker-supplied image height for in-range y). One integer argument or one crafted image yields hundreds of thousands to millions of stacked frames, exhausting the process stack: an attacker-scalable denial of service (CWE-400).

evidence.reason: Uncontrolled recursive self-call at line 63 inside the span loop: with attacker-chosen x=0, border=7, color=8 and unclamped y=-10000000, every level recurses with y+1 (line 56 passes for any negative y), stacking one frame per row until the process stack is exhausted (CWE-400). No depth counter, iteration cap, or explicit worklist exists anywhere in the function.

Second recursive sink: for an in-range start on a tall attacker-crafted image with no border-colored pixels, this Above-branch call recurses once per row upward, giving depth proportional to the attacker-controlled image height (sy), again with no depth bound in this code.

Origin of the unvalidated value: only the upper bound of y is clamped (symmetrically x at line 13); there is no 'if (y < 0)' arm, so a negative caller-supplied y flows unchanged into gdImageGetPixel/gdImageSetPixel (lines 21/24) and into the recursive calls, enabling depth proportional to |y|.

assumptions: im->sx and im->sy have no assignment in the shown code; they are treated as attacker-influenced because gdImageFillToBorder is an exported public API whose image state derives from parsed image files (e.g., PHP's imagefilltoborder passes user x/y directly), but the producing parse/creation statements are not quotable here.

Behavior of the unshown gdImageGetPixel/gdImageSetPixel for out-of-range coordinates is assumed to be clipping/returning a well-defined value (documented library behavior). If they did NOT clip, negative y would additionally give an out-of-bounds write, so the vulnerability conclusion holds a fortiori; the in-range trigger (line 47 recursion scaled by image height) does not depend on this assumption.
Stack-exhaustion depth (~10^5-10^6 frames) assumes typical 8 MB stacks and ordinary frame sizes; the attacker-controlled |y| or image height makes exceeding it straightforward.
limitations: The exact out-of-range return value of gdImageGetPixel is unknown; the attacker must choose border (>= 0, per the line 8 guard) and color distinct from it, which is a small search space but not fully quotable from the given code.

The 'color' parameter is passed unvalidated to gdImageSetPixel; any memory-safety consequence depends entirely on the unshown callee body (special color constants such as gdStyled/gdBrushed) and could not be characterized, so no separate finding is claimed for it.

evidence.reason: strcpy writes pipePath.size()+1 bytes into the fixed stack buffer local.sun_path (104/108 bytes inside sockaddr_un) with no bound; any endpoint.name() of length >= sizeof(sun_path) produces an out-of-bounds stack write with attacker-chosen content and length. No length check, clamp, mask, truncating copy, or rejecting branch exists on any path (line 5 only rejects duplicate paths).

evidence.snippet: string pipePath = endpoint.name();
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: the content-bearing parameter of the non-static member function is taken verbatim into pipePath with no documented or asserted length contract anywhere in this code, making the string attacker-data that reaches the strcpy sink at line 15.

assumptions: FATAL_FAIL is assumed to abort/throw on the -1 sentinel of socket()/bind()/chmod(); its definition is not shown, but it cannot bound pipePath.
sun_path width is taken from the platform header (108 on Linux, 104 on macOS/BSD); the overflow holds for any such width.
limitations: unlink(local.sun_path) deletes a caller-named filesystem path before bind; impact depends on what the deploying process may unlink and is not instantiated here.
Race window between bind (line 18) and chmod (line 21) leaves the socket with umask-default permissions briefly; exploitation requires unshown timing and attacker position.
::listen(fd, 5) return value is unchecked and the tail of sun_path past the strcpy NUL is uninitialized when passed to bind; both are robustness issues with no quotable security sink.
If bind fails after the overflow-free case (path length within bounds), the socket fd and the unlinked path are left in a partially initialized state; no security consequence is exhibited.

verdict.summary: elo_probe contains no instantiated security defect. The only memory-safety sink, interface_to_usbdev(to_usb_interface(hdev->dev.parent)), is guarded on the only path by the quoted first statement 'if (!hid_is_usb(hdev)) return -EINVAL;'. Reference counting is exactly balanced on every path: 'priv->usbdev = usb_get_dev(udev);' is followed, on both failure gotos, by 'usb_put_dev(udev);' in err_free, and usb_get_dev returns its argument unchanged so the put drops exactly the acquired reference (NULL-in/NULL-out is symmetric). The delayed work is queued only on the success path immediately before 'return 0', so no free-after-queue UAF exists within this code. Residual candidates (dangling hdev->driver_data after a failed probe, work-vs-remove UAF, NULL wq) require UNSOURCED values or not-shown consumers and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: hdev is a valid struct hid_device pointer supplied by the HID core, which serializes probe against remove for the same device.
elo_work, elo_broken_firmware, wq, ELO_PERIODIC_READ_INTERVAL, and the hid_device_id match table are defined outside the given code; wq is created in the not-shown module init.
hid_is_usb is a framework inline that returns true only for the USB transport, in which case hdev->dev.parent is the USB interface set by usbhid when registering the hid_device.
usb_get_dev increments the refcount and returns the same pointer (NULL in, NULL out); usb_put_dev decrements only when the argument is non-NULL; kzalloc returns zeroed memory or NULL.
On a successful probe, the not-shown elo_remove balances the usb_get_dev reference with usb_put_dev and cancels priv->work.
limitations: Candidate (a): NULL dereference at 'interface_to_usbdev(to_usb_interface(hdev->dev.parent))' for a non-USB HID device — dismissed: guarded by the quoted 'if (!hid_is_usb(hdev)) return -EINVAL;' at the function head, verified to lie on the only path to the use (this is the historical elo_probe segfault, already fixed in the given code).

Candidate (b): usb device reference-count imbalance — dismissed: 'usb_put_dev(udev);' in err_free is the exact counterpart of 'usb_get_dev(udev);', both gotos occur after the get, and the NULL edge is symmetric (no reference taken, no reference dropped).

Candidate (c): use-after-free of priv from the queued delayed work — not instantiated in this code: 'queue_delayed_work(wq, &priv->work, ELO_PERIODIC_READ_INTERVAL);' is reachable only on the success path immediately before 'return 0;'. A UAF would require the not-shown elo_remove to omit cancel_delayed_work_sync, which cannot be characterized from the given code.

Candidate (d): after a failed probe, hdev->driver_data still points to the freed priv because 'hid_set_drvdata(hdev, priv);' precedes err_free's 'kfree(priv);' and err_free never clears drvdata. The impact chain requires a not-shown consumer reading driver data after a failed probe (HID core callbacks are bound only after a successful probe), so the impact is not instantiated here.

Candidate (e): 'wq' is UNSOURCED — it is never assigned in the given code (created in the not-shown module init), so neither a NULL-wq crash nor a module-unload/queued-work race can be instantiated from this code.

elo_broken_firmware(priv->usbdev) dereferences device-controlled USB state inside a not-shown callee, but the call site passes an in-domain, referenced device pointer, so no defect exists at the call statement.

verdict.summary: update_topline() contains no instantiated security defect: it performs no memory indexing, copying, allocation, injection, or crypto operations; all internal loops are bounded by quoted in-body guards ('if (lnum >= curbuf->b_ml.ml_line_count || n >= halfheight) break;', 'if (lnum <= 0 || line_count > curwin->w_height + 1) break;', 'if (n >= *so_ptr) break;') that execute before each first use per iteration; the temporary 'scrolloff' mutation is provably restored on every path; and the only remaining candidates (signed overflow of 'curwin->w_topline + *so_ptr' with a near-LONG_MAX option value, and the long-to-int truncation 'int save_so = *so_ptr;') depend on option/state values this code never assigns and whose only consequence is a branch choice or option mis-store inside unshown scroll functions.

Incoming values of curwin->w_p_so, p_so, mouse_dragging, curwin->w_height, w_cursor.lnum, w_topline, w_botline, w_topfill, w_filler_rows, w_empty_rows, w_skipcol and curbuf->b_ml.ml_line_count are produced elsewhere; none is assigned in this code, so their magnitudes are UNSOURCED for trigger purposes.

limitations: C1 (CWE-190, speculative): 'lnum < curwin->w_topline + *so_ptr' and 'lnum >= curwin->w_botline - *so_ptr' can overflow signed long arithmetic if 'scrolloff' is near LONG_MAX; the option value is unsourced in this code and the only consequence is which scroll_cursor_* branch runs (callees not shown).

C2 (CWE-191, speculative/cosmetic): 'int save_so = *so_ptr;' truncates a long option; '*so_ptr = save_so;' would restore a wrong value if the option exceeded INT_MAX; value unsourced, and the consequence is option mis-store, not a security impact.

C3 (CWE-400/835, speculative): the loff while-loop relies on botline_forw(&loff) to advance loff.lnum; a misbehaving not-shown callee could stall the loop, but botline_forw's behavior is not characterizable from the given code.

If a producer outside this code delivered inconsistent state (e.g., w_cursor.lnum beyond ml_line_count or w_botline below topline), wrong scroll decisions could result, but no memory-unsafe use occurs within this code; the quoted loop guards ('lnum >= curbuf->b_ml.ml_line_count', 'lnum <= 0') bound every iteration regardless.

verdict.summary: getInfoForId performs an unvalidated map lookup on the attacker-controlled parameter id; when find() returns end(), the error arm only logs (STFATAL) with no quotable return/throw/exit, so the past-the-end iterator is dereferenced at 'return it->second;' — an out-of-bounds read that returns memory-adjacent garbage as a TerminalUserInfo (disclosure) or faults. Even if STFATAL aborts by convention, the same attacker-supplied unknown id causes an attacker-triggered fatal process abort (denial of service); the abort semantics are not shown in this code, so no guard on the not-found path is quotable.

evidence.reason: The failure-sentinel test for find() (line 3) is performed before the first use, but the error arm contains no return/throw/exit statement whose effect is quotable from this code, so control falls through to the dereference at line 6 with it == idInfoMap.end(). Trigger instantiated with attacker-data: any non-static-caller-supplied id absent from the map (e.g., an arbitrary or empty string) makes find() return end(), producing an out-of-bounds/invalid-iterator read at the sink and returning the garbage TerminalUserInfo to the caller.

assumptions: STFATAL is a macro whose definition is not shown; if it aborts (the common FATAL-logging convention), execution stops at line 4 and the realized impact of the same attacker trigger is a fatal process abort (denial of service) rather than the line-6 dereference. Because no statement in this code documents or enforces that abort, the error arm is treated as having no guard effect.
idInfoMap contents are never assigned in this code; the trigger does not depend on them, only on the attacker supplying an id that is not a key.
limitations: Callers of getInfoForId are not shown; per the entry-point rule the id parameter is treated as attacker-data. If a not-shown caller pre-validated ids against the map, reachability would depend on that unshown code, which cannot be used as a guard here.

If STFATAL provably terminates the process in the real build, the CWE-125 dereference is unreachable and the finding reduces to an attacker-triggered abort (CWE-20-class denial of service) with the same trigger and evidence lines.
No concurrent mutation of idInfoMap is shown, so no race candidate was instantiated.

verdict.summary: In _inplace_src_spans, a span with partial coverage (0 < coverage < 0xff) reaches the else branch, which writes len = spans[1].x - spans[0].x bytes into the fixed-size mask buffer (memset at line 85) with no bounds check on any path. The only length test, len >= r->u.composite.run_length, is ANDed with coverage == 0xff and thus never protects the partial-coverage arm, so attacker-controlled span coordinates produce a heap out-of-bounds write with attacker-chosen length and byte value (memory corruption).

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write (CWE-787): for any span with partial coverage this arm writes len = spans[1].x - spans[0].x attacker-controlled bytes into the mask buffer pointed to by m, with no bounds, clamp, or capacity check anywhere on the path. Trigger instantiated with spans = {{x=0, coverage=0x80},{x=100000000, coverage=0}}: line 83 writes one byte, then memset at line 85 writes 99,999,999 bytes of value 0x80 past the finite pixman mask buffer, corrupting the heap.

Origin of the tainted size: len is computed directly from attacker-controlled span coordinates (up to ~2^31-1). The only length guard in the function, len >= r->u.composite.run_length, is ANDed with spans[0].coverage == 0xff, so it applies solely to the full-coverage composite arm and never bounds the memset in the partial-coverage else arm.

assumptions: The exact capacity of r->mask is not assigned in this code (r->mask, r->u.composite.run_length, r->src, r->u.composite.dst, src_x, src_y are all UNSOURCED here); however, pixman_image_get_data returns a finite allocation fixed at image creation, and since len is unbounded in this code (int span coordinates), an attacker-chosen len exceeds any finite capacity — the overflow conclusion is independent of the exact size.

This is a non-static span-renderer callback; its spans/num_spans parameters carry content derived from rendered (potentially attacker-supplied) paths, so they are treated as attacker-data per the data-origin impact model.
pixman_image_composite32 calls are treated as characterizable library callees that clip to destination bounds; no defect is attributed at those call sites.
limitations: num_spans == 1 causes reads of spans[1] at line 15 (do-while body runs before the count test; the line 9 guard only excludes 0), a potential OOB read, but whether spans[1] lies outside the caller's allocation depends on the caller-side buffer size, which this code never assigns (UNSOURCED) — not counted as evidence.
Integer overflow of spans[1].x - spans[0].x (int subtraction) occurs only at extreme coordinate values and is subsumed by the primary path, which needs only a large positive len.
Accumulated walk-off of m across many small partial-coverage spans is the same missing-bounds defect as the primary finding and is covered by the same fix.

verdict.summary: dynamicGetbuf's read path is guarded: both branches bound rlen by remain = dp->logicalSize - dp->pos ('if (remain >= len) { rlen = len; }' and 'if (remain <= 0) { return EOF; } rlen = remain;'), so the memcpy at the sink reads within [dp->pos, dp->logicalSize) and returns EOF on exhaustion; edge cases (len==0, remain==0, remain<0, remain==len) are all handled. All identified defect candidates (negative len passed by an unseen caller yielding rlen<0 in memcpy, logicalSize exceeding the actual allocation, negative entry pos, NULL ctx/dp/data, undersized buf) depend on UNSOURCED preconditions with no producing or attacker-routing statement in this code, so none could be instantiated.

assumptions: dp->logicalSize, dp->data, and the entry value of dp->pos are initialized by context-creation code not shown in this snippet; analysis assumes the standard dynamic-ctx invariant that logicalSize does not exceed the allocated size of dp->data and pos starts at 0, but no statement in the given code enforces this.
len is assumed non-negative and consistent with the size of buf per the gdIOCtx getbuf interface convention; this contract is not documented, asserted, or checked anywhere in the given code.
ctx is assumed non-NULL and to point to a valid dpIOCtx whose dp field is valid; the cast at 'dctx = (dpIOCtxPtr) ctx;' is unchecked.
EOF is the standard -1 failure sentinel used by the surrounding io layer.
limitations: C1 (not confirmed): there is no 'if (len <= 0)' check anywhere in this code; in branch 'if (remain >= len) { rlen = len; }' a negative len (e.g., -1 with remain >= -1) is copied verbatim into rlen and then into memcpy's size_t parameter, causing a near-SIZE_MAX copy (OOB write into buf and OOB read of dp->data). Searched all fix forms (range check, clamp, mask, error arm on len) on every path: absent. Trigger precondition 'caller passes len < 0' is UNSOURCED: the function is static with no call site or callback registration shown, and no attacker data path to len exists in the given code, so it may not instantiate a finding; recorded as a hardening gap.

C2 (not confirmed): the memcpy bound is logicalSize, never an allocation-size field; if dp->logicalSize could exceed the allocated size of dp->data (invariant maintained in context-creation code not shown), the quoted rlen<=remain guard would still permit an out-of-bounds read. logicalSize has no assignment in this code (UNSOURCED), so the harmful value could not be instantiated.

C3 (not confirmed): a negative entry value of dp->pos would inflate remain and make the memcpy read before dp->data ('(char *) dp->data + dp->pos'); this code only advances pos ('dp->pos += rlen;' with rlen >= 0) and never checks or clamps its entry value, but no in-code or shown-caller producer of a negative pos exists.

C4 (not confirmed): 'dctx = (dpIOCtxPtr) ctx; dp = dctx->dp;' and the use of dp->data are unchecked NULL dereference sites if ctx, dctx->dp, or dp->data is NULL; no producer of such values appears in the given code.

C5 (not confirmed): if a caller passed a buf smaller than len, 'memcpy(buf, ..., rlen)' with rlen = len would write out of bounds; the buf/len size relation is an unquoted caller contract with no producer in this code.

verdict.summary: PipeSocketHandler::listen copies the attacker-supplied endpoint name into local.sun_path with strncpy using the full field size and no length validation, so a name of length >= sizeof(sun_path) (108) leaves sun_path without a NUL terminator; unlink(local.sun_path) and chmod(local.sun_path, 0700) then scan past the end of the sockaddr_un object on the stack (out-of-bounds read) and hand the garbage-terminated byte sequence, including leaked stack content, to destructive filesystem syscalls, or trip FATAL_FAIL and kill the service.

evidence.snippet:
strncpy(local.sun_path, pipePath.c_str(), sizeof(local.sun_path));
  unlink(local.sun_path);
evidence.reason: Root cause: strncpy with bound exactly sizeof(local.sun_path) writes no NUL when strlen(pipePath) >= 108, leaving sun_path non-terminated; the very next statement, unlink(local.sun_path), scans for a NUL past the end of the 110-byte sockaddr_un local (sun_path is its last member) into adjacent stack memory, an out-of-bounds read whose result is used as a filesystem path. The same non-terminated buffer is scanned again by chmod(local.sun_path, S_IRUSR|S_IWUSR|S_IXUSR) at line 21. No length check, clamp, truncation, or explicit terminator write exists on any path. Trigger: caller of this non-static handler passes endpoint.name() of length >= 108 (attacker-data parameter, line 4, unvalidated).

evidence.snippet: string pipePath = endpoint.name();
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: the endpoint name enters as a content-bearing parameter of this non-static member function and is stored with no length or content validation before being copied into the fixed 108-byte sun_path buffer at line 15.

assumptions: sizeof(local.sun_path) is 108 bytes on POSIX platforms (platform constant; the code itself only references sizeof(local.sun_path) and sizeof(sockaddr_un)).

FATAL_FAIL terminates the process on a non-negative-error sentinel of the wrapped call (its definition is not shown); the unlink at line 16 does not use it, so its out-of-bounds read occurs regardless.
initServerSocket(fd) is a not-shown callee; its return value is not consumed here.
limitations: TOCTOU/arbitrary-path unlink (CWE-367): unlink at line 16 runs unconditionally before bind, so a race exists between unlink and bind, and a caller-chosen path naming a victim file would be destroyed. The trigger requires an attacker able to plant or replace a filesystem object at the chosen path, a precondition no statement of this code instantiates, so it is not counted as a primary finding.
::listen(fd, 5) return value is unchecked, unlike the other syscalls; worst direct effect is a degraded listening socket with no memory corruption, bypass, or amplification, so it is robustness only.
The caller-visible path length is not bounded by this code; if an external caller enforced a shorter limit, the C1 trigger would not fire from that entry point, but no such bound can be quoted here.

verdict.summary: stl_remove_degenerate uses the int parameter facet to index stl->facet_start[facet] and stl->neighbors_start[facet] with no bounds check on any path. The only early-out, 'if (stl->error) return;', tests the error flag and does not constrain facet, and no range check, clamp, mask, checked accessor, or rejecting error arm exists anywhere in the function. As a non-static entry point whose index parameter is attacker-data (no documented or asserted range contract in the given code), any facet outside [0, facet_count) triggers an out-of-bounds read at the very first memcmp (lines 14-17), again at the later memcmps and the neighbors_start[facet] reads, and flows unvalidated into stl_remove_facet. Out-of-bounds write candidates via the stored neighbor/vnot fields were also identified but their trigger values have no producer in this code (UNSOURCED) and are recorded as limitations.

evidence.reason: First use in execution order of the unvalidated index parameter facet: the memcmp dereferences stl->facet_start[facet] with no bounds check anywhere on any path (the preceding 'if (stl->error) return;' does not test facet). Instantiated trigger: caller of the non-static function passes facet = N (one-past-limit), -1, or any out-of-range int; stl->error is clear; memcmp (characterizable standard callee) reads sizeof(stl_vertex) bytes out of bounds — an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) caused by missing index validation (CWE-129).

evidence.snippet: stl_remove_degenerate(stl_file *stl, int facet) {
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: the index facet enters here as an int parameter of a non-static function with no documented, asserted, or checked range contract anywhere in the given code, making it attacker-data per the intake rules; every subsequent facet_start[facet]/neighbors_start[facet] access and the stl_remove_facet(stl, facet) calls consume it unvalidated.

assumptions: The given code begins at the function name with no visible 'static' qualifier or return type, so the function is treated as non-static and its parameters as attacker-data per STEP 1; if a storage-class qualifier was trimmed, caller control would be a contract question, but no quotable contract exists either way.

Uncharacterizable callees: stl_remove_facet(stl, facet) at lines 22 and 69 receives the unvalidated facet, and stl_update_connects_remove_1(stl, neighborN) at lines 49, 52, 72 receives neighbor values checked only against -1; these are project functions whose behavior cannot be characterized from the given code, so in-callee out-of-bounds effects cannot be confirmed. Recorded as a limitation because the material impact of a caller-induced crash (denial of service across a trust boundary in a shared or higher-privileged process) requires deployment context that is an assumption per discipline 3 and cannot be quoted from the given code; the primary out-of-bounds-read finding stands independently.

verdict.summary: The DIE-parsing loop bound `i < abbrev->count - 1` underflows when abbrev->count == 0 (size_t wraps to SIZE_MAX). Because no check, clamp, mask, or error arm anywhere in the function rejects a zero count, the loop runs essentially unbounded, and the loop body performs out-of-bounds writes via memset(&die->attr_values[i], ...) and via parse_attr_value storing into &die->attr_values[i], plus an out-of-bounds read of &abbrev->defs[i]. A crafted binary whose abbreviation declaration carries a zero attribute count triggers heap corruption or a crash in the process parsing the file.

evidence.snippet:
for (i = 0; i < abbrev->count - 1; i++) {
		memset(&die->attr_values[i], 0, sizeof(die->attr_values[i]));
evidence.reason: Root cause: unsigned underflow in the loop bound. With abbrev->count == 0 (attacker-crafted DWARF abbreviation decoded from the parsed binary), `abbrev->count - 1` evaluates to SIZE_MAX, so the loop condition `0 < SIZE_MAX` is true and iterations continue past the capacity of die->attr_values. The memset on line 7 then writes out of bounds (as does parse_attr_value's store into &die->attr_values[i] on line 10, and &abbrev->defs[i] is read out of bounds on line 9). The trigger value abbrev->count == 0 is producible by the abbrev-section parser (not shown); the underflow and the absence of any guard in this function are fully verified from the given code.
limitations: Whether the unshown abbrev parser can actually emit count == 0 could not be quoted from the given code; if it provably guarantees count >= 1 (e.g., by always counting a sentinel entry), the underflow trigger would be speculative. The absence of any guard in this function remains a verified defect.
buf_end - buf (line 9) could underflow to a huge size_t if the unshown parse_attr_value ever advances buf past buf_end; no producer of buf > buf_end is visible in this code.

strdup(comp_dir) on line 30 relies on the unshown parse_attr_value to guarantee NUL termination of DW_FORM_string content within the section; a non-terminated string would cause an OOB read in strdup, but the producer is not in this code.

verdict.summary: copy_page_to_iter_pipe reuses a pipe_buffer ring slot and reinitializes it for a page-cache-backed buffer (setting ops, page, offset, len) but never resets buf->flags. A stale PIPE_BUF_FLAG_CAN_MERGE value left by a previous anonymous-pipe-write buffer survives on the published page-cache buffer, so the standard pipe write path later merges attacker-controlled data directly into the read-only page-cache page of the spliced file. This is the Dirty Pipe vulnerability (CVE-2022-0847), fixed upstream by adding buf->flags = 0 at exactly this site.

evidence.reason: This reinitialization sequence converts a reused pipe_buffer slot into a page-cache-backed buffer and publishes it (line 41: pipe->head = i_head + 1), yet never assigns, clears, or checks buf->flags anywhere in the function. The slot may previously have held an anonymous pipe-write buffer whose flags included PIPE_BUF_FLAG_CAN_MERGE; that stale value persists on the page-cache buffer. Trigger: attacker (1) fills a pipe via a normal write, (2) drains it so tail advances while the slot retains CAN_MERGE, (3) splices a target file into the pipe so this function publishes a page-cache buffer carrying the stale merge flag, (4) writes to the pipe, and the pipe write path merges attacker data into the read-only page-cache page, allowing modification of arbitrary readable files.

evidence.snippet: buf = &pipe->bufs[i_head & p_mask];
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted slot: the function selects a ring slot by index mask and reuses it without any statement that scrubs or resets the slot's prior contents beyond the four fields set at lines 35-39, so buf->flags retains leftover data from the slot's previous occupant (CWE-457, leftover value in reused memory reaching a security decision).

assumptions: sanity(i) (line 17) and pipe_full() (line 32) are called but their bodies are not shown; they were credited only as opaque pass/fail checks and not as validating any buffer field.

The only potential guard, STFATAL aborting the process, is not defined in the given code and therefore cannot be relied on.

Trigger: any caller-supplied id (attacker-data parameter of a non-static method) absent from idInfoMap makes find return end() (produced by line 3), and the dereference reads past the container's valid elements — out-of-bounds read / UB, crash or garbage data returned.

If it aborts or throws (as FATAL-level logging commonly does, e.g., glog LOG(FATAL)), the miss path never reaches line 7 and the code would be safe. Per the guard-anchoring discipline this unquotable behavior is not treated as a guard; it is recorded here instead.

idInfoMap population/erasure and the callers of getInfoForId are not shown; the id parameter is classified as attacker-data per discipline 3. The log text itself ("an id that no longer exists") indicates missing ids are an anticipated case.
limitations: idInfoMap is UNSOURCED in this code (no assignment shown); the trigger does not depend on its content because any finite map, including an empty one, yields a find-miss for some attacker-chosen id.

The precise memory effect of dereferencing end() (reading the container's end/header node vs. other undefined behavior) depends on the standard library implementation; downstream consumption of the returned garbage TerminalUserInfo is not shown and no claim is made about it.

verdict.summary: In the R_DYLDCACHE_FILTER path of create_cache_bins, the dependency-walk loop reads depArray with an unbounded index k (initialized from the file-parsed extras[j].dependentsStartArrayIndex and incremented with no upper bound; termination depends only on the file-controlled 0xffff sentinel, which the attacker can simply omit from the in-bounds array), causing out-of-bounds reads of depArray. Each read entry is masked with & 0x7fff and used directly as an index into deps (sized cache->hdr->imagesCount, itself file-controlled) at deps[dep_index]++ and into img at &img[dep_index], with no range check anywhere on any path. A malicious dyld cache file therefore yields attacker-chosen-offset heap out-of-bounds writes (increments) and reads. Additionally, deps is sized from hdr[0].imagesCount (line 19) but indexed with j < hdr->imagesCount of every sub-cache header, a further mismatch for n_hdr > 1.

evidence.reason: Sink of the primary defect. k starts at the file-parsed extras[j].dependentsStartArrayIndex and is incremented with no bound against cache->accel->depListCount (OOB read of depArray when the file omits any 0xffff sentinel), and dep_index (file value masked to at most 0x7fff) is used to index deps with no check against the array's size — heap out-of-bounds write at deps[dep_index]++ with attacker-chosen offset. Trigger simulated: imagesCount=1 (4-byte deps), depListCount=4, depArray={0x0005,...} with no 0xffff → k walks past the 8-byte depArray and deps[5]++ (or deps[0x7fff]++ for value 0x7fff) writes far past the allocation.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted data: depArray is filled directly from the untrusted dyld cache file, so both the loop's termination sentinel (0xffff) and the index values consumed at lines 79-81 are attacker-controlled; the return-value check only verifies the read length, not the content or any index bound.

evidence.snippet: deps = R_NEWS0 (int, cache->hdr->imagesCount);
evidence.reason: The write target bound that dep_index (up to 0x7fff from line 80) is never checked against: deps holds cache->hdr->imagesCount (hdr[0]) ints, a file-controlled count with no relation to the depArray values. It is also the source of the secondary mismatch: later loop iterations index deps[j] with j < hdr->imagesCount of each sub-cache header, with no statement constraining hdr[i].imagesCount to hdr[0].imagesCount.

assumptions: cache->buf, cache->hdr, cache->accel, cache->n_hdr and cache->maps are populated by not-shown parsing of the dyld cache file; per the data-origin model they are treated as attacker-data, not trusted state.

The confirmed trigger was deliberately re-instantiated without depending on any unshown validation inside these callees (k=0 start plus sentinel-free file content suffices).
The code runs when the operator sets R_DYLDCACHE_FILTER; the malicious input is the parsed cache file, and this function is the intake point for that file data.
limitations: Uninitialized magicbytes: r_buf_read_at (cache->buf, pa, magicbytes, 4) has its return value ignored; if the read fails, r_read_le32 consumes uninitialized stack bytes. Speculative because va2pa's bound behavior (whether pa always lies within readable buffer range) is not shown, so a failing 4-byte read could not be exhibited concretely.

The deps[j] sizing mismatch across sub-caches (line 19 vs lines 58/103) is instantiable only when n_hdr > 1 with hdr[i].imagesCount > hdr[0].imagesCount; it is subsumed by the same missing-bounds class as the primary finding.

verdict.summary: Stack buffer overflow in the BMP v4/v5 header path: when the file-supplied biSize is 108 or 124, ReadOK(fd, buffer, Bitmap_File_Head.biSize - 4) reads 104 or 120 bytes into the 64-byte stack array 'buffer' (declared as unsigned char buffer[64]), writing 40-56 bytes of attacker-controlled file content past the end of the buffer. No bounds check, clamp, or larger buffer exists on any path to this read.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds stack write (CWE-787). The destination 'buffer' is declared at line 4 as 'unsigned char buffer[64];' but the attacker-controlled biSize (108 or 124, parsed from the file) makes this ReadOK read biSize - 4 = 104 or 120 bytes into it, overflowing the 64-byte stack buffer by up to 56 bytes with attacker-controlled file content. Trigger fully instantiated: file with 'BM' magick, biSize field = 108 reaches this branch; no check, clamp, mask, alternate buffer, or error arm anywhere on the path bounds the read size against sizeof(buffer).

evidence.snippet: Bitmap_File_Head.biSize = ToL(&buffer[0x00]);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted size value: biSize is parsed directly from the input file's header (4 bytes read from fd at line 68), and its value (108 or 124) selects the overflowing read length 'Bitmap_File_Head.biSize - 4' consumed at line 194.

assumptions: ReadOK behaves as a file-read helper that reads its size argument's bytes into the destination buffer, inferred from its consistent usage (ReadOK(fd, magick, 2), ReadOK(fd, buffer, 12), etc.) and characterizable read-function semantics.

The struct types/widths of Bitmap_Head and Bitmap_File_Head fields are not shown; ToL/ToS return widths are unknown, but the overflow finding does not depend on them (104 and 120 exceed 64 for any width).
Deployment context (how the BMP file reaches this function) is not evidenced in the code; the file content consumed at this function's own entry point is treated as attacker-data.
limitations: fclose(NULL) on failed fopen: line 16 'if (!fd)' leads to 'goto cleanup' (line 19) and 'fclose(fd);' with fd == NULL (undefined behavior, likely crash). Whether line 352 executes depends on whether at_exception_fatal (line 18) returns or longjmps out before the goto; that callee is not shown and not characterizable, so the trigger is not fully instantiated.

ColormapSize can be negative: 'ColormapSize = (Bitmap_File_Head.bfOffs - Bitmap_File_Head.biSize - 14) / Maps;' (line 253) has an upper clamp ('if (ColormapSize > 256) ColormapSize = 256;') but no lower bound, and a negative value can be passed to ReadColorMap (line 334). ReadColorMap is not shown; its handling of a negative count cannot be characterized, so impact is not instantiated.

How ReadImage consumes masks is not shown, so the impact of the uninitialized read is not instantiated (CWE-457 potential).

at_bitmap_init at line 350 truncates biWidth/biHeight (guarded to be up to 0x7fffffff / biBitCnt) to unsigned short, creating a metadata/storage size mismatch whose effect depends on the not-shown at_bitmap_init and downstream consumers.
