The only absent checks (sq_reservestack return value, thread-state validation) could not be triggered to a security consequence from the given code: the former requires attacker-uninducible allocation failure, and the latter's impact depends entirely on unshown sq_call/SQVM internals, so no primary candidate survives.

assumptions: stack_get(v,1) and nparams = sq_gettop(v) >= 1 are assumed valid because native delegate methods are invoked by the VM's calling protocol with 'this' at slot 1; this protocol is not quotable from the given code.

The target thread's stack slot 0 is assumed to hold the closure placed at thread creation (newthread contract) and sq_call's layout (closure at -(params+1), stackbase = _top - params, params counting 'this' plus arguments) is relied on as characterizable framework semantics per the callee boundary rule.
_thread(o)->_roottable, _thread(o)->_lasterror and v->_lasterror are state fields never assigned in this code; they are only read/copied and never used as bounds, indices, or sizes.
limitations: The return value of sq_reservestack (line 6) is not checked; exploitation would require an allocation failure inside the callee that no attacker input can deterministically induce, and the push API's own growth behavior is not shown.

No thread-state check exists before sq_call: calling 'call' on a suspended thread makes sq_call fetch its closure slot from the suspended frame region, an arbitrary stack slot. Whether that yields anything beyond a VM-level error or a type-safe dynamic call is decided entirely inside unshown SQVM::Call/StartCall code (parameter-count validation, stack resize), so no memory-safety or bypass impact can be instantiated here.

Whether nparams+3 suffices for the callee's own execution frame (func->_stacksize) during sq_call is decided inside SQVM::Execute/StartCall, which is not given; this code's own pushes (exactly nparams) fit its own reservation with margin 3.

A hypothetical caller invoking this static function with an empty v stack would make stack_get(v,1) read out of bounds, but the only caller is the VM's native-dispatch protocol, which by documented semantics always supplies slot 1; this contract is not quotable in the given code.

verdict.summary: In mobi_parse_index_entry, the raw pointer control_bytes (initialized to buf->data + buf->offset) is advanced once per TAGX entry with control_byte == 1 (control_bytes++) and dereferenced (control_bytes[0]) with no bounds check against the buffer, on any path. The number of advances is bounded only by tagx->tags_count, an attacker-controlled count from the parsed MOBI file, so a crafted INDX/TAGX record whose entry label ends at the end of the record buffer makes control_bytes[0] read arbitrarily far past the heap allocation (at least one byte past with a single leading control tag). The out-of-bounds byte is used in control flow (value != 0), stored into parsed index tag values, and can crash the process: heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: Root cause: control_bytes is advanced by one byte for every attacker-controlled tag entry with control_byte == 1, with no comparison against buf->data + buf->maxlen or any other bound, and then dereferenced at control_bytes[0]. Instantiated trigger: file-supplied idxt.offsets place the entry so that buf->offset + entry_length == buf_maxlen - 1 (passes the line 16 check), the file-supplied label byte makes the label consume the whole entry (line 22 check is '>', so label_length == entry_length - 1 passes), so buf->offset reaches buf_maxlen - 1; a TAGX record whose first tag has control_byte == 1 and second has control_byte != 1 then reads data[buf_maxlen] — one byte past the buffer — and K leading control tags read data + buf_maxlen - 1 + K for any file-chosen K up to tags_count. The loop bound 'while (i < tagx->tags_count)' caps nothing relative to the buffer, and no check, clamp, mask, or error arm touches control_bytes anywhere between its initialization and the dereference.

evidence.snippet:
control_bytes = buf->data + buf->offset;
    mobi_buffer_seek(buf, (int) tagx->control_byte_count);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted pointer: control_bytes is captured as a raw pointer (buf->data + buf->offset) that bypasses the bounds-checked MOBIBuffer accessors, and the subsequent mobi_buffer_seek advances only buf->offset while leaving control_bytes unclamped and unchecked relative to the buffer; all later advancement of control_bytes is the unbounded control_bytes++ in the tag loop.

assumptions: This function is part of a MOBI-file parser; the structs indx (entries_count, total_entries_count, ligt_entries_count), idxt (offsets[]), tagx (tags_count, tags[], control_byte_count), ordt, and the MOBIBuffer contents are populated by earlier parsing of the attacker-supplied file, so their content fields are classified attacker-data. No statement in the given code assigns them.

buf->data is a finite heap allocation whose size is at least the record length buf->maxlen saved at line 15; the exact allocation size is not shown, but it is irrelevant because the number of control_bytes advances is unbounded (up to tagx->tags_count).

The buffer helpers mobi_buffer_get8, mobi_buffer_setpos, mobi_buffer_seek, mobi_buffer_get_varlen are assumed to enforce buf->maxlen internally (they are the bounded accessors this code otherwise relies on); control_bytes bypasses them, which is the defect.
INDX_LABEL_SIZEMAX, INDX_TAGVALUES_MAX, and MOBI_NOTSET are compile-time constants; the numeric value of INDX_LABEL_SIZEMAX is not quotable from the given code.
limitations: Lines 29/31 reassign label_length from the returns of mobi_getstring_ordt / mobi_indx_get_label without re-clamping it against sizeof(text) (INDX_LABEL_SIZEMAX, line 26) before strncpy reads label_length + 1 bytes from text (line 38). If either helper can return a length larger than INDX_LABEL_SIZEMAX (e.g., UTF-8 expansion in the ORDT path), this is a stack out-of-bounds read copied into the heap label; the helpers' behavior is not characterizable from the given code, so this is not confirmed.

Line 7 indexes idxt.offsets[curr_number + 1] with no check in this code that curr_number + 1 is within the offsets array; the array's size and the caller's loop bound are not shown and the code's own flow produces no out-of-range curr_number, so an out-of-bounds offsets read is not instantiated here.

malloc(tagx->tags_count * sizeof(MOBIPtagx)) (line 52) and malloc(tagx->tags_count * sizeof(MOBIIndexTag)) (line 82) could overflow the size multiplication only for tags_count near SIZE_MAX / sizeof(...); the declared width of tags_count is not quotable here, so this is speculative.

text[INDX_LABEL_SIZEMAX] may be partially uninitialized when strncpy copies label_length + 1 bytes (line 38) if the label helpers write fewer bytes than the copy length; the resulting uninitialized stack bytes would flow into the stored label (CWE-457/CWE-908), but the copy length equals the helper's own return, so this depends on unshown helper behavior.

The unsorted-offsets underflow at line 7 (idxt.offsets[curr_number + 1] - idxt.offsets[curr_number] wrapping) is neutralized in this code: the line 16 check tests the same expression that is assigned to buf->maxlen at line 20, so buf->maxlen never exceeds buf_maxlen - 1 and all helper reads remain in-bounds.

Several early error returns (e.g., lines 36, 55) leave buf->maxlen at the reduced entry value instead of restoring buf_maxlen; the reduced value is always smaller than the original, so no out-of-bounds access results, only a parse-state inconsistency for the caller.

verdict.summary: st21nfca_connectivity_event_received() parses the controller-supplied EVT_TRANSACTION frame without validating its fields. The only sanity check uses && instead of ||, so short frames with the AID tag 0x81 pass. The transaction object is allocated as skb->len - 2 bytes (never accounting for the fixed struct header or the parameters), and two memcpy calls use lengths read directly from the frame (aid_len = skb->data[1], params_len = skb->data[aid_len + 3], each up to 255) with no bound against the aid[] array, the allocation, or skb->len. A 7-byte frame with data[1]=0xFF makes memcpy write 255 bytes into a 5-byte heap allocation, a kernel heap out-of-bounds write with attacker-chosen length and partially attacker-controlled content; the params memcpy overflows for any spec-compliant frame as well. OOB reads of skb (aid_len+2, aid_len+3 indices, and both memcpy sources) accompany the writes.

verdict.summary: In gopherToHTML, the line-length guard clamps gopherState->len + llen to at most TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1, but the terminator write uses index llen+1: when a gopher server sends a line whose accumulated length equals exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 (attacker fully controls line lengths in the socket-read response), the statement line[llen + 1] = '\0' writes one NUL byte past the end of the TEMP_BUF_SIZE buffer 'line' (and the gopherState->buf spill path makes the state length code-assigned, so the trigger needs no unsourced state). Additionally, the unescaped 'host' (and embedded ':port') string from the server response is inserted raw into the generated HREF HTML (gopher://%s/ and http://%s/ links) while name and selector are escaped, allowing the malicious gopher origin to inject arbitrary HTML/script into the page served to the browsing client. Primary defect: off-by-one out-of-bounds write (CWE-787).

evidence.reason: This is the only bound on llen: it fires only at >= TEMP_BUF_SIZE, so it admits gopherState->len + llen == TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1 (and its clamp itself yields post-increment llen == TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1). The origin of the faulty value: it bounds the memcpy length to TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 but the subsequent terminator write consumes llen + 1, reaching index TEMP_BUF_SIZE.

Off-by-one out-of-bounds write (root cause). llen is attacker-chosen (gopher server response line length); after 'llen += gopherState->len' it can equal exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1 (e.g., call 1 leaves a 1-byte partial line in gopherState->buf via lines 85-86, call 2 supplies a TEMP_BUF_SIZE-2 byte line ending in '\n' so the guard at line 77 does not fire). The memcpys then write TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 in-bounds bytes, but 'line[llen + 1]' writes the NUL terminator at line[TEMP_BUF_SIZE], one element past the array declared 'LOCAL_ARRAY(char, line, TEMP_BUF_SIZE)'. No check, clamp, mask, or error arm anywhere in the function bounds the index llen + 1.

evidence.snippet: snprintf(tmpbuf, TEMP_BUF_SIZE, " %s\n", icon_url, host, gtype, escaped_selector, html_quote(name));
evidence.reason: HTML injection (CWE-79) into the proxy-generated menu page. 'host' is raw server-response data (all bytes except TAB/NUL allowed; after port[0]=':' it also embeds the port text) and is inserted into the HREF attribute with no html_quote or rfc1738 escaping, while 'name' is html_quote'd and 'selector' escaped; a malicious gopher server can send a menu line whose host field is \"><script>...</script> to inject arbitrary markup/script that is appended to the client response via outbuf.append(tmpbuf) and entry->append/flush. The telnet branch at lines 224/228 applies rfc1738_escape_part(host), proving this path's omission is a defect.

assumptions: gopherState fields not assigned in this code (entry, conversion, buf and its allocated size, the initial value of len, HTML_header_added, cso_recno) are initialized by the GopherStateData constructor/setup not shown; in particular gopherState->buf is assumed to hold at least TEMP_BUF_SIZE bytes and len is assumed to start at 0.

LOCAL_ARRAY(char, line, TEMP_BUF_SIZE) declares a fixed array of exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE chars (stack or static per the macro definition outside this code); TEMP_BUF_SIZE is a positive constant used consistently for both the array size and the guard bound.
inbuf/len carry the gopher server's socket response read by the surrounding gopher state machine (untrusted origin per discipline 3); this function is the decode/render boundary for that data.
limitations: If the UNSOURCED initial value of gopherState->len could ever be >= TEMP_BUF_SIZE, the clamp at line 79 would produce a negative llen and a length-converted memcpy at lines 91-92; this code's own statements keep every assigned len value <= TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1, so that variant is speculative and not counted.

The practical impact of the one-byte NUL write depends on the LOCAL_ARRAY storage class (static vs stack) and adjacent object placement, which are not visible in the given code; the write itself is out-of-bounds regardless.

The stale byte at line[llen] (terminator written at llen+1) can fold one leftover byte of a previous, longer line from the same server into the parsed port text; this is same-origin data reuse, not a cross-trust-boundary disclosure, so it is not counted as a finding.
The port[1]/port[2] reads at line 151 stay within the line buffer (indices <= llen+1) and at worst read the same stale byte; no out-of-bounds read is instantiated.
snprintf truncation of tmpbuf on long fields causes loss/truncation of rendered link data only; not a security effect.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write in the octet-counting framing parser: every received digit byte is stored with `*(pThis->pMsg + pThis->iMsg++) = c;` (line 42) with no bound on iMsg. The only guard on that path, `if(pThis->iOctetsRemain <= 200000000)` (line 33), bounds the accumulated count value, not the number of digit writes; leading '0' bytes keep iOctetsRemain at 0 forever, so a remote sender can drive iMsg arbitrarily far past the iMaxLine pMsg domain that this code itself enforces everywhere else (lines 102, 113-115), corrupting heap memory with attacker-chosen length.

evidence.snippet: *(pThis->pMsg + pThis->iMsg++) = c;
evidence.reason: Root cause: unbounded write into pMsg in the octet-counter digit state. The only check on this path is line 33 `if(pThis->iOctetsRemain <= 200000000)`, which bounds the accumulated count, not iMsg; the error arm (lines 35-40) also falls through to this write. Instantiated trigger: attacker sends N leading '0' bytes in octet-counted framing; each keeps iOctetsRemain = 0 (line 34), passes the line-33 check, and executes this write with iMsg = 0..N-1, so for N > iMaxLine the writes at indices iMaxLine..N-1 are out of bounds (the iMaxLine domain is enforced by this code's own guards at lines 102 and 113-115).

evidence.snippet: char c = **buff;
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: the first byte of the received TCP buffer (the code's own strings, e.g., line 36 "Framing Error in received TCP message:", establish this as received network data), which flows through isdigit at lines 14/32 into the unbounded pMsg write at line 42.

assumptions: pThis->pMsg is allocated outside this code; its safe domain is taken as iMaxLine because this code's own statements enforce iMsg < iMaxLine for every other pMsg access (lines 102, 113-115) — the allocation size itself is not shown.
The trigger requires pThis->bSuppOctetFram to be enabled (line 14); this flag is set outside this code, but octet-counted framing is a primary supported mode the state machine here fully implements.
iMaxLine is a global configuration constant never assigned in this code; any positive value leaves the leading-zero overflow exploitable, since the digit count is bounded by nothing.
buffLen is produced by the caller (network read length) and is assumed to accurately describe *buff; the digit-path defect does not depend on it.
limitations: Signed overflow of `octatesToCopy + pThis->iMsg` (line 112) could skip the clamp and cause a huge memcpy, but it requires a single receive buffer of ~2e9 bytes and an iMaxLine above ~147,000,000 — neither value is sourced anywhere in this code (UNSOURCED: buffLen bound, iMaxLine value); speculative.
doSubmitMsg (lines 81, 93, 124) is not shown; its effect on iMsg cannot be quoted, but the guarded write at line 102 and the reset at line 64 make no finding depend on it.

verdict.summary: Array.prototype.splice captures the object's length once (line 16), then performs argument conversion (njs_value_to_integer) which invokes attacker-supplied valueOf code that can shrink the receiver array mid-call. start and delete are clamped only against the stale length (lines 26, 42), so in the fast-array path the memcpy at lines 115-118 writes items elements at &array->start[start] beyond the array's real capacity, a heap out-of-bounds write with attacker-controlled njs_value_t content; the preceding njs_array_copy_within call (lines 104-105) likewise receives to/from indices beyond array->length and a negative count.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink. start is clamped only against the stale length captured before the conversions (line 26), while the buffer guarantee comes from njs_array_expand(vm, array, 0, delta) sized from the fresh array->length, not from start+items. Trigger: arr of length 10; arr.splice({valueOf(){ arr.length = 2; return 10; }}, 0, v1, v2) gives start=10, delete=0, items=2, delta=2; expand ensures capacity for 2+2=4 elements while existing capacity is at most 10, then memcpy writes slots 10-11 past the end of the allocation with attacker-supplied values.

Origin of the taint. length was read from this at line 16 before this call, but njs_value_to_integer performs ToPrimitive and runs attacker-controlled valueOf/toString that can shrink or mutate the receiver array; the subsequent clamp njs_min(start, length) and the delete clamp (line 42) use the stale length, so start/delete can exceed the array's actual internal length and are then used for raw memory operations (lines 61-63, 104-105, 115-118) with no re-validation anywhere in the function.

assumptions: njs_value_to_integer invokes ToPrimitive (valueOf/toString) for object arguments, per standard ECMAScript conversion semantics relied on under the callee boundary rule; this is the reentrancy vector.
njs_object_length is assumed to set *length on all non-error returns (implementation not shown); the given code checks only ret == NJS_ERROR at line 17.

Shrinking a fast array's length (arr.length = 2 in the valueOf) is assumed to keep its fast_array status and either preserve or shrink its capacity; the OOB write at the memcpy holds under both capacity behaviors, but if the array lost fast-array status the property-based slow path would be taken instead.

njs_array_copy_within with a negative count is assumed to perform a count-bounded copy loop (no iterations, returns NJS_OK); if it is memmove-based, the call at lines 104-105 itself faults with a huge size, which is still a memory-safety failure at this call site; if it returned an error, the function would return before the memcpy.

verdict.summary: st21nfca_connectivity_event_received parses the device-sourced EVT_TRANSACTION skb and allocates the destination with devm_kzalloc(dev, skb->len - 2, GFP_KERNEL), a size that excludes struct nfc_evt_transaction's fixed members and is never tied to the aid_len/params_len values later copied. The initial validation is a fail-open conjunction (skb->len < NFC_MIN_AID_LENGTH + 2 && skb->data[0] != NFC_EVT_TRANSACTION_AID_TAG), so a 7-byte frame with data[1]=16 passes and memcpy(transaction->aid, &skb->data[2], 16) writes 16 bytes into a 5-byte heap allocation (15-byte kernel OOB write). The params bound (skb->len - 2) - sizeof(struct nfc_evt_transaction) underflows unsigned whenever skb->len < 23, so params_len up to 255 is memcpy'd at struct offset into the undersized allocation, yielding an attacker-length, attacker-content kernel heap overflow plus OOB reads of the skb.

evidence.snippet:
memcpy(transaction->aid, &skb->data[2],

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds WRITE sink: aid_len (up to 16, taken from attacker byte skb->data[1] and bounded only against sizeof(transaction->aid), never against skb->len or the skb->len - 2 allocation) is copied into transaction->aid at struct offset 4. Instantiated trigger: skb->len = 7, data[1] = 0x10 → allocation of 5 bytes at line 26, aid_len = 16 passes the line-33 check, memcpy writes p[4..19] — a 15-byte kernel heap overflow with attacker-controlled bytes, plus an 11-byte OOB read of the skb.

evidence.snippet: transaction = devm_kzalloc(dev, skb->len - 2, GFP_KERNEL);
evidence.reason: Origin of the faulty value (CWE-131 buffer size miscalculation): the transaction buffer is sized solely from attacker-controlled skb->len - 2, excluding sizeof(struct nfc_evt_transaction)'s fixed members (~21 bytes: aid_len, aid[16], params_len) that lines 30, 36, 44 and 50 write. The comment at line 46 ('Total size is allocated (skb->len - 2) minus fixed array members') shows the author believed the allocation included them. For any skb->len < 23 the struct writes exceed the allocation.

Fail-open bound via unsigned underflow: when skb->len - 2 < sizeof(struct nfc_evt_transaction) (e.g. skb->len = 20 → 18 - 21 wraps to 2^64-3 in size_t), the check never rejects, so params_len (up to 255, read from attacker byte data[aid_len+3] at line 44) is memcpy'd at struct offset ~21 into the skb->len - 2 allocation. Instantiated trigger: skb->len = 20, aid_len = 16, data[18] = 0x82, data[19] = 200 → ~200 attacker-controlled bytes written past an 18-byte heap allocation, plus a 200-byte OOB read of the skb.

Missing-check site (fail-open validation): the conjunction rejects only frames that are BOTH shorter than 7 bytes AND mistagged. Edge values: skb->len = 7 (exactly at limit) passes with any tag; skb->len = 2 with data[0] = 0x81 passes, yielding a 0-byte allocation whose fixed-member writes at lines 30/36/44 immediately overflow. The required guard was '||' plus a length bound tying aid_len/params_len to skb->len; no such form exists anywhere on any path.

assumptions: skb->len and skb->data[] are device-sourced (HCI EVT_TRANSACTION frame from the ST21NFCA controller) delivered to this handler callback; per the data-origin impact model they are attacker-data and this function is the intake/validation point.

struct nfc_evt_transaction layout is not shown in the given code; the canonical kernel definition (include/net/nfc.h: u32 aid_len; u8 aid[16]; u8 params_len; u8 params[]; __packed, sizeof = 21) is assumed. The primary aid-memcpy finding is layout-independent (allocation of 5 bytes vs. at least 17 bytes of struct writes); only the exact underflow threshold of the second finding (sizeof >= 19) depends on it, and the code's own usage (aid_len <= sizeof(aid) with 16-byte copies, plus aid_len and params_len fields) bounds sizeof >= 18.
devm_kzalloc semantics: devres allocates sizeof(struct devres) + size from the slab and returns a valid non-NULL pointer for small sizes including 0; failure returns NULL and is tested at line 27.
NFC_MIN_AID_LENGTH = 5, NFC_EVT_TRANSACTION_AID_TAG = 0x81, NFC_EVT_TRANSACTION_PARAMS_TAG = 0x82, NFC_MAX_AID_LENGTH = 16 (external constants used as comparators).
limitations: skb->len < 2 makes skb->len - 2 wrap to ~4 GiB at line 26; devm_kzalloc then fails and the quoted NULL check at lines 27-28 returns -ENOMEM, so this path yields no corruption.
skb->data[0] is read at line 23 even when skb->len = 0 (1-byte read into skb tailroom); folded into the fail-open gate finding rather than a separate OOB-read verdict.

Behavior of the not-shown callee nfc_se_transaction with the corrupted transaction is not characterized; the impact (heap OOB write) completes at the memcpys in this code, so the chain does not depend on it.

Every successful EVT_TRANSACTION permanently retains sizeof(struct devres) + skb->len - 2 bytes in devres until device removal (no devm_kfree exists), and skb is leaked on the early-return paths at lines 24, 28, 34, 42 and 48 — attacker-scalable memory retention (CWE-400-class), secondary to the confirmed out-of-bounds writes.
Precise heap-exploitation consequences (which adjacent devres/slab objects are corrupted) are environment-dependent; the corruption primitive itself is fully instantiated.

verdict.summary: No security vulnerability found. The mb_ptr2len loop advances an index to the terminating NUL and breaks safely; lbr_chartabsize's returned width is only applied on the next iteration when not already at the NUL; the temporary space-buffer write is protected by an explicit NULL check and a non-negative width; and cursor positioning, backspace counting, and Replace-stack adjustments all remain consistent with the actual line length.

assumptions: Assumed the lbr_chartabsize helper returns the screen width of the current character, and mb_ptr2len returns its byte length including the NUL terminator; both are consistent with how the loop indexes the buffer.
Assumed alloc returns a NULL-terminated temporary buffer of the requested size, which the code then uses only for temporary space insertion.
limitations: Unchecked arithmetic like `Insstart.col -= insstart_less` could in principle make Insstart.col negative or beyond line length, but the surrounding conditions bound the values, and no observable out-of-bounds effect was traced.

The Replace-stack push loop `while (start_col < (int)curwin->w_cursor.col || replaced)` relies on replaced being cleared after one push; this affects only Replace-stack sizing, not memory safety, and was not traced further.

verdict.summary: The statusline redraw appends flags to the fixed MAXPATHL-byte global NameBuff without any capacity check: when the buffer name is exactly MAXPATHL-1 bytes, the raw append `*(p + len++) = ' '` overwrites the sole NUL terminator and pushes len to MAXPATHL. The following `vim_snprintf(p + len, MAXPATHL - len, ...)` receives size 0 (writes nothing, no re-termination), and `len += (int)STRLEN(p + len)` then reads past the end of NameBuff — an out-of-bounds read of adjacent global memory whose content is rendered on the status line by screen_puts; with the corrupted len, the truncation `*p = '<'` can additionally write out of bounds depending on adjacent memory layout. Trigger: an attacker-influenced buffer/file name of exactly 1023 bytes (e.g., a planted read-only file, making b_p_ro true) opened in a window drawn through the plain statusline path.

evidence.reason: Origin / missing-check site: an unbounded manual append into the fixed global buffer NameBuff. When len == MAXPATHL-1 (buffer name exactly fills the array), this statement overwrites the sole NUL terminator and increments len to MAXPATHL; no bounds check, clamp, or re-termination exists on any path (the MAXPATHL-len snprintf sizes at 57/63/73/78 do not guard this write).

evidence.snippet:
vim_snprintf((char *)p + len, MAXPATHL - len, "%s", "[+]");
	    len += (int)STRLEN(p + len);
evidence.reason: Sink: instantiated trigger (1023-byte modified buffer name, bufIsChanged true) reaches line 73 with len == MAXPATHL, where vim_snprintf gets size MAXPATHL - len == 0 and writes nothing, leaving the string unterminated past index MAXPATHL-1; line 74's STRLEN(p + len) then reads from NameBuff + MAXPATHL, one past the end of the char_u[MAXPATHL] global — out-of-bounds read whose length corrupts len and whose unterminated content is later displayed by screen_puts(p, ...) at line 118. Equivalent sinks at lines 58/64/79.

assumptions: NameBuff is the fixed-size global char_u NameBuff[MAXPATHL] with MAXPATHL = 1024; the code's own sizing expressions `MAXPATHL - len` (lines 57/63/73/78) evidence the intended capacity invariant len < MAXPATHL.

get_trans_bufname() (not shown) fills NameBuff with the buffer's NUL-terminated translated file name and does not truncate a 1023-byte path; a full path of exactly MAXPATHL-1 bytes is constructible on common OSes (PATH_MAX 4096 on Linux), so len == MAXPATHL-1 at line 46 is reachable.

vim_snprintf follows snprintf semantics: with size 0 it writes nothing (no NUL is added); if this Vim-internal emulation instead wrote a truncation NUL at str[0], the call at line 73/78 would itself be a one-past-end write — defective either way.
ru_col, Columns, has_mbyte, p_stl are globals with no assignment in this code (UNSOURCED); the analysis does not rely on their values.
limitations: OOB-write escalation at lines 105-106 / 113-114 (`*p = '<'`): requires the first NUL past NameBuff to lie at least this_ru_col-1 bytes beyond the array end — adjacent-global memory layout is not characterizable from this code, so only the out-of-bounds reads are confirmed as layout-independent impact (same root defect).

If get_trans_bufname can write more than MAXPATHL bytes for names longer than 1023 bytes, that overflow occurs inside the unshown callee; line 46's STRLEN would then already read out of bounds, but the producer is not shown.
Pathological negative ru_col (UNSOURCED global) could produce negative screen_fill end columns at line 119-120; depends on unshown clamping inside screen_fill.
Trigger requires a buffer name of exactly MAXPATHL-1 bytes; names of MAXPATHL-2 bytes were verified safe at the boundary (space at index 1022, snprintf n=1 writes NUL at 1023, STRLEN returns 0).

verdict.summary: compile_xclass_matchingpath is an internal static helper of the PCRE2 JIT compiler. It walks a serialized compiled-pattern fragment, which is the already-validated output of pcre2_compile, not raw user input. The trust boundary for pattern validity sits at the upstream parser, which is not part of this code. All potentially hazardous reads in this function are bounded either by the XCL_END sentinel of that validated stream, by fixed tables sized at build time, or by byte-masking that constrains the offset to the table's own width. No unvalidated attacker-controlled value reaches a memory, index, size, or injection sink here.

assumptions: The cc stream walked by this function is assumed to be well-formed, XCL_END-terminated, and validated by the upstream pattern compiler not shown here. This is an inferred contract from the surrounding PCRE2 architecture, not something quotable from the given code.
SLJIT_ASSERT statements are assumed to be active and enforced; in a release build they may compile out, meaning the asserted invariants would not be runtime-checked here.

The compiled-pattern properties referenced by cc[1] are assumed to name valid entries in ucd_boolprop_sets and ucd_script_sets, sized consistently with the byte range of cc[1]. This consistency is an upstream compile-time property, not something this code checks.
limitations: The emitted JIT machine code reads memory at ucd_boolprop_sets + (cc[1] >> 5). This code contains no bounds check on that offset against the size of ucd_boolprop_sets. Exploitation would require a compiled pattern carrying an out-of-range property index, which the upstream validation not shown here is expected to prevent. The impact chain therefore breaks at a link outside the given code.
Reads of cc[1] and cc[3] for property payloads assume the fragment extends at least that far, backed only by upstream serialization, not by a length check visible here.

A desynchronized or negative compares counter would cause the emitted jump table to select an incorrect code path. This is a correctness concern for the generated machine code, not a memory-safety defect reachable from the given statements.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. All memory writes into the growarray are preceded by ga_grow() checks in execution order (ga_grow(&ga, 120) at loop top before fgets; ga_grow(&ga, 1) before buf[ga.ga_len++] = NUL), buflines indexing is guarded each iteration by 'if (sp->buf_lnum >= sp->buflines.ga_len) break;', and every buf[len-1] access is reached only with len >= 1 established by the quoted producing statements (non-NULL fgets result or the post-concat NUL append). Failure sentinels of ga_grow, ga_concat's bounded append contract, and fgets NULL are all tested before first use.

assumptions: ga_grow() honors the documented growarray contract: returning OK guarantees room for at least the requested number of additional items; failure sentinel FAIL tested at each call site before any write.
ga_concat() internally grows the destination and performs a bounded append of the NUL-terminated source string; ga_init2(&ga, 1, 250) establishes element size 1 (bytes).

sp->fileformat's initial value (EOL_UNKNOWN/EOL_DOS) is set by code outside this function; all reads of it in this code occur inside the USE_CRNL block where a wrong initial value yields at worst a wrong-separator warning, not memory unsafety.
limitations: Potential fgets size underflow if ga.ga_len could exceed ga.ga_maxlen: no statement in this code produces that state (every ga_len advance is preceded by a successful ga_grow), so the trigger precondition is unsourced and speculative.
Read of buf[len-1] with len == 0: unreachable, since on the file path a non-NULL fgets result implies at least one byte read, and on the buffer path 'buf[ga.ga_len++] = NUL' guarantees len >= 1.
int truncation of STRLEN's size_t return would require a single sourced line over 2GB in a growarray whose ga_maxlen is itself an int; not reachable as written.

Under USE_CRNL, after replacing a trailing CR the escaped-NL parity scan uses the decremented len (stale-length quirk matching upstream Vim); all boundary cases (len 1 and 2) simulated in bounds, cosmetic at worst.
Memory leak of ga.ga_data on the FAIL/break early-exit arms before have_read is set: robustness only, no security impact.

verdict.summary: ex_retab here is the patched form of Vim's retab: the virtual-length overflow is stopped by the quoted 'if (vcol >= MAXCOL) { emsg(_(e_resulting_text_too_long)); break; }' arm before any length reaches the allocation, and the vartabstop aliasing double-free is stopped by the quoted 'if (new_vts_array == NULL) { new_vts_array = curbuf->b_p_vts_array; new_ts_str = NULL; }' invariant combined with the 'if (new_ts_str != NULL)' gate on the freeing block. All buffer writes (two mch_memmove calls and the tab/space fill loop) are bounded by an allocation sized from the same expressions as the copy lengths ('new_line = alloc(old_len - col + start_col + len + 1); if (new_line == NULL) break;'), with the col < STRLEN(ptr) invariant maintained by the 'if (ptr[col] == NUL) break;' statement ordered before every column advance, and boundary cases (trailing whitespace at the NUL, start_col == 0, empty lines) verified to land exactly at, never past, the allocation limit. The non-vartabs tabstop argument is range-checked ('if (new_ts < 0 || new_ts > TABSTOP_MAX)' plus the zero replacement). No instantiated memory-safety, injection, bypass, or amplification defect remains.

assumptions: tabstop_set(eap->arg, &new_vts_array) validates vartabstop entries (positive, at most TABSTOP_MAX) and returns FAIL on invalid input; its internals are not shown, so array element values are unverifiable from this code.
tabstop_fromto(), tabstop_count(), tabstop_first(), tabstop_eq() handle NULL and partial arrays and return non-negative results; not shown.
set_string_option_direct() copies the passed string (or otherwise does not leave the option owning new_ts_str), which makes the final 'vim_free(new_ts_str);' safe; semantics not shown.
ml_get(lnum) returns a valid NUL-terminated line for every lnum in eap->line1..eap->line2; ex-command range clamping happens in command-processing code not shown.
mb_ptr2len never advances past the NUL terminator (returns 1 for truncated or invalid multibyte sequences); this preserves the col < old_len invariant but is callee behavior not shown here.

The entering value of curbuf->b_p_ts is kept in 1..TABSTOP_MAX by the option layer; UNSOURCED in this code (only the exit-time assignments 'curbuf->b_p_ts = tabstop_first(new_vts_array);' and 'curbuf->b_p_ts = new_ts;' are present).
limitations: Historical retab virtual-column overflow (huge alloc / size wrap) is fixed here by the quoted 'if (vcol >= MAXCOL)' error arm; any 32-bit overflow of 'old_len - col + start_col + len + 1' additionally needs a line length near 2^31 together with a 32-bit long, and a wrapped negative would simply make alloc fail and hit the quoted 'if (new_line == NULL) break;'. Trigger speculative on an unshown 32-bit target and an unsourced line-length scale.

Historical vartabstop aliasing double-free at the end block is fixed by the quoted new_vts_array/new_ts_str invariant; 'new_ts_str != NULL' implies a freshly allocated array on every path, so no aliasing trigger can be instantiated.
A hostile entry inside new_vts_array (zero or negative tabstop) would depend on tabstop_set validation that is not shown (UNSOURCED); cannot be instantiated from this code.

getdigits truncation on huge numeric arguments (e.g., 4294967297 truncating to 1 in int) is real but every truncated value either fails the quoted '< 0 || > TABSTOP_MAX' check or lands in-domain; worst case is a wrong-but-safe tabstop, no security consequence.
Tab-expansion amplification is capped below MAXCOL by the quoted guard and by quoted allocation-failure handling; the bound is fixed and not attacker-unbounded.

ml_replace returning not-OK would leave new_line as a leaked owned allocation that this code only reassigns, never dereferences as freed or double-frees; no use-after-free link is characterizable within the given code.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability instantiated in this code. All attacker-controlled sinks are guarded in execution order: the 'name=' option is checked for empty (if (!param->size)), length (if (param->size > MAX_CGROUP_ROOT_NAMELEN - 1), correctly reserving one byte for the NUL terminator), and a strict [\w.-]+ character whitelist before storage, with a duplicate-name rejection before assignment; duplicate 'source' and 'release_agent' options are rejected before their stores; all fs_parse error sentinels (-ENOPARAM and opt < 0) are handled before any use of param fields; and the kernel isalnum macro safely casts to unsigned char before indexing the ctype table. Residual risks (fc->source can be set to NULL when 'source' is passed as a bare flag; the stored release_agent path and ctx->name being consumed by later, not-shown cgroup code) have their impact chains entirely outside this function and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: fs_parse is the standard kernel parameter parser: for fsparam_string specs ('release_agent', 'name') it enforces fs_value_is_string type and a non-NULL param->string and returns a negative error otherwise, so reaching those case arms implies param->string != NULL.

Framework producers (vfs_parse_fs_string for both mount(2) data and fsconfig(2) FSCONFIG_SET_STRING) construct string parameters with param->size == strlen(value) and a NUL-terminated param->string, so the loop for (i = 0; i < param->size; i++) reading param->string[i] is in-bounds for any size passing the quoted caps.
The kernel isalnum macro is defined with an (unsigned char) cast before indexing the 256-entry _ctype table, so bytes 0x80-0xFF in a name do not cause an out-of-bounds table read.
MAX_CGROUP_ROOT_NAMELEN is 64 and downstream consumers size their name buffer accordingly; the -1 in the length check reserves the NUL byte.

ctx->release_agent and ctx->name store attacker-supplied strings whose security-relevant consumption (release-agent execution, root-name use) happens in code not given; the famous release_agent container-escape class (CVE-2022-0492-adjacent) requires privileged cgroup-v1 mounting and its impact chain lies outside this function.

If a future or out-of-tree producer ever created a string fs_parameter with param->size exceeding the allocated string, the Opt_name loop would read out of bounds; no such producer is characterizable in the shown framework paths.
cgroup_no_v1_named is a boot-time global never assigned in this code (UNSOURCED); it is only used to reject the 'name=' option, never as a guard protecting a sink.

verdict.summary: No instantiated vulnerability found. All memory-access sinks reachable from attacker-controlled compressed data (stored-block memcpy, window/output match copies, literal writes, header extra/name/comment buffer writes, code-length array writes) are guarded by quoted bounds checks, clamps, or error arms on every execution path, and the one arithmetic-underflow candidate (extra_max - len in the EXTRA gzip-header copy) is provably unreachable because the code's own assignments maintain the invariant len <= extra_max. Residual risk concentrates in not-shown components (inflate_table table construction, updatewindow window bookkeeping, the local bit-input macros, and the sane flag's initialization), which cannot be audited from the given code and are recorded as assumptions and limitations.

assumptions: The local macros BITS, DROPBITS, NEEDBITS, PULLBYTE, BYTEBITS, INITBITS, LOAD, RESTORE, CRC2, CRC4, and UPDATE_CHECK are defined in inflate.c's private header 'inflate.h', which is not part of the given code; their standard zlib semantics (input-availability checks in NEEDBITS/PULLBYTE, hold/bits save-restore in LOAD/RESTORE) are assumed, not quoted.

struct inflate_state field capacities (lens[320], codes[ENOUGH], work) and the gz_header fields extra_max, name_max, comm_max being caller-provided buffer sizes are defined in not-shown headers (inflate.h, zutil.h); the CODELENS bound nlen+ndist <= 316 is safe only relative to those not-shown capacities.

inflate_table() (called at the LENLENS and CODELENS exits) is not shown; the assumption that it rejects over-subscribed and incomplete code sets (making single-lookup indexing of lencode/distcode safe) is a documented zlib contract, not a quotable statement in this code.

state->sane, state->wsize, state->whave, state->wnext, and state->window are assigned by inflateInit2/inflateReset/updatewindow, none of which appear in the given code; the MATCH window-arithmetic safety relative to these fields rests on those unshown invariants.

Build-configuration macros (GUNZIP, INFLATE_STRICT, INFLATE_ALLOW_INVALID_DISTANCE_TOOFAR_ARRR, PKZIP_BUG_WORKAROUND) determine which arms are compiled; the analysis treats the shown #ifdef structure as-is and notes that with INFLATE_STRICT undefined the dmax distance check is absent, though the MATCH whave check still bounds reads to actual window history.
limitations: Candidate: out-of-bounds window read in MATCH when copy > state->whave and state->sane == 0 with INFLATE_ALLOW_INVALID_DISTANCE_TOOFAR_ARRR undefined (execution falls through into window arithmetic with an unclamped copy). Trigger precondition state->sane == 0 is UNSOURCED: no assignment to state->sane exists in the given code, so the candidate is neither confirmed nor usable as a guard.

Candidate: unsigned underflow of state->head->extra_max - len in the EXTRA zmemcpy when len > extra_max. Disproved by an inductive invariant over the quoted statements: len = extra_len - state->length starts at 0 (EXLEN sets both from the same hold), the unclamped arm preserves len <= extra_max, and the clamped arm sets len to exactly extra_max; len can therefore never exceed extra_max and the underflow cannot be instantiated.

Candidate: unbounded-depth table indexing in LEN/DIST via state->lencode[BITS(state->lenbits)] and the second-level last.val + (BITS(...) >> last.bits) lookup. The harm depends on inflate_table (not shown) failing to reject incomplete codes; per the CALLEE BOUNDARY RULE this behavior is not characterizable from the given code, so the candidate is a limitation, not a finding.

Candidate: heap exposure through updatewindow(strm, strm->next_out, out - strm->avail_out) at inf_leave. The callee is not shown and its internal window bookkeeping cannot be characterized; the passed size (bytes produced this call) is non-negative by construction, so no out-of-domain argument is passed at this call site.

Candidate: acceptance of distances beyond dmax when INFLATE_STRICT is not defined. Not memory-unsafe in this code because MATCH's quoted 'if (copy > state->whave)' check with the sane error arm bounds all window reads to history actually produced; residual impact would be decompression of data outside the declared window, a data-integrity concern whose consequence lies in not-shown consumers.

verdict.summary: r_bin_java_inner_classes_attr_new reads the 2-byte number_of_classes field at buffer offset 6 without validating sz >= 8. The only size check in the function, `if (offset + 8 > sz)`, sits inside the loop body and therefore executes after this read. An attacker-supplied class file with an InnerClasses attribute of size 6 or 7 whose 6-byte header parses successfully causes a heap out-of-bounds read (crash of the binary-parsing process, potential disclosure).

evidence.reason: Root cause: R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT(buffer, offset) reads buffer[6..7] with offset == 6 and no check that sz >= 8 anywhere before this statement; the function's only bounds check (`if (offset + 8 > sz)`) is inside the loop and runs after this read. Instantiated trigger: attacker supplies an InnerClasses attribute with sz = 7 (or 6) and a valid 6-byte header, the header parser returns non-NULL (this code's own `offset += 6` documents the callee consumes only the first 6 bytes), and the 2-byte read at indices 6-7 goes past the end of the buffer.

Origin of the tainted offset: `offset += 6` advances the read cursor past the 6-byte attribute header, and the only validation on the callee result is a NULL test — sz is never compared against offset before the number_of_classes read at line 14, so any sz in [6,7] with a successful header parse reaches the out-of-bounds read.

assumptions: sz is the number of valid bytes reachable from buffer (caller contract; not checked in this code).
R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT(buffer, offset) reads 2 bytes at buffer[offset] and buffer[offset+1] (framework macro).

r_bin_java_default_attr_new consumes the 6-byte attribute header, as documented by this code's own `offset += 6;` at line 8; whether it additionally enforces sz >= 8 cannot be quoted and is therefore not relied on as a guard.
limitations: Lines 40-43 and 46-49: obj from r_bin_java_get_item_from_bin_cp_list can be NULL (the code tests it, prints, then passes obj anyway to r_bin_java_get_item_name_from_bin_cp_list). Whether that callee dereferences a NULL obj is not characterizable from the given code, so no finding is emitted.
Fallback path assigns icattr->name = r_str_dup(NULL, "NULL") and then free(icattr) without freeing the name — memory leak only, no security impact.
R_BIN_JAVA_GLOBAL_BIN is used for constant-pool lookups instead of the bin parameter; the global is UNSOURCED in this code, so any wrong-object consequence is uninstantiable here.

Loop-body reads (lines 27-33) were verified safe: the quoted guard `if (offset + 8 > sz) { break; }` runs at the top of every iteration before any read, uses the correct operator, and offset (max 524296) cannot overflow ut64.

verdict.summary: No exploitable defect is provable within the given code. The attacker-controlled rule content reaches only iteration, dispatch through kernel-resident ops tables, and allocation sizing. The zero-action case fails closed (num_actions == 0 returns -EOPNOTSUPP); both allocation results (nft_flow_rule_alloc, kzalloc) are NULL-checked before first use; every error arm sets err before ERR_PTR(err); ctx/flow are freed exactly once per path. The main structural concern - the action count in the first loop (offload_action predicate) versus actions appended by expr->ops->offload callbacks in the second loop - cannot be instantiated here because whether any not-shown offload callback appends more entries than counted is uncharacterizable from the given code, and the arguments passed at the call site are valid pointers. Integer overflow of num_actions, concurrent rule mutation between the two loops, and a NULL expr->ops similarly lack any instantiable producer in this code.

The precondition 'a callback appends uncounted entries' has no source in the given code - it lives in not-shown per-expression offload callbacks - so the trigger is UNSOURCED and the impact chain is uncharacterizable.

verdict.summary: In the CP950 branch of the Big5-to-wchar conversion filter, the linear search over cp950_pua_tbl (lines 51-55) can terminate without a match, leaving k equal to the table entry count; the code then reads cp950_pua_tbl[k][2] and cp950_pua_tbl[k][0] (lines 57-61) with no bounds check on k, an out-of-bounds read past the end of the static table. An attacker supplies a CP950 stream whose lead byte (e.g. 0x81) passes the line 18 lead test and whose second byte lies in 0x3a-0x3f, admitted by the loose `c > 0x39` trail tests on lines 31 and 48 but below the 0x40 trail anchor of every table range (evidenced by the `& 0xff) == 0x40` check and the 0x40/0x62 offsets on lines 57-58), so no range matches and k exits at the bound. The out-of-bounds-derived value flows into the converted output.

evidence.reason: The search loop's exit condition allows k to reach the entry count without the break on line 53 ever executing when c2 lies outside every table range; the loop bound on line 51 does not constrain the post-loop use. Line 57 then reads cp950_pua_tbl[k][2] with k == N (out of bounds), and lines 58-61 read cp950_pua_tbl[k][0] and [k][2] again, computing w from out-of-bounds data that is emitted to the output on line 71. Instantiated trigger: CP950 stream 0x81 0x3a — lead accepted by line 18, second byte admitted by lines 31/48, index w = (0x81-0xa1)*157 + (0x3a-0x40) = -5030 clamped to w = 0 on line 40, c2 = 0x813a matches no range, k exits at the bound.

Origin of the out-of-domain lookup key: the entry condition uses the loose trail test `c > 0x39`, admitting second bytes 0x3a-0x3f which are below the 0x40 trail anchor of every cp950_pua_tbl range (the code's own arithmetic on lines 57-58 keys ranges at trail 0x40 and 0xa1). Line 50 then forms c2 = c1 << 8 | c for such bytes, producing a key that cannot match any table range and drives k to the loop bound, enabling the out-of-bounds read on line 57.

assumptions: This is a non-static mbstring-style conversion filter callback; each call's parameter c is one byte of an attacker-controlled encoded stream, and the source encoding (CP950 vs Big5) is chosen per conversion request, so filter->from->no_encoding is treated as attacker-selectable configuration.

filter->status is initialized to a value other than 1 before the first call by the framework; within this code status==1 is only ever set together with filter->cache (lines 19-20), so cache is never read uninitialized on any in-code path.

MBFL_WCSGROUP_MASK / MBFL_WCSPLANE_MASK are masks that bound the emitted fallback values; big5_ucs_table_size is assumed consistent with big5_ucs_table, and the guard on line 37 makes the lookup safe regardless of its exact value.
c is typically 0-255; out-of-range or negative values are handled by the masked else arms on lines 21-25 and 74-78.
limitations: cp950_pua_tbl contents are not part of the given code. The claim that trail bytes 0x3a-0x3f fall outside every [k][2]..[k][3] range rests on characterizing the table as covering canonical CP950 second bytes (0x40-0x7e, 0xa1-0xfe), which the given code corroborates through its range arithmetic (line 57's `(cp950_pua_tbl[k][2] & 0xff) == 0x40` test and line 58's 0x40/0x62 trail offsets), and on the known upstream php-src fix that added exactly the missing post-loop bounds check on k in mbfl_filt_conv_big5_wchar.

Even when the loop finds a match, the PUA formula on line 58 assumes the found range's trail span matches the 0x40/0x62 anchoring; a mismatched table entry could yield an out-of-range PUA code point, but this cannot be evaluated without the table data.

If a caller ever invoked the filter with filter->status == 1 before any lead byte was seen, c1 on line 30 would be an uninitialized member; no in-code producer of that state exists, so this is not treated as a finding.

verdict.summary: In tipc_crypto_key_rcv, the attacker-controlled key length read from a received TIPC MSG_CRYPTO message (skey->keylen, from ntohl of message bytes at data + TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME) is used as the memcpy length at line 26-27 before any validation that it fits the kmalloc(size) allocation. The only sanity check, `if (unlikely(size != tipc_aead_key_size(skey)))` at line 30, executes AFTER both memcpy calls, so it can only free an object whose adjacent heap was already overwritten. With size = 36 and the message's length field set to 65535, the memcpy writes ~65531 attacker-controlled bytes past a 36-byte heap object; with size < 32 the fixed 32-byte copy into skey->alg_name overflows by itself. This is a remotely triggerable kernel heap out-of-bounds write (memory corruption), not merely a crash.

evidence.reason: Sink: memcpy uses skey->keylen (fully attacker-controlled, read at line 24 from the received message, up to 65535 after ntohl/truncation) as the copy length into skey->key, which lives inside a kmalloc(size) allocation (line 17) of at most 65535 bytes with destination offset >= 32. No statement before this copy bounds keylen against size; the only sanity check `size != tipc_aead_key_size(skey)` (line 30) runs after the copy in execution order and merely kfree()s the already-overflowed object. Instantiated trigger: message with msg_data_sz = 36 and length bytes 0xFFFF yields a ~65531-byte attacker-controlled heap overflow. The line-25 memcpy (fixed 32 bytes into a size-byte allocation) is an alternate instantiation of the same missing pre-copy bound (size < 32, or size = 0 where kmalloc returns ZERO_SIZE_PTR and line 24 itself writes out of bounds).

evidence.snippet:
u16 size = msg_data_sz(hdr);
	u8 *data = msg_data(hdr);
evidence.reason: Origin of the taint: size and data are decoded directly from the network-received TIPC message header. size (0..65535) becomes both the kmalloc length at line 17 and the value the too-late check at line 30 compares against, while the message bytes at data + TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME supply the unbounded copy length at line 24. This code is the trust-boundary intake for the key message, so these values cannot be assumed validated elsewhere.

assumptions: The layout of struct tipc_aead_key (keylen field of width u16 at offset TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME, key array following it) and the semantics of tipc_aead_key_size come from kernel headers not included in the given code; the finding does not depend on the exact widths because keylen's reachable maximum (>= 65535, or 2^32-1 if the field is wider) exceeds any allocation of size <= 65535.
kmalloc(0) returns the non-NULL ZERO_SIZE_PTR per standard kernel allocator semantics; if it returned NULL instead, only that alternate instantiation path is closed, not the primary trigger.

rx->skey == NULL on the fresh-session path: the initial assignment is in the not-shown crypto initialization; this code itself manages the field (rx->skey = skey at line 38) and is the designed first-key intake, and the attacker initiates the key exchange, so the permissive state is the protocol default rather than a value forced to be safe by any statement here.
msg_data_sz/msg_key_gen/msg_data/msg_key_mode are message-header accessors whose values come from the wire; no bound on the payload size is enforced anywhere in this code.
limitations: Potential NULL dereference of tx at line 46 (`tx->wq`): tx is assigned at line 3 from tipc_net(rx->net)->crypto_tx, a lookup whose result this code never checks and whose producer is not shown; the precondition tx == NULL is UNSOURCED here, so this is recorded as a limitation, not a finding.

The out-of-bounds READ side of the same memcpy (reading data + 36 + keylen bytes from a size-byte message payload, and the 4-byte read at data+32 when size < 36) is instantiated on the same trigger but is subsumed by the primary out-of-bounds write.

If keylen = 0 and size = 36, the line-30 check passes and a zero-length key is stored and scheduled; any weak-key or empty-key impact depends on the not-shown work handler (tipc_crypto_work / key attaching) and cannot be characterized from this code.
No race condition was instantiated: the state check and the copy run under `spin_lock(&rx->lock)`.

verdict.summary: processDataRcvd accumulates the octet-counted frame length from attacker-supplied TCP digits with no bound (line 33), so a 10+ digit counter (e.g. "3000000000 ") overflows int and wraps negative. The invalid-count check at line 40 only logs an error and falls through to line 54, and neither clamp on the copy path (lines 100 and 103, both upper-bound tests) catches a negative value, so the negative count reaches memcpy at line 108 as a size_t of ~1.8e19, producing a massive heap out-of-bounds write. Remote, pre-authentication, memory corruption (practically an immediate crash) on any listener with octet-counted framing support enabled.

evidence.reason: Sink and faulty computation. octatesToCopy is assigned from the attacker-overflowed iOctetsRemain (line 98, into the int declared at line 11). Both guards are upper-bound clamps only: line 100 (buffLen < octatesToCopy) is false for any negative value, and line 103 (octatesToCopy + iMsg > iMaxLine) is false for any negative value with iMsg >= 0. A negative count therefore reaches memcpy unclamped; the int converts to size_t near SIZE_MAX (e.g. -1294967296 becomes ~1.8e19), and memcpy copies exactly that many bytes past pMsg: out-of-bounds write. Trigger instantiated: TCP peer sends a frame header of 10 digits forming a value >= 2^31 followed by a space and payload bytes.

evidence.snippet:
if(isdigit(c)) {
			pThis->iOctetsRemain = pThis->iOctetsRemain * 10 + c - '0';
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value. The octet counter is accumulated once per attacker-supplied digit with no bound anywhere in the code; with 10 digits the multiplication overflows int (INT_MAX = 2147483647) and wraps negative. The fail-open at lines 40-44 (if(pThis->iOctetsRemain < 1) only calls DBGPRINTF/errmsg.LogError, no state reset, no FINALIZE) lets the negative count flow into the copy path at line 98. Independently of the struct field's width, line 98 truncates it into int octatesToCopy, so a wider counter also yields a negative length.

assumptions: bSuppOctetFram (consumed at line 14) gates entry into octet-counted framing mode; it is set by listener configuration not shown in this code and is not assigned anywhere here. It is recorded because the methodology demands sourcing; it cannot serve as a guard either, and the defective path is a framing mode this function itself implements.

The declared width and signedness of pThis->iOctetsRemain and pThis->iMsg are not visible in the snippet; the code's own statements treat them as int (assigned into the int at line 11, compared with int buffLen at line 100, printed with %d at lines 35/44/49), and the truncating assignment at line 98 makes the negative-length path reachable even if the struct field were wider.
pMsg is allocated elsewhere (not shown); the primary defect is immaterial to its size, since a ~1.8e19-byte copy exceeds any conceivable allocation.
The caller advances *buff by one element per invocation (the -1 adjustment at line 111 is calibrated to that convention); caller behavior is otherwise not shown.
iMaxLine is a global configured elsewhere; its concrete value does not affect the primary defect (both clamps fail for every negative octatesToCopy regardless of iMaxLine).
limitations: Octet count 0 (the case the TODO at line 41 flags): lines 108-111 execute with copy=discard=0, so *buff += -1 moves the buffer pointer back one byte and the frame is submitted; the security consequence depends on the unshown caller's loop/advancement behavior and cannot be characterized from this code.

A negative buffLen (caller-supplied) would propagate into memcpy identically via line 101, but no statement in this code can produce a negative buffLen and its producer (the socket read) is not shown; treated as a caller-contract question, not a confirmed finding.

Oversize positive counts (iMaxLine < iOctetsRemain < INT_MAX) were verified safe: lines 100-106 clamp the copy to iMaxLine - pThis->iMsg and account for the discarded remainder in the decrement at line 110 and the pointer adjustment at line 111.
The emergency-flush scan (lines 64-68) and the %.*s LogError (lines 69-70) were edge-tested against buffLen boundaries (0, 1, exactly buffLen) and are bounded by buffLen; no defect found.

The remaining candidates fail instantiation: the ut64 wrap in 'buf_offset + offset + 8' requires a buf_offset near 2^64 that no statement in this code can produce, and the possible NULL passed to r_bin_java_get_item_name_from_bin_cp_list has an impact chain that depends entirely on the unshown callee's NULL handling, which the code's own downstream NULL handling suggests is tolerated. The caller's production of buf_offset (accumulated class-file offsets) is not shown; whether it is always far below 2^64 is assumed, not quotable here.
r_bin_java_default_attr_new's own bounds handling of buffer/sz/buf_offset is not shown and is not relied upon for any verdict.

verdict.summary: No fully instantiated vulnerability exists in the given code. Every direct memory operation in write_entry is guarded by a quotable statement (mailbox/mdata NULL ternaries, the !value->len short-circuit before memcmp, the if(mailbox) guard before highestmodseq access, checked return codes for _annotate_getdb and read_old_value, and the fail-closed !maywrite check). The remaining candidates all break at links not characterizable from the given code: the unvalidated keylen from the unshown make_key used as a length at cyrusdb_delete/cyrusdb_store, an authz fail-open contingent on the unquoted IMAP_PERMISSION_DENIED constant being zero, and NULL-deref scenarios whose malformed struct buf producers are not shown. These are recorded as limitations, not findings.

assumptions: IMAP_PERMISSION_DENIED is assumed to be a nonzero error constant (com_err convention; 0 denotes success). It is never defined in the given code, so the fail-closed behavior of 'if (!maywrite) { r = IMAP_PERMISSION_DENIED; if (r) goto out; }' technically rests on this unquoted constant; if it were 0 the check would fall through and permit unauthorized writes.

make_key, read_old_value, _annotate_getdb, annotate_begin, annotate_putdb, make_entry, mailbox_quota_check, mailbox_annot_changed, key_as_string and cyrusdb_delete/cyrusdb_store are not shown; only their names and signatures are available, and their internal bounds handling (especially make_key's keylen semantics) is not characterizable.
struct buf is assumed to maintain s != NULL when len > 0 for values supplied by callers; no statement in this code establishes that invariant.
DEBUG is assumed not defined, so the syslog blocks (which print the possibly non-NUL-terminated value->s with %s) are not compiled into the analyzed binary.
limitations: keylen from 'keylen = make_key(mboxname, uid, entry, userid, key, sizeof(key));' is never validated against sizeof(key) or checked for a failure sentinel before being used as the key length in read_old_value, cyrusdb_delete and cyrusdb_store, and in the DEBUG key_as_string call. No guard of any form (range check, clamp, sentinel test) exists on any path in this code (verified in STEP 5). If make_key can return an oversized (e.g., snprintf-style would-be length) or negative length for attacker-controlled entry/userid/mboxname content, this yields an out-of-bounds read of the stack buffer key at the cyrusdb call sites (CWE-125/787 family). The trigger could not be instantiated because make_key's implementation is not shown and is not a characterizable standard-library function; the CALLEE BOUNDARY RULE therefore places this in limitations rather than evidence.

If IMAP_PERMISSION_DENIED were 0, 'if (!maywrite) { r = IMAP_PERMISSION_DENIED; if (r) goto out; }' would fall through and perform cyrusdb_store/cyrusdb_delete without authorization (CWE-862). The constant is never defined in this code (UNSOURCED), so this authorization-bypass trigger cannot be instantiated; com_err convention indicates it is nonzero.

'if (oldval.len == value->len && (!value->len || !memcmp(oldval.s, value->s, value->len)))' would pass NULL to memcmp if value->s (or oldval.s) were NULL with positive len. The code's own later check 'if (!value->len || value->s == NULL)' shows the authors consider value->s == NULL reachable, but only after the memcmp, and no producer of s==NULL with len>0 exists in this code (value comes from unshown in-file callers; oldval is filled by the unshown read_old_value). Speculative NULL-deref (CWE-476).
If a caller passed value == NULL, 'value->len' at the identical-value test dereferences NULL (CWE-476). No producer or quoted non-NULL contract exists in this code (UNSOURCED).

Under #if DEBUG, syslog prints value->s with %s; struct buf data is not guaranteed NUL-terminated, allowing an out-of-bounds read and attacker-controlled log content (CWE-125/CWE-117). Guarded only by the unquoted DEBUG compilation flag.

'if (!userid) goto out;' exits with r == 0, reporting success while silently not storing the annotation. Any security consequence depends on an unshown caller relying on the write having occurred; the chain breaks at caller behavior not characterized in this code.

The identical-value early exit precedes the !maywrite check, so a caller without write permission gets a 1-bit equality oracle on stored annotation values (return 0 vs IMAP_PERMISSION_DENIED). Exploitation requires an unshown caller path reachable without read permission; not instantiated here.

The 'do { ... } while (r == CYRUSDB_AGAIN);' retry loops are unbounded, but no interleaving of two ordered operations in this code sustaining CYRUSDB_AGAIN can be exhibited, so a denial-of-service trigger is speculative.

verdict.summary: string_scan_range dereferences its 'bf' parameter at the very first statement ('RBin *bin = bf->rbin;') before the NULL guard 'r_return_val_if_fail (bf, -1);' that appears later in the function. In execution order the guard can never protect the dereference: if a caller passes bf == NULL — an input the function's own guard explicitly anticipates and intends to handle by returning -1 — the process crashes with a NULL pointer dereference before the check runs. All other buffer accesses in the function were verified guarded (range checks on from/to/len, bounds checks on the tmp writes, and pointer dereferences on buf/str_start all precede their uses in execution order).

evidence.reason: Root cause: use-before-check NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476). Line 3 executes 'RBin *bin = bf->rbin;' which dereferences 'bf' unconditionally, while the only NULL guard, 'r_return_val_if_fail (bf, -1);', sits at line 10 — after the dereference in execution order. The presence of the guard proves the code's own contract anticipates bf == NULL (intended behavior: return -1), but the misplaced check never protects the first statement. Trigger: any invocation with bf == NULL crashes at line 3 before any validation runs; no earlier check, clamp, or error arm exists on any path (verified by the STEP 5 fix-form search). Consequence: NULL dereference crash / denial of service.

assumptions: The UTF decoders (r_utf8_decode, r_utf16le_decode, r_utf32le_decode) and r_read_le32 honor their length arguments, bounding reads to the supplied size; this is their core documented semantics, and all buffer accesses were additionally verified against the quoted bounds checks ('needle < to', 'needle + 4 < to', '(to - needle) > 8 + rc', 'i < sizeof (tmp) - 4', '(i + 32) < sizeof (tmp)', 'str_start - from > 1', 'str_start - from > 3').

r_utf_block_list returns -1-sentinel-terminated arrays with freq_list parallel in length to block_list; the callee is not shown, so the parallel indexing in the freq_list loop cannot be proven safe or unsafe from the given code.
r_return_val_if_fail is assumed active (non-debug build keeps the check); the finding does not depend on this, since the defect is the check's position, not its absence.

bf->buf, bf->o, bf->loadaddr, bf->size, bf->strmode and strings_db are struct state assigned outside this code (UNSOURCED); they are used only after the line-10 check and never as copy/index bounds inside this function.
limitations: Integer overflow: 'int outlen = len * 4;' overflows to a negative int when the scan range len exceeds 2^29 bytes (about 512MB) while RABIN2_CHARSET is set, passing a negative capacity to r_charset_encode_str. The impact could not be instantiated: the callee is a project function whose behavior with a negative size is not characterizable, and within this code the replacement buffer 'calloc (len, 4)' (4x the original length) keeps all subsequent loop reads (bounded by 'needle < to', i.e. the original length) inside the allocation, so no in-code memory violation occurs. Also requires the caller to supply a >512MB scan range.

'r_buf_read_at (bf->buf, from, buf, len);' ignores the return value; a short or failed read leaves the calloc-zeroed buffer, which scans as empty — no corruption, disclosure, or amplification in this code (robustness only).

After a successful charset re-encode, 'len = res; ... buf = out;' replaces the buffer with encoded data while the loop bound 'to' still maps to the original length; reads remain within the 4x-sized 'out' allocation so it is memory-safe, but the address-to-data mapping of the re-encoded buffer is inconsistent (functional defect, not a security impact).

Reachability of the NULL-bf trigger depends on a caller not shown (the function is static); per the analysis rules the caller was not assumed safe, and the code's own NULL guard at line 10 was treated as in-code evidence that bf == NULL is an anticipated input, which is why the finding stands despite moderate confidence.

verdict.summary: qh_help ignores its len parameter, the only bound on the attacker-supplied query buffer buf, and never verifies NUL termination before passing buf to strcmp, qh_find_handler, and '%s' in nsock_printf_nul. A query filling the buffer without a terminator is scanned past its end, and at line 25 the over-read bytes are transmitted back to the querying party on socket sd, giving a remote out-of-bounds read with memory disclosure and crash/DoS potential.

evidence.reason: Sink: buf is consumed by qh_find_handler (line 22, scans until NUL) and by '%s' in nsock_printf_nul (line 25, copies until NUL) with no termination or length check on any path; the only guard in the function (buf == NULL at line 5) bounds nothing about content. Trigger: attacker sends a query of exactly len bytes with no NUL (e.g. "help \x90\x90..."); strcmp at lines 5 and 12 mismatch in-bounds, qh_find_handler over-reads and returns NULL, and line 25 copies past the end of buf and writes the adjacent memory bytes to the attacker's socket sd — out-of-bounds read with direct disclosure (root cause: the buffer's declared bound len is never enforced).

evidence.snippet: static int qh_help(int sd, char *buf, unsigned int len)
evidence.reason: Origin: the interface supplies unsigned int len as the only bound on the attacker-controlled content of buf, but the function body never references len (no buf[len-1] check, no strn* call, no %.*s width, no clamp), so every string operation on buf in lines 5, 12, 22, 25, and 29 is unbounded relative to the actual buffer size.

assumptions: sd is the descriptor of the peer that submitted the query (implied by this handler replying with nsock_printf/nsock_printf_nul on sd); the peer's exact privilege level is not shown in the given code.

qhandlers, qh_find_handler, and nsock_printf_nul are program-internal helpers; nsock_printf_nul is treated as a printf-family function that writes formatted output plus a NUL to sd, and qh_find_handler as a name lookup returning NULL on miss.
buf carries socket-supplied command content per the handler role of this function ('help <name>', 'list'); no statement in the given code guarantees NUL termination of buf within len bytes.
limitations: The function-pointer call qh->handler(sd, "help", 4) at line 27 would be a control-flow hijack primitive if an attacker could register or corrupt a handler entry, but no statement in this code lets external data alter the qhandlers list — that trigger precondition is UNSOURCED here.
A concurrent (un)registration racing the list walk at line 14 is speculative: no two interleavable ordered operations are exhibited in this code.

If the not-shown dispatcher that invokes qh_help always NUL-terminates buf within len, the over-read is unreachable; that contract is unquotable in the given code, and the unused len parameter indicates termination is not part of this interface's guarantee, so the candidate could not be demoted on it.
Lines 5, 12, and 22 also over-read an unterminated buf with crash/DoS-only impact on those paths; this is subsumed by the confirmed disclosure at line 25.

verdict.summary: addBinding validates attacker-supplied namespace URIs and prefixes safely: allocation sizes are guarded against int overflow by quoted checks (len > INT_MAX - EXPAND_SPARE, plus a size_t-scale check under #if UINT_MAX >= SIZE_MAX) placed before every allocation on every path; buffers are allocated from the same expression (len + EXPAND_SPARE) that bounds the memcpy length (len); REALLOC/MALLOC failure sentinels are tested before first use; the static namespace-array comparisons are bounded by len > xmlLen / len > xmlnsLen short-circuits; the separator write b->uri[len-1] is preceded by len++ so len >= 1; and reserved-prefix/namespace enforcement (xml, xmlns, xmlns URI) rejects all hostile combinations, including the mustBeXML corner case which I proved unreachable-different from upstream. verdict.summary: This Guile primitive (scm_mkdir) converts its two inputs through checked converters before the single syscall sink: the optional mode defaults to the in-range constant 0777 via SCM_UNBNDP, and any supplied mode passes through scm_to_uint, whose characterizable semantics bound it to unsigned int and raise an error for out-of-range or non-integer values rather than returning a sentinel. The path reaches the raw mkdir syscall (not a shell) as a valid C string whose conversion raises on non-string input. The return value is checked on every path (if (rv != 0) SCM_SYSERROR), so there is no fail-open success reporting. No memory, size, index, format, or injection sink consumes unvalidated data; creating a directory at a caller-specified path is the API's documented function, and any further impact requires deployment assumptions not instantiated by this code.

assumptions: STRING_SYSCALL is a Guile macro whose documented semantics convert the SCM string to a stable, NUL-terminated C string (or signal an error for a non-string) before the syscall body executes; the body runs with a valid c_path or not at all.
scm_to_uint is a Guile checked converter that returns a C unsigned int or signals a wrong-type-arg/out-of-range error; it never returns NULL, a sentinel, or a wrapped value on out-of-range input.
mode_t is at least as wide as unsigned int on the build targets of this code (32-bit on POSIX systems Guile supports); no truncation from unsigned int to mode_t is exercised by the code as written.
SCM_SYSERROR raises a Scheme error incorporating errno on syscall failure; it does not fall through to a success return.
limitations: On a hypothetical platform where mode_t is narrower than unsigned int (e.g., 16-bit), a mode value between 2^16 and UINT_MAX would be truncated before mkdir; this width behavior is not exercised by the code's declared types and the platform width is UNSOURCED, so it remains speculative.

The path argument is passed to the raw mkdir syscall without path validation by design; whether the executing Scheme program is trusted is a deployment/interpreter policy question outside the given code, so no path-traversal or injection impact could be instantiated here.

verdict.summary: size = bytes_per_line * hh (line 87) multiplies the attacker-controlled width-derived bytes_per_line (up to 0x20000000 from line 85) by the attacker-controlled height in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic and stores the wrapped result in int size. verdict.summary: In the Opt_name handler, each attacker-controlled byte of the cgroup1 mount option value is loaded into a signed char (line 71) and passed to isalnum() (line 72). The kernel isalnum macro indexes its fixed-size _ctype table with (int)c and performs no range check, so a name byte >= 0x80, which is negative as a signed char on the dominant kernel targets, reads out of bounds before the table. The out-of-bounds byte then gates the [\w.-] validation, so an invalid byte can be accepted into ctx->name when the adjacent out-of-bounds memory happens to carry the alnum bits. No cast, range check, clamp, or mask bounds the byte on any path; the only guards (lines 65, 67) bound the length, not the content.

evidence.reason: The loop walks the attacker-supplied mount option value; 'char c = param->string[i];' loads an arbitrary attacker byte into a signed char, and 'if (isalnum(c))' passes it as the index into the kernel's fixed-size ctype lookup table without bounding the value to the table domain. Trigger instantiated: mount option name=<byte 0x80> gives c = -128 on x86_64, so _ctype[(int)(-128)] is an out-of-bounds read before the global table, and the out-of-bounds value (ANDed with _U|_L|_D) decides whether an out-of-charset byte is accepted as a valid cgroup root name. The quoted guards at lines 65 and 67 bound only param->size (loop iterations), never the byte value; no cast, range check, clamp, or mask exists on any path.

assumptions: fs_parse (not shown) is relied on per the callee-boundary rule for characterizable parse semantics: it returns a positive Opt_* id when the key matches the spec with a compatible type, and negative sentinels on error; no in-code statement enforces this.

The kernel isalnum expands to a ctype-table lookup of the form ((_ctype[(int)(c)] & (_U|_L|_D)) != 0) with no range check (include/linux/ctype.h); the _ctype table covers only ASCII/unsigned-char range plus an EOF slot, so negative indices read before the table under every layout variant. The table itself is not shown.
Plain 'char' is signed on the primary kernel targets (x86_64); on targets where char is unsigned the out-of-bounds read requires the table to cover fewer than 256 entries.

The code ignores len, so if a caller ever passes a buffer filled to its exact length without a terminating byte, strcmp would read past the allocation; the named unsourced field is the dispatcher's termination behavior.

verdict.summary: No trigger could be instantiated from the given code. The one genuinely unguarded sink is the fixed-headroom copy sequence STRCPY(s, dp->d_name) followed by STRCPY(buf + len, "/**") / STRCPY(buf + len + 3, path_end): no statement between dp = readdir(dirp) and the copy bounds d_name's length in any form (checked: no length check, clamp, mask, realloc, or d_name-derived allocation exists). All other sinks are verifiably guarded in execution order (vim_regexec is behind the quoted short-circuit regmatch.regprog != NULL, opendir is NULL-checked, d_name[2] is read only behind d_name[1] != NUL, fnamencmp reads e - s bytes of a component that is a verbatim copy of the original path component, recursion depth is capped by the quoted stardepth < 100, and qsort is behind matches > 0).

Callees not shown (rem_backslash, file_pat_to_reg_pat, vim_regcomp, vim_regexec, mb_ptr2len, fnamencmp, mch_has_exp_wildcard, backslash_halve, mac_precompose_path, addfile, mch_getperm, mch_lstat) were characterized only by their standard Vim semantics under the CALLEE BOUNDARY RULE.
