verdict.summary: gopherToHTML writes the string terminator at line[llen + 1] while its own overflow check (gopherState->len + llen >= TEMP_BUF_SIZE) and clamp permit llen to reach TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1, producing a one-byte out-of-bounds write past the TEMP_BUF_SIZE line buffer; gopher server response data fully controls the trigger. Additional confirmed findings: the gopher 'host' field is inserted raw into generated HREF attributes (HTML/XSS injection, CWE-79), and 'port' is dereferenced (*port) in the telnet branch without a NULL check after strchr can return NULL (CWE-476 denial of service).

evidence.reason: Off-by-one out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The line buffer is declared LOCAL_ARRAY(char, line, TEMP_BUF_SIZE) (line 6), so valid indices are 0..TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1. The terminator is stored at index llen+1, but llen can equal TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1: with gopherState->len == 0 and a gopher response line of TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 bytes (including the newline), the check at line 77 (0 + TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 >= TEMP_BUF_SIZE) is false, memcpy fills indices 0..TEMP_BUF_SIZE-2, and this statement writes line[TEMP_BUF_SIZE]. Trigger instantiated with a two-chunk sequence: partial line of k bytes sets gopherState->len = k (line 87), then a chunk whose first line ends after T-2-k bytes makes combined llen = T-1 via lines 92-94, again writing line[T]. The written value and index are fixed; the write itself is the memory corruption, driven entirely by untrusted gopher server data.

Origin of the faulty value: this is the only bound on llen, and it is off by one relative to the sink. It permits llen = TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1 (boundary case len + llen = TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1 passes the >= test), and on the clamp path it sets llen to exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE - gopherState->len - 1, so the combined llen after line 94 is TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1 in every path — precisely the value that makes line[llen + 1] write one past the buffer. No statement anywhere clamps llen to TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 2 or checks llen + 1 < TEMP_BUF_SIZE.

evidence.snippet: snprintf(tmpbuf, TEMP_BUF_SIZE, " %s\n", icon_url, host, rfc1738_escape_unescaped(selector + 5), html_quote(name));
evidence.reason: HTML/attribute injection (CWE-79). 'host' is a raw, attacker (gopher server) controlled field taken directly from the response line (host = strchr(selector, TAB); ++host at lines 125/129) and is placed unescaped inside the double-quoted HREF attribute, while name and selector are escaped. A host value such as 'h" onmouseover="alert(1)' breaks out of the attribute and injects script into the HTML that line 339 (entry->append(outbuf.rawBuf(), outbuf.size())) sends to the client. The same unescaped host appears in the standard-link snprintf at lines 248-249; the telnet branch escapes it (rfc1738_escape_part(host), line 229), proving the omission here. No validation of host exists on any path.

evidence.snippet:
port = strchr(host, TAB);

                    if (port) {
evidence.reason: Origin of the NULL value: strchr returns NULL when the gopher line contains selector and host but no third TAB. The if (port) guard only wraps the port-chopping block (closes at line 154) and does not cover the later *port dereference, so a NULL port flows on to the telnet formatting branch.

NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476, denial of service). For a gopher line with gtype GOPHER_TELNET (e.g. '7x\tsel\thostonly\n'), port = strchr(host, TAB) at line 130 returns NULL, the if (port) block is skipped, and this statement evaluates *port with port == NULL, crashing the process that processes untrusted network data. There is no NULL or emptiness check on port between line 130 and this sink on any path; the same defect appears at line 233 in the else snprintf.

assumptions: gopherState->buf is assumed to be a TEMP_BUF_SIZE-byte buffer; its allocation is not in this code. The clamp at lines 77-81 keeps gopherState->len + llen <= TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1, which makes memcpy at line 86 in-bounds only under that assumption.

gopherState->len's initial value is assigned outside this code; within this code lines 87 and 95 maintain it in [0, TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1]. The candidate-1 trigger was instantiated without relying on the initial value (two-chunk sequence).
gopherState->conversion, ->entry and ->HTML_header_added are set outside this code; they select code paths but never sizes.
html_quote, rfc1738_escape_part, rfc1738_escape_unescaped and mimeGetIconURL are escaping/lookup helpers relied on per their documented semantics; their implementations are not shown.
LOCAL_ARRAY declares a fixed TEMP_BUF_SIZE-byte array; TEMP_BUF_SIZE's numeric value is not shown, and only relative bounds against it are used.
inbuf and len are supplied by the gopher state machine from socket reads; their CONTENT is attacker (gopher server) controlled, so they are treated as attacker-data per the data-origin impact model.
limitations: Integer overflow of gopherState->len + llen at line 77 would bypass the clamp and cause a huge memcpy at lines 86/92/93, but it requires the caller to pass len near INT_MAX with a matching ~2GB inbuf; no statement in this code produces that scale, so the trigger is speculative.

The reads port[1] and port[2] at line 152 can index up to two bytes past line[] only when a stale TAB from a previous longer line sits at index TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1; this depends on prior-iteration residue (line[llen] is never cleared) combined with a maximal-length line and was not simulated as a clean standalone trigger.
line[llen] is never NUL-terminated, so exactly one stale byte from a previously processed line can be parsed as part of the current line (in-bounds logic defect with no direct memory-safety impact).
The gopherState->overflowed flag set at line 80 is consumed by code not shown; its handling was not evaluated.

verdict.summary: BinaryBroadcastFiveFold consumes params.broadcast_shape[0..4] as the sole loop bounds and copy counts for reading both inputs and writing the output, with no validation anywhere in the function: the RuntimeShape parameters (unswitched_input1_shape, unswitched_input2_shape, output_shape) that define the true buffer extents are accepted but never read. A caller/model supplying broadcast_shape whose product exceeds the real input/output sizes drives elementwise_f/scalar_broadcast_f to write y0*y1*y2*y3*y4 elements through an output pointer advanced by the same tainted counts, producing attacker-controlled heap out-of-bounds writes (and out-of-bounds reads of both inputs), i.e. the missing broadcast-shape validation class of TFLite model-parsing vulnerabilities.

evidence.reason: Sink: the innermost loop is bounded only by the tainted y3, and elementwise_f is called with the tainted count y4 and raw input/output pointers, then output_data_ptr is advanced by y4 each iteration. Over the full loop nest the output pointer advances y0*y1*y2*y3*y4 elements past output_data with no check against the actual output extent (the output_shape parameter is never read anywhere in the function). Instantiated trigger: broadcast_shape = {2,2,2,2,2} with a 1-element output buffer makes the very first call write out[1] out of bounds and every subsequent iteration writes further out of bounds, a heap OOB write whose size is attacker-controlled.

Origin: all loop bounds and copy counts are read directly from params.broadcast_shape, an attacker-supplied parameter of this non-static function with no documented, asserted, or checked precondition anywhere in the given code, and never compared against the passed RuntimeShape extents. These five unvalidated ints are the sole determinants of how many elements are read from input1_data_ptr, input2_data_ptr and written through output_data_ptr.

assumptions: elementwise_f and scalar_broadcast_f process exactly their count argument (y4 / y3) elements, reading from the two input pointers and writing to the output pointer; this framework-callback semantics is relied on per the CALLEE BOUNDARY RULE (count argument plus the lockstep pointer advancement by the same count in this code).

The true extents of input1_data, input2_data, and output_data are defined by the accompanying RuntimeShape parameters; this code receives them but contains no statement that reads or enforces them, so the mismatch between broadcast_shape and actual buffer sizes is not rejected anywhere in this function.
limitations: The intended TFLite contract is that a Prepare stage derives broadcast_shape from the input/output shapes before calling this helper; that derivation and any validation live outside the given code and could not be quoted, so per GUARD ANCHORING it neither instantiates a safe path nor serves as a guard here.

Secondary edge case, same root cause: when y4 <= 0 the 'else if (input1_data_ptr != nullptr)' arm still executes the scalar branch (the condition tests a pointer, not the count), writing y0*y1*y2*y3 elements even when a y4 == 0 broadcast product implies an empty output.

Out-of-bounds reads of input1 (including the in-code dereference *input1_data_ptr in the scalar branch) and input2 follow from the same unvalidated broadcast_shape values; they are recorded as part of the primary finding rather than as separate evidence entries.

verdict.summary: DoCompute validates only the RANK relationship between updates, indices, and params ('updates.dims() == indices.dims() + params->dims() - 1') and only the PREFIX relationship (StartsWith), but never checks that the trailing dimensions of updates equal params.shape[1:]. An attacker supplies updates shaped [2,7] against a variable of shape [4,5] with indices [2]; every check passes, updates_flat becomes a 2x7 matrix while params_flat is a 4x5 matrix, and the ScatterFunctor call scatters update rows of width 7 into params rows of width 5, writing past row bounds (for the last row, past the end of the params buffer) with attacker-controlled values. The symmetric mismatch (updates narrower than params rows) yields an out-of-bounds read of the updates buffer whose contents are stored into the readable variable. The call statement passing the mismatched matrix dimensions is the defect: no path in this code validates them.

evidence.reason: updates_flat is built with inner width num_updates/N (attacker-controlled updates shape, e.g. 7) while params_flat (line 43) has inner width params.shape[1:] (e.g. 5); nothing on any path equates them, so the ScatterFunctor call scatters update rows wider than params rows, writing past the row and, for the last row, past the params buffer (heap OOB write), or narrower rows, reading past the updates allocation (OOB read into a readable variable). Trigger fully instantiated: params [4,5], indices [2], updates [2,7] passes all quoted checks.

evidence.snippet:
updates.dims() == 0 ||
                    updates.dims() == indices.dims() + params->dims() - 1,
evidence.reason: This is the only shape-consistency check, and it compares only the RANK (number of dimensions), not the dimension values. The invariant the kernel itself states ('updates.shape = indices.shape + params.shape[1:]') is therefore unenforced on values, letting mismatched inner dimensions reach the shaped<2> view and the scatter functor.

assumptions: Index is int32 (DataTypeToEnum<Index>) and the scatter functors are the framework's standard ScatterScalarFunctor/ScatterFunctor whose documented semantics are writing each update row into params[index] after validating index bounds; their internals are not shown and were not used to demote any candidate.
Input dtypes (indices of type Index, updates of type T) are enforced by op registration at the framework level.
params' shape is set at variable creation by the graph author; in the untrusted-model threat model the attacker controls it, and even feed-only attackers control the runtime updates/indices shapes.
limitations: params->dim_size(0) (line 29) is evaluated without any check that params->dims() >= 1; for a rank-0 variable it reads an indeterminate dimension, but the consequence (TensorShape internal behavior) is not shown, so the trigger's harmful value is not instantiated here.

This code takes no lock on the variable (v->mu()), unlike standard resource-variable kernels; a concurrent reshaping assign could race the checks at lines 11/29 against the use at lines 64-68. The window is exhibitable, but the harmful value it produces (inner-width mismatch) is already statically reachable without a race, so it widens rather than creates the primary finding.

The exact OOB direction (write past params rows when updates rows are wider vs read past the updates buffer when narrower) depends on the not-shown functor's inner loop bound; both directions are out-of-domain accesses and the write direction is the primary characterization.

verdict.summary: No fully instantiated vulnerability in the given code. The only dangerous memory operation, memcpy(data, ch->sample->data, ch->sample->dataLength), is guarded in execution order by an allocation sized from the identical expression (gf_filter_pck_new_alloc(ch->pid, ch->sample->dataLength, &data)) plus a failure-sentinel test (if (!pck) return GF_OUT_OF_MEM) on the sole path to the sink. All log format strings are literals. Remaining candidates fail trigger proof: the stale count vs gf_list_get candidate and the unchecked pck_data candidate each depend on mutation/return behavior of not-shown callees (isoffin_configure_pid, gf_filter_pck_get_data, isoffin_push_buffer) that this code neither quotes nor characterizes, and the arithmetic candidates (sample_dur *= nb_pack, dep_flags u8 packing) produce only non-security metadata effects.

assumptions: gf_filter_get_udta(filter) returns a valid ISOMReader*; no NULL check on read exists in this code and the framework's constructor guarantee is not quotable here.
gf_list_get(read->channels, i) for 0 <= i < gf_list_count(read->channels) returns non-NULL; this code never stores NULL into read->channels, but the insertion code is not shown.

isor_reader_get_sample/isor_reader_get_sample_from_item set ch->sample, ch->last_state, and advance ch->sample_num such that the while (nb_pck) loop terminates at track exhaustion; the parser is not shown.
ch->isLeading, ch->dependsOn, ch->dependedOn are 2-bit values and ch->sample->IsRAP is within the GF_FilterSAPType range; the producing parse code is not shown.
gf_filter_pck_new_alloc zeroes/initializes the output data pointer on failure so that the if (!pck) return arm precedes any use of data.
limitations: Stale count after channel-list reconfiguration: count = gf_list_count(read->channels) is captured once at function entry, then isoffin_configure_pid(filter, read->pid, GF_FALSE) is invoked in the DASH-switch retry path with no re-read of count and no NULL check on the ch returned by gf_list_get(read->channels, i) before if (!ch->playing). A NULL-deref (CWE-476) would require isoffin_configure_pid to shrink read->channels; that mutation is not shown in this code, so the trigger precondition is UNSOURCED and the candidate cannot be confirmed.

Unchecked packet-data pointer in memory-load mode: pck_data = gf_filter_pck_get_data(pck, &data_size); isoffin_push_buffer(filter, read, pck_data, data_size); has no NULL/emptiness sentinel test between the accessor and the callee. A NULL or unset size would require gf_filter_pck_get_data to return its failure sentinel for a fetched packet and would manifest inside the not-shown isoffin_push_buffer; neither link is characterizable from the given code.

min_offset_plus_one = 1 + ch->last_valid_sample_data_offset wraps to 0 if the offset equals U64_MAX, silently skipping isoffin_purge_mem (retained memory); no statement in this code can produce an U64_MAX offset, so the precondition is UNSOURCED.

sample_dur = ch->au_duration; sample_dur *= ch->sample->nb_pack; is an unchecked u32 multiply on attacker-influenced parsed values; the direct consequence is only an incorrect duration property on the output packet (no memory or control-flow effect), so it is not a security finding in this code.

dep_flags packing (dep_flags = ch->isLeading; dep_flags <<= 2; ... dep_flags |= ch->redundant;) has no & 3 mask on its inputs; if the not-shown parser allowed values > 3 the u8 would lose high bits, but the result is only stored as packet dependency metadata with no memory/indexing use.

The stsd-skip path (if (read->stsd && (ch->last_sample_desc_index != read->stsd) && ch->sample) { isor_reader_release_sample(ch); continue; }) does not decrement nb_pck, so one process call may parse and discard every remaining sample of a track; the work is linear in the input's own sample count, which is not attacker-scalable amplification.

(GF_FilterSAPType) ch->sample->IsRAP casts an attacker-influenced s32 with no range check; the out-of-range value is only stored on the packet and any harmful consumption would occur in downstream code not given.

verdict.summary: No instantiated security vulnerability in the given code. The empty-stack guard 'if (stack->top == 0) { return; }' covers every wddx_stack_top use in execution order and contains the historical WDDX stack-desync UAF (CVE-2016-9912); all stack pops are gated so top never goes negative and each entry is freed exactly once. The remaining defects are memory leaks (CWE-401): the EL_FIELD arm frees the entry without zval_ptr_dtor(&ent->data) or efree(ent->varname), and the UNDEF early-return path plus the non-container-parent path leak varname/data references. These retain memory only until PHP request shutdown, scale linearly with attacker input size, and cause no corruption, disclosure, bypass, or unbounded amplification, so they are not security vulnerabilities under the impact model. Object instantiation of attacker-chosen classes with property merge and __wakeup is inherent deserializer semantics whose harmful consequence would occur in not-shown gadget classes.

assumptions: expat delivers NUL-terminated element names ('name'), so the strcmp comparisons are in-domain; the given code only ever compares name against fixed constants, so no content-bearing sink exists for it.

php_wddx_push_element and php_wddx_process (not shown) push one fresh entry for every push-able element and set ent->data to string/array/undef types; consequently every elements[top-1] slot read by wddx_stack_top is a valid allocated entry, and ent1->data at the EL_BINARY arm is IS_STRING or IS_UNDEF (the UNDEF case being explicitly guarded by 'if (Z_TYPE(ent1->data) == IS_UNDEF)').

ent1->varname / stack->varname strings are NUL-terminated when produced by the not-shown push handler, so 'strlen(ent1->varname)' cannot over-read; no producer or terminator guarantee exists in the given code itself.
wddx_stack_top returns stack->elements[stack->top-1] without side effects; the given code guarantees top >= 1 at every call through the quoted entry guard and the 'stack->top > 1' gates.
php_base64_decode (characterizable standard-API semantics) always returns an allocated zend_string in non-strict mode; NULL occurs only on OOM, where PHP bails out before ZVAL_STR consumes it.

call_user_function_ex initializes *retval on success; its characterizable failure path for a missing method on an object without __call is a fatal-error bailout, so the subsequent zval_ptr_dtor(&retval) never consumes an uninitialized stack zval.

stack, entries, target_hash, and varname are never stored into any userland-visible container by any statement in this code, so __wakeup (attacker-selected class) cannot free or mutate the C-level stack state during the call.
limitations: EL_FIELD arm: 'wddx_stack_top(stack, (void **)&ent); efree(ent); stack->top--;'' omits zval_ptr_dtor(&ent->data) and efree(ent->varname) (upstream later added the dtor). Confirmed by STEP 5 fix-form search (no dtor, no varname free, no ownership-transfer call in that arm). Impact is a request-scoped memory leak bounded linearly by packet size and reclaimed at request shutdown by PHP's memory manager; no UAF is possible because the refcount is only left undecremented, never decremented twice. Not a vulnerability under the impact model.

Additional CWE-401 leaks: the IS_UNDEF early-return path 'stack->top--; efree(ent1);' leaks ent1->varname; the path where ent2->data is neither array nor object drops ent1->data without a dtor before 'efree(ent1);'. Same bounded, request-scoped impact; the 'worst case' is peak memory growth capped by memory_limit, not attacker-scalable unbounded retention.

Type confusion at the EL_BINARY sink (Z_STRVAL/Z_STRLEN on a hypothetical non-string, non-UNDEF ent1->data) is not instantiable: the only type producers are the not-shown push/process handlers, and the quoted UNDEF guard covers the only in-code-derivable non-string case. UNSOURCED precondition: a push handler assigning a non-string type.
'strlen(ent1->varname)' over-read requires an unterminated varname; the producer is not shown and no statement in this code creates varname strings. UNSOURCED precondition.

Uninitialized 'retval' reaching 'zval_ptr_dtor(&retval)' requires call_user_function_ex to return without initializing retval; the only characterizable such path (missing method, no __call) bailouts out first. Any other failure mode depends on not-shown zend_call_function internals.

Deserializer object injection (attacker-chosen pce via zend_hash_find_ptr on an attacker string, zend_hash_merge of attacker properties, __wakeup invocation) is by-design deserializer behavior identical to unserialize; the security consequence exists only in gadget classes not given, so the impact chain breaks at uncharacterizable code.
The known WDDX OOB write (CVE-2017-11143) resides in php_wddx_push_element, which is not part of the given code; nothing can be concluded about it here.

Stack desync via unbalanced poppable end tags (the pre-fix CVE-2016-9912 trigger) is fully contained by the quoted entry guard 'if (stack->top == 0) { return; }': with top==1 the EL_FIELD arm frees a valid entry, leaves top==0, and the next pop returns at the guard before any dereference.

verdict.summary: No instantiated security vulnerability. The allocation/memset size expressions are verbatim-identical and bounded by UBYTE m_ucCount (max 255), so no integer overflow or size mismatch is reachable (max 16320 bytes); the array write m_ppDownsampler[i] is guarded on every path by the loop condition i < m_ucCount, which holds at both boundary values 0 and 255; and the m_pLargestScale call is guarded. The remaining candidates — memset on an unchecked AllocMem result (possible NULL only on allocation failure of a small, non-attacker-scalable request), the unchecked ComponentOf(i) dereference (requires an unsourced relation between m_ucCount and the frame component count), and the unchecked CreateDownsampler result (consumer not shown) — are recorded as limitations because their trigger preconditions cannot be instantiated from the given code.

assumptions: m_pEnviron->AllocMem may throw rather than return NULL on failure (Accusoft convention) — not quotable from the given code; the verdict does not rely on it, since allocation sizes are bounded at 16320/2040 bytes and failure is not attacker-inducible.
m_ucCount is assumed to equal the frame's component count, as set elsewhere in the codebase — no assignment to m_ucCount exists in the given code (UNSOURCED).
m_pFrame, m_pLargestScale, m_ulPixelWidth, m_ulPixelHeight, and m_bSubsampling are members initialized outside this function (UNSOURCED).
Deployment context (library vs. tool, privilege level) is unknown and was not used to demote or promote any candidate.
limitations: Missing NULL check on the AllocMem result before memset at both allocation sites (CWE-476 pattern): `m_ppEncodingMCU = ...AllocMem(...); memset(m_ppEncodingMCU,0,...)` and the analogous m_ppDownsampler pair. Step 5 confirmed no check of any form exists on any path, but the trigger requires an allocation failure of at most 16320 bytes (UBYTE-bounded), which no attacker input in this code can induce.

Unchecked dereference `comp->SubXOf()` on `m_pFrame->ComponentOf(i)`: no NULL check in this code, but triggering requires ComponentOf to return NULL or i to exceed the frame's component table — the m_ucCount/component-count relation is UNSOURCED and the callee is not characterizable.
The return of DownsamplerBase::CreateDownsampler is stored without a NULL check; any harmful use occurs in code not shown and cannot be characterized.
No NULL check on m_pEnviron or m_pFrame before member calls; both are UNSOURCED with no in-code producer of NULL.

verdict.summary: The function is a small, fail-closed VM routine. The only memory-access sink on a parameter is the dereference c->mt, whose NULL-table consequence is guarded by 'if (h && mt_del(mrb, h, mid)) return;' before the call, and the error path raises NameError rather than silently succeeding. The format string is a literal constant, so no format-string injection is possible. The remaining candidate shapes (NULL class pointer from a caller, invalid symbol id, stale method table) all require trigger preconditions or impact links located in code not given (unshown callers, uncharacterizable callee internals, unsourced struct fields), so none is an instantiated vulnerability in this code.

assumptions: mrb is a valid mrb_state* execution context; this code performs no validation of it and the C-API contract is not shown.
MRB_CLASS_ORIGIN's macro body is not given; in mruby it reads c->tt and redirects an ICLASS to its origin class, i.e. it dereferences c. Its behavior cannot be quoted from the given code.
mt_del is assumed to be a hash-table delete that hashes/masks the symbol key (no raw indexing by mid) and returns nonzero only if the key was found; its internals are not shown.
mrb_name_error is assumed to raise a NameError exception; its %n and %C formatting internals are not shown.
Callers of this exported function (e.g., mruby's module-level remove_method shim) are not shown; whether they can ever pass NULL or a non-interned symbol is unknown from the given code.
limitations: C1 (CWE-476 shape): a NULL c reaches the dereference 'h = c->mt;' with no guard anywhere in this code (verified absent in STEP 5), causing a process crash. Not counted as a finding: the trigger requires an unshown caller to pass an invalid reference, and the denial-of-service impact requires a party across a trust boundary whose reach to this function is not exhibited by any statement in the given code.

C2: a never-interned mrb_sym passed by a C caller would reach mt_del (safe under hash-table semantics) and the '%n' formatter of mrb_name_error; any mishandling of such an id occurs inside an uncharacterizable callee, and this code contains no producer of non-interned symbol ids.
C3: c->mt is UNSOURCED in this code (no assignment exists here), so staleness or corruption of the method table pointer cannot be triggered or excluded from the given code alone.

C4: the absence of a frozen-class check before removal is a language-semantics matter (mruby performs such checks elsewhere in its codebase); no security state is misrepresented on any path in this code.

verdict.summary: AutoParallel::Initialize indexes each apply-gradients node's input list with a fixed position from gradient_pos (values 2 through 9) without ever checking the node's actual input count. A malicious GraphDef (model file) containing an apply-gradients op node with fewer inputs than its designated gradient position causes an out-of-bounds read at apply_gradients_node->input(...) and an out-of-bounds write when a std::string is assigned through the pointer returned by mutable_input(...), corrupting process memory in the release build of the graph-optimization path.

evidence.reason: The index gradient_pos[apply_gradients_op] is a fixed constant (2-9, from the map initialized at lines 50-60) applied to the node's input list, whose length is attacker-controlled serialized graph content. No statement in the function compares the index against input_size(). With a node {name: "adv", op: "ApplyAdam", input: ["var"]}, input(9) reads out of bounds and mutable_input(9) = div_node->name() writes a std::string through an out-of-bounds element pointer, yielding memory corruption (CWE-787) caused by unvalidated index handling (CWE-129).

Origin of the tainted value: a node is admitted to apply_gradients_nodes_ solely on its op string; its input list (attacker-controlled content from item.graph) is never validated for length, so a malformed apply-gradients node with fewer inputs than its gradient position flows unvalidated into the out-of-bounds input()/mutable_input() accesses at lines 67 and 70.

assumptions: The GrapplerItem passed to Initialize is treated as attacker-data (deserialized model/GraphDef content) per the data-origin impact model, since the method consumes serialized graph state at its entry point.

Protobuf RepeatedField/RepeatedPtrField accessors (input(), mutable_input()) index the container without release-mode runtime bounds checks (only DCHECK in debug), a characterizable standard-library behavior relied on per the callee boundary rule.

AddNodeDivConst/AddNodeDiv/ComputeTransitiveFanin/IsDequeueOp are not-shown helpers; their observable behavior at these call sites was characterized only by their signatures and return-value handling in this code.
limitations: Line 123 logs all_nodes_.size() under the label "Number of shared nodes" — a cosmetic logging inaccuracy with no security effect.

The result of AddNodeDivConst() (line 48) is not checked for NULL before use at lines 49 and 68, but the helper is not shown and standard C++ allocation failure terminates via exception; no security impact could be instantiated in this code.

The dequeue_node pointer dereference at line 106 is safe: input_nodes is populated only inside the if (dequeue_node) branch at lines 88-92, so the loop over input_nodes executes zero iterations when dequeue_node is null.

If two nodes share a name and the first-inserted one is not an apply-gradients op, gradient_pos[apply_gradients_op] default-constructs index 0 via map operator[]; this is subsumed by the confirmed missing input-count check (index 0 with an empty input list is out of bounds).

verdict.summary: The MklRequantizePerChannel Compute kernel derives `depth` solely from input_min_vec.NumElements() and never checks it against the input tensor's channel dimension (input.dim_size(3)), yet passes the depth-sized `scales` vector to mkldnn set_output_scales with mask 2 (per-output-channel scales). An attacker supplying, e.g., a 4-D input with 256 channels and a 1-element min/max vec passes all three OP_REQUIRES checks, so the MKL-DNN reorder indexes scales[0..255] against a 1-element (4-byte) heap allocation, reading up to ~1020 bytes out of bounds; the OOB-read floats directly scale output tensor elements readable by the attacker (heap disclosure) and large channel counts can push the read far past the allocation (crash/DoS of the shared process).

evidence.snippet:
mkldnn::primitive_attr reorder_attr;
    reorder_attr.set_output_scales(2, scales);
evidence.reason: Sink: set_output_scales(2, scales) registers per-output-channel scales (mask 2) indexed by the input's channel count input.dim_size(3), but `scales` was allocated at line 42 as std::vector<float> scales(depth) where depth comes only from the min-vec. No statement in this code relates depth to the channel dimension, so with input [1,1,1,256] and min/max vecs of shape [1] (depth=1), the reorder reads scales[1..255] out of bounds of a 4-byte heap allocation; the OOB floats scale attacker-readable output values.

evidence.snippet: size_t depth = input_min_vec.NumElements();
evidence.reason: Origin of the faulty value: depth is taken from the attacker-controlled min-vec element count. The only subsequent checks (input.dims() == 4 at line 20, input_min_vec.dim_size(0) == depth at line 24, input_max_vec.dim_size(0) == depth at line 28) are rank and min/max-vec self-consistency checks; none compares depth to input.dim_size(3), which is the missing-check site for the undersized scales array.

assumptions: Input dtypes (qint32 input, float min/max/requested tensors) are presumed constrained by the TensorFlow op registration, which is not part of the given code; flat<T>() dtype enforcement is therefore treated as an interface contract.

MKL-DNN semantics relied on per the CALLEE BOUNDARY RULE: set_output_scales(mask=2, scales) stores per-output-channel scales that the reorder kernel indexes by channel, and TFShapeToMklDnnDimsInNCHW(input.shape(), FORMAT_NHWC) maps input.dim_size(3) to the channel dimension.
out_type_ and cpu_engine_ are kernel configuration set outside this code; the confirmed trigger is independent of their values.
limitations: The loop counter `int i` compared against `size_t depth` (line 43) can only misbehave when depth > INT_MAX (an ~8 GB min-vec); after signed overflow the promoted comparison ends the loop, and indices remain in-bounds for i in [0, depth), so no instantiated security impact.
If both requested min and max are 0.0, requested_min_max is 0 and scales become inf/NaN; this produces garbage output values but no memory-safety, disclosure, or amplification effect.
DCHECK(input_requested_min_float < 0.0f) at line 32 is a debug-only assertion; in release builds it is a no-op, but no reachable sink in this code depends on the asserted invariant for memory safety.
A 0-dimensional (scalar) min-vec would make dim_size(0) access depend on TensorFlow TensorShape internals not shown; this edge is subsumed by the primary finding and not separately instantiated.

verdict.summary: All memory-safety sinks executed in this code are guarded by quotable, edge-tested checks: the narrowing cast is preceded by 'if (example_weights.size() >= std::numeric_limits<int>::max())' with an error return, label tensor length is checked with 'if (example_labels.size() != num_examples)', and the flat-tensor accesses are bounded by the loop 'for (int example_id = 0; example_id < num_examples; ++example_id)'. Real gaps exist (dense_features_inputs size is never validated against num_dense_features before being passed to CreateDenseFeatureRepresentation; sparse_feature_values_inputs may be empty while num_sparse_features > 0; num_features_ = num_sparse_features + num_dense_features can overflow signed int; the tensorflow_cpu_worker_threads() pointer is dereferenced unchecked), but each of these has its harmful use inside helper code not given, so no impact chain is instantiated within this code.

assumptions: This Initialize is assumed to be called by the TensorFlow op framework with OpKernelContext; the framework's behavior of context->input/input_list (fetching session-supplied tensors) is taken as documented framework semantics.
The device on which the kernel runs is not constrained by any statement in this code; whether tensorflow_cpu_worker_threads() can return null for it is unknown from the given code.
The contents and behavior of CreateSparseFeatureRepresentation, CreateDenseFeatureRepresentation, and ComputeSquaredNormPerExample are not given and were not relied on for any conclusion.
limitations: Missing size validation of dense_features_inputs against num_dense_features: this code checks 'sparse_example_indices_inputs.size() != num_sparse_features' and the analogous checks for sparse_feature_indices and (conditionally) sparse_feature_values, but no statement compares dense_features_inputs.size() to num_dense_features before the call 'TF_RETURN_IF_ERROR(CreateDenseFeatureRepresentation(worker_threads, num_examples, num_dense_features, weights, dense_features_inputs, &examples_))'. If the not-shown callee indexes dense_features_inputs[i] for i in [0, num_dense_features), an out-of-bounds read (OpInputList operator[] is unchecked in release builds) would result; the harmful use is in code not given, so the impact chain is not instantiated here.

When num_sparse_features_with_values <= 0, sparse_feature_values_inputs is never fetched (the fetch is inside 'if (num_sparse_features_with_values > 0)') and is passed empty to CreateSparseFeatureRepresentation while num_sparse_features may be positive; whether the callee handles the empty list is not shown.

Signed integer overflow candidate: 'num_features_ = num_sparse_features + num_dense_features;' can overflow (e.g., num_sparse_features = INT_MAX, num_dense_features = 2) since neither parameter is bounded anywhere in this code, and the wrapped value persists in the member; however num_features_ is never consumed in the given code, so no impact is instantiated.

Potential NULL dereference: 'const DeviceBase::CpuWorkerThreads& worker_threads = *context->device()->tensorflow_cpu_worker_threads();' dereferences an unchecked pointer; the precondition (a device whose tensorflow_cpu_worker_threads() returns null) is UNSOURCED in this code.

Resource consumption: an attacker-supplied example_weights tensor of up to INT_MAX-1 elements (after passing the quoted size check) drives examples_.resize plus per-example nested resizes, i.e., memory retention proportional to the attacker's own input size with a bounded constant factor; classified as proportional use on attacker-supplied size with a terminal allocation failure, not attacker-scalable amplification beyond the input's own footprint.

Casts and flat accessors were verified safe only with respect to the guards quoted in the given code; behavior of Eigen TensorMap accessors outside the verified bounds was not exercised because the loop bound and size-equality checks keep every access in range.

verdict.summary: In the run-mode branch of the JPEG-LS sample-interleaved scan decoder, the decoded run length from DecodeRun(length, m_lRunIndex[0]) is never validated against the remaining line length before the fill loop. The loop 'while(run) { ... *lp[cx]++ = a[cx] << preshift; ... run--,length--; }' writes one sample per component per iteration and decrements length with it. A crafted entropy-coded scan that decodes run > length makes the loop write past the end of the line buffers (heap out-of-bounds write), underflows the signed length counter, and because 'if (length)' (line 83) is true for negative values and the outer 'do {...} while(--length)' never reaches zero from below, the decoder continues unbounded out-of-bounds writes with attacker-influenced sample values.

evidence.reason: The fill loop is bounded only by the decoded run value, not by the remaining samples on the line. lp[cx] was set to the start of a line buffer of exactly m_ulWidth[0] samples (line 41), and length = m_ulWidth[0] (line 36). When the attacker-decoded run exceeds length, iteration W+1 executes '*lp[cx]++ = a[cx] << preshift;' past the end of the line buffer (out-of-bounds write), and 'run--,length--;' underflows the signed length counter, so the subsequent 'if (length)' (line 83) and 'while(--length)' (line 155) never terminate the decoding, continuing OOB writes. No check, clamp, mask, error arm, or failure-sentinel test anywhere in this code bounds run to length before the first write.

evidence.snippet: LONG run = DecodeRun(length,m_lRunIndex[0]);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: the run length is a parse of the attacker-controlled entropy-coded scan segment. Its result is used as the loop bound at line 69 with no range validation on any path in this code; a crafted JPEG-LS scan decodes a run larger than the remaining line length, which is the instantiated trigger of the out-of-bounds write at line 75.

assumptions: DecodeRun is not shown; per guard anchoring, an unquoted clip inside it cannot be assumed. Its result is treated as attacker-controlled parse output because it decodes the attacker-supplied bitstream. If DecodeRun itself guaranteed run <= length, the fill loop would be safe, but no such bound is quotable from the given code.

m_ucCount is assigned outside this code (scan header); a sample-interleaved scan with m_ucCount >= 1 is assumed so that the write loop executes. 'assert(m_ucCount < 4);' (line 26) is the only quoted check on it and is compiled out in release builds (NDEBUG).
LONG is assumed a signed type of at least 32 bits (the code's error-mapping logic relies on signed values).
m_ulWidth[0], m_ulRemaining[0], m_ucLowBit, m_lLimit, m_lJ, m_lRunIndex, and m_pFrame->HeightOf() are set by the frame/scan parser not shown; their bounds cannot be quoted here.
limitations: int truncation: 'int lines = m_ulRemaining[0];' (line 4) could yield negative lines if m_ulRemaining[0] exceeded INT_MAX, but the magnitude of m_ulRemaining[0] is not producible or quotable in this code (UNSOURCED); the DNL path 'if (m_pFrame->HeightOf() == 0) { lines = 8; }' and 'if (lines > 8) lines = 8;' cover the shown cases.
UBYTE overflow in 'preshift = m_ucLowBit + FractionalColorBitsOf();' (line 5) or a shift >= type width in 'a[cx] << preshift' cannot be instantiated: both operands are UNSOURCED here.

m_ulWidth[0] == 0 would make the inner do-while execute once and then run 'while(--length)' with length = -1, causing OOB writes; m_ulWidth[0] is never assigned in this code (UNSOURCED), so this trigger is not instantiated.
m_ucCount >= 4 in a release build would index line[4]/lp[4]/a[4]/d[4] out of bounds; only an assert (line 26) guards this and the value is UNSOURCED here.
The bounds of m_lRunIndex[0] relative to the m_lJ[] array in 'GolombDecode(k,m_lLimit - m_lJ[m_lRunIndex[0]] - 1);' (line 101) cannot be verified from the given code.

verdict.summary: This DeleteSessionTensor kernel validates every value it consumes where a guard is required within this code: the input tensor's scalar shape is enforced by 'OP_REQUIRES(ctx, TensorShapeUtils::IsScalar(handle.shape()), errors::InvalidArgument("`handle` must be scalar"))' before the scalar accessor, and the session-state pointer is enforced non-null by 'OP_REQUIRES(ctx, session_state != nullptr, ...)' before 'session_state->DeleteTensor(name)'. The attacker-controlled string 'name' flows only into a keyed delete whose error status is propagated with OP_REQUIRES_OK (no fail-open). No injection, memory-safety, or authz sink exists at any quoted statement. The one unvalidated precondition (input dtype before 'handle.scalar<tstring>()()') could not be triggered from this code because the dtype-binding machinery is not shown; it is recorded as a limitation, not a finding.

assumptions: The op's input dtype (DT_STRING) is fixed by op registration/kernel dispatch machinery not present in this code; this code itself performs no dtype check.
session_state->DeleteTensor(name) is assumed to perform a standard keyed delete returning a Status; its implementation is not shown.
OP_REQUIRES/OP_REQUIRES_OK are assumed to return from Compute with an error status when the condition fails (standard TF macro semantics).
limitations: Type-confusion/OOB-read candidate at 'const string& name = handle.scalar<tstring>()();': this code checks scalar shape (quoted, lines 3-4) but never checks the tensor dtype. A non-DT_STRING scalar reaching this line would be reinterpreted as a tstring. The trigger precondition (a mismatched-dtype tensor reaching this kernel) is UNSOURCED in the given code, since dtype binding occurs in not-shown registration/dispatch; the candidate is therefore speculative and does not affect the verdict.

Authz impact of deleting an arbitrary session tensor by attacker-chosen name could not be evaluated: whether session state crosses a trust boundary depends on deployment context not quotable from this code.

verdict.summary: HttpFileImpl::save writes an uploaded file to a destination built by appending the client-controlled upload filename (fileName_) to the target directory without validating it. The only guard on fileName_ is an emptiness check ('if (fileName_.empty()) return -1;'), and the anchoring logic at lines 7-9 inspects only the caller-supplied path argument, never the filename. Because std::filesystem operator/ retains '..' components lexically and replaces the whole path when the appended filename is absolute, a multipart filename such as '../../www/shell.php' or '/etc/cron.d/x' escapes the upload directory and yields an arbitrary file write with attacker-controlled content.

evidence.snippet: return saveTo(fsPath / fsFileName);
evidence.reason: Sink: the destination path is constructed by concatenating the base directory with fsFileName, which is derived from the client-supplied upload filename and is never checked for absoluteness or '..' components on any path in this code. Instantiated trigger: with fileName_ = '../../app_www/shell.php' and path = 'media', this call becomes saveTo('/srv/app/uploads/media/../../app_www/shell.php'), writing attacker content to /srv/app/app_www/shell.php; with an absolute filename the operator/ semantics replace the base entirely, giving an arbitrary-path write. Root cause: missing validation of the externally controlled filename component before the filesystem write.

evidence.snippet: filesystem::path fsFileName(utils::toNativePath(fileName_));
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: the client-supplied multipart filename (fileName_) enters path construction here; the only check it undergoes anywhere in this code is the emptiness test 'if (fileName_.empty()) return -1;' at lines 4-5, which rejects only the empty string and passes traversal ('../..') and absolute ('/etc/...') filenames through to the sink at line 27.

assumptions: fileName_ is populated from the client-supplied multipart Content-Disposition filename by the framework's request parser, which is not part of the given code; per the data-origin model it is treated as attacker-controlled request content (this class is the server-side HTTP upload abstraction, as evidenced by HttpAppFrameworkImpl::instance().getUploadPath() and the save-to-disk purpose).

utils::toNativePath is characterized as path-separator conversion (its name and role); nothing indicates it strips '..' components or absolute roots, and the absolute-filename case survives any separator conversion.

saveTo (not shown) is characterized per the callee boundary rule as writing the uploaded file's content to the given path; the defect is the unvalidated destination argument at the call site, which this code constructs.
limitations: The 'path' parameter is deliberately passed through when it begins with '.' or '..' (lines 7-9) and embedded '..' components are never normalized; traversal through this argument requires an application to forward request-derived data as the save path, which is not shown here, so that trigger is not instantiated in this code.
assert(!path.empty()) compiles out under NDEBUG; the empty-path case is anchored to the upload path by '!fsPath.has_parent_path()' at line 8 and has no identified security effect.
The upload base directory returned by getUploadPath() is framework configuration not assigned in this code; no guard depends on its value, and the filename-based traversal escapes regardless of it.

verdict.summary: Analysis of this TensorFlow TensorHandleOp Compute method found no fully instantiable security vulnerability. The code stores an input tensor in the tensor store and produces a handle (ResourceHandle or string) referencing it. Error handling via OP_REQUIRES_OK is present at allocation and store-addition points. A theoretical type confusion exists in the else branch where handle->flat<tstring>() assumes DT_STRING output dtype without explicit verification, but the trigger requires an op registration with a non-RESOURCE non-STRING output type which is not shown in the given code and cannot be instantiated from it.

assumptions: The op registration for this kernel restricts the output dtype to DT_RESOURCE or DT_STRING, as suggested by the code structure (if/else for resource vs legacy V1 string) and the comment 'Legacy behavior in V1'.
MakeResourceHandle<Tensor> creates a ResourceHandle struct by filling fields without a failure mode requiring error checking.
ctx->tensor_store() and ctx->session_state() return non-null pointers during op execution as guaranteed by the TensorFlow framework.
GetNewId() produces unique 64-bit IDs from a session-wide counter with no realistic overflow concern.
limitations: Type confusion candidate: the else branch calls handle->flat<tstring>() without verifying expected_output_dtype(0) == DT_STRING. If the op registration allowed output dtypes other than DT_RESOURCE and DT_STRING, this would cause type confusion (CWE-843). However, the op registration is not shown in the given code, making this trigger precondition UNSOURCED. The op registration field would need to be inspected to confirm or deny this.

Tensor store growth: an attacker executing graphs with many TensorHandleOp nodes could accumulate stored tensors without consumption, potentially exhausting memory. This is a general resource management characteristic of the tensor store mechanism managed at the session level, not a specific defect in this code.

verdict.summary: The RequantizePerChannel kernel's requested_max validation is a copy-paste of the requested_min check: the OP_REQUIRES guarding input_requested_max tests input_requested_min.NumElements() == 1, so input_requested_max is never validated. An attacker feeding an empty (0-element) DT_FLOAT tensor as requested_output_max reaches input_requested_max.flat<float>()(0), an out-of-bounds heap read in release builds; the leaked value is written verbatim to the output_max tensor the attacker can read back.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the guard meant to validate requested_output_max re-checks input_requested_min.NumElements() == 1 (line 31) instead of input_requested_max, so no check on requested_max exists on any path. Instantiated trigger: attacker supplies a 0-element DT_FLOAT tensor at kRequestMaxIndex (line 29) while requested_min is a valid scalar; the wrong-variable check passes and line 34 reads flat<float>()(0) from a 0-element view, an out-of-bounds heap read (TF flat bounds assert is DCHECK-only in release). The read value flows into requested_min_max and is written to output_max->flat<float>()(0) = input_requested_max_float, giving a disclosure path to attacker-readable output.

assumptions: TensorFlow release builds compile out the DCHECK bounds assertion in flat<T>()(i), so the element access at line 34 is unchecked for a 0-element tensor (standard framework semantics relied on per the callee boundary rule).
Tensor::flat<T> enforces dtype DT_FLOAT with a CHECK, so the attacker supplies an empty float tensor rather than a mismatched dtype.
Op kernel Compute is a trust-boundary intake point: tensor contents and shapes at ctx->input(...) are attacker-data per the handler-function rule, regardless of deployment.
limitations: Signed/unsigned mismatch in 'for (int i = 0; i < depth; ++i)' with size_t depth: triggering requires a >=2^31-element (8GB+) input_min_vec, and the int wrap converts to a huge size_t making the loop exit before any out-of-bounds access; not a memory-safety defect here.

depth is never validated against input.dim_size(3) (channels); a mismatched scales vector relies on mkldnn set_output_scales/reorder primitive-desc validation throwing mkldnn::error, which this code catches and converts to an error status (characterizable callee); no corruption in this code.
Float division by zero when both requested scalars are 0.0f produces IEEE inf/NaN scales and garbage output, but no crash or memory-safety effect.
out_type_ and cpu_engine_ are UNSOURCED members (no assignment in this code); out_type_ is first consumed at line 36, after the confirmed sink, so it neither gates the trigger nor serves as a guard.

The QINT8 branch checks input_requested_min_float < 0.0f while its error message names requested_output_max, and the requested_max error message names the wrong variable; these are cosmetic validation-message inconsistencies, not security-state misrepresentation.
A non-float requested_max tensor would trigger a TF CHECK abort (DoS in a shared process); this is subsumed by the confirmed out-of-bounds read on the same unvalidated input.

verdict.summary: All memory-relevant sinks in this op kernel are guarded by quotable checks in execution order: dims must be a 1-D vector (OP_REQUIRES IsVector), must have exactly input.dims() elements (OP_REQUIRES input_dims == dims.dim_size(0)), input rank is capped at 8 (OP_REQUIRES input_dims <= 8) before the 0..8 switch dispatch, and the output allocation status is checked (OP_REQUIRES_OK) before output is used. The residual gaps — no dtype check on dims before dims.vec<bool>() and no default arm in the switch — were trigger-simulated: a non-bool dims tensor yields an in-bounds under-read (every TF dtype has element width >= 1 byte, so reading dim_size(0) bytes never overruns the buffer) with only semantic confusion inside the not-shown HandleReverseCase; a switch fall-through requires a negative tensor rank, which no statement in this code can produce (UNSOURCED). No instantiated trigger reaches a memory-corruption, disclosure, bypass, injection, or amplification impact at any quoted or characterizable statement.

assumptions: context->input(0) and context->input(1) return valid live tensors when this kernel runs; input-slot existence is enforced by the not-shown executor, not quotable in this code.
Tensor rank (input.dims()) is non-negative because TensorShape forbids negative rank in the not-shown framework; this code contains no statement producing or checking a lower bound on rank.

The registered op signature constrains the dtype of the dims tensor in the not-shown framework; this code itself performs no dtype check, and the analysis did not rely on the framework constraint as a guard.
OP_REQUIRES / OP_REQUIRES_OK macro semantics (return from Compute on failure) are standard TensorFlow framework behavior relied on for the allocation and validation guards.
limitations: Candidate: missing dtype validation on dims before dims.vec<bool>() (CWE-125/CWE-843 style type confusion). Trigger instantiated (non-bool dims tensor), but at the quoted call site the read of dim_size(0) bytes is in-bounds for every TensorFlow dtype (minimum element width 1 byte), so no out-of-bounds access occurs in this code; the only misuse of the confused booleans happens inside HandleReverseCase, which is not shown and is not characterizable per the callee boundary rule. Recorded as a latent robustness/correctness gap, not a vulnerability in this code.

Candidate: switch (input_dims) has no default arm, so a rank outside [0,8] would fall through and leave output 0 unset. Upper bound is blocked by the quoted 'input_dims <= 8' check; the lower-bound precondition (negative rank) has no producer in this code and is UNSOURCED, so the trigger is speculative.

HandleReverseCase<Device, T, NDIMS> is not shown; if it mishandles the dims bool values or the output tensor, that defect would live in the callee. This code passes arguments verified in-domain: a 1-D bool-viewed vector of length exactly NDIMS and a non-null allocated output.

verdict.summary: BinaryBroadcastFiveFold consumes attacker-controlled broadcast dimensions (params.broadcast_shape[0..4]) as loop bounds and pointer increments with no validation anywhere in the function, despite receiving the input and output RuntimeShape parameters that could be used to bound them. The total number of elements written through elementwise_f/scalar_broadcast_f (y0*y1*y2*y3*y4) is never checked against the output buffer size, so a caller passing broadcast_shape inconsistent with the allocated buffers causes an out-of-bounds write past output_data, and out-of-bounds reads past the input buffers.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values: the five loop-bound/pointer-increment dimensions are read from caller-supplied params.broadcast_shape with no validation. The function receives unswitched_input1_shape, unswitched_input2_shape and output_shape (lines 2, 4, 6) that could bound these values, but never reads them, so no guard exists on any path.

Out-of-bounds write sink (general path): output_data_ptr is advanced by y4 for every i3 iteration (and input pointers likewise), so the callbacks write y0*y1*y2*y3*y4 elements total. With no check that this product fits the output buffer, a caller passing broadcast_shape = {2,2,2,2,2} against an 8-element output buffer writes elements 8 and 9 past the buffer on the second i1/i2 pass. Trigger fully instantiated from this function's own parameter surface.

Second write sink (y4 <= 1 path, including the boundary value y4 == 0 which this branch accepts instead of rejecting): scalar_broadcast_f writes y3 elements at output_data_ptr and dereferences *input1_data_ptr, advancing by y3 per iteration for y0*y1*y2*y3 total writes, again with no bound against the output buffer or the input buffers.

assumptions: Deployment context (e.g., that callers are TFLite kernel wrappers that validate shapes against tensor buffers before calling) is not quotable from this code and was not used to demote any candidate.

elementwise_f/scalar_broadcast_f are callback function pointers whose bodies are not shown; their write behavior (write count elements at the output pointer) is characterized only by this code's comment ('The innermost loop is an elementwise add of sections of the arrays') and their call signatures, per the callee boundary rule.
limitations: Out-of-bounds READS of the input buffers are partially covered by a documented contract in the given comment ('input1.shape.FlatSize = y0 * y1 * y2 * y4, input2.shape.FlatSize = y0 * y2 * y3 * y4'), so the read-side trigger requires the caller to violate a documented precondition; the write-side (output buffer size) has no documented contract or check and is the primary finding.

Candidate C4: if broadcast_category is neither fast-broadcast category, the switched_params/data swap mispairs quantization offsets and inputs, but the shown consequence is arithmetic mis-computation, not memory corruption or bypass; impact outside this code is not characterized.

Candidate C3: integer overflow of y0*y1*y2*y3*y4 is not exercised as written because pointer advances are incremental (+= y4 per iteration) and no single wide product is used for allocation or copy sizing in this code.
Null initialization of input2_data_ptr (lines 49, 78) is always overwritten before first use on every path where the loops execute (lines 51, 80 precede the calls); no defect.

verdict.summary: patternRow renders effect columns by indexing the fxColors and extFxColors palettes with the raw pattern cell value pat->data[i][index], which is content parsed from a user-loaded song file. The only checks are an ==-1 sentinel test and a one-sided <0x10/<0xe0 bucket chain: a negative value other than -1 passes '<0x10' and indexes fxColors with a negative index, and any value above 0xff falls into the unbounded else arm extFxColors[value-0xe0]. Sibling columns are fully guarded (instrument: '<0 || >=insLen'; volume: clamps to [0,127]), proving the omission, so a crafted song file causes out-of-bounds reads (crash/DoS or garbage memory consumed as color) when the pattern is displayed.

evidence.snippet:
if (pat->data[i][index]<0x10) {
            ImGui::PushStyleColor(ImGuiCol_Text,uiColors[fxColors[pat->data[i][index]]]);
evidence.reason: The effect cell pat->data[i][index] (signed, file-derived) is checked only against ==-1 (line 194) before this use; any negative value other than -1 satisfies '<0x10' and reaches fxColors with a negative index, which is out of bounds for any C array. Trigger instantiated with a crafted song file containing an effect cell of -2 in a visible, non-collapsed channel; execution order verified: the ==-1 test at 194 is the first use and does not cover -2.

evidence.snippet:
} else {
            ImGui::PushStyleColor(ImGuiCol_Text,uiColors[extFxColors[pat->data[i][index]-0xe0]]]);
evidence.reason: The final else arm of the effect-color chain has no upper bound: every value >= 0xe0 from attacker-controlled pattern data indexes extFxColors at value-0xe0, which for a signed cell reaches 32671 (e.g., a file cell of 0x2000 yields index 7936, reading far past the palette). No clamp, mask, range check, or error arm exists anywhere on the path, unlike the instrument column's explicit bounds check at line 120.

evidence.snippet: const DivPattern* pat=patCache[j];
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted data: the DivPattern object reached through the patCache parameter holds pattern content parsed from a user-loaded song file (untrusted serialized state per discipline 3); its effect cells are consumed as array indices at lines 200 and 218 with no validation on any path in this code.

assumptions: DivPattern::data is a signed integer array; signedness is evidenced in-code by the ==-1 sentinel tests (lines 116, 154, 194), but the exact declared width (short in the codebase) is not shown, so the 32767 maximum used for the extFxColors index is assumed from that width.

fxColors and extFxColors are fixed-size color palettes (intended domains 0x00-0x0f and 0xe0-0xff per the chain's own bucket structure); their sizes are not declared in the given code. The fxColors negative-index finding does not depend on the size; the extFxColors finding assumes the palette is not 32672 entries.

Pattern data, chanShow/chanCollapse, effectRows, patLen and insLen originate from a song file loaded by code not shown; no decode-side constraint on effect cell values is quotable, and per the rules such unshown constraints may not be relied upon.
limitations: chans (parameter) is used as loop bound and as patChanX[chans] index with no check against the channel-array sizes; triggering harm requires a caller passing chans exceeding those arrays, and neither the caller nor the array sizing is shown — contract unquotable, cannot be instantiated from this code.

The row guard 'if (i<0 || i>=e->song.patLen)' bounds i only against the file-settable song field; if a file could set patLen beyond the pattern array's row count (width not shown), pat->data[i][...] would read out of bounds — the array row count is unshown and not characterizable here.

verdict.summary: All attacker-reachable memory, index, and size sinks in this requantization-calibration kernel are guarded by a complete, execution-order-verified OP_REQUIRES chain: input_min.NumElements() == depth covers input_min_data[i]; depth is defined as input_max.NumElements() so input_max_data[i] is in bounds by construction; input.dims()==4, input.dim_size(3)==depth and input.NumElements()>0 bound chip<0>(i) for every i < depth; ranges is allocated from the same depth expression that bounds the loop; depth==0 is unreachable because it would force input.NumElements()==0, which is rejected. The remaining genuine defects are numerical/portability/race issues (out_min_max initialized to std::numeric_limits<float>::min(), i.e. the smallest positive float, so outputs can never fall below ~1.18e-38; std::abs on INT32_MIN is signed-overflow UB; static_cast<float>(1L << 31) is negative on LLP64/Windows; the MSVC OpenMP path omits reduction(max:out_min_max) causing a data race; is_non_negative has a benign same-value race). Their triggers either depend on platform/build configuration or produce only wrong calibration scalars consumed by code not shown; none constitutes memory corruption, out-of-bounds access, injection, bypass, security-state misrepresentation, or attacker-scalable amplification. This code appears to be the patched form of the historical RequantizePerChannel missing-validation issue (the shape checks are present).

assumptions: Input dtypes (qint32 for input, float for input_min/input_max) are enforced by op registration outside the given code; within this code, Tensor::flat<T>()/flat_inner_dims<T>() CHECK-fail (abort) on dtype mismatch rather than reinterpreting memory, so the worst case of a dtype mismatch is a process abort, not corruption.

TensorShape::dim_size(0) is called on input_min/input_max before any dims()>=1 check; the assumed framework behavior (returning -1 for an out-of-range index in current TensorFlow, or CHECK-failing) rejects scalar tensors either way because -1 widens to SIZE_MAX and cannot equal depth.
OP_REQUIRES/OP_REQUIRES_OK return from Compute on failure, so all six shape checks execute before input_min.flat<float>().data(), the loop, and every sink, on the single control-flow path.
clip_value_max_ is a member with no assignment in this code (UNSOURCED); it is used only as a float clamp on output magnitude and cannot cause memory unsafety.
Tensors reaching an op kernel have concrete (non-partial) shapes at execution time.
limitations: std::abs(min_per_channel)/std::abs(max_per_channel) is undefined when the per-channel qint32 minimum is INT32_MIN (signed overflow, CWE-190-adjacent). Trigger fully instantiable by attacker tensor content, but the concrete consequence is only a wrong (negative) ranges[i] and hence wrong calibration scalars; impact exists only in unshown downstream consumers, so it is a correctness bug, not a security vulnerability in this code.

out_min_max is initialized to std::numeric_limits<float>::min() (smallest positive normalized float, ~1.18e-38) instead of 0 or lowest(), so when every channel's range is 0 (e.g., zero input with zero min/max scales) the op emits min=0, max=1.18e-38 instead of 0/0, and under the OpenMP max-reduction the floor persists. Numerical correctness defect only.

static_cast<float>(1L << 31) is 2147483648 on LP64 but overflows into the sign bit on LLP64/Windows (long is 32-bit), in practice yielding -2147483648 and sign-flipped ranges on every iteration; defect requires a Windows/MSVC build configuration and produces only wrong calibration values.

Under ENABLE_ONEDNN_OPENMP with _MSC_VER the pragma omits reduction(max:out_min_max), producing a data race (lost maxima) on the shared reduction variable, and is_non_negative is written by multiple threads without synchronization (all writers store the same value false, benign in practice). Build-configuration-dependent; consequence is wrong scalar outputs only.

std::vector<float> ranges(depth) can throw std::bad_alloc (terminate) for very large depth, but depth equals input_max.NumElements(), so the attacker must already have allocated an equally large input_max tensor; cost is proportional with no amplification.

NaN or infinite attacker-supplied input_min/input_max values propagate into ranges/out_min_max (std::max comparisons with NaN return the first argument), producing garbage calibration scalars; the attacker already controls those input values and no security sink is reached.

No dims()>=1 check precedes input_min.dim_size(0)/input_max.dim_size(0); safety for scalar-shaped inputs rests on the framework dim_size sentinel behavior (see assumptions), not on a check in this code.

With an attacker-supplied 'ApplyAdam' node with input_size()=3, input(9) reads out of bounds and mutable_input(9) = div_node->name() writes a std::string through an out-of-bounds pointer, corrupting the heap. Trigger fully instantiated from attacker graph content; protobuf repeated-field accessors index the container with no release-mode bounds enforcement.

verdict.summary: GetVariableInput dereferences the result of GetMutableInput without checking it for nullptr. GetMutableInput is an accessor that returns nullptr when the requested input index is out of the node's input range or the input is absent (optional tensor), and index is an unvalidated int parameter of this exported helper whose content comes from untrusted model/operator wiring. The very first use, tensor->is_variable, is a pointer dereference with no preceding NULL test on any path (the body is two straight-line statements; the ternary tests is_variable, not tensor). Untrusted parsed-model content can therefore drive a NULL-pointer dereference and crash the interpreter process, a denial of service across the trust boundary.

  return tensor->is_variable ? tensor : nullptr;
evidence.reason: The lookup GetMutableInput(context, node, index) can return nullptr (out-of-range or absent input index), and the very next statement dereferences it via tensor->is_variable with no NULL check on any path. Trigger: attacker-supplied model/operator wiring selects a variable-input index beyond the node's inputs (or an absent optional input), GetMutableInput returns nullptr, and the first use is the unchecked member read, crashing the process. The ternary condition tests is_variable, not tensor, so it cannot guard the dereference it contains.

verdict.summary: UnstageOp::Compute reads a tuple of tensors from a shared, named staging buffer and validates only the element count against ctx->num_outputs(). verdict.summary: In the quantized uint8 branch of the TFLite Div Eval kernel, the zero-divisor guard TF_LITE_CHECK_DIV_NON_ZERO(uint8_t) compares raw quantized bytes against 0 instead of against the divisor's quantization zero point (params->input2_offset). A byte equal to the zero point represents real value zero yet passes the check, so EvalQuantized is invoked with a zero divisor and performs an integer division by zero, crashing (SIGFPE) the process inferring an attacker-supplied model - a denial of service.

evidence.reason: The uint8 branch invokes the zero-divisor check and then passes input2 to EvalQuantized. The check (macro body at line 20) tests the raw byte against 0, but the quantized divisor is the zero-point-shifted value input2_data[i] - params->input2_offset; a raw byte equal to the zero point (e.g., 0x80 with zero point 128) passes the guard while representing real zero, so the division kernel divides by zero. Trigger instantiated: attacker model with output->type=kTfLiteUInt8, input2 constant byte 0x80, input2_offset=128; check passes (128 != 0), EvalQuantized computes divisor 128-128=0, integer division by zero crashes the process (DoS from untrusted model content).

evidence.snippet: TF_LITE_ENSURE(context, input2_data[i] != 0);                   \
evidence.reason: This is the actual guard statement (macro TF_LITE_CHECK_DIV_NON_ZERO body). It enforces the wrong invariant for the quantized case: it compares the raw uint8 byte to 0 rather than to params->input2_offset (the zero point), so quantized zero divisors are not rejected. No alternative guard form (clamp, mask, error arm, zero-point comparison) exists anywhere in the given code.

assumptions: The TFLite interpreter parses the attacker-supplied model file into tensor data, input2->bytes, output->type, and TfLiteDivParams (including input2_offset/zero point); these values are attacker-controlled serialized model state per discipline 3, although the assignments occur in code not shown (parser/Prepare).

EvalQuantized (not shown) performs division on zero-point-shifted input2 values, i.e., divisor = input2_data[i] - params->input2_offset; characterized per the callee boundary rule from the given code's macro name TF_LITE_CHECK_DIV_NON_ZERO, the passing of params into EvalQuantized, and the float-branch comment stating that a zero-divisor check is required for the non-float paths.
GetInputSafe/GetOutputSafe abort Eval with kTfLiteError when the requested tensor is missing (standard TFLite 'Safe' accessor semantics).
limitations: Potential NULL dereference of input2_data at the check loop if the model sets input2->type different from output->type (e.g., output INT32, input2 INT8): impact depends on the unshown GetTensorData<T> behavior on type mismatch and on unshown Prepare-time type equality validation; trigger precondition not instantiable from the given code.
Potential out-of-bounds reads in EvalDiv/EvalQuantized for models with broadcast-incompatible shapes depend on shape validation and indexing entirely inside code not shown; not instantiable here.

The float32 path intentionally skips the zero-divisor check (quoted comment: 'Div by zero seems ok in this case... infinities are returned'); IEEE float semantics make this consistent with upstream TF, so it is not treated as a defect.

If a deployment always used symmetric quantization with zero point 0 the trigger would not fire, but nothing in the given code constrains params->input2_offset, and asymmetric uint8 quantization (zero point != 0) is the norm.

With attacker-controlled fileName = 'foo/../../tmp/pwned', begin()->string() is 'foo' (not '.'/'..'), so the path is anchored under the upload root and the embedded '..' components escape it; a path starting with '..' makes the condition false and the path is then used unanchored relative to the process CWD. The missing member in this rejection list is the root cause of the unchecked NULL reaching the sink.
