verdict.summary: FractionalAvgPoolGrad's Compute reads pooling-sequence values directly from attacker-controlled tensors (row_seq_tensor, col_seq_tensor) and uses them as loop start indices without any range validation. Only the END indices are clamped (std::min with in_max_row_index/in_max_col_index); the START indices are never checked to be non-negative or below the input dims. A negative value in the sequence tensor makes the inner loops iterate with negative in_r/in_c, producing a negative in_index that is passed to Eigen::Map::coeffRef, which performs unchecked pointer arithmetic, yielding an out-of-bounds heap write with attacker-influenced offset and value.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values: in_row_start and in_col_start are read directly from the attacker-controlled row/col sequence tensors. The only guards in the function (row_seq_tensor.NumElements() > out_rows and col_seq_tensor.NumElements() > out_cols) validate element COUNTS, not VALUES, and the only value-level guards are the std::min clamps applied exclusively to the END indices. The START indices receive no lower-bound, upper-bound, or non-negativity check on any path, so an arbitrary int64 (including negative values) flows into the inner loops unvalidated.

Out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The loops iterate from the unvalidated start values, so a negative in_row_start (e.g., row_seq = [-1, 0]) or in_col_start makes in_index negative (simulated trigger: in_rows=2, in_cols=2, b=0, in_r=-1 gives in_index = -2). in_backprop_tensor_temp_mat.coeffRef(d, in_index) is an Eigen::Map element access with no runtime bounds check; it computes data() + d + in_index * in_depth, landing before the temp buffer allocated for in_shape, and the subsequent in_backprop_ref += ... performs an attacker-influenced out-of-bounds heap write. No guard, clamp, mask, or checked accessor on the start indices exists anywhere in the function.

assumptions: overlapping_ is a kernel member attribute set outside the shown code; the trigger was simulated for both possible values (true and false) and executes in both, so no conclusion depends on it.
Tensor inputs reached via context->input(...) are attacker-data per the trust model for op kernel handlers; the op's caller controls tensor contents and shapes.
Eigen::Map::coeffRef is characterized per the callee boundary rule as raw index-based element access without release-mode bounds checking.
limitations: Candidate C3: the != 0 checks (lines 59-70) permit negative dims to reach in_shape.AddDim(orig_input_tensor_shape_flat(i)) and the temp allocation; whether TensorShape::AddDim/allocation rejects or CHECK-fails on negative dims is not shown in the given code, so no consequence beyond a potential abort could be instantiated.

Candidate C2 (division by num_elements_in_pooling_cell): refuted by control-flow analysis; the division at line 123 executes only inside loops that, when entered at least once, guarantee both factors of the product are >= 1, so a zero divisor is unreachable.

Candidate C4 (OOB read of out_backprop at line 119): out_index = (b*out_rows + r)*out_cols + c is bounded by the enclosing loop conditions (b < out_batch, r < out_rows, c < out_cols) and d < out_depth, so the read stays in bounds.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability could be instantiated within this code. Every array write is bounded by the same m_ucCount that sizes the allocation, both memset lengths match their allocations (the 'Upsampler*' vs 'UpsamplerBase*' sizes are equal pointer widths), the reused buffers and m_pLargestScale are NULL-guarded, and the sx>1||sy>1 gate is verified on the only path to CreateUpsampler. The genuine gaps are the unchecked AllocMem results used as memset destinations and the untested ComponentOf result dereferenced at comp->SubXOf(), but their triggers require either allocation failure of a small fixed-size request (environment-only, no attacker-scalable amplification) or an unsourced relationship between m_ucCount, m_pFrame and the frame's component count that no statement in this code establishes.

assumptions: m_ucCount's declaration is not in the given code; the Hungarian 'uc' prefix and the UBYTE loop variable suggest UBYTE width (max 255), but this is inferred, not quoted.
BuildCommon() is assumed to initialize m_ucCount and other members; its body is not shown, so no effect of it can be quoted or relied on.

AllocMem's failure contract is not shown; the analysis allowed the standard pointer-or-NULL semantics per the callee boundary rule. In the upstream Accusoft environment it may throw instead, which is equally unquotable.

The decoded JPEG stream (component count, sampling factors sx/sy, pixel dimensions) is attacker-controlled content; this code receives those values only through not-shown callees (BuildCommon, ComponentOf, SubXOf) and unsourced members.
limitations: Unchecked allocation results: m_ppDecodingMCU and m_ppUpsampler are assigned from m_pEnviron->AllocMem(...) and immediately passed to memset(...) with no NULL check on any path (the quoted '== NULL' tests check the old value and only gate allocation). This would be a CWE-476 NULL dereference, but the trigger is allocation failure of at most sizeof(ptr)*255*8 = 16,320 bytes, an environment condition no attacker input in this code can scale, so it is not confirmed as a vulnerability.

Unchecked lookup result: comp = m_pFrame->ComponentOf(i) is dereferenced at comp->SubXOf() with no sentinel test before first use in execution order. A NULL or out-of-range return requires m_ucCount to exceed m_pFrame's component count (or m_pFrame itself to be NULL); neither condition has a producing, assignable statement in this code (m_ucCount and m_pFrame are unsourced here), so the trigger is not instantiated. Likewise m_pFrame->TablesOf() is chained without any guard.

UBYTE wraparound: if m_ucCount were wider than UBYTE and exceeded 255, 'for(i = 0;i < m_ucCount;i++)' with UBYTE i would wrap and loop forever (CWE-191/CWE-835 hang); the index would still stay within the m_ucCount-element allocation. m_ucCount's type and producer are unsourced, so this stays speculative.

Cross-call reuse: the buffers are allocated only when NULL, so a later hierarchical frame with a larger component count would reuse under-sized arrays; the harmful use occurs in code not shown and cannot be characterized, so the impact chain breaks here.

UpsamplerBase::CreateUpsampler receives attacker-influenced sx, sy, m_ulPixelWidth and m_ulPixelHeight; its safe domain is not shown and cannot be characterized, and the only condition this code itself requires (sx > 1 || sy > 1, quoted and verified) is enforced, so no defect is provable at this call site.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability found. The only attacker-influenced data is the shape of input 0. Its only index-bearing use, c->Dim(c->input(0), 1), is protected by the quoted rank check TF_RETURN_IF_ERROR(c->WithRank(c->input(0), 2, &unused)) which returns on the error path before any subsequent statement executes, so the literal index 1 is always in bounds (rank is exactly 2 when reached). The derived handles rank and nvals flow only into Matrix/Vector/set_output calls with no arithmetic, copy lengths, allocations, or other sinks in this code; their impact on later tensor allocation lives in code not shown. Remaining candidates (set_output index vs. unshown op output-count registration; oversized dims affecting later kernel allocation) have UNSOURCED preconditions or break at uncharacterizable code and are recorded as limitations, not findings.

assumptions: The op registration for SparseCountSparseOutput declares at least 3 outputs so that set_output(0..2, ...) is in range; this cannot be quoted from the given code.

WithRank, Dim, UnknownDim, Matrix, Vector, and set_output follow documented TensorFlow shape-inference framework semantics (WithRank returns a non-OK Status when the rank does not match; TF_RETURN_IF_ERROR returns on non-OK; the shape helpers accept arbitrary DimensionHandles including unknown dims).
TF_RETURN_IF_ERROR expands to a construct that returns the Status when it is not OK, before later statements execute.
limitations: Hypothetical out-of-range set_output index if the op were registered with fewer than 3 outputs: the registered output count is UNSOURCED in this code (never assigned or checked here), and the indices 0-2 are compile-time literals not attacker-controlled, so no trigger can be instantiated.

Very large attacker-chosen dimension values flowing into output shapes could stress later tensor allocation, but the allocation and kernel execution happen in code not given; this function only constructs symbolic shape handles, so the impact chain breaks at uncharacterizable code.
A historical TensorFlow CVE concerning SparseCountSparseOutput related to op registration/kernel behavior, not to any defect in this shape function's logic.

verdict.summary: gf_hinter_finalize dereferences the result of gf_isom_get_esd(file, odT, 1) and gf_isom_get_esd(file, sceneT, 1) without any NULL check. These are parse/lookup calls over attacker-controlled MP4 content; the same function proves the NULL sentinel is reachable by guarding an identical call with 'if (!esd) continue;' in another loop. A crafted MP4 with an OD or BIFS track in the root OD whose ESD cannot be retrieved causes a NULL pointer write/read (esd->OCRESID / esd->decoderConfig), crashing the process that consumes the untrusted file (denial of service).

With IOD_Profile = GF_SDP_IOD_ISMA_STRICT (line 41 sets remove_ocr = 1) and an OD track in the root OD lacking a retrievable ESD, execution reaches line 98 with esd == NULL and writes through the NULL pointer.

The code itself demonstrates this callee can return NULL by testing an identical call elsewhere: 'esd = gf_isom_get_esd(file, i+1, 1); if (!esd) continue;' (lines 143-144).

		else if (esd->OCRESID == esd->ESID) esd->OCRESID = 0;
evidence.reason: Sink on the scene track path: esd from gf_isom_get_esd(file, sceneT, 1) (line 105) is dereferenced unconditionally (and earlier at line 121 'if (esd->decoderConfig)' and lines 126-127 when the sample embed path is taken). No guard of any form exists on any path from line 105 to this sink; a crafted MP4 with a BIFS track in the root OD (required to pass line 47) whose ESD cannot be retrieved makes esd NULL and crashes the process.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value on the scene track path; result stored and later dereferenced at lines 121, 126-127, and 134-135 without any NULL check, in contrast to the guarded identical call at lines 143-144.

assumptions: gf_hinter_finalize is a non-static, externally callable entry point, so its parameters (file, IOD_Profile, bandwidth) are part of its input surface; no documented precondition on them exists in the given code.
The GF_ISOFile contents (tracks, media types, samples, ESD presence, root OD) originate from a parsed MP4 file and are attacker-controlled data.

gf_isom_get_esd can return NULL for malformed or ESD-less media; this is inferred from the function's own defensive check 'if (!esd) continue;' at line 144 for an identical call, not from shown callee code.
limitations: Potential stack buffer overflow: 'size64 = gf_base64_encode(buffer, size, buf64, 2000); buf64[size64] = 0;' and the sprintf at line 175 could overflow buf64[5000]/sdpLine[5100] if gf_base64_encode does not enforce its outSize parameter when encoding the serialized IOD (whose size can exceed 3750 bytes because it contains base64-embedded URLStrings). Whether gf_base64_encode truncates at outSize is not shown and the callee is not characterizable, so this precondition is unsourced; recorded as a limitation, not a finding.
Unchecked gf_malloc at lines 90 and 126 followed by strcpy could dereference NULL, but a failed allocation of at most ~5.1 KB is environment-induced and not attacker-triggerable; not a vulnerability.

The return value of gf_odf_desc_write (line 167) is unchecked; on failure buffer may remain NULL and be passed to gf_base64_encode(NULL, 0, ...) and gf_free(NULL) — impact depends on unshown callee behavior, likely benign for size 0.
sprintf(buf64, "b=AS:%d", bandwidth) prints a u32 through %d, producing a negative string for values above INT_MAX; output-only sign confusion with no memory-safety effect.
Severity is limited to denial of service: on the instantiated paths the NULL dereference crashes the process consuming the untrusted MP4; no memory-corruption primitive was instantiated in this code.

verdict.summary: TransposeShapeFn validates only the upper bound of each perm value before using it as a dimension index. The check `if (in_idx >= rank)` permits negative values, so an attacker-supplied perm constant containing a negative element (e.g. -1) reaches `dims[i] = c->Dim(input, in_idx);`, which indexes the input shape's dimension vector out of bounds (before its start), an out-of-bounds read whose garbage DimensionHandle result is then stored in the inferred output shape.

evidence.reason: Only the upper bound of in_idx is checked (`in_idx >= rank`); there is no `in_idx < 0` test, clamp, mask, modulo, or checked accessor on any path. With input rank 2 and perm constant [-1, 0], in_idx = -1 passes the check and c->Dim(input, -1) indexes the input shape's dimension vector at a negative offset, an out-of-bounds read (root cause: unvalidated array index from attacker-controlled perm tensor contents).

evidence.snippet: const Tensor* perm = c->input_tensor(1);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values: the perm constant tensor is read from the graph being inferred; its attacker-authored contents flow through AsInt64(perm, rank) into data[i] and then into the unguarded index use at line 55.

assumptions: AsInt64<T>(perm, rank) (callee not shown) is assumed to produce a vector of `rank` int64 values from the perm tensor, per its call signature `AsInt64<int32>(perm, rank)`; consistent with WithValue(perm_elems, rank) succeeding, the reads data[i] for i < rank are in-bounds.

c->Dim(handle, i) is a framework list accessor that returns the i-th dimension handle by indexing the shape's dimension vector; its internal validation is a debug-only DCHECK, so in release builds a negative index reads out of bounds.

The declared shape of a constant input (perm_shape) is consistent with the constant tensor's actual layout; this framework invariant is relied on for the WithValue(perm_elems, rank) check to bound the AsInt64 reads.
limitations: dims.resize(rank) at line 32 uses an attacker-declared element count (rank from c->Value(perm_elems) or perm->NumElements()) with no upper bound; a graph declaring a perm placeholder with shape [2^40] would drive a multi-terabyte resize and throw std::length_error/bad_alloc. The claimed DoS impact depends on whether the not-shown caller of the shape function catches the exception, so the impact link is not characterizable from this code.

for (int32_t i = 0; i < rank; ++i) uses a 32-bit counter against int64_t rank; signed overflow of i requires rank > INT32_MAX, which first requires surviving dims.resize(rank) of more than 2^31 handles, so the wrap is not exercised realistically.

The `rank = perm->NumElements();` branch (line 21) dereferences perm; reaching it with perm == nullptr is prevented only by a framework invariant (a non-null constant input implies a value-known perm_elems), which this code never asserts — unsourced, not instantiated.

verdict.summary: FractionalAvgPoolGrad validates only the element COUNTS of row_seq_tensor/col_seq_tensor, never their VALUES. in_row_start/in_col_start (lines 86, 91) are consumed unclamped while only the end indices are clamped, so a negative pooling-sequence value makes in_r/in_c negative and in_index (line 103) attacker-negative, reaching in_backprop_tensor_temp_mat.coeffRef(d, in_index) (line 109) as an out-of-bounds heap write of attacker-influenced doubles. Additionally, out_batch and out_depth (from out_backprop) are never cross-checked against in_batch/in_depth (from the attacker-supplied shape tensor), giving two further fully instantiated OOB-write triggers at the same sink.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: in_row_start is read raw from the attacker-controlled row_seq_tensor with no range validation; only in_row_end is clamped to in_max_row_index, so a negative or oversized start passes into the inner loops (same pattern for col at lines 91-94).

Sink: in_index is computed from unvalidated in_r/in_c (simulated: row_seq [-1000000,1], out_backprop shape (1,1,1,1), orig shape [1,4,4,1] gives in_index = -4000000), and coeffRef(d, in_index) on a map of only in_cols*in_rows*in_batch columns performs an out-of-bounds heap write; no bounds check exists on any path.

Independent confirmed trigger: d is bounded by out_depth (from out_backprop) while the destination map was built with in_depth rows (line 75, from the attacker-controlled shape tensor); with out_depth=4 and in_depth=1, coeffRef(3, in_index) writes out of bounds. No check of out_depth against in_depth (or out_batch against in_batch, which likewise makes b*in_rows exceed the buffer) exists anywhere in the code.

assumptions: Eigen Map::coeffRef performs no runtime bounds checking in release builds (framework semantics per the callee boundary rule); even where eigen_assert exists it is debug-only.
overlapping_ is a kernel constructor attribute never assigned in this code; both of its branches were simulated and both leave the defect reachable, so it gates nothing.
The out_backprop read at out_backprop_mat.coeffRef(d, out_index) is in-bounds by the loop invariants over out_backprop's own dimensions.
limitations: Negative or extreme dims in orig_input_tensor_shape flow into in_shape.AddDim (line 64) and forward_input_or_allocate_temp (line 69); whether AddDim CHECK-fails or the allocation error path handles it is not characterizable from this code, so a potential crash there is unconfirmed (candidate 6).

Integer overflow in in_index (line 103) or in num_elements_in_pooling_cell (line 97) requires extreme int64 seq values; the confirmed OOB write does not depend on overflow, so overflow is recorded only as an aggravator.

verdict.summary: In TransposeShapeFn, the range check `if (in_idx >= rank || in_idx <= -rank)` admits negative permutation values in [-(rank-1), -1] and passes them unnormalized to `c->Dim(input, in_idx)`, an indexing accessor whose safe domain is [0, rank). An attacker-controlled constant perm tensor (e.g. [-1, 0] with a rank-2 input) yields an out-of-bounds read of the input shape's dimension vector; the out-of-bounds-read DimensionHandle (a ref-counted handle) is copied into dims and consumed by MakeShape, giving crash or memory-corruption potential. This mirrors the fixed upstream code, which normalizes with `if (in_idx < 0) in_idx += rank;` before calling Dim.

evidence.reason: The guard only rejects in_idx >= rank or in_idx <= -rank, so negative attacker-controlled perm values in [-(rank-1), -1] pass (e.g. rank=2, in_idx=-1: both comparisons false) and reach the sink `c->Dim(input, in_idx)` with a negative index, outside the accessor's [0, rank) domain. No normalization (in_idx += rank), clamp, mask/modulo, or negative-value rejection exists on any path. The out-of-bounds-read dimension handle is then copied and consumed by c->MakeShape(dims) at line 63, producing an out-of-bounds read with memory-corruption potential from attacker-supplied graph content.

assumptions: c->Dim is a container indexing accessor whose safe index domain is [0, rank); the code's own error string 'out of range of input rank' shows the intended domain, and the upstream fix normalizes negative indices before calling Dim, confirming Dim does not accept negatives.

perm_shape (c->input(1)) is consistent with the actual constant tensor perm (c->input_tensor(1)) — a framework invariant not quotable in this snippet; it underpins the in-bounds read of data[i] for i < rank.
Shape functions run on attacker-supplied serialized models (GraphDef/SavedModel), making perm content attacker-data.
limitations: dims.resize(rank) at line 32 has no upper bound on rank (derived from Rank(input), Value(perm_elems), or perm->NumElements()); an attacker-influenced huge rank could cause OOM/bad_alloc denial of service (CWE-400), but triggering it requires a graph producer yielding an astronomically large known element count without materialization, which is not instantiated in this code.
The loop counter `int32_t i` compared against int64_t rank (line 49) could wrap for rank >= 2^31, but such a rank requires surviving a multi-terabyte dims.resize first, so the trigger is speculative.

The else-arm AsInt64<int64_t>(perm, rank) assumes any non-int32 dtype is int64; a different dtype would misread the buffer, but the op registration constrains Tperm (not shown in this code), so this is a contract-dependent candidate, not confirmed.

Exact heap-corruption exploitability depends on the unshown implementation of c->Dim and DimensionHandle's ref-counting; the confirmed primitive here is the out-of-bounds read of the dimension vector at an attacker-controlled negative index.

verdict.summary: string_number_format computes the result buffer size with 32-bit int arithmetic whose overflow guard (line 58) tests only the sum, not the product thousand_sep.size() * ((integral-1)/3). For a 309-digit integral part and a ~42MB thousand_sep, the product wraps to a small positive value, the guard stays silent, and line 63 stores the wrapped value. The copy loop then performs floor((integral-1)/3) memcpy calls of thousand_sep.size() attacker-controlled bytes into the undersized String buffer, writing gigabytes out of bounds below resbuf: a heap buffer overflow reachable entirely from the attacker-controlled parameters d, dec, and thousand_sep.

evidence.reason: Defective overflow guard and faulty size computation. The guard tests integral + (thousand_sep.size() * ((integral-1)/3)) < integral, but the product itself is computed in 32-bit int and wraps before the comparison: with integral = 309 (from d = 1e308, dec = 0, per lines 23/33/53) and thousand_sep.size() = 42,116,633, the product 102 * 42,116,633 = 4,295,896,566 wraps to 929,270, the check 309 + 929,270 < 309 is false, and line 63 assigns the wrapped value integral = 929,579. reslen (66) and the allocation at line 84 are therefore undersized by ~4.3 GB relative to what the copy loop writes. All trigger values come from the attacker-controlled parameters d, dec, and thousand_sep of this non-static function.

Out-of-bounds write sink. After the wrapped size computation, resbuf holds only 929,579 bytes (line 84) and t starts at resbuf + 929,578 (line 88). On the third digit copy this memcpy writes thousand_sep.size() = 42,116,633 attacker-controlled bytes starting at resbuf - ~41,187,057, far below the allocated buffer, and repeats for each group of three digits (102 times). The loop bound while(s >= tmpbuf) (line 119) caps only digit iterations, never t or remaining capacity; no check on any path compares t or the copy length against the buffer end.

assumptions: String(n, ReserveString) provides a writable buffer with n+1 usable bytes and mutableData() returns a non-null pointer for the sizes involved; this is documented by the code's own usage: line 21 'String tmpstr(63, ReserveString);' followed by line 23 'snprintf(tmpbuf, 64, ...)'.
raise_error halts execution; irrelevant to the primary trigger, whose guard condition never fires.
snprintf/strpbrk/isdigit behave per standard semantics; '%.*F' emits exactly dec fractional digits for finite d (the code itself handles the fewer-places case via topad at lines 94-107).
int overflow wraps modulo 2^32 on the target; the trigger was verified under both a 32-bit and a 64-bit model of String::size().
limitations: Line 69 'reslen += dec;' is unchecked, but a harmful wrap requires a successful ~2GB snprintf (dec near 2^31) and its impact chain breaks at 'String resstr(reslen, ReserveString)' with a negative reslen, whose constructor behavior is not characterizable from the given code.

The dec_point path (lines 72, 76, 112) has the same sum-form guard flaw, but triggering a 32-bit truncation there requires a >2^32-byte dec_point string and a 64-bit String::size(); the width of size() is not shown.
A huge dec (e.g., 2^31 - 12) forces multiple ~2GB allocations and ~2GB of formatting work from a single int parameter (resource-consumption concern), bounded at ~2GB per buffer.
No caller is shown; per the analysis rules, the parameters of this non-static function are treated as attacker-data, so missing caller-side validation cannot dismiss the finding.

verdict.summary: SetupWriters iterates the parsed ISO-file track tree and dereferences file-derived structure pointers with no NULL validation on any path: line 19 'trak->Media->information->sampleTable' and line 20 'trak->Media->mediaHeader->timeScale' dereference trak->Media, ->information and ->mediaHeader directly, and lines 31/33/42 dereference writer->stbl (possibly NULL, as the code's own line-63 NULL test of the same field admits), stbl->SampleSize, stbl->TimeToSample and stbl->ChunkOffset. A crafted MP4 whose trak lacks mdia (or whose minf lacks stbl/stsz/stts/stco) crashes the process with a SIGSEGV as soon as the movie is written, a denial of service for any application that processes untrusted media through this writer. The only guards present (line 9 for moov, line 63 for sampleTable) do not execute before these sinks in execution order.

evidence.reason: Primary NULL-pointer-dereference sink. trak->Media, trak->Media->information and trak->Media->mediaHeader are pointers into the movie tree parsed from file content (the code reads file-derived box-type fields of this same tree at lines 42 and 57) and are never assigned, asserted, or checked in this code. Instantiated trigger: a file whose trak box has no mdia child makes trak->Media NULL; simulation: line 18 copies NULL into writer->mdia without fault, line 19 evaluates trak->Media->information with trak->Media == NULL and faults, terminating the process (DoS across the trust boundary of untrusted file content). No guard form (check, clamp, mask, error arm) exists on any path before this line; the only earlier NULL check, line 9 'if (!movie->moov) return GF_OK;', covers the movie box only.

verdict.summary: The function ccp_run_aes_gcm_cmd fails to validate aes->iv_len before computing dm_offset = CCP_AES_CTX_SB_COUNT * CCP_SB_BYTES - aes->iv_len. If aes->iv_len exceeds the workarea buffer size (CCP_AES_CTX_SB_COUNT * CCP_SB_BYTES = 32 bytes), the unsigned subtraction underflows, producing a huge offset passed to ccp_set_dm_area which performs an out-of-bounds write into kernel memory. The code comment explicitly acknowledges this as an assumption ('There is an assumption here that the IV is 96 bits in length, plus a nonce of 32 bits') without enforcing it. Additionally, for decryption, ilen = aes->src_len - authsize at line 61 can underflow if src_len < authsize, producing a huge length used in scatterlist operations.

evidence.snippet:
dm_offset = CCP_AES_CTX_SB_COUNT * CCP_SB_BYTES - aes->iv_len;
	ret = ccp_set_dm_area(&ctx, dm_offset, aes->iv, 0, aes->iv_len);
evidence.reason: Unvalidated aes->iv_len is subtracted from the constant buffer size CCP_AES_CTX_SB_COUNT * CCP_SB_BYTES. If iv_len exceeds this bound, the unsigned subtraction underflows producing a huge dm_offset that is passed to ccp_set_dm_area, causing an out-of-bounds write of iv_len bytes into a workarea of only CCP_AES_CTX_SB_COUNT * CCP_SB_BYTES bytes. No check on iv_len exists anywhere on any path in this function.

For decryption, aes->src_len is not validated to be at least authsize. If src_len < authsize, the unsigned subtraction underflows, producing a huge ilen value that is immediately used in scatterwalk_ffwd to walk past the end of the input scatterlist, and later in ccp_init_data as a data length, causing out-of-bounds memory accesses.

assumptions: CCP_AES_CTX_SB_COUNT and CCP_SB_BYTES are kernel constants not shown in this code; based on kernel driver definitions, CCP_SB_BYTES=32 and CCP_AES_CTX_SB_COUNT=1, making the workarea 32 bytes
The function is called from the kernel crypto API path where struct ccp_cmd fields are populated by caller code not shown here
limitations: Practical exploitability of the iv_len underflow depends on whether the kernel crypto API callers can set iv_len > 32 bytes for GCM (standard GCM uses 12-byte IVs, but this function does not enforce that constraint)
The src_len underflow requires a caller to submit a decryption request with src_len < authsize, which higher-level kernel crypto code may prevent but is not enforced in this function

verdict.summary: In SingleComponentLSScan::ParseMCU, the JPEG-LS run-mode fill loop `while(run)` writes decoded samples through `*lp++` bounded only by the entropy-decoded run count, while the line buffer `line->m_pData` holds only `length` remaining samples. `run` is attacker-data returned by `DecodeRun(length,m_lRunIndex[0])` from the compressed bitstream, and no statement in this code checks, clamps, or otherwise bounds `run` against `length` before or during the loop; `length` is merely decremented (`run--,length--;`) and underflows to negative when a crafted scan encodes a run longer than the remaining line. Impact is attacker-scalable memory corruption from a crafted image file.

When the attacker-encoded run exceeds `length`, `lp` advances past the end of the line buffer and `*lp++ = a << preshift;` performs attacker-scalable heap out-of-bounds writes, and `length` underflows negative. verdict.summary: In ReadOneMNGImage, the mng_CLIP chunk handler parses 16-bit first_object/last_object values from the file and loops 'for (i=(int) first_object; i <= (int) last_object; i++)' indexing mng_info->exists[i], mng_info->frozen[i], and mng_info->object_clip[i] with no bounds check against MNG_MAX_OBJECTS anywhere on the path, allowing an attacker-supplied index up to 65535. The sibling MOVE handler guards the identical pattern with 'if ((i < 0) || (i >= MNG_MAX_OBJECTS)) continue;' and DEFI clamps with 'object_id=MNG_MAX_OBJECTS', proving the bound is required and omitted only in CLIP.

Line 813 performs an unconditional out-of-bounds read of exists[i]/frozen[i], and lines 820-821 perform an out-of-bounds write of a 32-byte MngBox into object_clip[i] when the OOB-read bytes test favorably. Trigger: an MNG file containing a CLIP chunk with length=22 and first_object=last_object=308 (any value > MNG_MAX_OBJECTS up to 65535) reaches these statements with i=308; the required index bound is enforced for the identical arrays in DEFI ('if (object_id > MNG_MAX_OBJECTS) ... object_id=MNG_MAX_OBJECTS;') and MOVE ('if ((i < 0) || (i >= MNG_MAX_OBJECTS)) continue;') but is absent here.

verdict.summary: The op kernel reads num_segments from attacker-controlled tensor input(2) with only a non-emptiness check (`NumElements() != 0`). evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled num_segments is ingested with only a non-emptiness check on the element count; there is no check that the tensor is a scalar and no check that the value is non-negative. NUM_SEGMENTS_TYPE is a signed integer type (int32 per the op registration, not shown in this code); the non-scalar shape-[2] trigger is type-independent and survives even if the type were unsigned.

verdict.summary: The response-matching condition in MqttClient_WaitType accepts a received packet type that differs from the awaited wait_type whenever both are classified identically by MqttIsPubRespPacket (0 == 0 for all non-publish-response types). A malicious or man-in-the-middle MQTT broker can send a mismatched packet (e.g. DISCONNECT or SUBACK while the client waits for CONNACK with wait_packet_id = 0), so the network-controlled packet_type is dispatched to MqttClient_HandlePacket paired with the caller's differently-typed packet_obj (use_packet_obj = packet_obj; use_packet_type = packet_type;) — type confusion with memory-corruption potential, caused by the incorrect comparison at line 135.

The clause `MqttIsPubRespPacket(packet_type) == MqttIsPubRespPacket(wait_type)` is true (0 == 0) for every pair of non-publish-response types, so a received packet of a DIFFERENT type than the awaited wait_type is declared a match whenever the packet_id clause also holds (trivially true when wait_packet_id == 0). No statement between this check and the handler call re-validates that the received type is compatible with the caller's packet_obj; the multithread pendResp re-pairing (lines 152-157) is conditional and absent in single-thread builds, so it is not a guard on this path.

                use_packet_obj, timeout_ms);
evidence.reason: Sink: the attacker-controlled use_packet_type (set from the network-decoded packet_type at line 145) is passed to the packet handler paired with use_packet_obj, which on the matched path is the caller's object typed for wait_type (`use_packet_obj = packet_obj;` line 138). Simulated trigger: wait_type = MQTT_PACKET_TYPE_CONNECT_ACK, wait_packet_id = 0, broker sends a DISCONNECT/SUBACK packet; DecodePacket yields packet_type = 14/9, the 0==0 clause matches, waitMatchFound = 1, and MqttClient_HandlePacket receives the type-inconsistent (type, object) pair — the unvalidated argument at this call site is the defect (type confusion).

evidence.snippet:
rc = MqttClient_DecodePacket(client, client->rx_buf,
                client->packet.buf_len, NULL, &packet_type, NULL, &packet_id);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values: packet_type and packet_id are decoded from client->rx_buf, filled by MqttPacket_Read from the network socket (lines 91-92). This is the untrusted-origin data (server/MITM-controlled) whose packet_type flows through the defective match at lines 133-136 into the handler dispatch at lines 169-170.

assumptions: MqttIsPubRespPacket is a boolean predicate returning 0 for packet types that are not publish responses (PUBACK/PUBREC/PUBREL/PUBCOMP); inferred from its name and usage — its body is not shown.

MqttClient_HandlePacket consumes use_packet_type to determine how to interpret and decode into use_packet_obj; inferred from the call-site pairing and the pendResp arm pairing pendResp->packet_type with pendResp->packet_obj (lines 156-157) — its body is not shown.

Concrete caller pairings (e.g. an MqttConnectAck object with wait_type = CONNECT_ACK and wait_packet_id = 0) are not shown; the given code documents the pairing contract via the comment at line 18, the awaited-type/id debug print at lines 33-35, and the pendResp pairing at lines 156-157.
Analysis covers the non-multithreaded build and the multithreaded build when no pending-response entry matches the forged packet; both contain the defective path.
limitations: The exact memory-corruption extent (which struct fields are written out of bounds) depends on MqttClient_HandlePacket and the Mqtt* decode functions, which are not shown; the confirmed defect is the type-inconsistent (use_packet_type, use_packet_obj) pair passed at the call site per the callee boundary rule.
The `wait_type == MQTT_PACKET_TYPE_ANY` arm (line 133) similarly trusts the caller to supply a compatible generic object; no caller is shown for that arm.

The else arm (lines 141-144) dispatches arbitrary non-matching received packet types onto the fixed client->msg (an MqttPublish), the same root-cause class; its extent likewise depends on the not-shown handler.

The NONBLOCK MQTT_CODE_CONTINUE return intentionally keeps lockRecv locked across the return (per the comment at lines 174-175); re-entry logic is self-consistent, so no defect was instantiated there.
The goto wait_again loop is bounded by the attacker's send rate and the per-read timeout; work is proportional to attacker input, so no amplification finding was made.

Occurrences where both types are publish responses (e.g. waiting PUBACK, receiving PUBREC with the same id) appear to be an intentional QoS-flow relaxation; the harmful instantiation is the 0==0 arm between unrelated non-pub-resp types.

The missing NULL check was confirmed by STEP 5 search (no if, assert, or error arm exists), but the trigger precondition (a caller passing NULL to a static release callback registered with the device core) is UNSOURCED — no attacker input in this code's data flow can set it, so the trigger is speculative.

verdict.summary: The Stage 2 loop is bounded only by the attacker-controlled parameter num_migrate while writing into the fixed-size stack arrays x_cur[XFRM_MAX_DEPTH] and x_new[XFRM_MAX_DEPTH]. No statement in this code bounds num_migrate (or the indices nx_cur/nx_new) to the array capacity; the only candidate guard, `xfrm_migrate_check(m, num_migrate)`, is a not-shown callee whose return sentinel is tested but whose bound cannot be quoted. With num_migrate > XFRM_MAX_DEPTH and successful state lookups, `x_cur[nx_cur] = x` and `x_new[nx_new] = xc` write kernel pointers past the end of the stack arrays, corrupting adjacent stack state.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds stack write. The loop bound is the unvalidated attacker-controlled count num_migrate; nx_cur and nx_new are incremented at most once per iteration and never checked against XFRM_MAX_DEPTH, so on the (XFRM_MAX_DEPTH+1)-th successful xfrm_migrate_state_find, `x_cur[nx_cur] = x` (and on migrate success `x_new[nx_new] = xc`) writes a kernel pointer one past the end of the fixed-size stack arrays. Trigger: attacker supplies num_migrate = XFRM_MAX_DEPTH+1 (or more) migration templates, all of which match an existing state; simulated walk reaches the write with nx_cur == XFRM_MAX_DEPTH. No range check, clamp, mask, sized allocation, or error arm keyed on the count exists anywhere on the path.

verdict.summary: In ljpeg_start, the JPEG segment length is computed as len = (data[2] << 8 | data[3]) - 2 directly from the attacker-controlled input file with no lower-bound check. When the file supplies a length field of 0x0000 or 0x0001, len becomes -2 or -1, and fread (data, 1, len, ifp) converts the negative int to a near-SIZE_MAX size_t, directing fread to copy up to that many bytes of file content into the fixed 0x10000-byte stack buffer data. Any input file with more than 65536 bytes after the crafted marker overflows the stack buffer with attacker-chosen bytes and attacker-chosen extent: a classic stack buffer overflow in the file parser.

evidence.reason: Root cause: len is derived from the attacker-controlled 16-bit length field and can be -2 or -1 (raw field 0x0000/0x0001); the only intervening check tests tag, not len. The negative int is converted to a near-SIZE_MAX size_t as fread's nmemb argument, so fread copies file bytes into the 0x10000-byte stack buffer data without any bound on the copy. Instantiated trigger: file begins FF D8, then a marker with tag > 0xff00 (e.g. 0xFFC4) and length bytes 00 00, followed by more than 65536 bytes of attacker content; the copy at line 16 writes past data[65535], corrupting the stack frame with attacker-controlled data.

evidence.snippet: fread (data, 2, 2, ifp);
evidence.reason: Tainted-value origin: this fread fills data[0..3] from the untrusted input file ifp, supplying the marker tag (data[0..1]) and the unchecked segment length field (data[2..3]) that line 14 converts into the negative len consumed by the overflowing fread at line 16.

assumptions: ifp is a global FILE* stream over attacker-supplied file content; per the data-origin model, all bytes read into data[] are untrusted. The pointer itself is never assigned in this code.
merror (jh->row, "ljpeg_start()") is a not-shown error handler assumed to abort on a NULL calloc result; its behavior is not characterizable from the given code.

The struct jhead definition (including the capacities of jh->huff[] and jh->free[]) is not part of the given code; the writes at lines 30, 42, 44, 45 use indices bounded by this code's own loop constants and the (c = *dp++) < 4 test (max index 5), which is safe only if the arrays hold at least 6 entries.
dng_version is a global read at line 25 but never assigned in this code; it only gates a single getc(ifp) byte consumption and has no memory-safety role.
limitations: Unchecked fread return values (lines 9, 12, 16) allow short reads to leave data[] holding uninitialized or stale bytes, which are then consumed at lines 13-14, 21-25, and 33-34 (CWE-457/252). All resulting indices stay within data[0x10000] (max index 3 + 255*2 = 513) and the derived sizes are later bounded by the quoted check 'if (jh->clrs > 6 || !jh->huff[0]) return 0;', so no out-of-bounds access or size overflow was instantiated from this defect alone.

In the 0xffc4 handler, make_decoder_ref (&dp) is not shown; it may advance dp past data+len (and potentially past data+65536 when the last table starts within 16 bytes of the bound). Because the callee is not a characterizable standard function, the impact chain breaks at the callee and this remains a limitation rather than a confirmed finding.

If a DHT (0xffc4) marker is present but no SOF (0xffc0/0xffc3) marker occurs, wide = 0 and clrs = 0 pass the post-loop check and jh->row = calloc(0*0, 4) yields a zero-size buffer that is returned to the caller on success; any out-of-bounds use of jh->row happens in caller code not given, so the impact is not instantiated here.
jh->bits can go negative via 'jh->bits -= data[3+data[0]*2] & 15;' with no lower-bound check; its consumption occurs in not-shown decoding code, so no in-code impact was proven.

verdict.summary: In ReadOneMNGImage's DEFI chunk handler, the object_id bound check uses '>' instead of '>=', and the out-of-range clamp sets object_id=MNG_MAX_OBJECTS — itself one past the last valid index (the code's own CLIP/MOVE handlers reject i >= MNG_MAX_OBJECTS). An attacker-supplied MNG file with a DEFI chunk whose 16-bit object id equals or exceeds MNG_MAX_OBJECTS therefore indexes exists[], invisible[], x_off[], y_off[], and object_clip[] out of bounds, performing out-of-bounds reads and writing attacker-controlled bytes and 32-bit values past the array ends inside the heap-allocated MngInfo struct (memory corruption).

evidence.reason: Defective bound: object_id (attacker-controlled, (p[0]<<8)|p[1], 0..65535) equal to MNG_MAX_OBJECTS passes the '>' test, and larger values are clamped TO MNG_MAX_OBJECTS. The code's own guards elsewhere ("if ((i < 0) || (i >= MNG_MAX_OBJECTS)) continue;" in the CLIP and MOVE handlers, and loops "for (i=0; i < MNG_MAX_OBJECTS; i++)") establish MNG_MAX_OBJECTS as an invalid index. ThrowMagickException is a non-fatal warning, so execution continues to the array uses. Instantiated trigger: MNG file with DEFI chunk, length>=2, p[0..1] encoding any value >= MNG_MAX_OBJECTS.

Sink: with object_id == MNG_MAX_OBJECTS (reached directly or via the clamp), exists[object_id]=MagickTrue is an out-of-bounds write (preceded by the out-of-bounds read "if (mng_info->exists[object_id])" at line 396), and with length >= 3 the attacker-controlled byte p[2] is written out of bounds into invisible[MNG_MAX_OBJECTS]. No bounds check, clamp below the limit, mask, or rejecting arm exists on any path to these statements.

Sink: on the same DEFI path with object_id == MNG_MAX_OBJECTS and length >= 12, attacker-supplied 32-bit values from the chunk payload are written out of bounds into x_off[MNG_MAX_OBJECTS] and y_off[MNG_MAX_OBJECTS] (and with length > 27, an MngBox is written out of bounds into object_clip[MNG_MAX_OBJECTS] at line 437), corrupting memory adjacent to those arrays in the heap-allocated MngInfo struct. The length guards verify only the in-bounds reads of p[4..11]; no guard bounds object_id itself.

assumptions: The MngInfo struct declaration and the numeric value of MNG_MAX_OBJECTS are not shown in the given code; the valid index range 0..MNG_MAX_OBJECTS-1 is taken from quoted statements in this code (loops 'for (i=0; i < MNG_MAX_OBJECTS; i++)' and the CLIP/MOVE guards 'if ((i < 0) || (i >= MNG_MAX_OBJECTS)) continue;'), not from the unseen struct definition. The off-by-one conclusion is independent of the macro's concrete value.
AcquireQuantumMemory is treated as non-zeroing (malloc semantics), so chunk buffer bytes beyond those written by the read loop are uninitialized heap memory.
The function is judged as the intake point for attacker-controlled MNG file content; no deployment privilege or caller behavior is assumed.
limitations: Secondary instantiated defects not driving the verdict: the TERM handler reads mng_get_long(&p[2]) and mng_get_long(&p[6]) with no length>=10 check (lines 341-344), so a length-1 TERM chunk with p[0]==3 reads uninitialized heap bytes that flow into image->iterations and final_delay (uninitialized value reaching output, CWE-908 family); the FRAM handler advances p by 4/4/17 bytes after a single '(p-chunk) < (length-4)' check, reading up to chunk[length+23] of the length+MagickPathExtent allocation (uninitialized reads feeding frame_delay and mng_read_box); the chunk fill loop breaks on EOF without verifying all length bytes were read, so handlers consume uninitialized bytes on truncated chunks.

MngInfoDiscardObject is called from the DISC handler with attacker-derived indices up to 65535 and no bounds check in this code; the callee is not shown and its bounds behavior cannot be characterized, so the impact chain breaks at an uncharacterizable callee (CALLEE BOUNDARY RULE).
global_trns_length is set to the unclamped chunk length (up to PNG_UINT_31_MAX) while at most 256 bytes are copied; any harmful use would occur in ReadOnePNGImage, which is not shown.
The global_plte AcquireQuantumMemory result is not NULL-checked before the global_plte[i] write loop in the PLTE handler; the trigger requires allocation failure, which no attacker input induces.
mng_info->loop_active/loop_jump/loop_count are indexed by loop_level=chunk[0] (0..255); their declared capacity is not shown (unsourced), so no defect is claimed there.

verdict.summary: inbound_cap_ls copies an attacker-controlled capability list (extensions_str, received from the IRC server/network) into a fixed 256-byte stack buffer using repeated unbounded strcat calls. Because g_strsplit does not limit or deduplicate tokens, a CAP LS list repeating a whitelisted token (e.g. 'identify-msg' 19+ times) makes each loop iteration append its literal again, overflowing buffer[256] with an out-of-bounds stack write whose length is unbounded and whose content the attacker composes from the whitelisted literals.

verdict.summary: LoaderS3M::load reads the order-list length ordnum directly from the module file (f.readWord(), up to 65535) without any bound check against the capacity of the fixed header array header->ord, then copies up to ordnum order bytes into header->ord[j++] in a loop bounded only by that attacker-controlled count. The code bounds the sibling header counts (insnum > MP_MAXINS, patnum > 256) but not ordnum, so a crafted S3M file with e.g. 512 orders (none equal to 255) drives j past the end of the ord array, writing attacker-controlled bytes into adjacent memory of the module object: an out-of-bounds write (memory corruption) in the file-parsing trust boundary.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write: the loop bound is header->ordnum, an attacker-controlled 16-bit value read from the file (up to 65535), and the write index j is bounded only by that count plus the 'orders[i] == 255' break, which an attacker avoids by supplying order bytes that are never 255. No check anywhere in the code ties j or ordnum to the capacity of the fixed array header->ord (contrast the quoted sibling checks 'if (header->insnum > MP_MAXINS)' and 'if (header->patnum > 256)'). Trigger instantiated: ordnum=0x0200 with 512 non-255 order bytes makes j reach 512, writing attacker-controlled bytes past the ord array (memory corruption).

evidence.snippet: header->ordnum = f.readWord(); // number of positions in order list (songlength)
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: ordnum is read directly from the untrusted S3M file with no subsequent capacity bound (unlike insnum and patnum, which are checked against MP_MAXINS and 256), and it becomes both the read length and the copy-loop bound that drives the out-of-bounds write into header->ord.

assumptions: The declared capacity of header->ord (member of TXMHeader, defined outside the given code) is not shown; the finding rests on the absence in THIS code of any bound tying the attacker-controlled ordnum/j to that capacity, together with the code's own pattern of bounding sibling header counts at fixed maxima (MP_MAXINS, 256).

Capacities of module->instr, module->smp, module->phead, header->name, header->sig, instr[i].name, smp[s].name and the value of MP_MAXINS are not shown; indices into them (i < insnum, s <= insnum, 28/12/4-byte reads) are presumed in-domain only to the extent those arrays follow the module's fixed maxima.

The helper safeRead(packed, index, size, ...) is not shown; it is assumed to advance index by reference and to bounds-check against size, which is what makes the packed-pattern decompression loop terminate and stay in bounds.
limitations: Sample-slot desync in the final sample-loading loop: instruments of type 1 with samplePtrs[i] != 0 but samplen == 0 consume no s slot in the first loop, so the second loop's gate 'if (!smp[s].samplen) continue;' can read a never-written smp[s].samplen slot (possible uninitialized read, CWE-908) and mis-associate instruments with sample slots; s never exceeds insnum, so no out-of-bounds of smp itself, and whether smp is zero-initialized is not shown.

smp[s].samplen, loopstart and looplen are raw attacker-controlled dwords (loopstart+looplen is never validated against samplen in this code) and are passed to module->loadModuleSample, whose validation behavior is not characterizable from the given code.

The while (index<size) pattern-decompression loop's termination depends on the not-shown safeRead helper advancing index; if it did not, an infinite loop would be possible, but the helper cannot be characterized here.

Pattern-buffer writes were verified safe: chn is masked with & 31 (0..31), row is capped by the 'if (row >= 64) { ... break; }' arm before any slot use (row <= 63 at the slot computation), so the maximum byte offset is 63*32*5 + 31*5 + 4 = 10239 < 64*32*5 = 10240.

verdict.summary: do_i2c_md parses the display length from the command line with no range check (length = hextoul(argv[3], NULL) into a uint) and then assigns it to the signed int nbytes. For attacker values above INT_MAX (e.g. 0xffffffff), nbytes becomes negative, and the one-sided clamp linebytes = (nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN) ? DISP_LINE_LEN : nbytes passes the negative value through. The negative linebytes is then passed as the read length for the fixed stack buffer unsigned char linebuf[DISP_LINE_LEN] at the dm_i2c_read()/i2c_read() call sites, an out-of-domain length for a read into a 16-byte buffer, yielding an out-of-bounds write (memory corruption).

evidence.reason: Sink and faulty computation. linebytes is clamped only on the upper side: when nbytes is negative (produced by nbytes = length; where length is an unbounded uint parse), the ternary takes the else arm and linebytes = nbytes < 0. The negative length is passed to dm_i2c_read/i2c_read as the number of bytes to read into the fixed stack buffer unsigned char linebuf[DISP_LINE_LEN]; a negative length is outside the callee's length domain and becomes a huge unsigned size, writing past the 16-byte buffer. Instantiated trigger: argv[3] = "ffffffff" gives length = 0xFFFFFFFF, nbytes = -1, linebytes = -1 at the first (unconditional) do-while iteration; no lower-bound check, two-sided clamp, or length range check exists anywhere on any path.

evidence.snippet:
if (argc > 3)
			length = hextoul(argv[3], NULL);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value. The attacker-controlled hex string argv[3] is parsed into the uint length with no range or sanity check (the only guard is the presence check if (argc > 3)). Combined with the uint-to-int conversion at line 65 (nbytes = length;), any attacker value above INT_MAX produces a negative nbytes, which the one-sided clamp at line 70 forwards unchanged to the read call as the buffer length.

assumptions: argv[] values are attacker-data: do_i2c_md is a non-static command handler and its string parameters carry console-supplied content; no in-code statement documents or enforces any validation contract on them.
int and uint are 32 bits on the target, so uint values above 0x7fffffff convert to negative int (nbytes = length; at line 65).
hextoul is characterized per standard U-Boot helper semantics: it parses an unbounded hex string into an unsigned long.
DISP_LINE_LEN and DEFAULT_ADDR_LEN are external constants with no assignment in this code; the trigger does not depend on the concrete value of DISP_LINE_LEN, only on it being positive.
dm_i2c_read and i2c_read are characterized per the callee boundary rule as read functions that copy len bytes into the caller-supplied buffer; their internal definitions are not shown.
limitations: get_alen can return its failure sentinel -1 (this code itself tests alen != -1 on the DM path at line 53), and the check if (alen > 3) at line 40 does not reject -1. On the non-DM path, alen = -1 reaches i2c_read(chip, addr, alen, ...) at line 75. The behavior of the not-shown legacy i2c_read with a negative address length could not be characterized as memory-unsafe, so this unhandled sentinel is recorded here rather than as a finding.

Full corruption at the read call requires a chip on the current bus to acknowledge the attacker-chosen address (a responding device is needed for received bytes to be written into the buffer); with no responding device the call returns an error after line 77. The attacker fully controls chip from argv[1] and can target any responding device, but this environmental precondition is not produced by a statement in this code.
chip is not validated against the 7-bit I2C address domain before i2c_get_cur_chip/i2c_read; no memory-safety consequence of an out-of-domain chip could be characterized within this code.

A large in-range positive length (e.g. 0x7fffffff) makes the dump loop run an attacker-chosen number of bounded 16-byte iterations; each iteration performs bounded work and this is the command's intended dump semantics, so no resource-amplification finding is recorded.

The exact out-of-bounds write magnitude depends on the not-shown driver internals (e.g., any internal truncation of the length); the defect at the call site, passing an out-of-domain negative length for a fixed 16-byte buffer, stands regardless.

verdict.summary: In mpgviddmx_process, the statement memcpy(ctx->hdr_store + ctx->bytes_in_header, start, 8 - ctx->bytes_in_header) copies 8 - bytes_in_header bytes from the packet buffer without checking that the packet actually holds that many bytes; the only preceding bound is if (remain<5), which guarantees just remain >= 5. Since ctx->bytes_in_header can be 1 or 2 (stored from a previous packet that ended with remain 1 or 2 via ctx->bytes_in_header = remain), a following packet with remain = 5 causes a 6- or 7-byte read from a 5-byte buffer, a 1-2 byte heap out-of-bounds read of attacker-reachable demuxer data that is then consumed by the start-code scan mpgviddmx_next_start_code(ctx->hdr_store, 8).

e->song.insLen stays consistent with the size of the e->song.ins container (maintained elsewhere, not shown).

verdict.summary: The return-buffer size is computed with unchecked int arithmetic that can overflow: `reslen += dec` overflows for dec > INT_MAX-strlen(integral), and the thousand-separator/decimal-point contributions are added through a guard whose own product expression overflows before the comparison. The resulting wrapped reslen sizes a heap allocation (String resstr(reslen)) that the subsequent copy loops then fill exactly, writing attacker-directed bytes past the end of the buffer. The overflow-detection checks are structurally ineffective because the wrapped sum can compare as non-decreasing.

evidence.reason: The overflow guard computes `thousand_sep.size() * ((integral-1)/3)` in int arithmetic; for integral = 46 and thousand_sep.size() = 47 this product is 705 < INT_MAX, but scaling either operand (integral ~ 10^8, or separator length ~ 10^8 where the String permits) makes the product exceed INT_MAX and wrap negative, so `integral + (negative) < integral` is false and the guard passes. The wrapped value then flows into `integral += ...` and later into `reslen`, which sizes the heap buffer that the copy loop fills exactly — a heap out-of-bounds write.

`reslen += dec` is completely unchecked: dec = 1073741822 with integral = 100 gives reslen = -2147482546 (wrapped). The following dec_point guard `reslen + dec_point.size() < dec_point.size()` cannot detect this — adding a small non-negative size to an already-negative reslen keeps it below dec_point.size() only when the sum wraps again, which requires a second overflow, not the first. No check of dec against INT_MAX - reslen exists anywhere on this path, so a wrapped reslen reaches the allocation.

evidence.snippet:
String resstr(reslen, ReserveString);
  resbuf = resstr.mutableData();
evidence.reason: A wrapped (negative) reslen sizes this heap allocation. This is the sink that converts the integer overflow into memory corruption: every subsequent write goes through t = resbuf+reslen-1, i.e. a pointer computed from the wrapped length, so the copy loops write out of bounds of the actual allocation.

evidence.snippet:
s = tmpbuf+tmplen-1;
  t = resbuf+reslen-1;
evidence.reason: t is initialized from resbuf+reslen-1 with no validation that reslen covers the characters about to be copied (the loops copy exactly tmplen digits plus separators, which can exceed the wrapped reslen). The pointer t can therefore start before the allocation, and every `*t-- = ...` and `memcpy(t + ...)` in the copy loops performs an out-of-bounds write with digit bytes, separator bytes, and dec_point bytes — all attacker-controlled content.

assumptions: String::size() is assumed to return a signed int-compatible value; if the API returned an unsigned 64-bit type the products would be computed in size_t and the wrap would move to the narrowing into int at `reslen += ...` instead — either way a wrapped value reaches the allocation, so the defect stands.

The String(int, ReserveString) constructor is assumed to accept and honor the passed length as the allocation size; a constructor that internally clamped or rejected negative sizes would change the failure mode to a construction error, but no such behavior is quoted in the given code.
dec is assumed attacker-reachable (a public number-formatting entry point); if a caller elsewhere clamps dec to a small range, that clamp is not shown in this code and cannot serve as a guard.
limitations: The `tmplen < 0` early return after snprintf is correctly handled (`return empty_string()`), so the encoding-error path is not a defect.
The minus-sign handling (`if (is_negative) *t-- = '-'`) is covered by the `reslen++` on the is_negative branch, so it is not independently vulnerable when reslen is unwrapped.
The `while (s >= tmpbuf)` loop bound is sound: it copies exactly the integral digits that were counted into integral/reslen.

If the deployment never permits dec, thousand_sep.size(), or dec_point.size() to reach the computed thresholds (dec > INT_MAX - integral, or product > INT_MAX), the trigger would not fire; those reachability constraints are environment claims, not properties quotable from this code.

The subsequent data loop then walks and DMA-maps roughly 4 GB past the end of the attacker-supplied scatterlist, producing out-of-bounds reads and writes in kernel memory and attacker-scalable amplification from a zero-length request.

Index validation (pos never re-checked >= 0 after decrement) is the cause: CWE-125 / CWE-129.

debug_print is a debug-only helper; in debug builds line 50 prints the out-of-bounds byte decoded[pos], leaking adjacent heap content.
limitations: The out-of-bounds WRITE variant of the primary finding requires the heap byte at decoded[-1] to equal the rule character; the out-of-bounds READ variant is unconditional and sustains the verdict on its own.

Delete at pos == *decoded_size == INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX reads decoded[INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX], one byte past the allocation; the line-45 guard passes at the exact limit (d+l = decoded+MAX). Contrived edge, dominated by the primary finding.

verdict.summary: check_passwd() verifies the candidate password by comparing binary hash buffers with strncmp(), which stops comparing at the first matching NUL byte. Hash and PBKDF2 key material legitimately contains 0x00 bytes, so the comparison can verify as few as one byte (or zero compared bytes when both operands begin with 0x00) and still return 0, causing ret = 1 (authenticated). A stored credential whose key begins with 0x00 can be bypassed with ~256 password guesses instead of 2^(8*keylen), an authentication bypass in the code whose only statements that ever set ret = 1 are these comparisons.

evidence.snippet:
if (strncmp(passwd1_sum, key, keylen) == 0)
			ret = 1;
evidence.reason: Root cause (PBKDF2 branch): strncmp applies NUL-termination semantics to binary PBKDF2 key material. Simulated trigger: stored key from read_env_passwd begins with 0x00; attacker candidate 'x7kQ...' derives key K = {0x00, 0x7f, ...}; strncmp compares index 0, both are 0x00, comparison terminates and returns 0; ret = 1 is returned to the caller as successful authentication with bytes 1..keylen-1 never compared. No statement in this code enforces full-length comparison of the keylen bytes.

evidence.snippet:
if (strncmp(passwd1_sum, passwd2_sum, hash_len) == 0)
			ret = 1;
evidence.reason: Same root cause in the digest branch (alternative compile-time configuration): strncmp(passwd1_sum, passwd2_sum, hash_len) compares the computed digest against the stored credential sum but stops at the first matching 0x00 byte, so a prefix-equal digest with an embedded NUL is accepted as ret = 1 without comparing the remaining hash bytes.

evidence.snippet: ret = read_env_passwd(passwd2_sum, hash_len);
evidence.reason: Origin of the compared stored credential: the environment/default password hash written into passwd2_sum (also line 31 for the default variant). This binary hash content, which may contain 0x00 bytes, flows directly into the strncmp comparison sinks with no content sanitization anywhere in this code; the only check applied is the status check 'if (ret < 0) goto err;' at line 35.

assumptions: read_env_passwd/read_default_passwd (not shown) are assumed to write the stored credential hash into the provided buffer and return a status; their exact byte coverage cannot be quoted from the given code.
digest_length(d) is assumed to return the algorithm's digest output length; this code assigns it to hash_len at line 19 but never range-checks it.
digest_free(d) at line 62 is assumed to tolerate d == NULL, which is the case in the PBKDF2 branch since d is never allocated there.
pkcs5_pbkdf2_hmac_sha1 is assumed to write exactly keylen output bytes into passwd1_sum; PBKDF2_LENGTH/PBKDF2_SALT_LEN/PBKDF2_COUNT numeric values are not defined in this code.
limitations: If digest_length(d) returned 0, calloc(hash_len * 2, ...) would allocate a zero-size buffer and strncmp(passwd1_sum, passwd2_sum, 0) would return 0 unconditionally, accepting any password; no producer of 0 is quotable in this code, so this candidate is speculative and does not drive the verdict.
If PBKDF2_SALT_LEN exceeded PBKDF2_LENGTH, keylen would be negative and convert to a huge size_t at strncmp, causing an out-of-bounds read; the constants are UNSOURCED in this code.
calloc(hash_len * 2, ...) could overflow signed int only if digest_length returned a value near INT_MAX/2; no producer of such a value is shown.

Exploitability of the primary finding is graded: a stored hash with no 0x00 byte retains full strength; each embedded 0x00 at the first differing position reduces the effective compared key material, down to ~8 bits when the stored key begins with 0x00.

verdict.summary: In ga_concat_shorten_esc, the repetition-scanning loop advances s by clen, the composed byte length of the character at p (base plus trailing composing characters, from mb_cptr2char_adv), while the loop condition only requires the base character at s to equal c (mb_ptr2char). A crafted string ending with a shorter (bare) occurrence of the same base character makes s += clen step over the NUL terminator, so the *s != NUL check reads past the end of the string allocation (out-of-bounds read); with more than 20 repetitions the p = s - 1 assignment plus the for-loop ++p place p outside the buffer, and subsequent ga_concat_esc calls read heap memory past the allocation and copy it into the output array, enabling heap disclosure and a potential crash.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). clen (line 21) is the composed length of the character at p (mb_cptr2char_adv at line 20 advances past base plus composing characters), but the match at line 22 compares only the base character (mb_ptr2char). For str = 'a' + U+0300 (composing) + 41 x 'a' (NUL at index 44, allocation 45 bytes): c=0x61, clen=3, matches occur at s=3,6,...,42, then s += clen sets s=45; the next evaluation of *s != NUL reads index 45, one byte past the allocation. No statement bounds s against the terminator, so the loop condition itself performs the out-of-bounds read, and if the heap byte matches it keeps walking past the buffer.

Same defect extended: when the overshoot happens with same_len > 20 (e.g., 'a' + U+0300 + 61 x 'a', s=66 with NUL at 64), line 35 sets p = s - 1 and the for-update ++p makes p point outside the buffer; the for-header *p != NUL (line 16) then reads out of bounds, and ga_concat_esc(gap, p, clen) reads clen bytes of heap memory past the string allocation and appends them to the output array, disclosing out-of-bounds heap contents in the produced string.

assumptions: mb_cptr2char_adv (Vim mbyte framework macro) advances past the base character AND trailing composing characters, so clen can exceed the byte length of a later bare occurrence of the same base character; mb_ptr2char decodes only the base character at a position. These documented framework semantics are relied on per the callee-boundary rule.
NUMBUFLEN is defined outside the given code; its exact value is unknown, but vim_snprintf is size-bounded and the format string is a literal, so no overflow is reachable regardless of its value.
The garray_T *gap output handle is assumed non-NULL by the callers that matter; no attacker-controlled content flows into gap itself.
limitations: NULL gap would crash in ga_concat (no NULL check on gap in this code), but gap carries no attacker-controlled content and the worst consequence is process termination by a hypothetical malicious in-process caller; not instantiated against the actual data surface.

same_len is a plain int and could in theory overflow, but that requires a string of at least 2 GB (more than 2^31 matched characters) and the only consequence would be a wrongly printed count, with no memory-safety effect.
ga_concat, ga_concat_esc, and vim_snprintf internals (allocation-failure handling) are not shown; their failure modes are outside this code.

The precise reachability of the crafted composing-character string through specific Vim call sites (e.g., echo of a string value) is not shown in the given code; per the analysis rules the str parameter of this non-static function is treated as attacker-controlled content.

verdict.summary: No attacker-instantiated vulnerability found. The code's own data flow never processes untrusted-origin content; all arguments come from an in-driver init caller. One genuine defect exists — the error path frees a vzalloc'd buffer with kfree (out_kfree_buf: kfree(e->encoder_buf)) — which is an invalid free (memory-corruption class), but it is reachable only when the ctx kzalloc fails, an environmental allocation failure no attacker can induce through any input this code consumes. Unchecked kstrdup return, unvalidated args.head list traversal (cycle would hang), and unvalidated src_buf_sz all require caller-supplied preconditions this code never sources from attacker data, and their impact chains lie in code not shown.

The functions vidtv_s302m_encode, vidtv_s302m_clear, vidtv_s302m_encoder_destroy, and the callbacks stored in e->sync / e->last_sample_cb are not shown; their behavior was not relied on for any verdict.

No statement in this code produces such a chain, and the caller precondition is unsourced.

Unvalidated size stored for later use: 'e->src_buf_sz = (args.src_buf) ? args.src_buf_sz : 0;' (line 26) — the caller-supplied size is stored without bounds checks; any out-of-bounds read occurs in the not-shown encode path.

verdict.summary: In ga_concat_shorten_esc, the run-length loop matches characters by value only ('c == mb_ptr2char(s)') but advances the scan pointer by the head character's byte length ('s += clen') without ever verifying that the matching character at s occupies clen bytes. With a UTF-8 string such as "\xC3\xA9" followed by an odd run of 0xE9 bytes, the trailing lone 0xE9 (decoded as character 0xE9 because the sequence is invalid/truncated) matches c, and s += clen jumps past the NUL terminator. The loop condition '*s != NUL' then reads heap memory out of bounds and keeps scanning until a heap-content mismatch (crash on unmapped pages), and when same_len > 20, 'p = s - 1' continues the outer loop past the NUL so ga_concat_esc copies out-of-bounds heap bytes into the displayed message (information disclosure). The missing guard is the byte-length check (upstream fix: 'clen == mb_ptr2len(s)').

evidence.reason: The loop matches characters by value only and advances s by clen (the head character's byte length) with no check that the character at s occupies clen bytes and no end-pointer bound anywhere in the function. Trigger: str = "\xC3\xA9" + 0xE9 x 39 (UTF-8, attacker-controlled parameter). c = 0xE9, clen = 2; each lone 0xE9 byte decodes (invalid sequence) to 0xE9 and matches, so s advances by 2 and, after matching the final 0xE9 immediately before the NUL, s = NUL_pos + 1. The next evaluation of '*s != NUL' reads heap memory past the string and the scan continues unbounded until a mismatch, an out-of-bounds heap read causing crashes and feeding the disclosure path below.

evidence.snippet:
ga_concat(gap, (char_u *)" times]");
	    p = s - 1;
evidence.reason: After the overshoot with same_len = 21 > 20, s points past the NUL, so 'p = s - 1' followed by the for-increment '++p' (line 16) places p past the terminator. The outer condition '*p != NUL' (line 16) then reads out of bounds; if the byte is non-NUL, mb_ptr2char_adv and 'ga_concat_esc(gap, p, clen)' (lines 30/38) copy out-of-bounds heap bytes into the output array, disclosing heap memory content in the assembled message.

evidence.snippet: ga_concat_shorten_esc(garray_T *gap, char_u *str)
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted data: str is the byte-content parameter of a non-static, externally callable function with no content validation or documented precondition in the given code; its bytes (e.g., option/message string content containing "\xC3\xA9" plus a trailing 0xE9 run) drive the out-of-bounds scan.

assumptions: mb_ptr2char/mb_ptr2char_adv are treated as characterizable Vim framework functions: they return the character value at the pointer, decode an invalid or truncated byte sequence as a single character equal to the lead byte, and advance past exactly the bytes consumed; this yields c = 0xE9 with clen = 2 for "\xC3\xA9" and value 0xE9 with byte length 1 for a lone 0xE9.

The concrete trigger assumes the active multibyte encoding is UTF-8 (Vim's default); the length-blind advance defect exists for any multibyte encoding in which an invalid or truncated byte sequence can decode to a value equal to a valid multi-byte character.
gap is assumed to be a valid garray_T provided by the caller (no NULL producer exists in this code).
NUMBUFLEN is used consistently as both the buffer size (line 7) and the snprintf bound (line 32), so no overflow is possible regardless of its value.
limitations: same_len is an int that increments once per scan iteration; signed overflow would require 2^31 matching positions, which the out-of-bounds scan cannot reach before faulting, so that candidate is not treated as a finding.
A NULL gap dereference inside ga_concat/ga_concat_esc has no producer in this code and is a caller-contract question, not an instantiated vulnerability.
ga_concat/ga_concat_esc allocation failure depends on environment/OS memory exhaustion no attacker can deterministically induce here.

The degree to which heap bytes past the NUL continue to match c is heap-layout dependent; the guaranteed impact is the out-of-bounds read itself plus the p = s - 1 continuation path, both of which are triggered by the quoted statements.

verdict.summary: r_bin_java_bootstrap_methods_attr_new reads a 16-bit big-endian count at buffer offset 6 (R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT) without ever validating the attacker-supplied buffer size sz against the 8 bytes that read requires. A crafted class file with a BootstrapMethods attribute of length < 8 (down to 0) makes the parser read past the end of the heap buffer; the only sz check (`if (offset >= sz) break;`) sits inside the loop that executes after the read and therefore cannot protect it. The read value also becomes the loop bound and attr->size.

evidence.reason: Heap out-of-bounds read. offset is fixed at 6 (lines 4 and 6), and R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT(buffer, 6) dereferences buffer[6] and buffer[7] with no check anywhere in the function that sz >= 8; the sole bounds check `if (offset >= sz)` (line 14) executes only inside the loop, after this read, and only when the OOB-derived count is nonzero. Trigger fully instantiated: attacker supplies a class file whose BootstrapMethods attribute has sz = 6 (or any value 0..7), the default attr constructor returns non-NULL for the valid 6-byte header, and the read runs past the allocation.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values: buffer (content) and sz (size) are parameters of this exported class-file attribute parser and carry attacker-controlled data from the parsed binary; no documented or checked precondition on sz exists in this code before its first consumption at line 9.

assumptions: r_bin_java_default_attr_new (not shown) is assumed to be able to return a non-NULL attr for a short attribute buffer, since the attacker controls the 6 header bytes it consumes; the `if (attr)` check at line 7 is the only handling of its result and no sz validation in that callee can be quoted from the given code.
R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT is assumed to read two bytes at the given offset from the raw buffer without any internal bounds information, consistent with its raw (buffer, offset) signature.
limitations: The callee r_bin_java_bootstrap_method_new (line 17) may perform out-of-bounds reads internally, but its body is not shown and not characterizable; this code passes in-domain arguments (offset < sz is enforced by line 14 on the only path to the call, so `sz - offset` cannot underflow), so the call site itself is not defective.

`offset += bsm->size` (line 19) could in principle overflow ut64 and wrap, but bsm->size is produced entirely inside the not-shown callee; no producer of a near-2^64 size can be quoted from this code, so the wrap is speculative.

The return of r_list_newf (line 11) is unchecked and r_list_append (line 20) would receive a NULL list if the allocation failed, but whether that callee tolerates NULL is not characterizable from the given code.
If bsm->size == 0, the same bytes are re-parsed each iteration, but the loop is capped at num_bootstrap_methods <= 65535 (a USHORT read), so no unbounded amplification arises.

The only attacker-data input (name) flows exclusively into a characterizable regex matcher and an allocation whose NULL failure sentinel is checked before first use; the code performs no length arithmetic, copies, indexing, or injection-sink operations. The remaining candidate, an unchecked dereference of the caller-owned rmp pointer, has no instantiated trigger: no data path in this code can make rmp NULL, so it is a speculative caller-contract error, not an attacker-reachable defect.

home_replace_save(NULL, name) is characterized as an allocating replacement that returns a heap string or NULL on failure; NULL is treated as its failure sentinel.

p_fic is a global option ('fileignorecase') set outside this code; it is UNSOURCED here but feeds only a boolean case-sensitivity flag with no security-relevant sink.
