verdict.summary: All memory-access sinks in do_i2c_md are guarded by quotable, edge-tested checks in execution order: argv accesses are guarded by 'if (argc < 3) return CMD_RET_USAGE;' and 'if (argc > 3) length = hextoul(argv[3], NULL);'; the stack buffer linebuf is protected by the clamp 'linebytes = (nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN) ? DISP_LINE_LEN : nbytes;' which provably keeps linebytes in [0, DISP_LINE_LEN] on every iteration, and 'nbytes -= linebytes;' cannot underflow because linebytes <= nbytes in both clamp branches; get_alen's failure sentinel (-1 stored into uint) is rejected by 'if (alen > 3) return CMD_RET_USAGE;' and the DM lookup/offset/read failure sentinels are tested with 'if (ret) return i2c_report_err(ret, I2C_ERR_READ);' before any use of dev or the read data. Remaining candidates fail trigger or impact instantiation: the repeat path (CMD_FLAG_REPEAT) bypasses the alen>3 check, but every value this code assigns to i2c_dp_last_alen was already validated <= 3 and no out-of-range producer exists in the shown code; an unbounded operator-requested dump length yields only a self-inflicted hang of the requester's own console session with no cross-boundary victim; a zero length causes one 0-byte read whose driver behavior is not shown.

assumptions: get_alen(argv[2], DEFAULT_ADDR_LEN) returns an address length of 1, 2, 3 or an error value; its error/-1 return is caught by 'if (alen > 3) return CMD_RET_USAGE;' because alen is uint, but its exact range is not shown in the given code.

dm_i2c_read/i2c_read fill exactly linebytes bytes and return nonzero on failure (standard read semantics); linebuf is only read after 'if (ret) return i2c_report_err(ret, I2C_ERR_READ);' tests the sentinel.
i2c_get_cur_bus_chip(chip, &dev) fills dev and returns 0 on success; dev is consumed only after ret == 0 is confirmed by 'if (ret) return i2c_report_err(ret, I2C_ERR_READ);'.
DISP_LINE_LEN is a positive constant equal to the declared size of linebuf (the declaration 'unsigned char linebuf[DISP_LINE_LEN];' uses the same constant).
limitations: Repeat path bypasses the alen validation: 'if (alen > 3) return CMD_RET_USAGE;' executes only inside 'if ((flag & CMD_FLAG_REPEAT) == 0)'. On a repeat, alen/chip/length come from i2c_dp_last_* globals whose out-of-range values would reach i2c_set_chip_offset_len/i2c_read unvalidated. Every assignment in this code ('i2c_dp_last_alen = alen;') stores a value already validated <= 3, so an out-of-range trigger requires the unsourced initial global value or a writer not shown (other i2c command handlers) plus a first call carrying CMD_FLAG_REPEAT; UNSOURCED, not instantiated.

'length = hextoul(argv[3], NULL)' is unbounded (up to 0xFFFFFFFF) and the 'do { ... } while (nbytes > 0);' loop contains no ctrlc/abort check, so a huge length blocks the console for ~2^28 iterations of I2C reads and output. The work is linear in the operator-requested dump length and the only blocked principal is the same console session that supplied the value; no cross-boundary victim or disproportionate-work mismatch is instantiated by any statement in this code, so this is a self-inflicted CLI hang (robustness), not a CWE-400 finding here.

length == 0 still executes one do-while iteration, calling dm_i2c_read/i2c_read with linebytes == 0 (a 0-byte bus read) and printing an empty line before 'i2c_dp_last_length = length;' saves the state. Whether a not-shown I2C driver mishandles a 0-length transfer cannot be characterized; within this code the effect is a spurious 0-byte call with no memory access (both j loops run zero times).

Attacker-controlled chip (0..0xFFFFFFFF via 'chip = hextoul(argv[1], NULL);') and addr are passed to i2c_get_cur_bus_chip/dm_i2c_read/i2c_read, whose in-callee domain checks are not shown; this code's only obligation, testing the returned sentinels with 'if (ret) return i2c_report_err(ret, I2C_ERR_READ);' before consuming dev or the data, is met. If the not-shown callee returns success without filling linebuf, stack data would be printed (CWE-457), but no such callee behavior is shown or characterizable.
hextoul returns unsigned long and is truncated into uint chip/addr/length on 64-bit builds; all subsequent uses are uint-consistent and wrap safely, so no width confusion reaches a sink in this code.

verdict.summary: In njs_object_iterate_reverse, the byte/ASCII-string path computes p = string_prop.start + from from the caller-supplied, entirely unvalidated index args->from, then reads one byte at p per loop iteration down to the equally unvalidated args->to ((void) njs_string_new(vm, &character, p, 1, 1)). No statement on any path bounds from or to against the string's length/size or against zero (the only tests in the branch are the encoding equality at line 77 and the loop condition i-- > to at line 84, both in the wrong unit/variables). Any from >= string length yields out-of-bounds reads past the buffer; any to < 0 yields reads before the buffer; the read bytes are copied into string values handed to the iterator handler, giving an attacker-offset heap information-disclosure read.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) caused by unvalidated index handling (CWE-129). `from` (int64_t, attacker-supplied) is added to the string's byte-buffer pointer with no bounds, NULL, range, or clamp check anywhere on the path: line 77 only tests the encoding, and the loop bound at line 84 compares against the equally unvalidated attacker index `to`, not the buffer size. Instantiated trigger: value = "AB" (string_prop.size = 2), from = 5, to = 0 gives p = start+5 and njs_string_new copies the byte at start+5 (then start+4, start+3, start+2) out of bounds; from = 1, to = -3 makes the loop read start-1 and start-2 before the buffer. The out-of-bounds byte becomes the string value passed to handler at line 88, disclosing heap memory adjacent to the string.

Origin of the tainted values: the indices `from` and `to` are read from the caller's args struct (int64_t) at function entry of a non-static function. The given code contains no assert, documented contract, range check, or clamp on either value before they reach the pointer arithmetic at line 80 and the byte read at line 86; per the trust model the caller's content-bearing indices are attacker-data, making this code the last line of defense and the missing validation the defect.

assumptions: njs_string_prop(&string_prop, value) (line 74) fills string_prop.start/string_prop.size with the string's byte-buffer pointer and byte size and returns the codepoint length; its definition is not shown, but this is its standard parse/lookup semantics.

njs_string_new(vm, &character, p, 1, 1) (line 86) copies exactly one byte from the address p into the new string value `character`; the code's own comment '/* This cannot fail. */' refers to allocation, not bounds.

njs_is_valid(&array->start[from]) (line 28) dereferences the address it is given, so if the line-27 comparison passes for a negative from, the out-of-bounds read occurs inside the guard expression itself.
The declared width of array->length (used in the line-27 comparison `from < array->length`) is not shown in the given code, so the comparison's signedness for negative from cannot be quoted.
limitations: Array path negative index (lines 27-30): with from = -1 and to = -2 the loop runs (from += 1 then from-- yields -1). verdict.summary: In _gdContributionsAlloc, the error cleanup path performs an unconditional unsigned decrement u-- when the per-row error condition is hit on the first loop iteration (u == 0), wrapping u to 0xFFFFFFFF. The subsequent cleanup loop for (i=0;i<=u;i++) then iterates about 2^32 times, reading res->ContribRow[i] far out of bounds and passing the read values (including an uninitialized row when overflow_error was set) to gdFree. The trigger is instantiated by an oversized windows_size (>= 2^29 makes overflow2(windows_size, sizeof(double)) fail at u=0, e.g. 0x20000000) or by a windows_size whose 8x-size allocation fails on the first row, with any line_length >= 1. Consequence: out-of-bounds reads and invalid frees, i.e. a crash or allocator-state corruption, with attacker-scalable amplification.

evidence.reason: Unsigned underflow at the sink: when the error arm is entered at u == 0, u-- wraps to 0xFFFFFFFF; the loop bound i<=u (both unsigned int) then admits ~2^32 iterations. Each iteration reads res->ContribRow[i] beyond the line_length-entry array (line 22 bounds only the allocation loop, not this one) and gdFree's the out-of-bounds-read value, causing out-of-bounds reads and invalid frees (first iteration frees an uninitialized Weights when overflow_error was set). Trigger: line_length = 1, windows_size = 0x20000000 (overflow2(windows_size, 8) true at u = 0) or a windows_size whose row allocation returns NULL at u = 0. No guard on u, no line_length bound, and no signed type exists anywhere in this loop.

Origin of the error arm reached on the first iteration: the per-iteration overflow2 check on windows_size (or a NULL return from gdMalloc for an oversized row) sets overflow_error / leaves Weights NULL at u == 0, sending control into the cleanup path that performs the faulty u-- at line 30. Unlike the line_length check, which is hoisted before its use (line 13 precedes line 17), the windows_size check is only inside the loop and is not accompanied by any handling of the u == 0 case.

assumptions: overflow2(a, b) is libgd's multiplication-overflow check returning nonzero when a*b would exceed the unsigned int range; inferred from its name and its quotable use at line 13 guarding the multiplication at line 17. Its implementation is not shown. Trigger B (gdMalloc returning NULL for a ~1 GiB row allocation at u == 0) reaches the same defective statement without depending on overflow2's behavior.
gdMalloc/gdFree behave as malloc/free (allocation returns a pointer or NULL; free deallocates the given pointer).

This function is static inline and its callers are not shown; per the analysis rules, line_length and windows_size are treated as attacker-controlled since this code documents, asserts, or checks no precondition on them. In the real libgd these parameters derive from image dimensions and scaling factors supplied to the public resizing API.
limitations: line_length == 0 causes the loop at line 22 to run zero iterations and returns res with LineLength 0 and a ContribRow from gdMalloc(0); the safety of that result depends on consumers not shown.

Exploitability beyond a deterministic crash (allocator abort on invalid free) depends on heap layout not characterizable from this code; the out-of-bounds reads, the uninitialized-value free, and the ~2^32-iteration amplification are directly instantiated by the quoted statements.

verdict.summary: In sctp_make_strreset_req, the chunk-size arithmetic narrows attacker-controlled sizes into 16-bit variables: stream_len = stream_num * sizeof(__u16) (line 6) and outlen = (sizeof(outreq) + stream_len) * out / inlen = (sizeof(inreq) + stream_len) * in (lines 12-13) truncate mod 65536. For attacker-chosen stream_num in [65529..65535] with out=true (or stream_num in [65533..65535] with in=true), outlen/inlen wrap to 2..14 / 1..6, so sctp_make_reconf allocates a payload of only outlen+inlen bytes (line 15), but the subsequent sctp_addto_chunk calls append the UNtruncated sizeof(outreq)=16 and stream_len (up to 65534) bytes (lines 26/29 and 37/40) of attacker-controlled stream IDs. Concrete trigger: stream_num=65535, out=true, in=false gives stream_len=65534, outlen=14, a 14-byte payload receiving 65550 bytes — an out-of-bounds heap write of ~65536 attacker-influenced bytes (or an attacker-triggered kernel BUG in the appender), with the parameter header additionally advertising the wrapped length htons(14).

evidence.reason: Sink: with the instantiated trigger stream_num=65535, out=true, in=false, stream_len has wrapped to 65534 and outlen to 14, so the chunk payload allocated at line 15 holds only 14 bytes; this code then appends the untruncated sizeof(outreq)=16 bytes plus stream_len=65534 bytes of attacker-controlled stream IDs, an out-of-bounds heap write of ~65536 bytes past the allocation. The only guards on this path, `if (outlen)` and `if (stream_len)`, are presence checks that the wrapped values (14, 65534) pass; no bounds, clamp, mask, or capacity check exists on any path.

Origin of the faulty value: outlen is computed in size_t as 16+stream_len (up to 65551) and then narrowed into the 16-bit outlen, wrapping to 14 for the trigger, while stream_len itself already wrapped at line 6 (`__u16 stream_len = stream_num * sizeof(__u16)` = 65534 for stream_num=65535). The allocation at line 15 is then sized from the wrapped outlen+inlen even though the copy lengths at lines 26/29 use the untruncated sizeof(outreq) and stream_len — the size mismatch between the allocation expression and the copy expressions is the root-cause integer truncation.

assumptions: sizeof(outreq)=16 and sizeof(inreq)=8 are inferred from the SCTP framework headers: sctp_paramhdr is {__be16 type; __be16 length} (4 bytes) and the struct fields used in this code show outreq = param_hdr + 3 x __u32 and inreq = param_hdr + 1 x __u32; the wrapped-outlen trigger only requires sizeof(outreq) > 15 for the line-26 overflow and stream_len >> outlen for the line-29 overflow, so the finding is robust to exact sizes.

Framework-callee characterizations per the callee boundary rule: sctp_make_reconf(asoc, size) allocates a RECONF chunk whose payload capacity equals its size argument (the code's own `if (!retval) return NULL;` treats it as an allocation), and sctp_addto_chunk(chunk, size, data) appends exactly size bytes of data to the chunk payload (memcpy-like). If the appender instead detects the overrun and panics, the impact is an attacker-triggerable kernel BUG/DoS rather than silent corruption — still a vulnerability, never demoted to robustness.
Allocation success is assumed (normal path); failure is handled by the quoted `if (!retval) return NULL;`.

stream_list is assumed to hold at least stream_num entries; the truncated stream_len = (2*stream_num) mod 65536 never exceeds 2*stream_num, so the source read stays within such a buffer — the out-of-bounds is on the destination chunk.
limitations: Candidate C4: outlen+inlen (line 15) can reach 131062 (stream_len=65519, out=in=true); if sctp_make_reconf's size parameter is 16-bit (as in the actual kernel prototype `__u16 size`), a third truncation undersizes the chunk even without per-term wrap. The callee's parameter width cannot be quoted from the given code, so this variant is not counted as primary evidence; the primary trigger (outlen+inlen = 14) does not depend on it.

The `in`-branch variant (lines 37/40, out=false, in=true, stream_num in [65533..65535] giving inlen in [1..6] and stream_len in [65530..65534]) is the same root defect on the symmetric branch and is not separately evidenced.

Whether any particular in-tree caller imposes its own cap on stream_num cannot be quoted from the given code; per the trust model, caller-side validation is not evidence and does not demote the candidate.

verdict.summary: In readconf_main, the return value of expand_string(host_number_string) is passed to Ustrtol without any NULL check, unlike every other expand_string call site in the same function (spool_directory, log_file_path, pid_file_path), which all test 'if (s == NULL)' and die gracefully. A configuration whose localhost_number expansion fails (including transiently, e.g. a lookup failure) makes expand_string return NULL, and Ustrtol(s, &end, 0) dereferences NULL, crashing the process during configuration loading.

uschar *s = expand_string(host_number_string);
  long int n = Ustrtol(s, &end, 0);
evidence.reason: The result of expand_string is used as the first argument of Ustrtol with no NULL check between the call and the first use. The same function quotes the idiom this site is missing (lines 236, 250, 310: 'if (s == NULL) log_write(0, LOG_MAIN|LOG_PANIC_DIE, "failed to expand ...")'), proving expand_string returns NULL on failure for config-derived strings. Trigger: a configuration file line 'localhost_number = <failing expansion>' (e.g. a dnsdb/lsearch lookup that fails) sets host_number_string; line 391 assigns s = NULL; line 392 calls Ustrtol(NULL, &end, 0), which dereferences the NULL pointer and crashes the process. The only guard on this path, 'if (host_number_string != NULL)' (line 387), tests the option, not the expansion result, and the config ownership check is gated on the unsourced config_changed flag, so the config content is boundary-crossing data at this intake point.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: the configuration file content read by get_config_line (line 115) is dispatched here, storing option values such as host_number_string, which later reaches the unchecked expand_string/Ustrtol use at lines 391-392. verdict.summary: php_wddx_pop_element stores the result of php_base64_decode() into a zval with ZVAL_STR without checking for NULL. A WDDX packet containing a <binary> element with invalid base64 makes the strict decoder return NULL, producing a {IS_STRING, NULL} zval that is subsequently dereferenced by zval_ptr_dtor(&ent1->data) (or Z_STRLEN(ent1->data) in the php_class_name path), crashing the process that deserializes attacker-controlled WDDX input (attacker-triggered NULL pointer dereference / denial of service).

evidence.reason: The result of php_base64_decode() is stored into ent1->data with ZVAL_STR without any NULL check. On attacker-supplied invalid base64 inside a <binary> element the decode returns NULL, so ent1->data becomes {IS_STRING, NULL}, a zval whose string pointer is NULL while the type claims a valid string; the old value was already destroyed by zval_ptr_dtor on the previous line, so the NULL is the only value carried forward. This unchecked store is the root-cause defect (CWE-476).

if (ent2->type == ST_FIELD && Z_ISUNDEF(ent2->data)) {

evidence.reason: Instantiated crash sink for the trigger: after ZVAL_STR(&ent1->data, NULL) at line 36, a packet such as <wddxPacket><struct><recordset><field name='a'><binary>%%%</binary></field>... makes ent2 the ST_FIELD entry with UNDEF data, so this branch is taken and zval_ptr_dtor(&ent1->data) executes on the {IS_STRING, NULL} zval; zend_string_release then dereferences the NULL zend_string pointer, crashing the process handling the untrusted packet. The equivalent dereference also occurs at line 67 (Z_STRLEN(ent1->data)) in the php_class_name path.

assumptions: The paired start-element handler (not shown) creates stack entries: character data of <binary> elements is accumulated as an IS_STRING zval, container tags push entries with types ST_STRUCT/ST_ARRAY/ST_FIELD, and the var name attribute is attached as ent->varname. php_base64_decode performs strict decoding and returns NULL when the input contains characters outside the base64 alphabet, mirroring userland base64_decode($s, true) returning FALSE.
The XML parser guarantees well-formed tag matching, so a </binary> end tag only arrives after a <binary> start tag pushed a string entry.
limitations: zval_ptr_dtor(&retval) at line 48 runs without checking the result of call_user_function_ex; if the callee could fail while leaving retval uninitialized and without a bailout, the dtor would run on uninitialized stack memory. A type-confusion candidate (non-string ent1->data reaching Z_STRVAL/Z_STRLEN in the EL_BINARY branch) is not instantiable because well-formed XML pairing ensures binary entries carry string data.
Object instantiation from attacker-chosen class names (zend_hash_find_ptr on EG(class_table)) is inherent to the WDDX format design and not by itself a defect in this snippet.

Framework semantics relied on per the callee boundary rule: pj_size_t is unsigned; PJ_MIN(a,b) is ((a<b)?a:b); pj_memcpy copies exactly n bytes; %.*s reads at most the precision bytes without requiring NUL termination; PJ_LOG emits conditionally on the configured log level.

verdict.summary: ljpeg_start ignores the return values of the fread calls that refill the header buffer inside its do-while loop. When the input file ends right after any segment header whose tag is in 0xff01-0xffff other than 0xffda, fread at EOF transfers nothing, data keeps its stale attacker-chosen bytes, the only exit guard `if (tag <= 0xff00) return 0;` never fires, and `while (tag != 0xffda)` can never become false, so the loop spins forever on a 6-byte crafted file: an attacker-triggerable infinite loop (unbounded CPU consumption / denial of service) in the parser of untrusted image files.

evidence.reason: The return value of `fread (data, 2, 2, ifp)` is ignored. At EOF it transfers no bytes, so `tag` is recomputed each iteration from the same stale attacker-controlled header bytes (e.g. 0xffdb from a file `FF D8 FF DB 00 02` followed by EOF). The sole guard `if (tag <= 0xff00) return 0;` tests that frozen value and never triggers, and no short-read/EOF check exists anywhere in the function.

evidence.snippet: } while (tag != 0xffda);
evidence.reason: Sink: the loop exit condition depends only on `tag`, which is frozen at an attacker-chosen value (any tag in 0xff01-0xffff except 0xffda) once the file ends and the unchecked fread stops transferring bytes. The condition can never become true, producing an unreachable exit (infinite CPU loop, denial of service) from a 6-byte input.

`struct jhead` member types and the sizes of `huff[]` and `free[]` are not shown; writes such as `jh->huff[c+1]` (index up to 5) and `jh->free[c]` (c < 4) are assumed to lie within the struct.

If the callee reads more than the remaining bytes, a stack out-of-bounds read occurs, but the callee is not shown and is not a standard/system/framework function, so per the CALLEE BOUNDARY RULE the impact link is not characterizable here.

Uninitialized/stale data use: all freads can be short (truncated file), leaving `data` holding uninitialized or previous-segment bytes that reach `jh->bits` (which `jh->bits -= data[3+data[0]*2] & 15;` can drive negative), `jh->high`, `jh->wide`, and `jh->psv` (0-255). verdict.summary: cvtchar, the termcap/terminfo escape decoder, handles a caret escape without testing for end of string: `c = UChar(*++sp);` can read the NUL terminator, and `len = 2;` is then set unconditionally, reporting two consumed characters when only the single '^' remains before the terminator. Every other arm of the same function sizes its length to stop at the terminator (case '\0': len = 1; len = (c != '\0') ? 2 : 1; len = (c != '\0') ? 1 : 0), proving the consumed-length contract; the parse position therefore advances one byte past the end of the string buffer and the next dereference reads out of bounds, continuing until a chance NUL in adjacent memory. A malicious terminfo/termcap source whose capability string ends with '^' triggers this heap out-of-bounds read in the tic/captoinfo conversion path.

evidence.reason: The caret arm reads the byte after '^' with `c = UChar(*++sp);` and never tests c == '\0', the end-of-string sentinel of that read; both the if and else arms fall through to the unconditional `len = 2;`. For an attacker-supplied capability string ending with '^' immediately before the NUL terminator (cvtchar called with sp pointing at that '^'), the simulation yields c = 0, nothing saved, and return value 2 although only one character remains. The parser advances two characters, stepping one byte past the terminator, and the subsequent dereference reads beyond the string buffer (out-of-bounds read of unbounded extent). No sentinel test, ternary length, clamp, case arm, or error return exists on any path to `len = 2;` — in contrast to the '\0' handling at lines 17-19 and the ternaries at lines 33 and 47.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted data: sp points into a NUL-terminated terminfo/termcap source string parsed from file content (untrusted per the data-origin model); a value ending in '^' flows from this parameter into the unguarded caret arm at lines 37-43.

verdict.summary: In SplashOutputDev::tilingPatternFill, the 32-bit integer product surface_width * (x1 - x0) in the sx computation can wrap to zero (e.g., 65536 * 65536 = 2^32 mod 2^32 = 0), making sx = result_width / 0 evaluate to +/-infinity. Then m1.m[0] *= sx becomes +/-inf, the matrix transform places inf into kx, and the pattern-size limiting loop 'while(fabs(kx) > 16384 || fabs(ky) > 16384) { m1.m[0] /= 2; ... }' can never terminate because inf/2 = inf. A crafted PDF (attacker-controlled bbox, ptm, xStep, x0/x1 and CTM) hangs the renderer in a permanent CPU-bound infinite loop: an attacker-triggered denial of service with no guard, clamp, finiteness check, or iteration cap anywhere on the path.

evidence.reason: Sink: loop with unreachable exit condition. When kx = +inf (m1.m[0] = +inf from the poisoned sx, width > 0), fabs(inf) > 16384 is always true and m1.m[0] /= 2 yields inf/2 = inf, so m1.transform(width, height, &kx, &ky) recomputes kx = inf*m[0]*width + 0*height + 0 = inf every iteration. No finiteness check, clamp, or iteration cap exists on any path to this loop (the only std::isfinite checks, on ctm[], run earlier and inspect different values; the 0x800000 area check at line 81 inspects only pre-loop surface values and passes for e.g. 65536x1). Instantiated trigger: bbox width=1, xStep=1, ptm scaled so kx_first = 65536, x1-x0 = 65536, result_width = 1, giving sx = 1/0 = +inf and an eternal CPU hang (DoS).

Origin of the faulty value: surface_width * (x1 - x0) is a 32-bit int product of two attacker-influenced values with no overflow check; when it wraps to exactly 0 (65536 * 65536 = 2^32 wraps to 0) while result_width is nonzero, sx = result_width/0.0 = +/-inf. m1.m[0] *= sx then sets the matrix entry to +/-inf, and the transform on line 68 propagates inf into kx, which reaches the halving loop that cannot reduce it. This is the root-cause integer overflow (CWE-190) feeding the infinite loop (CWE-835) at lines 85-90.

assumptions: Parameters ptm, bbox, mat, xStep, yStep, x0/y0/x1/y1, paintType and the GfxState CTM originate from PDF pattern dictionaries and content streams and arrive at this non-static entry point with no documented or asserted contract in the given code; they are treated as attacker-data.

state->getHDPI()/getVDPI() are not assigned in this code; the trigger requires nonzero DPI, which holds in any functioning render, and the attacker scales ptm[0]/ptm[3] to hit the needed kx_first for whatever the actual DPI is.

Two's-complement 32-bit int wraparound and IEEE-754 semantics (x/0.0 = +/-inf, 0*inf = NaN, inf/2 = inf) are assumed, as universally implemented; the (int) cast of NaN/out-of-range doubles yielding INT_MIN (itself UB) is the common platform behavior and is only relied on for the secondary candidates.
limitations: NaN propagation path to out-of-domain bitmap dimensions: with ptm[0]=ptm[2]=0, kx becomes 0, surface_width = 0, sx = 0/0 = NaN (line 64), kx = NaN skips the halving loop, and '(int) ceil(fabs(NaN))' at line 91 yields INT_MIN, which passes both 'surface_width == 0 || surface_height == 0' checks (lines 94 and 119, which miss negatives) and the line-81 area check (which only tests the pre-recompute values). The unvalidated negative dimension then reaches 'bitmap = new SplashBitmap(surface_width, surface_height, 1, ...)' at line 127; whether this corrupts memory or fails safely depends on the unshown SplashBitmap constructor/gmalloc behavior and the quoted 'if (bitmap->getDataPtr() == nullptr)' recovery, so the impact is not characterizable from the given code.

First branch (fabs(kx)<1 && fabs(ky)<1): 'ky = 2 / kx' with kx == 0 produces inf, and the resulting (int) casts can yield INT_MIN surface dimensions with no zero/negative/area check in that branch at all; same uncharacterizable SplashBitmap impact as above.

result_width = tBitmap->getWidth() * imgData.repeatX (and the height counterpart) can overflow 32-bit int for attacker-large repeatX/repeatY (capped only by x1-x0/y1-y0); the overflowed values are passed to splash->drawImage and consumed by the unshown tilingBitmapSrc callback, so the impact cannot be confirmed here.

verdict.summary: In block_insert(), the append branch on short lines (b_insert == 0, bdp->is_short) allocates the replacement line as STRLEN(oldp) + spaces + s_len + (spaces>0 && !is_short ? ts_val - spaces : 0) + count + 1, but then copies count (= spaces) bytes of post-padding at newp + offset + spaces. When a TAB must be split, the code needs ts_val - spaces extra bytes but the allocation adds only count == spaces, so any ts_val > spaces under-allocates by ts_val - spaces bytes and the memset writes past the end of the allocated buffer: a heap out-of-bounds write whose geometry is controlled by attacker-supplied buffer text (tabstop configuration derived from the text, gap size from the block edge). All other candidates (OOM NULL, negative spaces, mb_head_off pointer arithmetic, tail calls) were dismissed with quoted guards or with unproducible trigger preconditions.

evidence.reason: Alloc-size miscalculation: in the append branch on a short line (bdp->is_short), count was set to spaces (line 61) and spaces = (oap->end_vcol - bdp->end_vcol) + 1 (line 62), so the allocation reserves only spaces bytes for post-padding. When the character at the block edge is a TAB that must be split, the code writes ts_val - spaces bytes at newp + offset + spaces (post-padding memset at lines 113-114), but the allocation adds only count == spaces bytes for it. With a tabstop wider than the gap (e.g. ts_val = 8, spaces = 1: allocation adds 1, memset writes 8), the memset writes past the end of the allocated buffer: an attacker-influenced heap out-of-bounds write driven by buffer text (tabstop configuration and gap geometry). The STEP 5 exhaustive search found no size correction, clamp, or runtime bound anywhere in the function.

assumptions: Assumed standard Vim semantics for the ml_get/alloc/mch_memset/mch_memmove/STRMOVE/STRLEN helper calls (they behave as documented: bounds-checked line lookup by ml_get, allocation, byte-wise memset, byte-wise memmove, NUL-terminated copy, string length).

Assumed tabstop values in the range 1-80 are configurable by the user through buffer content (modelines) or editor settings, which puts the ts_val > spaces precondition within attacker reach; the calculation does not depend on ts_val being large, since any ts_val > spaces under-allocates.
Assumed bdp->end_char_vcols reflects the tabstop-derived virtual column of the block edge, per block_prep's documented behavior, making the overflow geometry content-dependent.
limitations: The mb_head_off call at oldp + offset + spaces with spaces + offset beyond the end of a short line could read out of bounds, but no path in this code produces such a state (the maximum offset + spaces is bounded by bdp->textcol + bdp->textlen and the end_vcol-based spaces computation), so the trigger could not be instantiated.

The tail calls changed_lines(oap->start.lnum + 1, 0, oap->end.lnum + 1, 0L) and inserted_bytes(lnum, startcol, s_len) assume the documented Vim behavior of clipping line/column arguments to buffer bounds; a misbehavior there would be a defect in code not given.

If Vim's internal memory allocator placed guard pages or redzones around every alloc, the overwrite would crash rather than corrupt, but no such behavior is quoted in the given code, so the heap-corruption classification stands.

The size arithmetic was checked for 32-bit unsigned wraparound (size_t sums near SIZE_MAX); it is not reachable because STRLEN(oldp) + spaces + s_len are bounded by line length and block geometry far below the wrap threshold, so no wrap-based trigger exists.

verdict.summary: Fractional max-pool OpKernel reads out of bounds: the pooling-sequence start indices (height_start, width_start) are used as loop initializers and array indices without any clamp or validation, while only the end indices are clamped to height_max/width_max. GeneratePoolingSequence's documented contract only bounds terminal values by gen_max (ceil(input/ratio)) < input_size when ratio > 1, so for hs==0 the start can equal input_size[1] itself. The innermost loop then executes with h = input_size[1] and computes in_offset one full row past the Eigen-mapped input buffer, which in_mat.col(in_offset) reads out of bounds; the read value is written to the output tensor, giving a memory-disclosure-capable read primitive triggered entirely by attacker-controlled tensor shape attributes.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read sink: h is initialized from height_start with no bound. Simulated trigger: input_size[1]=16, pooling_ratio_[1]=2 → gen_max=8, GeneratePoolingSequence emits height_cum_seq[0]=8..16; take cum[0]=16 → hs==0 gives height_start=16, height_end=min(16,15)=15 (overlapping_) or 15 (non-overlapping), so the loop body executes exactly once with h=16==input_size[1] (h <= height_end is false only for h>15; the body runs because the initializer is evaluated before the condition). in_offset = (0*16+16)*input_size[2]+0 indexes in_mat one full row past its mapped extent of input_size[2]*input_size[1]*input_size[0] columns, reading uninitialized/out-of-bounds memory that is then written into the output tensor. Only the end indices are clamped ('height_end = std::min(height_end, height_max);' / 'width_end = std::min(width_end, width_max);'); no clamp, check, mask, checked accessor, or loop-bound fix guards height_start/width_start on any path.

Origin of the unvalidated value: height_start is assigned directly from the random pooling sequence with no bound against height_max (input_size[1]-1). The sequence's first element can equal input_size[1] because GeneratePoolingSequence only guarantees terminal values are <= gen_max = ceil(input_size[1]/pooling_ratio_[1]), and the check 'input_size[i] >= pooling_ratio_[i]' permits ratio==1 making gen_max==input_size[1]; additionally each generated non-terminal value can be incremented ('if (cum_seq.back() >= input_size) --i; else ++cum_seq.back();') up to input_size, so height_start ∈ [gen_max, input_size[1]] while the valid row domain is [0, input_size[1]-1].

verdict.summary: The bounds check 'fd >= ctx->nr_user_files' correctly handles all out-of-range values including negative file descriptors. verdict.summary: DoCompute enforces only rank equality and a shape prefix for updates, never that updates' trailing dimensions match params->shape()[1:]. The code's own invariant ('updates.shape = indices.shape + params.shape[1:]') is thus reduced to a rank check, so updates_flat = shaped({N, num_updates/N}) can have a second dimension unequal to params_flat's inner dimension. The scatter functor call then writes each update row (attacker-chosen length) into a params row of a different width: with num_updates/N > params inner size it writes past the row (and past the buffer for the last row index); with num_updates/N < params inner size it reads past the updates buffer into the readable variable. evidence.reason: The sink: updates_flat is built as {N, num_updates / N} where num_updates/N is the product of updates' attacker-chosen trailing dims, while params_flat (line 37) has inner extent product(params->dim_size(1..)). No statement in this code equates the two, and the scatter functor call scatters each updates row of length num_updates/N into a params row of the (different) params inner width. With params [10,5], indices [3]={9,...}, updates [3,7] — which passes every check — the functor writes 7 attacker values into the 5-wide last params row, 2 elements past the heap buffer; bad_i is -1 because index 9 is valid, so no error is raised.

Instantiated trigger: mode=0x82 gives rle=true, palSize=2; palette[0..1] initialized; attacker byte 0x02 yields index=2, so palette[2] is uninitialized stack memory that is then copied into buf and pushed to the framebuffer by pb->imageRect (line 125).

evidence.snippet:
rdr::U8 index = (byte >> nbits) & ((1 << bppp) - 1) & 127;
              *ptr++ = palette[index];
evidence.reason: Same root cause in the packed-pixels path: for palSize=17 (bppp=8) the mask permits index up to 127 while only palette[0..16] were initialized; e.g. byte=0x7F gives index=127 and *ptr++ = palette[index] stores uninitialized stack memory into buf. For bppp=4 (palSize 5..16) index can reach 15 and for bppp=2 (palSize=3) index can reach 3, all beyond the initialized domain. No check of index against palSize exists on any path.

Origin of the uninitialized data: palette is declared without initialization and the fill loop's bound is palSize (<= 127), leaving entries [palSize, 128) uninitiated for the whole tile iteration; both confirmed sinks (lines 66 and 118) index into this unvalidated region.

assumptions: READ_PIXEL(zis) reads one PIXEL_T from the compressed stream; its definition is not shown.
pb->fillRect / pb->imageRect copy the tile into the pixel buffer (characterizable framebuffer accessor); pb and pf non-NULL is not checked or documented in this code.
rdr stream readU8/READ_PIXEL throw on exhausted input (framework behavior, not shown).
BPP and PIXEL_T widths are compile-time macros; the raw-path readBytes sizing is exact because __rfbmin clamps (lines 12, 16) cap every tile at 64x64.
limitations: int length = is->readU32() can be negative (e.g. 0x80000000 -> INT_MIN) and is passed unvalidated to zis->setUnderlying(is, length) at line 6; setUnderlying is not shown and not characterizable, so the impact chain breaks at the callee boundary and this is recorded as a limitation, not a finding.

Signed overflow of the RLE run length (len += b loops at lines 85 and 108) requires roughly 8-16 MB of 0xFF run bytes from one tile; a wrapped negative len skips the write loop ('while (len-- > 0)') and a wrapped positive len is still rejected by the quoted checks at lines 88 and 111, so no memory corruption was instantiated.
pb/pf NULL dereference at lines 29/125 has no producer in this code and no quotable contract, so it remains an assumption.

verdict.summary: get_complex_object reads a signed 32-bit length for a complex-number string directly from the parsed .pyc file (n1 = get_st32(buffer, &error)) into a ut32 with no range or sign check. When the attacker supplies 0xFFFFFFFF, the allocation-size expression malloc(n1 + 1) wraps to malloc(0), yielding a minimal non-NULL heap allocation, and rz_buf_read(buffer, s1, n1) then copies up to all remaining attacker-controlled file bytes past the end of that allocation. The only length check (if (size != n1)) executes after the overflowing read. The identical defect exists for n2/s2. Result: an attacker-controlled heap out-of-bounds write (content and length chosen by the input file) in an untrusted-file parser.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted length: a signed 32-bit value read from the attacker-controlled pyc buffer is stored into ut32 n1 with no bound or sign check; -1 becomes 0xFFFFFFFF. The branch is selected by the file's magic number (> 62061 selects this 4-byte path).

Sink of the primary defect: with n1 = 0xFFFFFFFF, n1 + 1 wraps to 0 in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic, so malloc(0) returns a minimal non-NULL allocation while rz_buf_read(buffer, s1, n1) writes min(n1, bytes-remaining) attacker-controlled bytes into it — a heap out-of-bounds write. No range, clamp, or sign check on n1 exists on this path, and the if (size != n1) check at line 28 runs only after the overflowing copy.

Second instance of the same confirmed defect: n2 = get_st32 (line 38) can hold 0xFFFFFFFF, malloc(n2 + 1) wraps to malloc(0), and rz_buf_read(buffer, s2, n2) overflows the minimal allocation with attacker file bytes; the size != n2 check at line 48 is post-use.

assumptions: pyc->magic_int has no assignment in this code; it is the parsed pyc file header value (attacker file content per discipline 3), and values > 62061 select the 4-byte length path — the mainstream format this else-arm exists to handle. The branch is treated as attacker-selected; the assignment itself is not quotable here.

malloc(0) returning a unique non-NULL minimal pointer is standard allocator behavior (glibc and most allocators); if it returned NULL, the if (!s1)/if (!s2) checks would abort the path before the overflow.
get_ut8/get_st32 read values from the buffer and set *error on failure (characterizable parse functions); rz_buf_read copies up to len bytes clamped to the data available in the buffer.
limitations: Memory leaks on error paths (lines 23-25 free nothing on malloc(s1) failure, lines 39-41 and 43-45 return without freeing previously allocated s1/ret) — bounded retention proportional to input size, not promoted to a finding.

s1[n1] = '\0' at line 33 would also be out of bounds under the wrap, but on the wrapped trigger the function returns at line 28 first; it is subsumed by the primary write at line 27 and would require a buffer with >= 0xFFFFFFFF bytes remaining to pass the size check.
The rz_str_newf call uses a constant format string with NUL-terminated arguments — no format-string injection; dismissed after verification.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read at id->name[SNDRV_CTL_ELEM_ID_NAME_MAXLEN] caused by incorrect operand ordering in the loop condition: the array access id->name[i] is evaluated before the bounds check i < SNDRV_CTL_ELEM_ID_NAME_MAXLEN due to C's short-circuit && evaluation order, resulting in a one-byte read past the 44-byte name array when all name bytes are non-zero. The read stays within the containing struct and does not influence the hash output.

evidence.snippet:
for (i = 0; id->name[i] && i < SNDRV_CTL_ELEM_ID_NAME_MAXLEN; i++)
		h = MULTIPLIER * h + id->name[i];
evidence.reason: The loop condition evaluates id->name[i] (array read) BEFORE checking i < SNDRV_CTL_ELEM_ID_NAME_MAXLEN. When all 44 name bytes are non-zero attacker data, the loop reaches i=44 and reads id->name[44] — one byte past the unsigned char name[44] array — before the bounds check executes. The correct form would place the bounds check first: i < SNDRV_CTL_ELEM_ID_NAME_MAXLEN && id->name[i].

assumptions: MULTIPLIER is defined elsewhere and is a constant suitable for hash computation
SNDRV_CTL_ELEM_ID_NAME_MAXLEN equals 44 based on the standard ALSA struct definition
The struct snd_ctl_elem_id has the name array followed by the index field within the same allocation, keeping the OOB read within the struct
limitations: The OOB read value at name[44] is never incorporated into the hash result (loop body does not execute at i=44 in either branch), so no information disclosure or output corruption occurs
The read stays within the containing struct snd_ctl_elem_id in typical memory layouts, so no page fault or crash occurs
SNDRV_CTL_ELEM_ID_NAME_MAXLEN and the exact struct layout are not shown in the given code, so the precise byte being read OOB is inferred from standard ALSA definitions

verdict.summary: No instantiable vulnerability: the attacker-controlled name length is bounded by a quoted, execution-order-correct check (dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN) that fires before the only variable-length read, and the buffer is sized from the same constant (sizeof(squashfs_dir_entry_2) + SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1), so even the boundary value dire->size = SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN-1 stays exactly in bounds including the NUL write; the directory entry count is likewise capped by the quoted dir_count > SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT check, and every inner iteration strictly advances bytes while consuming finite on-disk data, guaranteeing termination. Remaining concerns (possible NULL from read_inode before (*i)->mode is read, check_name semantics, read_directory_data behavior, bitfield signedness, SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT/SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN values) depend on unshown code or unsourced type layouts and cannot be instantiated from the given statements.

assumptions: squashfs_dir_header_2.count and squashfs_dir_entry_2.size bitfield widths/signedness, and the placement of the name member, are not in the given code; the analysis of guard (a) is robust to any layout because offset_of(name) <= sizeof(squashfs_dir_entry_2) and the buffer adds SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1 bytes.
Values of SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN and SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT are not defined in the given code; both quoted guards use these constants consistently with the buffer sizing expression.

Semantics of read_directory_data (returns FALSE on failure/EOF, fills the destination on success), read_inode (may or may not return NULL), check_name, squashfs_closedir, MEM_ERROR, and SQUASHFS_SWAP_DIR_* macros are not shown; only their success/failure sentinel usage within this code is relied on.
Globals swap and sBlk.s.directory_table_start are consumed but never assigned in this code (UNSOURCED state).
limitations: Potential NULL dereference: *i = read_inode(block_start, offset) is not checked before dir->mode = (*i)->mode; trigger requires read_inode to return NULL on corrupt data, which is unshown internal code and cannot be characterized, so the trigger is speculative.

If dirh.count were a signed type, a negative dir_count could bypass the '>' check; requires an unsourced struct definition, and each inner iteration still consumes finite file data (EOF ends the loop), so no unbounded primitive is instantiable.

Path traversal via dire->name depends on the unshown check_name implementation and on extraction code not given; the guard call check_name(dire->name, dire->size + 1) is present at the correct execution-order position in this code.

Integer overflow of bytes (int) would require roughly 2^31 bytes of physically present directory data to be read successfully, making it input-proportional rather than attacker-scalable amplification, with no memory-corruption consequence in this code.
Passing dire->size + 1 <= 0 to read_directory_data is only reachable if dire->size is negative, which requires an unsourced signed bitfield; under any unsigned reading the minimum read length is 1.

verdict.summary: clone_private_mount validates the attacker-selectable mount on every path in execution order: it rejects unbindable mounts (IS_MNT_UNBINDABLE), mounts outside the current namespace including detached and internal ones (check_mnt), and mounts with locked children under the target dentry (has_locked_children); it tests the clone_mnt failure sentinel with IS_ERR before the sole dereference (new_mnt->mnt_ns = MNT_NS_INTERNAL), and namespace_sem is released exactly once on both exits. No trigger with a sourced precondition reaches any sink: memory-safety, cross-namespace, and fail-open paths are all cut by quoted guards, and the only unguarded candidate (a NULL path/mnt deref) has no attacker-reachable producer through this code's input surface.

assumptions: Semantics of real_mount, IS_MNT_UNBINDABLE, check_mnt (compares mnt_ns against current->nsproxy->mnt_ns), has_locked_children (iterates mnt_mounts testing is_subdir of each child mountpoint against the target dentry), and clone_mnt (allocates a mount and dgets the root, returning ERR_PTR on failure) are characterized from mainline kernel behavior; these callees are not shown in the given code.

Callers are in-kernel (overlayfs and related VFS code) that pass struct path values produced by successful kernel lookups, so path->mnt/path->dentry pointer validity and pairing are established upstream; the attacker controls only which mount/dentry is selected.
Writers of the mount tree (attach/umount) take namespace_sem for writing, so the down_read(&namespace_sem) held during has_locked_children and clone_mnt serializes those reads.
limitations: NULL/invalid path or path->mnt would be dereferenced at 'real_mount(path->mnt)' / 'IS_MNT_UNBINDABLE(old_mnt)' with no NULL check in this code (CWE-476 class), but the trigger precondition (a caller passing NULL or a malformed path) is UNSOURCED: no statement of this code or attacker input surface can produce it, so it is speculative and does not flip the verdict.

A reference leak of the longterm clone is possible only if a caller violates the contract this code itself documents ('/* Longterm mount to be removed by kern_unmount*() */'); the misuse and its impact would occur entirely in unshown caller code.
A race during has_locked_children would require some other code mutating mnt_mounts without namespace_sem; no such statement is shown, so the window is not instantiated in this code.
Any vulnerability fixed in this function after the knowledge cutoff of this analysis cannot be reflected here.

verdict.summary: In the PseudoClass path, colormap_index is allocated with only image->colors+1 entries (lines 26-27), but the final pixel loop indexes it with ScaleQuantumToMap(GetPixelIndex(image,q)) (lines 149-150), a file-derived pixel index that can be as large as MaxColormapSize-1. No statement in this code validates the pixel index against image->colors, and the memset/initialization block is skipped for PseudoClass images. A malformed palette-based image whose pixel index exceeds the colormap size causes a heap out-of-bounds read; the garbage value is then stored as a pixel colormap index and consumed by subsequent colormap operations.

evidence.snippet:
SetPixelIndex(image,(Quantum) colormap_index[ScaleQuantumToMap(
        GetPixelIndex(image,q))],q);
evidence.reason: Heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125, index-handling cause CWE-129): the pixel index GetPixelIndex(image,q) is file-derived attacker data and is never validated against image->colors anywhere in this code; for a PseudoClass image with colors=2, a pixel index of 100 makes colormap_index[100] read element 100 of a 3-element heap buffer. The OOB-read value is then cast to Quantum and stored as the pixel's colormap index via SetPixelIndex.

Origin of the undersized buffer: colormap_index is sized from image->colors+1 for PseudoClass images, while later code indexes it with values bounded only by MaxColormapSize-1. In the PseudoClass case the initialization block (guarded by 'if (image->storage_class != PseudoClass)' at line 34) is skipped, so no bound and no sentinel exist for indexes >= image->colors.

assumptions: ScaleQuantumToMap is an ImageMagick inline macro/function not shown in the given code; per its documented framework semantics it maps a Quantum value into [0, MaxColormapSize-1]. If it did not clamp, the non-PseudoClass path (allocation MaxColormapSize+1, lines 29-30) would also be affected.

GetPixelIndex/SetPixelIndex are ImageMagick pixel accessors that read/store the pixel's colormap index; GetCacheViewAuthenticPixels returns a row pointer or NULL (NULL is checked at lines 63 and 142).

The Image struct fields (storage_class, colors, colormap contents, per-pixel indexes) are populated by image-file decoding before this function runs; per discipline 3 this function is the intake consumer of that untrusted content and no quotable caller contract restricts it.
AcquireQuantumMemory and AcquireImageColormap succeed for the simulated trigger (their failure paths are handled at lines 31, 38, 104).
limitations: Uninitialized read at the boundary: entry colormap_index[image->colors] (index exactly == colors) is within the colors+1 allocation but is never written on the PseudoClass path (writes via lines 100/119 cover only 0..colors-1); a pixel index exactly == colors would read an uninitialized ssize_t (CWE-908). This is subsumed by the stronger index > colors case which is confirmed as the primary finding.

Zero-size edge: if image->colors==0 on entry (e.g., a non-PseudoClass image with zero rows/columns, since line 44 sets colors=0 and the loop at line 51 never runs), colormap=AcquireQuantumMemory(0,...) at line 103 is followed by the write colormap[0]=image->colormap[0] at line 111 into a zero-sized allocation. This trigger depends on malloc(0) semantics and on reachability of colors==0 from the decoder, so it is not counted as primary evidence.

The OOB-read value stored as a pixel index may cause further out-of-bounds colormap accesses in downstream consumers of the modified image (including the shown call SetImageMonochrome at line 159 and later coders); the direct confirmed impact in this code is the heap out-of-bounds read itself.

verdict.summary: No fully instantiated vulnerability exists in the given code. All command-line-derived values (jas_optarg) either flow into not-shown callees (addopt, with the bound OPTSMAX passed at the call site) or are merely stored into fields whose consumers are not shown (debug, cmptno, max_mem, path/format strings). The one in-code memory access, argv[jas_optind] in the warning fprintf, is guarded by 'while (jas_optind < argc)' in execution order, uses a fixed format string, and has no negative-value producer in this code. malloc is checked and every struct member is initialized before use. Potential risks at the boundaries (addopt buffer handling, atoi/strtoull unvalidated parses including the strtoull '-1' wrap to ULLONG_MAX, possible NULL jas_optarg on missing option arguments) cannot be confirmed because their sinks lie in uncharacterizable code not given and the buffer size OPTSMAX is unsourced.

assumptions: jas_getopt is a getopt-like parser: it returns the id field of a matching entry in cmdoptions (all such ids have a case arm; unknown options reach default: badusage()), sets jas_optarg for JAS_OPT_HASARG entries, and advances jas_optind; none of this is quoted in the given code.
badusage() terminates the process (suggested by the preceding fprintf error message but not shown).
get_default_max_mem_usage() returns a sane default cap; its definition is not shown.

The code runs as an ordinary CLI where argv is supplied by the local user; per discipline 3 this assumption was not used to demote any candidate, but note the only party controlling argv here is the invoker.
limitations: addopt(cmdopts->inoptsbuf/outoptsbuf, OPTSMAX, jas_optarg) copies attacker-controlled strings into fixed buffers; the callee body, the true buffer sizes (cmdopts_t layout), and the OPTSMAX constant are all unsourced/not shown, so a buffer overflow (e.g., mishandled append bound or repeated -o/-O appends) cannot be confirmed or excluded. If addopt misuses the passed bound (classic strncat-style CWE-131), the defect would be in the callee, not at this call site, which passes a NUL-terminated string plus a length bound.

atoi(jas_optarg) for --debug-level and --cmptno: unvalidated parse, undefined behavior on out-of-range input; the parsed values are only stored here, and their downstream use (e.g., cmptno as a component index) is not shown.

strtoull(jas_optarg, 0, 10) for --memory-limit: no endptr/errno validation; input '-1' wraps to ULLONG_MAX (disabling the cap) and non-numeric input silently yields 0. The memory-limit consumer is not shown, so the impact is not instantiated.

A negative or otherwise out-of-range jas_optind would make argv[jas_optind] an out-of-bounds read; no statement in this code produces such a value, and the guard 'jas_optind < argc' handles the upper bound.
If jas_getopt can return an JAS_OPT_HASARG id with jas_optarg unset (option missing its argument), atoi/addopt/strtoull would receive NULL; jas_getopt's missing-argument semantics are not shown.

If badusage() returned instead of exiting, cmdopts_parse would return an incompletely specified options object; badusage's body is not shown, though no security-state misrepresentation (only a usage error) would result.

verdict.summary: ins_bs() performs guarded memory accesses: the previous-line trailing-space edit is protected by 'len > 0' before 'ptr[len - 1]', all ml_get_cursor()-1 reads are preceded by 'curwin->w_cursor.col > 0' in short-circuit order, the word-delete do-while is entered only with col != 0 and bounded by 'col > mincol' with mincol < original col, the replace-stack loop tests the -1 sentinel ('while (cc > 0)'), and the potentially uninitialized cpc[] is read only under the same enc_utf8 && p_deco condition that fills it. The sole unguarded path (revins_on bypassing the top backspace guard, potentially decrementing Insstart.lnum to 0 before ml_get) requires user-only reverse-insert configuration unsourced in this code, and its impact depends on not-shown memline behavior, so it is recorded as a limitation rather than a confirmed vulnerability.

assumptions: Vim-internal callees (ml_get, ml_get_buf, ml_get_cursor, dec_cursor/inc_cursor, getvcol, replace_pop, do_join, u_save, utfc_ptr2char) behave per upstream Vim semantics; their implementations are not shown and were not treated as guards.

Division at 'want_vcol = (want_vcol / ts) * ts' on the p_sta arm relies on get_sw_value(curbuf) never returning 0 (Vim maps 'shiftwidth' 0 to 'tabstop', minimum 1) — enforced in not-shown code, hence an assumption, not a quoted guard.
u_save is assumed to accept line numbers below 1 ((linenr_T)(curwin->w_cursor.lnum - 2) can be -1 or 0) as documented top-of-buffer semantics.
limitations: revins_on path: the top guard is wrapped in '!revins_on && (...)', and the delete-newline branch admits '|| revins_on', so '--Insstart.lnum; Insstart.col = (colnr_T)STRLEN(ml_get(Insstart.lnum));' could in principle be reached with Insstart.lnum == 1 (decrementing to 0, ml_get(0)). The trigger requires the user to enable reverse insert ('allowrevins' is a secure option not settable via modeline, so no attacker-input source in this code reaches it), and whether ml_get(0) is harmful is decided inside not-shown memline code — the impact chain breaks, so this stays speculative.

The ts divisor on the 'p_sta && in_indent' arm has no in-code nonzero check; only the other arm is covered by 'get_sts_value() != 0'. No statement in this code can produce ts == 0, so a divide-by-zero trigger is not instantiated here.

The space-insert loop 'while (vcol < want_vcol)' is bounded only indirectly by want_vcol derived from getvcol of a real cursor position; no statement in this code caps it explicitly, but no attacker input can push want_vcol beyond a value derived from an actual buffer position either.

verdict.summary: The sysfs store handler bounds the copy correctly: 'if (nbytes >= MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN) return 0;' rejects every value for which nbytes + 1 could exceed sizeof(drc_name), and since both the array dimension and the guard use the same MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN, strscpy(drc_name, buf, nbytes + 1) can write at most exactly MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN bytes into a MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN-byte buffer, with guaranteed NUL termination. The strncmp-with-newline stripping operates on a validly terminated in-bounds string. No out-of-bounds access, wrap, or injection sink is reachable from the attacker-controlled buf/nbytes within this code.

assumptions: MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN is defined outside this code; its numeric value is unsourced, but the guard and the array dimension use the same identifier, so the bound is structurally sound for any value of the macro.
The kernfs write path supplies buf/nbytes to this store callback; the contents of buf are treated as attacker-data and validated here only for length.
dlpar_add_slot's handling of the name string (lookup semantics, effects of arbitrary names) is not shown; this code passes it a NUL-terminated, in-bounds string.
limitations: Returning 0 instead of a negative error for oversized writes (line 8) could interact with the not-shown kernfs write loop's handling of a zero-byte-consumed return; the impact chain cannot be characterized from the given code and is not treated as a finding.

If dlpar_add_slot mishandles specific drc_name values (e.g., injection into a firmware call), that defect would live in the callee, which is not shown; no out-of-domain argument is passed at the call site.

verdict.summary: All memory sinks in squashfs_opendir are guarded by quotable checks correctly placed in execution order: the filename length check 'if(dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN)' runs before both the name read and the NUL write and rejects the boundary value (256) and every larger value for any field width >= 9 bits; the entry count check 'if(dir_count > SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT)' bounds the inner loop for all non-negative counts; allocation results for dir and ent are checked. Residual weaknesses (unchecked read_inode return, potential signed wrap of dir_count bypassing the > SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT check for 32-bit count fields, unchecked strdup, unverifiable check_name) each have impact chains that depend on unshown callees or field widths not declared in the given code, so they cannot be instantiated as vulnerabilities here.

assumptions: SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN is 256 and SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT is 256; the constants are not defined in the given code.

The buffer 'char buffer[sizeof(struct squashfs_dir_entry) + SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1]' places dire->name at offset offsetof(name) leaving a name area of at least SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1 bytes; the struct definitions are not part of the given code.
FALSE is 0 and read_directory_data returns FALSE on failure; the callee is not shown.
sBlk.s.directory_table_start is a global initialized outside this code; it is not assigned here.
limitations: The return value of read_inode is not NULL-checked before the first dereference 'dir->mode = (*i)->mode' and '(*i)->data'; whether read_inode can produce NULL is not determinable because the callee is not shown, so the NULL-dereference candidate is speculative (CWE-476 only if a NULL producer exists).

dir_count = dirh.count + 1 can wrap to a negative int if dirh.count is a 32-bit field holding a value near INT_MAX (e.g., 0x7FFFFFFF), bypassing 'if(dir_count > SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT)' and driving 'while(dir_count--)' for ~2^31 iterations; the count field's declared width is not in the given code (UNSOURCED), and the impact requires ~2^31 successful read_directory_data calls whose bounding/wrap behavior is in an unshown callee, so neither trigger nor impact is instantiated.
ent->name = strdup(dire->name) is not NULL-checked; the consumer of ent->name is outside this code, so the impact chain breaks.

check_name is called with (dire->name, dire->size + 1) but its implementation is not shown; whether it actually rejects '/', '.', and '..' (guarding against directory traversal at extraction time, CWE-22) cannot be verified, and the path-construction use is not in this code.

The widths of dire->size, dirh.count, and (*i)->data are not declared in the given code; edge cases that depend on those widths (negative size bypassing the >= check, signed conversion of count) cannot be instantiated.

bytes and size are signed ints accumulating attacker-influenced lengths; overflow requires ~2^31 bytes of successful reads from the unshown reader and bytes reaches no memory, index, or copy sink, so no security consequence is instantiated in this code.

verdict.summary: add_slot_store copies nbytes attacker-controlled bytes into drc_name and never NUL-terminates the buffer, then calls strchr on it. The only guard (nbytes >= MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN) bounds the copy but not the scan; at nbytes == MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN - 1 the array is completely filled with no possible in-bounds terminator. strchr therefore reads uninitialized stack bytes past the copied data and can run past the end of the stack array until it happens to hit a newline or NUL in adjacent memory.

evidence.snippet:
memcpy(drc_name, buf, nbytes);

	end = strchr(drc_name, '\n');
evidence.reason: memcpy copies exactly nbytes attacker bytes and no statement writes drc_name[nbytes] = '\0' or zeroes the remainder; strchr at line 13 then scans drc_name with no terminator guarantee, reading uninitialized stack bytes at indices nbytes..MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN-1 and potentially past the array. Trigger: write of nbytes = MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN - 1 bytes containing no newline or NUL fills the array completely, making an in-bounds terminator impossible and the scan unbounded.

evidence.snippet:
if (nbytes >= MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN)
		return 0;
evidence.reason: This is the only guard on nbytes and it bounds only the memcpy length, not the subsequent string scan; it admits the exactly-at-limit value nbytes = MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN - 1, which fills the entire array and leaves no byte for a NUL terminator, so the strchr on the next path has no enforced stopping point.

assumptions: The sysfs/kernfs layer may NUL-terminate the incoming buffer at buf[nbytes]; no statement in this code documents, asserts, or enforces that, so it is an unquotable contract and was not used to dismiss the finding. Even if true, the nbytes = MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN - 1 case leaves no in-array slot for that terminator.
The exact value of MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN is defined outside the given code; the trigger requires only that it is at least 1, which any usable definition satisfies.
Deployment privilege of who can write this sysfs attribute is not evidenced by the code and was not used to raise or lower severity.
limitations: The write *end = '\0' (line 16) becomes an out-of-bounds write only if the unbounded strchr finds a newline located past the array before any NUL; that depends on adjacent stack content not sourced from attacker input, so it is recorded as a conditional aggravation of the same unbounded scan, not an independent finding.

dlpar_add_slot may receive a string embedding uninitialized bytes when strchr stops in the uninitialized tail; the callee is not shown and its handling is not characterizable, so no downstream impact is claimed.
Returning 0 for oversized input silently swallows the write but has no security effect.

verdict.summary: Off-by-one bounds check in __io_sync_cancel: 'if (unlikely(fd > ctx->nr_user_files))' uses '>' instead of '>=', so fd == ctx->nr_user_files passes the check and is not clamped by array_index_nospec (which only masks indices strictly greater than the limit). The one-past-the-end index then indexes the fixed-file table at io_fixed_file_slot(&ctx->file_table, fd), reading out of bounds; the OOB-derived word is masked into cd->file and consumed by the cancel path. An attacker issuing a fixed-file cancel request with fd equal to the registered file count triggers the OOB read; the empty-table edge (nr_user_files == 0, fd == 0) also reaches the OOB slot read.

evidence.reason: The bounds check 'fd > ctx->nr_user_files' rejects only fd strictly greater than the table size; the boundary value fd == ctx->nr_user_files (one-past-the-end) passes. array_index_nospec does not repair this: it only clamps indices strictly greater than the limit, returning index == limit unchanged. io_fixed_file_slot then reads slots[nr_user_files], one past the last valid slot, an out-of-bounds read whose result is masked by FFS_MASK and stored into cd->file. Trigger instantiated with attacker-controlled cancel fd == nr_user_files (and also at nr_user_files == 0, fd == 0, which passes '0 > 0' and saturates to index 0 of an empty table).

evidence.snippet:
static int __io_sync_cancel(struct io_uring_task *tctx,
			    struct io_cancel_data *cd, int fd)
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted index: 'fd' is a parameter of this non-static function carrying the attacker-supplied file descriptor / fixed-file index from the cancel request (gated by cd->flags containing IORING_ASYNC_CANCEL_FD | IORING_ASYNC_CANCEL_FD_FIXED, both attacker-set in cd). No statement in this code constrains fd below nr_user_files before the defective check at line 11.

assumptions: ctx = cd->ctx is dereferenced without a NULL check; no statement in this code asserts or documents cd or cd->ctx non-NULL, and no NULL producer exists in this code, so this is an unquotable interface contract rather than an instantiated defect.

array_index_nospec semantics (mask/saturate index > limit, pass-through at index == limit) and io_fixed_file_slot as a pure array indexer are relied on per the documented kernel contracts; neither rejects index == limit, which is central to the confirmed off-by-one.

FFS_MASK width and the layout of io_file_slot are not shown; the OOB value's usability beyond the !cd->file test and the __io_async_cancel match is not characterized, so impact is scoped to the out-of-bounds read itself.
limitations: Whether the OOB-read file_ptr word can be turned into information disclosure beyond influencing which cancellation matches (and thus observable request completion behavior) depends on __io_async_cancel internals and the surrounding fixed-file machinery, which are not shown; the confirmed impact is the out-of-bounds read at the slot lookup.

Negative fd values widen to a huge unsigned index inside array_index_nospec, which then saturates to the limit (== nr_user_files), converging on the same one-past-the-end read rather than forming a distinct defect; this is subsumed by the primary finding.

verdict.summary: handleLWPolylineData parses the attacker-controlled DXF group-90 vertex count into maxVertices with only a lower-bound check (maxVertices>0) and then allocates with new double[4*maxVertices] while the initialization loop is bounded by the unwrapped maxVertices. For maxVertices greater than INT_MAX/4 (e.g., 1073741825), the 32-bit expression 4*maxVertices overflows and wraps to a tiny value (4), so a 4-element buffer is allocated and the loop then performs roughly 4.3 billion out-of-bounds heap writes (vertices[i*4..i*4+3]), corrupting the heap; the index expression i*4 itself later overflows int as well. A slightly different value (536870912) wraps the size to INT_MIN, producing a huge allocation and an uncaught std::bad_alloc, an attacker-triggered denial of service from file content.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds heap write (CWE-787) caused by integer overflow in the allocation size (CWE-190). The allocation is sized by 4*maxVertices in 32-bit int arithmetic, but the loop bound i<maxVertices uses the unwrapped count, so the write extent is 4*maxVertices elements. Instantiated trigger: group code 90 with value 1073741825 makes maxVertices=1073741825 (>0 passes the only check), 4*maxVertices wraps to 4, new double[4] allocates 4 elements, and the second loop iteration (i=1) writes vertices[4] out of bounds, continuing for ~10^9 iterations (with i*4 itself overflowing int at i>=2^29), corrupting the heap.

evidence.snippet:
maxVertices = toInt(groupValue);
        if (maxVertices>0) {
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted size: the attacker-controlled DXF group value is parsed into maxVertices and the only validation on any path is the lower-bound check maxVertices>0; no upper bound (e.g., maxVertices <= INT_MAX/4), clamp, or 64-bit size computation exists anywhere before the value is consumed by the allocation and loop at lines 9-10.

assumptions: maxVertices, vertexIndex and vertices are member declarations not shown in the snippet; int width of maxVertices (and therefore 32-bit wrap in 4*maxVertices) is inferred from the code's own int usage (for (int i=0; i<maxVertices; ++i), toInt) and not from a quotable declaration.

toInt parses the attacker-supplied group value string into an int without an upper bound; its implementation is not shown, but every int value including 1073741825 is a plausible parse result of file content.
groupCode and groupValue originate from parsing a DXF file in code not shown; this function is treated as the intake point for that untrusted content, so those values are attacker-data.
limitations: Pre-first-call values of vertices, maxVertices and vertexIndex are UNSOURCED (no constructor shown). If a constructor left vertexIndex >= 0 with vertices == NULL and maxVertices > 0, the writes at lines 31/34 could dereference NULL, but that trigger precondition cannot be instantiated from the given code.

If new at line 9 throws std::bad_alloc after delete[] at line 7, vertices dangles; exploitation as use-after-free requires a caller that catches the exception and re-enters this function, behavior not shown and not characterizable.

The pure DoS face of the primary defect (maxVertices = 536870912 making 4*maxVertices wrap to INT_MIN, producing a huge allocation and an uncaught std::bad_alloc) is subsumed by the primary corruption finding and does not drive a separate verdict.

verdict.summary: remove_slot_store copies only nbytes attacker bytes into the never-initialized stack buffer drc_name and then runs strchr over it BEFORE any NUL terminator is written. For any write of 0..MAX-1 bytes containing no newline, strchr scans uninitialized stack past the initialized region (and potentially past the end of the array), and the subsequent *end = '\0' can write out of bounds on the kernel stack; the garbage-terminated string is also passed to dlpar_remove_slot. The only guard (nbytes >= MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN) bounds nbytes, not the scan, and no zero-initialization, pre-termination, or length check on the scan region exists anywhere in the function.

evidence.reason: memcpy initializes only bytes [0, nbytes) of drc_name; the NUL terminator is written at line 17, AFTER strchr already scanned the buffer at line 14. On an attacker write of nbytes < MAX bytes containing no '\n' (e.g., a single 'A'), strchr reads uninitialized stack from drc_name[nbytes] onward, may run past the MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN-byte array, and the found pointer is then used in *end = '\0' at line 17, an out-of-bounds stack write when the first '\n' lies at index >= MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN. Trigger fully instantiated: nbytes and buf content are attacker-controlled store-callback parameters; the uninitialized tail is produced by this code's own memcpy leaving the line-5 buffer partially initialized.

evidence.snippet: char drc_name[MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN];
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted state: drc_name is declared without initialization and the only partial initialization is the nbytes-bounded memcpy at line 12, leaving drc_name[nbytes..MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN-1] uninitialized for the strchr scan at line 14.

assumptions: MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN is defined outside the given code; only its role as sizeof(drc_name) and as the bound at lines 9-10 is used, its numeric value is not relied upon beyond exceeding 1.
buf is assumed to contain the nbytes bytes that sysfs copied from user space; this is the standard contract of a kobj_attribute store and is not used to dismiss any candidate.
dlpar_remove_slot is not shown; no impact link depends on its behavior beyond receiving the NUL-terminated, garbage-containing drc_name string.
limitations: The fully out-of-array write (index >= MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN at line 17) additionally requires the uninitialized stack tail to contain no '\n' or NUL byte before the array ends; exact stack contents are not controlled by the given code. The unconditional consequences on the simulated path — use of uninitialized stack memory in the strchr scan (CWE-457), reading past the initialized region, and passing uninitialized stack bytes to dlpar_remove_slot — do not depend on this.

The oversize-input path returning 0 (lines 9-10) reports 0 bytes consumed rather than an error; this is accounting behavior with no security-state misrepresentation and is not counted as a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: sdb_edit executes an external editor chosen from the EDITOR/VISUAL environment variables with no validation: any value containing a space is composed into a shell command line and passed to system() (and space-free values go to execlp), yielding arbitrary command execution by any party that can influence the process environment. Additionally, the post-edit file length from ftell is narrowed with (int) when sizing the reallocation while the untruncated long is used as the fread length and the NUL-termination index, producing a heap out-of-bounds write for files larger than INT_MAX (and a body[-1] write on the unchecked ftell failure sentinel -1).

evidence.reason: OS command injection (CWE-78): the string passed to system() embeds the environment-derived editor value verbatim with no content validation anywhere in the function (the only checks are ==NULL for absence and a space test that merely selects between the system() and execlp sinks). An attacker-controlled EDITOR such as 'touch /tmp/pwned;#' is executed by /bin/sh when the child runs system(p).

Taint origin: the editor command is read from the EDITOR/VISUAL environment variables, an untrusted origin per the data-origin impact model; these getenv results are the only source of the value reaching the system()/execlp sinks and are never content-checked before use.

Integer truncation leading to heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-190/CWE-787): the allocation is sized from (int)len+1 (narrowed long from ftell, which is also never tested against its -1 failure sentinel), while the read length and the terminator index use the untruncated len. For a post-edit file of 5,000,000,000 bytes (producible by the environment-controlled editor command, e.g. system("truncate -s 5000000000 /tmp/sdXXXXXX") via the CWE-78 path), (int)len truncates to 705,032,704, so myfread is passed 5e9 for a ~672MB buffer and body[5000000000]='\0' writes far out of bounds; for len=-1L the size becomes 0 and body[-1] writes one byte before the buffer.

assumptions: omAlloc/omFree/omStrDup/myfread/si_wait/si_unlink/iiGetLibProcBuffer/Print are not shown; only standard functions (getenv, mkstemp, strchr, execlp, system, sprintf, strlen, fopen, fseek, ftell, fork, close, write, fclose) were relied on with documented semantics.

omAlloc's failure behavior (NULL return vs abort) is not shown and is not a standard-library contract, so unchecked allocation results at lines 56 and 79 are recorded as limitations rather than findings.
NUL-termination of pi->data.s.body after iiGetLibProcBuffer is not shown; strlen at line 39 depends on this unquotable contract.

myfread's exact prototype is unknown; the line 80 finding rests on the CALLEE BOUNDARY RULE (the call site passes the untruncated len against a buffer sized (int)len+1) and on the quoted body[len] write at line 81, which needs no callee characterization.
limitations: Unchecked omAlloc at lines 56 and 79: if omAlloc could return NULL on attacker-inducible sizes, myfread/body[len] would dereference NULL, but omalloc failure semantics are not shown and not characterizable.

strlen(pi->data.s.body) at line 39 over-reads if a caller supplies a non-NUL-terminated buffer; the over-read's extent and content depend on unshown caller allocations and heap layout, so the impact is not instantiated here.
write() at line 39 ignores its return value; a partial write is a robustness issue only.
The child exits with status 0 even when execlp fails (line 60), misreporting operational success, but no security-state (auth/verification) is presented.
If fork() fails (pid==-1), the parent still enters the pid!=0 branch and calls si_wait(&pid); behavior depends on the unshown si_wait and is at most a hang, not instantiated as attacker-controlled.

No temp-file race finding: mkstemp (characterizable O_EXCL/0600 creation) prevents other local users from reading or modifying the procedure body while it is staged in /tmp, and no in-code statement makes the path attacker-writable.

verdict.summary: squashfs_opendir dereferences the result of read_inode(block_start, offset) without any NULL check. read_inode is a parse/lookup call over attacker-controlled filesystem content and returns its failure sentinel NULL on malformed input; the very next statements dereference *i unconditionally (dir->mode = (*i)->mode; and the following field copies, plus (*i)->data later), causing a NULL pointer dereference and process crash. An attacker who supplies a crafted squashfs image with an unreadable/invalid directory inode triggers a reliable denial of service. No validation of *i exists anywhere in the function (all other failure sentinels — res, dir, ent — are tested, but *i never is).
