verdict.summary: No instantiated security vulnerability found. All pointer/index/size computations in ins_bs() are guarded by quoted, on-path checks in execution order: the col==0 join path is unreachable at lnum==1/col==0 due to the early-return guard; ml_get_cursor()-1 dereferences require col>0 conjuncts evaluated left-to-right in the same condition; the word-delete do-loop is bounded by col>mincol with mincol=0 initialized in-function; the FO_WHITE_PAR trim tests len>0 before ptr[len-1]; and the vcol insertion loop terminates because each inserted space strictly increases the virtual column toward the getvcol-derived want_vcol.

assumptions: Editor state (curwin->w_cursor, Insstart, revins_on, p_sts, b_p_vsts_array, replace stack) is assumed to be internal trusted state maintained by the editor rather than attacker-origin data; no external input surface into these fields is shown in this code.

Behavior of not-shown callees (ml_get, dec_cursor, inc_cursor, getvcol, do_join, u_save, replace_pop, del_char, ins_char, ins_str, mb_get_class) is assumed to match their documented Vim semantics, e.g. dec_cursor() not moving before column 0 of a line.
c and mode parameters are assumed to be internal keypress/mode constants dispatched by the insert-mode editor loop, not attacker-controlled content.
limitations: A hypothetical corruption of editor state (e.g. Insstart.lnum or curwin->w_cursor set out of range by a bug elsewhere in Vim) could make the u_save((lnum-2),(lnum+1)) call or dec_cursor() loops unsafe; no producer of such corrupt state exists within this function, so the trigger is speculative and not attributed to this code.

The guard `curwin->w_cursor.lnum == 1 && curwin->w_cursor.col == 0` prevents backspacing at the very start of the buffer, but its correctness for lnum>1 relies on the do-loop condition and BS_* option checks interacting correctly; a deep audit of can_bs semantics across all 'backspace' option values was not performed.

If stop_arrow(), u_save(), or ml_get() could fail in a way that leaves cursor state inconsistent (not shown), subsequent ml_get_cursor()/STRLEN uses could read stale pointers; this code checks the two FAIL sentinels it can observe (stop_arrow and u_save) but cannot characterize callee failure modes not given.

verdict.summary: ip6gre_err consumes the err_handler-supplied `offset` parameter without any lower-bound validation. The only guards, `pskb_may_pull(skb, offset + grehlen)` (lines 12 and 25), bound only offset+grehlen bytes: with offset = -4 the first pull checks 0 bytes and passes, so `greh->flags` reads before the buffer; with small non-negative offset (e.g. 0) both pulls pass while the code reads a full 40-byte struct ipv6hdr at skb->data (ipv6h->saddr/ipv6h->daddr in the lookup call), far beyond the pulled length. An attacker-supplied ICMPv6 error geometry reaching this registered handler produces an out-of-bounds read.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read. The pull guards only offset+grehlen bytes (4..12); nothing ensures 40 bytes at skb->data. Instantiated trigger: attacker-supplied offset = 0 with a short ICMPv6 error skb makes both pskb_may_pull(skb, 4) calls pass, then the lookup dereferences ipv6h->daddr (data[24..40)) and ipv6h->saddr (data[8..24)) beyond the pulled region. Root cause: the `offset` index is never validated against sizeof(struct ipv6hdr).

Origin of the tainted index and second OOB site. `offset` (attacker-data, err_handler parameter) is used unchecked: with offset = -4, offset + grehlen = 0 so pskb_may_pull(skb, 0) passes, and greh = skb->data - 4 makes `flags = greh->flags` read 2 bytes before the linear buffer. No lower-bound check, clamp, or 40-byte pull exists anywhere on any path.

assumptions: pskb_may_pull(skb, len) is treated per its standard semantics: returns true iff len bytes can be made linear (and skb->len >= len); with len 0 or small values on a non-empty skb it succeeds.

ip6_tnl_parse_tlv_enc_lim and ip6gre_tunnel_lookup are not shown; their kernel-documented semantics (parser returning 0/not-found or a validated in-packet offset; lookup reading the pointed-to fields) are relied on as characterizable callees.

This function is invoked as a registered ICMPv6 err_handler (function-pointer dispatch not shown); per the handler-function rule its type/code/offset/info parameters are treated as attacker-data, and any bound the real dispatcher places on offset (e.g. offset >= sizeof(struct ipv6hdr)) is unquotable in this code.
limitations: ICMPV6_PKT_TOOBIG: `mtu = be32_to_cpu(info) - offset` has no upper clamp and can wrap (info=0, offset=48 -> mtu=4294967248), which is then stored via `t->dev->mtu = mtu`; the harmful consequence depends on unshown consumers of dev->mtu in the xmit/fragmentation path, so it is not instantiated as a finding.

The PARAMPROB read `tel = (struct ipv6_tlv_tnl_enc_lim *) &skb->data[teli]; tel->encap_limit` relies on ip6_tnl_parse_tlv_enc_lim (not shown) returning an in-packet validated offset; a misbehaving return value cannot be instantiated without the callee's source.
`t->err_count++` is unbounded but is a reporting/rate-limit counter only; no security effect.
Signed overflow of `offset + grehlen` at extreme offset values converts to a huge unsigned length in pskb_may_pull, which fails and returns; no guard bypass was instantiated.

verdict.summary: ReadMATImageV4 only tests the ReadBlob failure sentinel (count == -1) after each pixel-row read; on a truncated MAT4 file ReadBlob returns a short byte count, and the partially-filled (otherwise uninitialized) heap buffer is passed whole to ImportQuantumPixels/SyncAuthenticPixels and committed as image pixel data, disclosing uninitialized process heap memory through the returned image. The second (complex) row loop repeats the identical sentinel-only check.

evidence.reason: The only validation of the row read is the failure-sentinel test `if (count == -1) break;` — a short read (e.g. 10 of 100 requested bytes on an attacker-truncated file) passes, and the full row width `depth/8*image->columns` of the partially-uninitialized heap buffer is subsequently imported into image pixels by `ImportQuantumPixels(...,pixels,...)` and `SyncAuthenticPixels`, leaking uninitialized heap memory into the returned image (CWE-908, out-of-domain read CWE-125). Instantiated trigger: file truncated mid-row → count==10 ≠ -1 → uninit bytes committed as pixel data.

evidence.snippet: pixels=(unsigned char *) GetQuantumPixels(quantum_info);
evidence.reason: Origin of the disclosed content: `pixels` is the quantum buffer obtained from AcquireQuantumInfo/GetQuantumPixels with no initialization statement anywhere in this code; on a short read the bytes beyond `count` retain uninitialized heap contents that reach output.

assumptions: ReadBlob returns the number of bytes actually read (a short count at end-of-file) and -1 only on hard error, per the characterizable semantics of a byte-count read primitive; the given code's `if (count == -1)` shows the sentinel convention.
AcquireQuantumInfo/GetQuantumPixels allocate but do not zero the pixel buffer; no initializing statement for `pixels` exists in the given code.
The MAT4 file content is untrusted input; this decoder is the trust-boundary intake point, so missing short-read validation is not deferrable to a caller.

InsertComplexDoubleRow/InsertComplexFloatRow consume the buffer as double/float rows of image->columns elements; their internal stride behavior is not shown, so the imagf==1 loop is evaluated only for its identical unguarded short-read at the ReadBlob call site.
limitations: SetImageExtent/QueueAuthenticPixels success guarantees the pixel cache matches columns/rows, but the quantum buffer's guaranteed extent versus `depth/8*image->columns` depends on AcquireQuantumInfo's internal sizing (not shown); if that extent were ever smaller than the row read length, a heap overflow would exist at the same call site — this code provides no quotable bound for it either way.

Ping-branch candidate: `SeekBlob(image, HDR.nCols*ldblk, SEEK_CUR)` can wrap in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic (e.g. nCols=0xFFFFFFFF, ldblk=2, imagf==1) yielding a wrong in-file offset; worst direct consequence is reading untrusted file bytes from a wrong position — no corruption, disclosure of out-of-file memory, bypass, or amplification is reachable from the quoted statements, so it is not treated as a vulnerability.
Mid-loop break paths (e.g. EOFBlob arm) leak the current quantum_info allocation — a bounded, non-attacker-scalable resource accounting defect with no security-state effect.
Unchecked return values of SetQuantumFormat/SetQuantumDepth/SetQuantumEndian/SetImageColorspace degrade gracefully (defaults apply) with no security-state misrepresentation.

Disclosed uninitialized bytes become externally visible only if a later encoder writes the returned image; that stage is not shown, but the uninitialized values already reach the function's security-relevant output (committed image pixels), so the finding stands on the in-code chain.

verdict.summary: seq_buf_alloc is a bounded allocation wrapper. Its only input, the unsigned long size parameter, is checked against the fixed constant MAX_RW_COUNT with an explicit error arm ('if (unlikely(size > MAX_RW_COUNT)) return NULL;') that lies on the only path to the sole sink, kvmalloc(size, GFP_KERNEL_ACCOUNT). The allocation is sized from the same expression consumed, no arithmetic is performed on the size, and the kvmalloc result (possibly NULL) is only returned, never dereferenced, in this code. Edge cases 0, MAX_RW_COUNT, MAX_RW_COUNT+1 and ULONG_MAX all resolve safely. No trigger for memory corruption, out-of-bounds access, amplification, or any other security impact can be instantiated within this code.

assumptions: MAX_RW_COUNT is a fixed compile-time constant on the order of INT_MAX page-aligned, standard in the kernel; the comparison semantics do not depend on its exact value.
kvmalloc follows kernel allocation semantics: it returns a valid pointer or NULL, supports a vmalloc fallback for large sizes, and treats a zero size as a valid zero allocation.
The function is declared static, so callers exist only in the same translation unit; their identity and the provenance of the sizes they pass are not shown.
limitations: kvmalloc can return NULL under memory pressure; this code returns that NULL to its unseen caller, so any missing NULL check would be a defect in the caller, which is not part of the given code.

Potential resource amplification from large (up to MAX_RW_COUNT, roughly 2 GB) allocations requires a caller that passes attacker-derived sizes repeatedly; no such caller is shown and the function is static, so this precondition is unsourced and the candidate is speculative.

verdict.summary: ip6gre_err() dereferences attacker-controlled ICMPv6 error payload without sufficient validation. First, `flags = p[0];` reads at skb->data+offset before any pskb_may_pull in this function. Second, the GRE key expression `*(((__be32 *)p) + (grehlen / 4) - 1)` double-counts `offset` (p already equals skb->data+offset while grehlen also includes offset), so the 4-byte read lands `offset` bytes past the `grehlen`-byte region validated by pskb_may_pull. A crafted ICMPv6 error embedding a GRE packet with the GRE_KEY flag triggers an out-of-bounds read of kernel heap memory past the end of the skb data.

evidence.snippet:
t = ip6gre_tunnel_lookup(skb->dev, &ipv6h->daddr, &ipv6h->saddr,
				flags & GRE_KEY ?
				*(((__be32 *)p) + (grehlen / 4) - 1) : 0,
				p[1]);
evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read sink. The key read address is p + 4*(grehlen/4) - 4 where p = skb->data + offset (re-based at line 25), i.e., absolute bytes [offset + grehlen - 4, offset + grehlen), while pskb_may_pull(skb, grehlen) at line 22 validated only [0, grehlen). With the instantiated trigger (crafted ICMPv6 error, embedded IPv6 header nexthdr=GRE with GRE_KEY flag, offset=40, grehlen=48, skb data length 48), the read touches bytes [84, 88) — 36+ bytes beyond the end of the data. Root cause is index handling: the base pointer already includes offset, so the index (grehlen/4)-1 overshoots by exactly offset bytes.

The insufficient guard and the computation producing the faulty value. The only validation guarantees grehlen linear bytes from skb->data, but p is then rebased at skb->data + offset, so any dereference of p at index (grehlen/4)-1 in 32-bit units lies offset bytes beyond the validated span. No check anywhere in the function bounds offset or the computed read address against the pulled region.

Second out-of-bounds read sink: `flags = p[0];` dereferences skb->data + offset before any pskb_may_pull in this function (the first pull is at line 22, after the read). For a crafted ICMPv6 error whose embedded packet is exactly the 40-byte inner IPv6 header with nexthdr=GRE (offset=40, data length 40), this reads 2 bytes past the end of the skb data — unvalidated, unpulled data that the code itself treats as potentially absent (otherwise the later pull would be unnecessary).

assumptions: The not-shown caller is the IPv6 ICMP error dispatcher that invokes this err_handler with skb->data at the embedded packet and offset pointing past the embedded IPv6 header; no reliance was placed on any unshown caller validation (per guard anchoring, the code's own pskb_may_pull at line 22 is the only quotable validation, and it demonstrably runs too late or with too small a bound).

skb contents and the parameters offset, type, code, info are attacker-craftable network data (ICMPv6 error payload); the canonical offset=40 (embedded IPv6 header size) is used for the trigger, and the key-read overshoot holds for any offset >= 4.
ip6gre_tunnel_lookup returns NULL or a valid tunnel; the NULL case is handled at line 31.
Whether the OOB reads stay inside the kmalloc'ed skb head (stale-heap read) or exit the allocation (potential fault) depends on runtime allocation sizing not determinable from this code.
limitations: ICMPV6_PKT_TOOBIG path (lines 65-68): `mtu = be32_to_cpu(info) - offset;` can unsigned-underflow (info=0, offset=40 gives mtu=0xFFFFFFD8), which bypasses the `if (mtu < IPV6_MIN_MTU)` clamp, and `t->dev->mtu = mtu;` then writes an attacker-chosen huge MTU and can also raise a previously lowered MTU. However, the trigger additionally requires ip6gre_tunnel_lookup to match a configured tunnel — deployment/configuration state this code never assigns (UNSOURCED) — and the security consequence materializes only in unshown consumers of dev->mtu, so it is recorded as a limitation rather than a confirmed finding.

ICMPV6_PARAMPROB path (lines 51-55): `teli` comes from the not-shown callee ip6_tnl_parse_tlv_enc_lim; the arguments this code passes (skb, skb->data) are in-domain and the zero sentinel is tested before use (`if (teli && ...)`), but whether a nonzero teli is bounded by the buffer is decided inside the callee and cannot be characterized from the given code.

The ipv6h->daddr/ipv6h->saddr reads at line 27 are covered by pskb_may_pull only when offset >= 36; if a dispatcher could pass a smaller offset these would also exceed the pulled region, but the dispatcher's computation of offset is not shown.

verdict.summary: No instantiated vulnerability in this code. All memory accesses use fixed indices (pool[0..3]), a verified mask bound (cycles & 3), or fixed sizes (sizeof(fast_pool->pool), sizeof(seed)) matching the passed objects; the input_pool lock is taken with spin_trylock and released on every continuing path with no early return in between. Remaining candidates fail trigger instantiation: fast_pool->count is never incremented here (so the count >= 64 fast-load path is unreachable from this code), but crng_init, the initial count, and the initial last value are never assigned in this code (UNSOURCED), and the claimed impact (delayed CRNG initialization affecting getrandom consumers) lives in code not given; get_reg receives a possibly-NULL regs, but its behavior is unshown and uncharacterizable; races on the per-CPU fast pool have no exhibitable interleaving window. These are recorded as limitations, not findings.

assumptions: struct fast_pool is the kernel's standard 4-element __u32 pool: the code's own unconditional writes to pool[0], pool[1], pool[2], pool[3] and the mask cycles & 3 imply at least 4 elements; the struct definition is not given, so a smaller pool would make the fixed writes OOB, but that cannot be confirmed from the given code.

arch_get_random_seed_long fills *seed when it returns true (standard fill-on-success seed-getter contract); if it returned true without filling, the uninitialized seed would be mixed in, but this callee is not shown.

This function resembles Linux drivers/char/random.c add_interrupt_randomness; functions get_reg, fast_mix, crng_fast_load, __mix_pool_bytes, credit_entropy_bits, random_get_entropy, and the globals crng_init/input_pool/net_rand_state are external to the given code.
limitations: fast_pool->count is never incremented in this code (only assigned 0 at the crng_fast_load reset and at the flush end); consequently fast_pool->count >= 64 can never become true through this code alone and the count < 64 term of the flush gate is always true. The trigger additionally requires crng_init == 0 and count >= 64, both UNSOURCED (never assigned in this code), and the impact (delayed or blocked CRNG initialization affecting getrandom callers, mitigated by other entropy sources not shown) lies outside this code, so this cannot be confirmed as a vulnerability here.

regs may be NULL (the code tests regs ? instruction_pointer(regs) : _RET_IP_), and NULL regs is passed to the unshown get_reg(fast_pool, regs) both in the cycles == 0 fallback and in the pool[3] ternary on 32-bit builds; get_reg's NULL handling cannot be characterized from the given code, so no dereference can be confirmed.

crng_init is read without synchronization and the per-CPU fast pool can in principle race with nested interrupt context; no two ordered statements in this code exhibit an attacker interleaving window, and the worst observable effect would be lost entropy or at most one extra credited bit per event path (bounded by credit + 1 with credit in {0,1}).

irq_flags is unused; irq, jiffies, and cycle-counter values (all low-grade or attacker-influenced) are mixed into the pool, but credit is fixed at one bit per flush (credit_entropy_bits(r, credit + 1)), so no over-crediting statement exists in this code.

verdict.summary: PresentationContext_new computes the surface buffer size as width * height * 4 in UINT32 arithmetic with no bounds, overflow, or zero check on the attacker-influenced width and height parameters. A crafted geometry (e.g., width=0x10000, height=0x10001) wraps the product to a small value (262144 bytes), so BufferPool_Take returns a drastically undersized heap buffer, which this code then pairs with the full width/height in h264_context_reset (line 18), video->createSurface (line 34), and yuv_context_reset (line 48). Decoders configured for the full-resolution surface then write past the end of the undersized buffer, yielding a remote-controlled heap out-of-bounds write.

evidence.snippet: ret->surfaceData = BufferPool_Take(priv->surfacePool, width * height * 4);
evidence.reason: The allocation size expression width * height * 4 is evaluated in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic and can wrap for large attacker-influenced dimensions (width=0x10000, height=0x10001 wraps to 262144). No check, clamp, mask, or overflow guard on width/height exists anywhere in the function, and the only error test (if (!ret->surfaceData)) inspects the pointer, not the size. The undersized buffer is then handed to consumers configured with the full width and height at lines 18, 34, and 48, so frame decoding writes out of bounds: integer overflow in buffer size calculation leading to heap memory corruption.

evidence.snippet: UINT32 x, UINT32 y, UINT32 width, UINT32 height)
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values: the width and height parameters (UINT32) carry presentation geometry received from the remote peer; no documented precondition, assertion, or bound on them exists in this code, so they are attacker-data whose unvalidated product reaches the allocation sizing sink at line 27.

assumptions: The static function's caller passes a valid non-NULL video context with a valid priv->surfacePool; this code neither documents nor checks that contract, but it is a context handle consumed by internal callers and is not data-carrying content, so it cannot instantiate a security trigger.
width/height originate from the presentation geometry parsed by the caller of this static helper (not shown); per the parameter-carries-external-content rule they are treated as attacker-data.
limitations: No upper bound on width/height also permits a single small geometry message to request multi-gigabyte allocations or a zero-size allocation (width or height = 0 gives BufferPool_Take size 0); the NULL return is handled at line 28, and the zero-size/exhaustion behavior depends on the not-shown BufferPool_Take and pool implementation, so this amplification candidate is not confirmed here.

The out-of-bounds write itself occurs in frame-decoding code not given; the confirmed defect is the overflowed size argument at the BufferPool_Take call site, which this code pairs with full-geometry consumers at lines 18, 34, and 48.

verdict.summary: The destructor deletes `mixer` (line 4) before using it: `mixer->isActive()`, `mixer->isDeviceRemoved(player)` and `mixer->removeDevice(player)` (lines 8-9) then operate on freed memory (use-after-free, including a mutating call) whenever mixer and player are both non-NULL, and dereference NULL whenever mixer is NULL and player is non-NULL. The `if (mixer)` guard at line 3 protects only the delete statement and runs before the free, so no statement certifies mixer live at the later uses.

evidence.snippet:
if (mixer->isActive() && !mixer->isDeviceRemoved(player))
			mixer->removeDevice(player);
evidence.reason: Unguarded use of `mixer` after it was freed at line 4: `mixer->isActive()` and `mixer->removeDevice(player)` read and mutate freed memory (CWE-416) whenever mixer was non-NULL, and dereference NULL (CWE-476) whenever mixer is NULL; no check, reassignment, or error arm exists between the free and this use on any path.

evidence.snippet:
if (mixer)
		delete mixer;
evidence.reason: Origin of the freed pointer: `delete mixer` executes before the player-cleanup block, so the subsequent member calls at lines 8-9 run on freed memory; the `if (mixer)` test only guards the delete itself and cannot serve as a liveness or NULL guard for the later uses.

assumptions: Members `mixer` and `player` are assigned in the class constructor and other methods, which are not part of the given code; the analysis treats both possible mixer states (NULL and non-NULL) explicitly rather than assuming one, and both are defective at line 8 whenever player is non-NULL.

`isActive`, `isDeviceRemoved`, and `removeDevice` are member calls whose concrete bodies are not shown; per the callee-boundary rule the defect is the freed/NULL `mixer` argument at the call sites in this code, and member invocation on a freed/NULL pointer is characterized by standard C++ semantics.
`delete[] audioDriverName;` and `delete listener;` are safe for NULL operands and were verified as non-defects.
limitations: A lifecycle inconsistency remains when mixer is NULL but player is non-NULL: the player is deleted without ever being removed from any mixer; whether that leaks a registration depends on Mixer behavior not shown and is not classified.

Exploitability of the use-after-free beyond a crash (e.g., control of the freed mixer's contents before line 8) depends on allocator behavior and timing outside this code; the direct quoted consequence is reading and writing freed memory.

verdict.summary: No instantiated security vulnerability. Every memory-safety sink is covered by a quotable guard in execution order: the key copy is bounded by the allocation ('if (keylen > password_len) { key = emalloc(keylen); memset(key, 0, keylen); memcpy(key, password, password_len); }'), the output buffer is sized from the same expression consumed by the decrypt calls ('outlen = data_len + EVP_CIPHER_block_size(cipher_type); outbuf = emalloc(outlen + 1);'), unknown ciphers are rejected ('if (!cipher_type) ... RETURN_FALSE;'), decryption fails closed on bad padding ('EVP_DecryptFinal ... else { efree(outbuf); RETURN_FALSE; }'), and all frees are ownership-guarded. Remaining candidates (signed overflow of data_len + block_size at ~2GiB requiring unsourced memory configuration, unchecked EVP_CIPHER_CTX_set_key_length with no memory-safety consequence, and design-level unauthenticated CBC/padded-key behavior) are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: php_openssl_validate_iv(&iv, &iv_len, EVP_CIPHER_iv_length(cipher_type)) normalizes/pads the IV and sets free_iv; callee not shown, inferred from signature and the free_iv ownership flag.
php_base64_decode (internal non-strict helper) always returns an allocated buffer and sets base64_str_len; callee not shown.
Legacy EVP_DecryptInit/EVP_EncryptInit safely initialize a stack-allocated EVP_CIPHER_CTX (framework semantics); EVP_DecryptUpdate sets its out-length parameter even on failure.
emalloc aborts the request (bailout/fatal error) on failure rather than returning NULL; zend_parse_parameters 's' rejects NULL and yields int lengths in [0, INT_MAX].
limitations: Integer overflow candidate (CWE-190): 'outlen = data_len + EVP_CIPHER_block_size(cipher_type);' can wrap only for data_len > INT_MAX-16 (~2GiB string). The precondition (a ~2GiB allocation succeeding under the runtime memory_limit configuration) is UNSOURCED in this code, and even then emalloc(outlen+1) converts to a huge size_t causing a per-request fatal-error bailout, not memory corruption (no small-wrap value is reachable). Not instantiable.

Unchecked return of 'EVP_CIPHER_CTX_set_key_length(&cipher_ctx, password_len);': if it fails (fixed-key cipher with longer password) the key read stays at keylen <= password_len bytes; if it succeeds (variable-length cipher) the read equals password_len bytes. No out-of-bounds in either arm; behavioral only.

If php_base64_decode could return NULL without setting base64_str_len, data_len would be uninitialized; the non-strict internal decoder always returns a buffer, and even a NULL with length 0 is memory-safe (Update with inl=0, Final fails, RETURN_FALSE). Not instantiated.

Design-level: decryption is unauthenticated CBC (padding-oracle surface) and short passwords are zero-padded to the cipher key length by 'memset(key, 0, keylen); memcpy(key, password, password_len);', yielding keys with only password_len bytes of entropy. The claimed impact requires an unshown application consumer of the TRUE/FALSE result; no MAC parameter exists in this code. Recorded as a design weakness, not a defect instantiated here.

verdict.summary: No instantiated vulnerability in the given code. The security-critical guards are present, fail-closed, and correctly ordered: the expression register is blocked when the command line is itself an expression prompt or a password is being typed ('if (ccline.cmdfirstc == '='  || cmdline_star > 0) { beep_flush(); c = ESC; }' lines 29-34), and the pasted cursor position is clamped into [0, cmdlen] (lines 55-61), verified at boundaries 0, cmdlen, cmdlen+1 and -1. The no_mapping/allow_keys increments and decrements are balanced with no early exit between them. The unvalidated register character reaching cmdline_paste (line 41) and the unchecked gotesc dereference (line 48) have no guard in this code, but their impact depends on a not-shown project-internal callee whose safe domain cannot be characterized here, and on a caller-supplied NULL with no instantiated producer, respectively; both are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: cmdline_paste(), get_expr_register(), plain_vgetc(), putcmdline(), beep_flush() and aborting() are project-internal functions whose semantics, register-name domain, and failure behavior are not shown in the given code and cannot be quoted; no reliance was placed on their presumed validation for the verdict.
The parameter 'int *gotesc UNUSED' is an out-parameter; no non-NULL contract is quotable from the given code, so the belief that the caller passes a valid pointer is an assumption, not a fact.
ccline.cmdfirstc, cmdline_star, ccline.cmdlen and ccline.cmdbuff are state fields with no assignment in this code (UNSOURCED here); their safety properties are maintained elsewhere.

The recursion and password guards exist only under #ifdef FEAT_EVAL; the analysis assumes the shown feature macro configuration; with FEAT_EVAL undefined the '=' path falls through to the unshown cmdline_paste, which cannot be evaluated from this code.
This appears to be an interactive editor command-line handler; per discipline 3, deployment context was not used to promote or demote any candidate.
limitations: Candidate A (arbitrary key code passed unvalidated to cmdline_paste at line 41, 'cmdline_paste(c, i == Ctrl_R, FALSE);'): the trigger was fully instantiated (attacker-controlled 'c' from 'i = c = plain_vgetc();'), and no guard of any form (range check, clamp, mask, membership test, error arm) bounds 'c' into a register-name domain on any path in this code. However, the claimed impact depends entirely on how the not-shown project-internal cmdline_paste handles out-of-domain register names; its safe domain is not characterizable from the given code, so the impact chain breaks and this is a limitation, not a finding in this code.

Candidate B (NULL dereference at '*gotesc = TRUE;' line 48): a NULL check is genuinely absent, but triggering it requires the not-shown caller to pass NULL; no attacker input reaches the pointer and no statement in this code produces that value (UNSOURCED precondition), so the trigger is speculative.

Candidate F (INT-scale overflow in the 'new_cmdpos > ccline.cmdlen' comparison, lines 58-61): would require new_cmdpos near INT_MAX; its producer set_cmdline_pos() is not shown and writes nothing quotable in this code, so the harmful value is not instantiated; the clamp itself is otherwise sound for all in-range values.
The aborting() early return skips redrawcmd(), leaving the quote prompt on screen; this is cosmetic with no security effect.
The caller-side contract for '*gotesc = TRUE' (freeing ccline.cmdbuff after history insertion) is honored in code not shown; no misuse is visible in this code.

verdict.summary: In the attribute namespace-declaration loop, the duplicate-check inner loop indexes element->attributes[j] where j is bounded only by nspace_declarations_count, not by element->attribute_count. Because each attribute contributes up to two declaration entries (namespace declaration plus value) and the element namespace adds one, nspace_declarations_count can exceed attribute_count, so element->attributes[j] reads a pointer past the attributes array and dereferences it. An element with two attributes each in out-of-scope namespaces plus an out-of-scope element namespace (all attacker-chosen parsed content) drives j to 2 with attribute_count=2, producing a heap out-of-bounds read at line 53.

evidence.snippet:
for(j = 0; j < nspace_declarations_count; j++)
            if(nspace_declarations[j].nspace == element->attributes[j]->nspace) {
evidence.reason: The inner duplicate-check loop bounds j only by nspace_declarations_count, which is not tied to the attributes-array size; the array's demonstrated domain is [0, attribute_count) (outer loop 'for(i = 0; i < element->attribute_count; i++)' at line 41). With attribute_count=2, an out-of-scope element namespace (count=1), attribute[0] in a distinct out-of-scope namespace (count=3 after its declaration and value entries), and attribute[1] in another out-of-scope namespace, j reaches 2 and element->attributes[2] is read out of bounds and dereferenced for ->nspace. Index confusion (j used where the current attribute i is required) is the root cause; no bound, clamp, mask, checked accessor, or error arm on any path limits j to the array domain.

evidence.snippet:
nspace_declarations[nspace_declarations_count].nspace = NULL;
      nspace_declarations_count++;
evidence.reason: Origin of the harmful bound: each processed attribute appends a value entry and increments nspace_declarations_count; combined with the element-namespace entry (line 36) and per-attribute namespace-declaration entries (line 65), the count grows beyond element->attribute_count while the buggy inner loop at line 53 still uses it to index element->attributes, enabling the out-of-bounds read.

assumptions: xml_writer->nstack, ->iostr, ->depth are writer-context state with no assignment in this code; analysis assumes the mainstream configuration in which the writer has a namespace stack and stream (the code dereferences iostr unconditionally at raptor_iostream_write_byte('<', iostr), and the entire declaration machinery guarded by if(nstack) is the function's primary path). These context fields are not the defect-deciding variables; the harmful index j and its bound nspace_declarations_count derive from attacker-controlled parsed element content.

element->attribute_count, element->attributes, element->name->nspace, element->xml_language and element->declared_nspaces are treated as attacker-data: they are content-bearing fields of the element parameter of this non-static writer function, populated from parsed document content, and no statement in this code validates them.
limitations: xml:lang buffer handling (lines 109-127): buf_length = XML_LANG_PREFIX_LEN + lang_len + 1 sizes the heap buffer for the UNESCAPED language length, raptor_xml_escape_string is passed maxlength = buf_length (larger than the post-prefix capacity lang_len) and its unchecked return advances p before the unconditional *p++ = quote; *p = '\0'; writes, and the RAPTOR_MALLOC result is never NULL-checked (unlike the calloc at line 24 which is checked). The claimed heap write-overflow depends on the not-shown raptor_xml_escape_string expanding XML-special characters beyond lang_len bytes and on its truncation behavior, which cannot be characterized from the given code (CALLEE BOUNDARY RULE); the NULL-deref path requires attacker-inducible allocation failure, which the small input-proportional allocation does not provide. Recorded, not confirmed.

The comparison at line 53 also implements the wrong predicate even for in-bounds j (compares declaration j against attribute j instead of the current attribute i), which can produce duplicate or missing namespace declarations in output; this is a correctness effect secondary to the out-of-bounds read and is not counted as a separate security finding.

nspace_max_count = element->attribute_count * 2 (line 14) could overflow int for attribute_count >= 2^30; any resulting huge calloc fails and is caught by the quoted check at lines 24-25, so no trigger is instantiable.

verdict.summary: All tagstack index and length arithmetic in do_tag is guarded by quotable clamps and range checks verified in execution order, including the boundary cases of count 0, negative count, count INT_MIN, huge count, empty stack, exactly-full stack, and index equal to tagstacklen (DT_POP and :tag count-0 arms). Every read of matches[cur_match] is preceded by an in-range clamp of cur_match. The two remaining memory-safety candidates have genuinely absent guards but unsourced trigger preconditions: the NOTAGFILE retry path dereferences the cached tagstack pointer without revalidating it against curwin->w_tagstack (the check exists only after find_tags inside the refresh branch), which is a UAF only if an autocommand can close the original window during a jumpto_tag call that returns NOTAGFILE, an internal behavior of the not-shown callee; and new_num_matches/new_matches are uninitialized locals consumed unconditionally after a find_tags whose failure-time output contract is not shown. Neither trigger could be instantiated from this code, so no vulnerability is confirmed.

verdict.summary: The function's internally derived arithmetic is sound (left accounting, alloc-failure sentinel tested before first use, head published after buffer fields, partial returns in [0,size]). Every remaining memory-safety candidate (size_t to ssize_t narrowing of size, PAGE_SIZE - off underflow, ring_size power-of-two mask assumption, unoccupied-buffer writes in the off-branch, race on pipe state, unbounded allocation) requires a trigger value that this code never assigns or produces: i->count, pipe->ring_size, pipe->tail/max_usage, and the data_start output (iter_head/off) are all UNSOURCED from the given code, and pipe_full/data_start bodies are not shown. Per the unsourced-value rule these candidates are speculative and cannot drive a verdict; no attacker input within this code's own surface is shown to reach any sink out of domain.

assumptions: Deployment context (Linux kernel pipe/iov_iter helper) is inferred from the code style; per discipline 3 it was not used to promote or demote any candidate.
pipe_full(iter_head, p_tail, max) is assumed to test head-tail >= max, but its body is not shown, so it is not credited as a quotable guard.

data_start(i, &iter_head, &off) is assumed to return an occupied buffer index and an offset < PAGE_SIZE, but its body is not shown, so neither safety nor exploitability of iter_head/off could be established.
The caller is assumed to hold any pipe lock and to pass non-NULL iter_headp/offp and a pipe-backed iov_iter; no such contract is quotable from the given code.
limitations: Integer narrowing (line 16 'left = size'): if i->count exceeded SSIZE_MAX, left would be negative, making 'buf->len = min_t(ssize_t, left, PAGE_SIZE)' store a negative len and 'if (left == 0) return size' return bogus full success. Trigger precondition i->count > SSIZE_MAX is UNSOURCED (never assigned in this code); not instantiable.

Underflow at line 21 'left -= PAGE_SIZE - off': if data_start returned off >= PAGE_SIZE, the subtraction wraps, and line 23 'pipe->bufs[iter_head & p_mask].len += size' or line 26 '.len = PAGE_SIZE' would over-claim valid data (corruption/info-leak class). The value off is produced by the unshown callee data_start and cannot be instantiated from this code.

Mask assumption at line 6 'unsigned int p_mask = pipe->ring_size - 1': a non-power-of-two or zero ring_size would make 'iter_head & p_mask' index outside the ring (OOB write at lines 23/26/30). pipe->ring_size is UNSOURCED.

Off-branch writes (lines 23, 26) touch pipe->bufs[iter_head & p_mask] with no occupancy check on that path; safety relies on the unshown data_start invariant that iter_head names the iterator's current (occupied) buffer. Not provable from this code.

Race candidate: p_tail snapshot (line 5) vs pipe->head update (line 42) against concurrent pipe users requires a locking context and interleaving party not exhibitable as two ordered operations in this code.
NULL output pointers iter_headp/offp (lines 18-19) would dereference NULL; the caller contract is not quotable and this is a static helper, so the trigger is unsourced.
Allocation-loop amplification (lines 29-45) is bounded only by the unshown pipe_full and the unsourced i->count; a bound on iterations cannot be quoted from the given code.

verdict.summary: The sysfs store handler bounds the input with 'if (nbytes >= MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN) return 0;' using the same constant that sizes the destination buffer 'char drc_name[MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN];', so strscpy's count (nbytes + 1) can never exceed the buffer at any boundary value (nbytes == MAX is rejected, nbytes == MAX-1 is an exact fit, nbytes == 0 yields count 1, and no wrap is reachable). strscpy's documented kernel semantics guarantee NUL termination for any nonzero count, so drc_name is always a bounded, terminated C string before strchr(), the '*end = '\0' write, and dlpar_remove_slot(); the callee's error sentinel is tested at 'if (rc) return rc;'. No unterminated-string, out-of-bounds, integer, or fail-open defect is present in this code; it is the fixed strscpy-based version of the earlier memcpy-based termination bug.

assumptions: buf is the kernel kernfs/sysfs write buffer of at least PAGE_SIZE bytes, so strscpy reading at most nbytes + 1 <= MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN bytes from it stays in bounds; the buffer itself is not shown in the given code.

MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN is a compile-time positive constant defined outside the given code; because the same constant sizes the buffer and bounds the guard, the analysis does not depend on its numeric value.

strscpy semantics relied upon per the characterizable-callee rule: for count > 0 it writes at most count bytes and always NUL-terminates the destination (at index count-1 on the -E2BIG truncation path); count == 0 writes nothing, but count = nbytes + 1 >= 1 on every path here.
limitations: dlpar_remove_slot() is not shown; its handling of an arbitrary attacker-supplied DRC name (including the empty string when nbytes == 0, which passes drc_name[0] == '\0') is uncharacterizable. This code passes it an in-domain argument (a bounded, NUL-terminated string), so any name-validation defect would live in the callee, not here.

The ignored strscpy return value means a too-long name is silently truncated to fit and passed to dlpar_remove_slot, which at worst fails the lookup and returns an error; no security effect in this code.
Returning 0 for an oversized write (line 10) instead of -EINVAL is a userspace semantics oddity, not a memory-safety or fail-open security issue.

verdict.summary: When a parsed networkstatus document supplies exactly two arguments to the network-status-version line and the second is an unknown flavor name, the code logs escaped(tok->args[2]) while having established only tok->n_args > 1 (i.e. n_args may be exactly 2). Index 2 is one past the argument array per the code's own i < tok->n_args convention, so the statement reads out of bounds from the heap and passes the value to a string-escaping routine, giving a remotely triggerable out-of-bounds read (potential crash or heap-content disclosure into logs).

evidence.reason: Root cause: improper index validation. The only bound quoted is `tok->n_args > 1`, which admits n_args == 2, yet the error path reads index 2. Instantiated trigger: attacker supplies a document whose network-status-version line has exactly two arguments with an unrecognized flavor (e.g. "network-status-version 3 zzz"); line 42 passes, line 43 returns flavor < 0, and line 46 reads tok->args[2] out of bounds before the goto err at line 47. The over-read value is consumed by escaped() as a C string, so the direct consequence is an out-of-bounds read with disclosure or crash. No check, clamp, mask, or alternate index exists on any path (STEP 5 search).

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted data: the document string parameter s is the trust-boundary input; this function is the parsing intake point, so all token arguments derived from s, including tok->n_args and the array read at line 46, are attacker-controlled content.

The code's own convention (loops of the form `for (i = 0; i < tok->n_args; ++i)` and `tor_assert(tok->n_args >= 6)` before accessing args[5]) treats indices as valid only below n_args.
Deployment context (who calls this parser and with what privilege) is not shown; per the data-origin model the document string is treated as untrusted network content because this function parses it.

escaped() is characterized as a standard string-escaping routine that scans its argument as a C string; the out-of-bounds read occurs at the index expression in this code regardless of escaped()'s internals.

If a malformed document omits a required keyword, a NULL dereference or internal assert abort (DoS) may result, but find_by_keyword's body is not shown, so whether it returns NULL or aborts internally is uncharacterizable; not counted as primary.

If routerstatus_parse_entry_from_string failed to advance s, the `while (!strcmpstart(s, "r "))` loop could allocate entries without progress (unbounded consumption); the callee body is not shown and non-advancement cannot be confirmed.

verdict.summary: In PresentationContext_new, the surface buffer size is computed as `s = width * height * 4ULL;`. Because `*` is left-associative, `width * height` is evaluated first in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic and wraps modulo 2^32 before the 4ULL promotion. The subsequent bound check `if (s > INT32_MAX)` therefore inspects only the wrapped value. With attacker-controlled dimensions such as width=65536, height=65537, the product wraps to 65536, s becomes 262144, the check passes, and BufferPool_Take allocates a 256 KB buffer that is then bound to a 65536x65537 surface via createSurface and used to configure the h264 and yuv decoders. The resulting allocation is far smaller than the geometry the context advertises, giving the downstream video pipeline a heap out-of-bounds write primitive.

evidence.reason: Root cause: `width * height` is computed in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic (both operands are UINT32) and wraps mod 2^32 before being promoted by 4ULL, so the guard `if (s > INT32_MAX)` only sees the wrapped value. Instantiated trigger: width=65536, height=65537 gives a wrapped product of 65536, s=262144, which passes the check although the true surface size is ~17.18 GB.

evidence.snippet: ret->surfaceData = BufferPool_Take(priv->surfacePool, s);
evidence.reason: The allocation sink consumes the wrapped size s (262144 bytes in the simulated trigger) with no statement in this code validating that s matches the true required size width*height*4; the only bound check (lines 8-9) examined the already-wrapped value.

evidence.snippet: ret->surface = video->createSurface(video, ret->surfaceData, x, y, width, height);
evidence.reason: The undersized buffer from BufferPool_Take is bound to a surface declared with the full attacker-controlled width and height, creating the buffer-size/geometry mismatch that the h264_context_reset, yuv_context_reset, and downstream frame pipeline consume, yielding a heap out-of-bounds write.

assumptions: UINT32 is a 32-bit unsigned type and size_t is 64-bit on the target platform (standard typedef semantics); the wraparound occurs in the 32-bit `width * height` sub-expression regardless of the later 4ULL promotion.
BufferPool_Take is characterized per the callee boundary rule as an allocator/pool accessor returning a buffer of the requested size (or NULL, which this code checks at line 34).
The caller of this static constructor passes a valid non-NULL `video` context in the normal operating path; no contract is quotable from the given code.

The actual out-of-bounds write executes in the video pipeline code that consumes the returned PresentationContext; the corrupted size/geometry pairing itself is fully created by the quoted statements at lines 7, 33, and 40 of this code.
limitations: C2 (CWE-476): `video->priv` at line 5 dereferences `video` with no NULL check, but the trigger requires the caller to pass NULL; no statement in this code produces a NULL video and no attacker input on this code's surface controls it, so the trigger is not instantiated.

Behavior inside h264_context_reset, yuv_context_reset, and the createSurface callback is not shown; their out-of-bounds behavior is inferred from the dimension/buffer-size mismatch passed at the call sites, not quoted.
priv->surfacePool is UNSOURCED in this code (assigned elsewhere); it is not relied on as either a guard or a trigger precondition.

verdict.summary: Operator-precedence error in the refresh cleanup loop: `*mdev_types[i]` parses as `*(mdev_types[i])`, indexing the mdev_types parameter itself (a pointer to the caller's single output variable, per the declared type virMediatedDeviceTypePtr **mdev_types) instead of the array it points to. On a refresh call with *nmdev_types >= 2 (a state this function's own success path produces: `*nmdev_types = ntypes;`), iteration i=1 reads one pointer slot past the caller's variable (out-of-bounds read), dereferences the garbage value, and passes the result to virMediatedDeviceTypeFree, causing an invalid free / heap corruption or a crash on a wild dereference. The correct form `(*mdev_types)[i]` appears nowhere in the code.

evidence.snippet:
for (i = 0; i < *nmdev_types; i++)
       virMediatedDeviceTypeFree(*mdev_types[i]);
evidence.reason: Due to C precedence, `*mdev_types[i]` equals `*(mdev_types[i])`, which indexes the parameter mdev_types (pointer to the caller's single output variable) rather than the array at *mdev_types. For i=0 this accidentally yields (*mdev_types)[0]; for i>=1 (any refresh where *nmdev_types >= 2, produced by this function's own prior success path `*nmdev_types = ntypes;`) it performs an out-of-bounds read past the caller's variable, dereferences the garbage pointer, and frees it via virMediatedDeviceTypeFree: invalid free / heap corruption, or a wild-deref crash. The loop bound `i < *nmdev_types` cannot guard this because the out-of-bounds target holds exactly one element regardless of the count.

evidence.snippet: virMediatedDeviceTypePtr **mdev_types,
evidence.reason: The declaration establishes that mdev_types points to the caller's single virMediatedDeviceTypePtr* variable (one element), so the indexing expression mdev_types[i] at line 11 reads past that single element for every i >= 1; no other statement in the code reinterprets, bounds, or parenthesizes the expression.

assumptions: mdev_types is read as virMediatedDeviceTypePtr ** (double pointer): the body's own statements `VIR_FREE(*mdev_types)` and `*mdev_types = g_steal_pointer(&types)` require it, and any single-pointer reading would not type-check.
virMediatedDeviceTypeFree(ptr) frees the passed object (characterizable free routine), and VIR_FREE frees and NULLs its argument.
Callers pass non-NULL mdev_types/nmdev_types; the code contains no quoted contract for this, but the instantiated corruption trigger does not depend on a harmful value for these pointers.
limitations: Trigger requires a refresh invocation with *nmdev_types >= 2 at entry; this state is produced by a previous successful call of this function (quoted lines 18-19) with a device exposing at least two mdev types, and the refresh case is documented by the code's own comment, so it is sourced, but it is not reachable on a first call with an empty output.

`sysfspath` is passed unvalidated into virMediatedDeviceGetMdevTypes (line 15); any path-safety defect would live in that not-shown callee, and the argument is an in-domain path string, so no defect is confirmed at this call site.
On refresh, elements 1..n-1 of the old array are never correctly freed (resource leak); this has no per-discipline-3 security impact and is not counted as a finding.

verdict.summary: fill_threshold_buffer is a non-static function that consumes caller-supplied pointers and integer lengths (src_width, left_offset, left_width, num_tiles, right_width) and passes them directly to memcpy at lines 9, 13 and 17 with no bounds, range, sign, or capacity check anywhere on any path. The first use of each size (line 9) precedes every statement in the body, the only if-statement in the code bounds only dead padding inside a compiled-out #ifdef, and there is no allocation, clamp, mask, or error arm. An untrusted caller (or any attacker data reaching these parameters) chooses copy lengths, count, and source offset freely, producing an out-of-bounds write of attacker-chosen length and content (and, at line 9, an out-of-bounds read via src_strip + left_offset). Negative int lengths also widen to ~SIZE_MAX at the size_t-parameterized memcpy call sites.

evidence.snippet:
memcpy(dest_strip, src_strip + left_offset, left_width);
    ptr_out_temp += left_width;
evidence.reason: Root cause: left_width and left_offset are unvalidated attacker-data parameters used as a memcpy length and source offset at their first use. No check, clamp, mask, allocation, or error arm exists before this statement. Instantiated trigger: call with left_width=100000 (or left_width=-1, which widens to ~SIZE_MAX as size_t) against a small destination, or left_offset=0x40000000 for an out-of-bounds read: memcpy copies exactly that many bytes, corrupting memory past the destination and reading past the source.

Second and third sinks of the same defect: the loop writes num_tiles * src_width bytes (both unvalidated parameters) at monotonically advancing ptr_out_temp with no per-iteration capacity check, then right_width more bytes at line 17. Total write extent is fully attacker-chosen with no bound anywhere in the function; e.g. num_tiles=INT_MAX, src_width=1 yields 2^31-1 sequential out-of-bounds copies.

evidence.snippet:
fill_threshold_buffer(byte *dest_strip, byte *src_strip, int src_width,
                       int left_offset, int left_width, int num_tiles,
                       int right_width)
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values: all six sizes/pointers are parameters of a non-static (externally callable) function with no documented precondition, assert, or validation anywhere in the given code, so per the trust model the caller controls their content and they are attacker-data.

assumptions: The destination and source buffer capacities are not derived, sized, or checked anywhere in this code (UNSOURCED); the analysis does not rely on them, since the defect is the total absence of any comparison between copy lengths and any bound.
No caller is shown; per the methodology the parameters of this non-static function are treated as an untrusted input surface and 'the caller should have validated' is not a valid dismissal.

PACIFY_VALGRIND and LAND_BITS are external, undefined in the given code (UNSOURCED); the ifdef block is assumed not compiled and in any case contains no bound on any copy: dest_strip - ptr_out_temp is <= 0 so the memset it guards never executes.
limitations: Real-world exploitability (which buffer overflows and with what content) depends on the not-shown caller's buffer sizing and on whether upstream decode stages constrain these parameters; no such constraint is quotable in the given code, so the finding stands on this code's own intake of the values.

The PACIFY_VALGRIND block computes negative padding (dest_strip - ptr_out_temp is negative after the copies), making its memset unreachable dead logic; it is not the primary defect and contributes no finding.

A pointer-overflow of ptr_out_temp via repeated += would require sizes near SIZE_MAX-scale; per-iteration memcpy corruption occurs far earlier, so this sub-candidate was folded into the primary overflow finding.

verdict.summary: njs_array_prototype_splice caches the array length (njs_object_length) before converting the attacker-supplied start/delete arguments, whose ToInteger conversion (njs_value_to_integer) can re-enter script via valueOf and shrink the array. All subsequent clamps (delete, delta) and the NJS_MAX_LENGTH check use the stale cached length while the fast path performs raw pointer operations: the deleted-copy loop reads array->start[n] past the truncated array (out-of-bounds read returned to script), array->length - (start + delete) can go negative and is passed to njs_array_copy_within, and array->length += delta underflows/corrupts the fast array's length field, enabling out-of-bounds access on any later use of the array.

evidence.reason: Origin of the defect: the array length is cached here, but the immediately following njs_value_to_integer on the attacker-supplied argument can execute user code (valueOf) that mutates the array, invalidating the cached 'length' used for every later bound.

Out-of-bounds read: 'delete' was clamped only against the stale cached length (line 32/42), and 'n' runs to start+delete-1 with no check against the array's current length; with a valueOf that shrinks the array during argument conversion (e.g. arr.length=1 with cached length 10), array->start[n] reads past the truncated array and the values are returned to script via 'deleted'.

evidence.snippet:
ret = njs_array_copy_within(vm, this, start + items, start + delete,
                                        array->length - (start + delete), 0);
evidence.reason: The count expression array->length - (start + delete) is computed from the post-mutation array->length against bounds clamped from the stale cached length; when the array shrank during argument conversion it evaluates negative (e.g. 1 - 10 = -9) and is passed unvalidated to njs_array_copy_within.

evidence.snippet: array->length += delta;
evidence.reason: Integer underflow / length-field corruption: delta was derived from the stale cached length (delta = items - delete with delete up to the old length), so after a valueOf-driven shrink this stores a negative (or unsigned-wrapped huge) value into the fast array's length field; every subsequent element access bounded by this length is out of bounds.

assumptions: njs_value_to_integer implements ECMAScript ToInteger, which invokes a user-supplied valueOf/toPrimitive on object arguments, re-entering script; treated as characterizable framework semantics analogous to memcpy.

Setting arr.length to a smaller value changes the array's actual length; the precise njs length-setter behavior (whether the backing allocation is shrunk/freed and whether the array remains a fast array) is not shown in the given code.
The declared width of njs_array_t.length is not shown; if unsigned, the underflow at line 115 wraps to a huge value instead of a negative one, with equivalent out-of-bounds consequences.
limitations: The exact heap effect of the reentrant shrink (in-place truncation vs. reallocation) is determined by the unshown njs length setter; if the mutation always converted the array to a slow array, the fast-path sinks would be unreachable and the slow path (property accessors) is bounds-safe.
njs_array_copy_within's behavior when passed a negative count is not shown; if it validated the count internally, the line-109 impact would be limited to the sinks at lines 62 and 115.

No fully in-code trigger exists without reentrancy: with the cached length equal to array->length, the clamps (lines 26, 42, 47) and the expand-before-copy order (line 103) keep the fast path within bounds, verified for delta>0 and delta<0.

verdict.summary: fill_threshhold_buffer performs three memcpy operations (left part, tile loop, remainder) whose lengths, source offset, and iteration count derive entirely from unchecked int parameters of a non-static function. memcpy(dest_strip, src_strip + left_offset, left_width);
    ptr_out_temp += left_width;

A peer on the vhost-user socket can exhaust host memory of the privileged backend process with a single small message and repeat it for ~2x peak footprint, since the new allocation happens before the old mapping is freed.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled num_queues (uint16, max 0xFFFF) and queue_size (uint16, max 0xFFFF) produce an unvalidated allocation of up to ~68 GB that memset then fully commits. Trigger instantiated: GET_INFLIGHT_FD message with num_queues=0xFFFF, queue_size=0xFFFF (or tuned smaller to guarantee mmap success) yields memory exhaustion of the shared backend process; each new request allocates a fresh region (line 54) before the previous one is freed (lines 62-64), roughly doubling peak footprint per iteration.

assumptions: inflight_mem_alloc behaves as an allocator (returns a pointer to a region of the requested size or NULL); its implementation is not shown, and the NULL result is checked at line 55 before any use.

All buffer operations use the truncated value consistently, so the direct consequence is truncated analysis coverage, not memory corruption; no OOB, bypass, or misrepresentation of security state results.

verdict.summary: vhost_user_get_inflight_fd accepts num_queues and queue_size directly from the vhost-user frontend message and, with no validation against the device's actual queue configuration or any cap, computes mmap_size = num_queues * pervq_inflight_size and passes it to inflight_mem_alloc, memsets the entire attacker-sized region, retains it in dev->inflight_info until the next call, and runs an init loop bounded only by the attacker values. A peer can turn a fixed-size 16-byte-payload message into a multi-gigabyte allocation, memset, and ~2^32-iteration write loop, and can repeat it at will, exhausting backend memory/hugepages and CPU (denial of service).

evidence.reason: The allocation size and memset length are computed exclusively from the peer-supplied num_queues and queue_size (loaded at lines 37-38) with no bounds check, clamp, or comparison against dev->nr_vring or negotiated vring sizes anywhere in the function. Trigger: frontend sends GET_INFLIGHT_FD with msg.size == sizeof(payload) (passes the line-13 check), num_queues = 0xFFFF, queue_size = 0xFFFF, producing an allocation/memset of up to ~100 GB from a fixed-size message; the region is retained at lines 69-71 until replaced and the packed init loop at lines 76-84 performs num_queues * queue_size (~2^32) writes. Attacker-scalable amplification and retention (CWE-400).

verdict.summary: The slice-building loop derives min_old_row/max_old_row directly from the unvalidated row_remapping input tensor (only its size is checked, not its values). With a single element INT64_MAX, row_start += slice_length overflows int64 (row_start = INT64_MAX + 1 wraps to INT64_MIN), re-entering the while loop with slice_length computed as 0, so the loop never terminates while tensor_slices.push_back grows without bound: a one-element attacker input causes an infinite loop and memory exhaustion. No clamp, range check against the checkpoint tensor's row count, slice_length positivity check, or iteration cap exists on any path before or inside the loop; the only shape validation (SliceTensorShape at line 141) runs only after the loop has completed.

evidence.reason: Root cause: signed int64 overflow on attacker-derived row bounds. Trigger instantiated: row_remapping = {INT64_MAX} (size matches num_rows_, values unchecked). Then max_old_row = row_start = INT64_MAX, slice_length = 1, and 'row_start += slice_length' overflows to INT64_MIN, so the loop condition 'row_start <= max_old_row' holds again with slice_length = 0 (max_old_row - row_start + 1 wraps to 0), producing a non-terminating loop whose tensor_slices.push_back grows unbounded: infinite loop plus memory exhaustion from a single attacker-controlled int64. Even without overflow, an attacker-chosen range up to 2^63 makes the iteration count and slice vector arbitrarily large (uncontrolled resource consumption). No guard of any form (bounds check vs tensor rows, clamp, slice_length > 0 check, checked arithmetic, iteration cap) exists on any path; SliceTensorShape validation at line 141 executes only after this loop finishes.

Origin of the tainted value: max_old_row is assigned directly from row_remapping(i), whose elements are attacker-controlled int64 input with no range validation anywhere in this code (only 'row_remapping.size() == num_rows_' is checked at line 9). Setting one element to INT64_MAX instantiates the overflow/infinite-loop trigger at lines 112-121.

verdict.summary: No trigger could be instantiated from the given code. The function contains genuinely unguarded arithmetic sinks — the divides `(8 * (runtime->oss.period_bytes - runtime->oss.buffer_used) + 7) / width`, `size * 8 / width`, and `runtime->control->appl_ptr % runtime->period_size`, plus the unvalidated silence write snd_pcm_format_set_silence(format, runtime->oss.buffer + runtime->oss.buffer_used, size) — with no bound, zero, or range check in any form on any path (verified by exhaustive search in STEP 5). However, every harmful value those sinks could consume (width == 0, period_size == 0, buffer_used > period_bytes, oss.buffer allocation size) is produced by statements outside this code (OSS parameter-change helpers and hw-params setup not shown), so per the sourcing rules each trigger precondition is UNSOURCED and the candidates are speculative, not provable vulnerabilities of this snippet in isolation. Lock/ref accounting and the f_flags save/restore were verified balanced on all paths; the only exhibited race (f_flags save/restore around the blocking DRAIN ioctl) corrupts only the O_NONBLOCK audio flag, which is not a security impact.

assumptions: pcm_oss_file is non-NULL and its streams[] entries are either valid substream pointers or NULL; this contract is enforced by the caller/ioctl dispatch, which is not shown.
substream->runtime is a valid, allocated runtime for the whole function body; snd_pcm_kernel_ioctl(SNDRV_PCM_IOCTL_DRAIN) does not free or replace the runtime.
snd_pcm_oss_make_ready, when it returns >= 0, leaves the stream with consistent period_size/oss.buffer state; this callee is not shown and not characterizable.
snd_pcm_format_set_silence writes exactly size frames within the target buffer; its bounds behavior is kernel-internal and not characterizable here.
runtime->control is non-NULL (allocated together with the runtime by core code not shown).
limitations: C1 (CWE-369 divide-by-zero): `size = (8 * (runtime->oss.period_bytes - runtime->oss.buffer_used) + 7) / width;` and `size * 8 / width` divide by `width = snd_pcm_format_physical_width(format)` with no zero check anywhere in this code. Trigger requires runtime->oss.format (UNSOURCED, set by the parameter-change path not shown) to map to a format with physical width 0, and buffer_used/period_ptr > 0 (UNSOURCED). Cannot be instantiated here.

C2 (CWE-369 divide-by-zero): `size = runtime->control->appl_ptr % runtime->period_size;` executes with no check that period_size != 0. The only in-code assignment to any oss field is `runtime->oss.buffer_used = 0;` (capture section, safe value); runtime->period_size has no producer in this code, so period_size == 0 is UNSOURCED.

C3 (CWE-787/190, most serious latent issue): `snd_pcm_format_set_silence(format, runtime->oss.buffer + runtime->oss.buffer_used, size);` performs a heap write whose offset (buffer_used) and length (derived from period_bytes - buffer_used, which underflows to a huge size_t when buffer_used > period_bytes) are entirely unvalidated in this code, with no allocation statement for oss.buffer present to anchor a same-expression sizing guard. Whether buffer_used can ever exceed period_bytes is decided by the OSS write/accumulate path (snd_pcm_oss_write and change_params), which is not given; the invariant is neither quotable nor refutable here.
C4 (CWE-190): `size * 8 / width` can wrap at size_t scale if period_bytes - period_ptr is near SIZE_MAX/8; both operands are UNSOURCED.

C5 (CWE-362, dismissed for impact not trigger): the f_flags save/mutate/restore around snd_pcm_kernel_ioctl(SNDRV_PCM_IOCTL_DRAIN, NULL) is an exhibitable race window interleavable by a concurrent thread, but the corrupted datum is the O_NONBLOCK audio flag on the substream — no memory corruption, bypass, or amplification, so it is not a security finding.

Reachability itself (a caller invoking snd_pcm_oss_sync with attacker-shaped runtime state via SNDCTL_DSP_SYNC or close) is provided by pcm_oss.c code outside the given snippet; if the parameter-change path (not shown) permits width == 0 or period_bytes == 0 states, C1/C3 would become real vulnerabilities in this function — this cannot be decided from the given code alone.

Every candidate defect (potential kfree of the stack array inline_vecs, UAF of iovec after -EIOCBQUEUED, count+truncated overflow in iov_iter_reexpand, io_size-count underflow in iov_iter_revert) depends on writeback/ownership/bounds behavior of not-shown callees (io_import_iovec, io_iter_do_read, iov_iter internals) that cannot be characterized from the given code, so no trigger precondition can be instantiated. verdict.summary: Stack buffer overflow in mcba_usb_start_xmit: the CAN frame DLC field cf->len (attacker-controlled content of the transmitted skb, width u8, values 0-255) is copied into usb_msg.dlc and used directly as the memcpy length into the fixed 8-byte stack array usb_msg.data. The only preceding check, can_dropped_invalid_skb(netdev, skb), contains no statement in this code bounding cf->len to the destination size (its framework semantics of this era permit lengths up to CANFD_MAX_DLEN=64), so any frame with len > 8 causes memcpy to write past usb_msg.data, corrupting adjacent kernel stack. Classic CAN frames sent to this netdev can therefore overflow a kernel stack buffer with data read from attacker-influenced skb memory.

evidence.reason: Root cause: usb_msg.dlc is assigned the attacker-controlled frame length cf->len with no bound, clamp, mask, or length check anywhere in this code, then used as the memcpy length into the fixed 8-byte stack array usb_msg.data (struct mcba_usb_msg_can). Trigger instantiated by a transmitted CAN frame with cf->len = 64: can_dropped_invalid_skb (the only validation, line 14) does not enforce a <=8 bound in this code, so the memcpy writes 64 bytes into the 8-byte stack array, overflowing 56 bytes into adjacent kernel stack (and reading past cf->data[8] in the skb). No fix form (bounds check, clamp, mask, sized allocation, error arm on length) exists on any path to this sink.

evidence.reason: Taint origin: the skb passed to this ndo_start_xmit handler carries attacker-supplied CAN frame content across a trust boundary; cf->len and cf->data read from this frame are the attacker-data that flows through line 43 into the unbounded memcpy at line 45.

assumptions: The width of usb_msg.data is not declared in the given code; the known driver definition of struct mcba_usb_msg_can is a __packed struct ending in u8 data[8] (classic CAN data length). The overflow analysis holds for this known width; the absence of any code-visible bound on usb_msg.dlc is independent of it.

can_dropped_invalid_skb is a CAN-framework helper not shown in the given code; its characterizable semantics in the kernel contemporary with this code reject only frames with cfd->len > CANFD_MAX_DLEN (64), not len > 8, for a classic-CAN-only device.

verdict.summary: memslot_get_virt validates the signed group_id parameter only against an upper bound (`group_id >= info->num_memslots_groups`); a negative group_id passes the check and is used directly as an index into info->mem_slots, so `slot = &info->mem_slots[group_id][slot_id]` computes an out-of-bounds pointer and `slot->generation` is read out of bounds (and leaked into the spice_critical log). evidence.reason: Sink: with the attacker-supplied signed parameter group_id = -1 (which passes the only check at line 10 because -1 >= num_memslots_groups is false for any count >= 0), line 22 computes `&info->mem_slots[-1][slot_id]`, an out-of-bounds pointer, and line 25 reads `slot->generation` from that out-of-bounds location. No lower-bound check, cast, mask, clamp, or checked accessor exists on any path to this read; the out-of-bounds value is also printed to the log at line 30 (information disclosure of adjacent host memory).

Origin of the defect: this is the only validation of group_id, a signed int. It enforces only the upper bound; there is no `group_id < 0` arm, so negative group_id values (down to INT_MIN) reach the array indexing at line 22. A correct guard would be `if (group_id < 0 || group_id >= info->num_memslots_groups)`.

assumptions: `info` is assumed non-NULL and initialized by the caller; no NULL check or documented contract exists in the given code.

`info->num_memslots_groups` and `info->num_memslots` are configured elsewhere (not assigned in this code) and are treated as non-negative counts; the primary defect holds for every value of num_memslots_groups >= 0, since the only scenario where the line-10 check would reject a negative group_id is a negative count, which a count cannot take.
`memslot_validate_virt` (not shown) is assumed to perform the intended bound check on h_virt + add_size before the pointer is returned at line 41; its semantics cannot be quoted from this code.
limitations: Negative `slot_id`: the check at line 16 (`slot_id >= info->num_memslots`) also lacks a lower bound, but slot_id is produced by the not-shown `memslot_get_id`, whose behavior cannot be characterized; no statement in this code produces a negative slot_id, so this trigger is not instantiated.

If the out-of-bounds `slot->generation` happens to match the computed generation, `slot->address_delta` (out-of-bounds memory) is added to h_virt at line 35 and the corrupted pointer is returned at line 41; what callers do with that pointer is not shown and not characterizable, so the downstream impact is not counted — the out-of-bounds read at line 25 is already confirmed independently.
The attacker-controllable `add_size` is passed to the not-shown `memslot_validate_virt` at line 37; the bound it enforces (if any) cannot be quoted from this code.
Deployment context (which process invokes this function and with what privilege) is not evidenced by the code and was not used to promote or demote any candidate.

verdict.summary: In get_lisp_indent(), the loop `while (*that && col)` (lines 97-101) advances `that` one multibyte character per iteration while decrementing `col`, a byte index (`col = pos->col`, the byte column of the enclosing paren). On a line containing multibyte characters before the opening paren (attacker-supplied buffer content, e.g. the line "\u00e9\u00e9("), the loop consumes past the paren and exits with `that` on the line's NUL terminator. The following if tests only for '(' or '[' and the else arm then executes the unconditional `that++` (line 114) with no NUL check, moving `that` past the end of the line buffer; the subsequent `VIM_ISWHITE(*that)` and scanning loops dereference out of bounds and can walk arbitrarily far past the allocation. This is a heap out-of-bounds read triggered by crafted file content during lisp indent computation.

evidence.reason: Origin of the faulty value: `col` holds the byte column of the enclosing paren (`col = pos->col`), but each iteration advances `that` by one multibyte character and decrements `col` once. With multibyte text before the paren on the paren line (e.g. "\u00e9\u00e9(" with the '(' at byte 4), the loop runs past the paren and exits with `that` pointing at the line's NUL terminator while col is still nonzero.

Sink: when the preceding loop exits with *that == NUL, this condition is false and the else arm executes `that++` with no NUL/emptiness check on any path, advancing `that` one byte past the line's NUL terminator. The next statement, `while (VIM_ISWHITE(*that))`, then dereferences out-of-bounds heap memory, and the loops further below can continue reading past the allocation until a NUL or whitespace byte is found. Trigger fully instantiated: attacker-controlled buffer line with multibyte characters before the unmatched '(' (e.g. line 1 = "\u00e9\u00e9(", cursor on line 2, lisp indent invoked) makes findmatch return col=4, the col loop land `that` on the NUL, and `that++` step past the end of the line buffer.

assumptions: `lbr_chartabsize_adv(line, &that, col)` advances `that` by one multibyte character (MB_PTR_ADV) and returns its display width, per well-established Vim internal semantics; the function body is not included in the given code.
`ml_get_curline()` returns the current buffer line as a NUL-terminated allocation; reading bytes after the NUL is out-of-bounds for that allocation.

`pos_T.col` / `w_cursor.col` are byte indices in Vim, and `findmatch(NULL, '(')` returns the position of the unmatched opening paren within the buffer, so pos->col is the byte offset of a real paren character on line pos->lnum.

Reaching this code requires the editor to compute a lisp indent (e.g. 'lisp' indent option with == or automatic indenting) on attacker-supplied buffer content; invocation context, not a guard, per the data-origin impact model.
limitations: Integer overflow of the `int amount` accumulator (lines 99, 120, 158-161) requires lines of hundreds of megabytes of wide tab expansion with no bound in this code; the resulting impact is a wrong indent value, so it is recorded as unconfirmed degradation rather than a vulnerability.
`lisp_match(that + 1)` when '(' is the final byte of the line passes a pointer to the in-bounds NUL terminator; string comparison stops at the first byte, so no out-of-bounds read occurs there.
Underflow of `--curwin->w_cursor.lnum` (line 33) would require cursor.lnum == 0 or pos->lnum == 0, which findmatch's valid positions (lnum >= 1) prevent; not instantiated.

The attacker-controlled loop size ((*i)->data) yields only input-proportional work; int overflow of the bytes accumulator has no memory-unsafe consumer. The unchecked read_inode return (potential NULL dereference at 'dir->mode = (*i)->mode') could not be confirmed because no statement in the given code characterizes read_inode's NULL behavior.

assumptions: Struct declarations for squashfs_dir_header_3/squashfs_dir_entry_3 and the constants SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN and SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT are not in the given code; per the known project headers the dir entry size field is an unsigned bitfield, which is what makes 'dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN' a complete guard (a signed field could be negative; the NUL write index dire->size+1 would then be <= 0, still in bounds, but the negative length passed to read_directory_data would be uncharacterizable).

read_directory_data is assumed to write exactly 'length' bytes into the caller buffer and to fail (FALSE) on exhausted/corrupt directory data, so the outer loop is bounded by actual image content; its implementation is not shown.
MEM_ERROR() is assumed to terminate the process on allocation failure; check_name and check_directory are assumed to validate/sort without memory-unsafe behavior; not shown.
The globals sBlk.s.directory_table_start and swap are set from the filesystem image outside this function; no assignment appears in the given code.
limitations: NULL dereference candidate: '*i = read_inode(block_start, offset);' is never NULL-checked before 'dir->mode = (*i)->mode;' dereferences it, but whether read_inode can return NULL (vs. exiting internally) depends on not-shown code that cannot be characterized, so the trigger precondition is unsourced and the candidate cannot be confirmed or demoted from here.

Integer overflow candidate: 'size = (*i)->data + bytes - 3;' with attacker-controlled data can produce size near INT_MAX; 'bytes' (int) can then overflow during the loop. Since bytes is only compared and incremented (never used as an index, pointer, or copy length), the consequence is at most an early loop exit with a partially built directory; no memory-safety impact, and triggering requires a multi-gigabyte crafted image.

Resource consumption: a large attacker-chosen directory size causes one dir_ent allocation plus a bounded strdup per entry, but each iteration must consume at least sizeof(dirh)+sizeof(*dire)+1 real image bytes, so memory use is a constant multiple of the input consumed rather than scalable amplification.

read_inode, read_directory_data, check_name, check_directory, and squashfs_closedir implementations are not shown; conclusions about their internal memory safety are outside the scope of this analysis.
