verdict.summary: LogFilePrep passes the caller-supplied strings fname and backup directly as the format argument to asprintf (lines 5 and 15) with no validation on any path. A caller-controlled fname or backup containing conversions beyond the single supplied argument (e.g. '%n', '%s') makes asprintf pop garbage values past the one real vararg: '%n' yields an out-of-bounds/arbitrary write (memory corruption) and '%s' yields out-of-bounds stack reads copied into the produced name (disclosure). The function is externally visible (no static), so per the intake rule its content-bearing parameters are attacker-data; the format interpretation is entirely local to the quoted call statements.

verdict.summary: vhost_user_set_inflight_fd processes the VHOST_USER_SET_INFLIGHT_FD message but never validates the frontend-supplied num_queues against the device's configured virtqueue count (dev->nr_vring) and never checks mmap_size against num_queues * pervq_inflight_size. The loop indexes dev->virtqueue[i] with the attacker-controlled count, reading past the array and then writing through the out-of-bounds-derived pointer (vq->inflight_split = addr) and past the attacker-sized mapping (desc_num = queue_size at base + i*pervq_inflight_size), yielding out-of-bounds read and write (memory corruption) in the backend process from a single crafted message.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the loop bound is the attacker-controlled num_queues with no check against dev->nr_vring (the only nr_vring use, line 45 'if (dev->nr_vring > 0)', gates only numa_node), so 'vq = dev->virtqueue[i]' reads past the array for i >= nr_vring (CWE-125). The same loop then writes 'vq->inflight_packed/split = addr' through the OOB-read pointer and writes desc_num at addr, which advances by pervq_inflight_size each iteration with no check that num_queues * pervq_inflight_size <= mmap_size, so writes land past the attacker-sized mapping (CWE-787). Instantiated trigger: num_queues = 0xFFFF, mmap_size = 4096, queue_size = 256, valid payload size and fd >= 0 (line 15) on a device with fewer than 65535 configured vqs: iteration i = nr_vring performs the first out-of-bounds read at line 81; a non-NULL garbage value flows to the pointer write at lines 86/89, and later iterations write at offsets up to 65534 * pervq_inflight_size beyond the 4096-byte mapping at lines 87/90.

Origin of the tainted values: all four fields are copied from the vhost-user message payload with no validation. The only check on the message, 'if (ctx->msg.size != sizeof(ctx->msg.payload.inflight) || fd < 0)' (line 15), verifies structural completeness and fd sign only, never the values of mmap_size (uint64_t), num_queues (uint16_t, up to 65535), or queue_size (uint16_t), which then drive the out-of-bounds loop at lines 80-93.

assumptions: vhost_user_set_inflight_fd is a vhost-user message handler: ctx carries a message received from the frontend over the vhost-user socket, so all payload fields and fds are attacker-data per discipline 3 (the caller is the untrusted frontend).

dev->nr_vring and the dev->virtqueue[] entries are assigned in other vhost-user handlers not shown (SET_VRING_NUM / SET_VRING_ADDR / vq allocation); the same frontend that sends SET_INFLIGHT_FD configured them, so their values cannot be assumed safe. limitations: The out-of-bounds read at line 81 requires num_queues to exceed the array's allocated length, i.e. nr_vring < num_queues. nr_vring has no assignment in the given code; the simulation instantiated nr_vring = 2 from the frontend's own earlier SET_VRING_NUM configuration, which is not part of the given code. The heap-corruption write at lines 86/89 requires the out-of-bounds-read pointer value at line 81 to be non-NULL ('if (!vq) continue;' filters only NULL); with NULL garbage the direct consequence degrades to the out-of-bounds read plus likely SIGSEGV (denial of service across the socket trust boundary), while non-NULL garbage yields the write primitive.

verdict.summary: No reachable memory-safety or validation defect. The allocation is sized by the same scan that the copy loop re-executes with identical escape alignment: pass 1 reserves 5 bytes per backslash-quoted special key, decrements 1 per interpolated brace pair, and both passes consume exactly/least 2 characters per backslash escape, so pass 2 never produces more than len-1 bytes plus the terminating NUL. Unterminated strings and stray braces are rejected by error arms that return before the copy loop, and the allocation result is NULL-checked before any write. The only overflow candidate is a signed-int wrap of len requiring a multi-gigabyte string literal, which is not instantiable at any realistic input scale and would fail allocation in any case.

assumptions: trans_special(&p, end, flags, FALSE, NULL) returns the number of bytes it wrote to end, returns 0 without writing on failure, and on success consumes at least the 4 characters of a minimal "\<x>" form while writing at most 9 bytes (3 modifier + 6 character); this is standard Vim semantics relied on per the callee boundary rule.
mb_char2bytes writes at most 3 bytes for a value <= 0xFFFF (\u with n=4) and at most 6 bytes for a 32-bit value (\U with n=8), both strictly less than the 6 or 10 input characters consumed.

MB_PTR_ADV and MB_COPY_CHAR advance/copy whole multibyte characters in both passes, so both passes stay character-aligned and a backslash-looking trail byte inside a multibyte character is never treated as an escape in either pass.
alloc(len) returns NULL on failure and otherwise returns a buffer of exactly len bytes, matching the len computed from the same scan that bounds the copy loop's output.
In interpolate mode the caller points *arg at the first character to scan such that off = 0 positions the scan at the content start; this affects only where the scan begins, not the sizing invariant.
limitations: len = (int)(p - *arg + extra) and extra += 5 use signed int; a string literal of roughly 4.3 billion characters (over 430 million "\<" sequences in one line) could wrap len past INT_MAX and produce an undersized or negative allocation. No statement in this code bounds the input length, but no attacker-realistic script reaches that scale, and in-range huge values make alloc fail, so the trigger is not instantiated (recorded as speculative integer overflow, CWE-190-class, field: unbounded p - *arg span).

The iemsg("eval_string() used more space than allocated") check after end += extra is post-hoc: if trans_special could ever write more than consumed + 5 bytes for a "\<...>" form, the writes would already have occurred before the check. The arithmetic invariant (consumed >= 4, produced <= 9) keeps it unreachable in this code, but the canary itself is not a guard.

In interpolate mode the fit is exact (len = S + 1 - N_pairs for S content chars and N brace pairs) with zero slack; the invariant holds because both passes consume 2 and produce 1 per pair, but any future edit to either pass's brace handling could turn this into an off-by-one overflow.

For \U the accumulated value nr can overflow a signed int at 8 hex digits (e.g. \U0010FFFF and above); the resulting negative value flows into mb_char2bytes, which then emits at most 1 byte, so no memory-safety effect occurs, only an encoding-correctness quirk.

Negative slot_id candidate: a negative return from memslot_get_id (unshown) would pass 'slot_id > info->num_memslots' and index mem_slots negatively; the return range of that callee is not characterizable from this code.

NULL-info candidate: 'info' is dereferenced at line 10 ('info->num_memslots_groups') with no NULL check; the trigger requires a caller passing NULL, no caller is shown, no attacker input maps to info, and the worst consequence is a crash (CWE-476) — speculative.

Unvalidated-translation candidate: h_virt = __get_clean_virt(info, addr) + slot->address_delta is returned to callers with all bounds validation delegated to memslot_validate_virt (line 37), which is not shown; potential defects there (virt + add_size wraparound, inactive slot whose zero generation matches a crafted generation value in addr, since slot->generation and slot->address_delta are UNSOURCED registration state) are neither provable nor disprovable here.

Caller-side overread candidate: the returned virtual pointer is valid for add_size bytes; whether unshown callers (e.g., red-parse.c draw-command decoding) access more than add_size bytes is outside the given code.

verdict.summary: build_dirs walks src until its NUL and advances q into dst in lockstep, writing *r='\0' (line 7), *q='\0' (line 20) and *r='/' (line 21) at offsets determined solely by src's content and the unvalidated dst_prefix_len; dst's length or allocation is never consulted and no bounds check, clamp, mask, error arm, or alternative loop bound exists on any path, so a dst buffer smaller than dst_prefix_len + strlen(src) - src_prefix_len + 1 suffers an out-of-bounds write whenever a source path component is an existing directory, followed by an out-of-bounds read of dst inside mkdir_attr.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink: q has been advanced in lockstep with p through src (line 8) and is dereferenced with no bound against dst's allocation. With the instantiated trigger (dst = 4-byte buffer holding "/c", dst_prefix_len = 2, src = "/a/bbbb/x", src_prefix_len = 2, "/a/bbbb" an existing directory), q = dst+7 when the component at src[7] is found, and *q = '\0' writes four bytes past the 4-byte dst buffer — heap memory corruption under attacker-controlled distance, followed by mkdir_attr reading the dst string past its allocation.

Origin of the faulty value: q and r are computed from the unvalidated dst_prefix_len, *r = '\0' immediately writes into dst with no check that dst_prefix_len lies within dst, and the loop's only bound (!last, set by *p == '\0') is src's terminating NUL — so how far the writes into dst advance is decided entirely by src's content, never by dst's size; no statement in the function bounds q or r.

assumptions: src and dst are NUL-terminated C strings at call time (no check exists in the code; assumed to match intended usage — if violated, the loop additionally walks past src unbounded).
mkdir_attr(const char *path, mode_t, uid_t, gid_t) creates a directory at path and reads path as a string (characterizable path-taking helper, per the callee boundary rule).
stat/mkdir semantics are the standard library ones.

The caller is treated as untrusted because the code documents, asserts, or checks no precondition on src, dst, src_prefix_len, or dst_prefix_len; with a visible caller that provably sizes dst as dst_prefix + src_suffix in a buffer of at least strlen(dst)+1 bytes, this specific out-of-bounds write would not be triggered by that caller — such caller behavior is not shown and per the rules cannot demote the finding.
limitations: TOCTOU between stat(src) (line 17) and mkdir_attr(dst) (line 23): no security consequence is instantiable within the given code (mkdir failure handling is out of view).
The return value of mkdir_attr (line 23) is ignored; any consequence of a failed mkdir happens only in stages not shown.

mkdir_attr receives the source directory's st_mode, which may include file-type and set*id bits; whether that creates a permission issue depends entirely on sanitization inside the unshown mkdir_attr.
If src_prefix_len >= strlen(src), p starts past src's NUL and *p reads / *p = '\0' writes fall outside src — same missing input-validation root cause as the primary finding, subsumed by it.

If src were not NUL-terminated, the loop would traverse past src's buffer (unbounded read with writes at matching offsets in dst); this requires the caller to pass an unterminated buffer and is recorded as the same caller-contract gap rather than a separate finding.

verdict.summary: bgp_capability_msg_parse reads a fixed sizeof(struct capability_mp_data) bytes with memcpy from pnt + 3 while the only length guard (if ((pnt + hdr->length + 3) > end)) bounds the available payload by the attacker-declared hdr->length. A BGP peer sending a Capability message with hdr->length in {0,1,2,3} (and the message ending exactly at pnt + 3 + hdr->length) causes the memcpy to read up to 4 bytes past the end of the received message buffer, an out-of-bounds heap read with crash/DoS and heap-byte disclosure potential via subsequent afi/safi debug logging.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the guard on line 43 only ensures hdr->length payload bytes are present, but the memcpy on line 51 unconditionally copies sizeof(struct capability_mp_data) (4 bytes: 16-bit afi per ntohs(mpc.afi), safi, reserved). Instantiated trigger: message [action=SET][code=CAPABILITY_CODE_MP][length=0x02][afi-hi][afi-lo] with length=5; the check at line 43 passes at the exact boundary (pnt+5 > end is false) and the memcpy reads pnt+3..pnt+6, two bytes past end. With hdr->length=0 and length=3, all 4 copied bytes lie past end. No check of hdr->length against sizeof(struct capability_mp_data) exists anywhere in the function.

evidence.snippet: hdr = (struct capability_header *)(pnt + 1);
evidence.reason: Taint origin: hdr->code and hdr->length are read directly from the peer-controlled message bytes at pnt+1/pnt+2; the attacker chooses hdr->length (including 0..3) that later controls how few payload bytes are guaranteed before the fixed-size memcpy at line 51.

assumptions: sizeof(struct capability_mp_data) = 4 bytes; the struct is defined outside the given code, but the code's own usage (ntohs(mpc.afi) implies a 16-bit field, mpc.safi one byte) shows at least 3 bytes are consumed, so even the minimal reading still leaves hdr->length in {0,1,2} triggering the over-read.
bgp_size_t is treated as a small unsigned message length (its FRR definition, uint16_t), so end = pnt + length cannot wrap.
bgp_notify_send, zlog_*, CHECK_FLAG, and the CAPABILITY_* constants have their documented standard semantics.
limitations: Potential out-of-bounds write at peer->afc_recv[afi][safi] = 1 (lines 88-96) would require bgp_map_afi_safi_iana2int to return success with afi/safi outside the afc array bounds; the callee is not shown and its success contract cannot be quoted, so this precondition is UNSOURCED and the candidate is not confirmed.

Pointer overflow in pnt + hdr->length + 3 would require pnt near the address-space maximum; hdr->length is uint8_t (max 255) and message lengths are small, so the wrap is not exercised by the code as written.

Disclosure impact of the over-read bytes depends on whether bgp_debug_neighbor_events-enabled debug logging renders iana_afi2str/iana_safi2str output containing the leaked values; the primary out-of-bounds read itself is fully instantiated regardless.

verdict.summary: do_cmdline() is the trust-boundary intake for command text, but every attacker-data path to a sensitive sink in this code is either guarded by a quotable check (recursion depth, vim_strsave/store_loop_line failure tests, breakpoint NULL tests, lines_ga repeat-path bounds check current_line < lines_ga.ga_len) or its only harmful instantiation requires pointer/index invariants established exclusively in callees not shown (do_one_cmd keeping next_cmdline inside cmdline_copy for STRMOVE, cstack push/pop bounds, store_loop_line ga_len growth). No trigger precondition for the remaining candidates is sourced in this code, so no vulnerability is instantiated here.

assumptions: FEAT_EVAL is enabled in the analyzed build; many guards and the whole cstack/lines_ga machinery exist only under it, and the non-FEAT_EVAL path (#define cmd_getline fgetline) was not the analysis target.

Globals consumed here (trylevel, did_emsg, did_throw, got_int, force_abort, debug_tick, ex_nesting_level, msg_list, p_mfd, p_verbose) are managed by other stages; their values are treated as environment, and every reset this code performs was quoted.

Semantics of getline_equal(), func_has_ended(), func_has_abort(), source_finished(), dbg_find_breakpoint(), store_loop_line(), get_loop_line(), do_one_cmd(), cleanup_conditionals(), rewind_conditionals(), free_cmdlines() are not shown; only their call sites in this code were analyzed.
Deployment context (interactive editor, plugin execution, privilege) is unknown and was not used to promote or demote any candidate.
limitations: C1 (CWE-416/787 candidate): STRMOVE(cmdline_copy, next_cmdline) after next_cmdline = do_one_cmd(&cmdline_copy, ...) would be a use-after-free or NULL write if do_one_cmd freed/reallocated cmdline_copy and returned a non-NULL pointer outside the live buffer. The code's own comment says "cmdline_copy can change, e.g. for '%' and '#' expansion", and the pointer-relationship invariant is maintained entirely in do_one_cmd, which is not shown; the harmful producer is UNSOURCED, so the trigger is speculative.

C2 (CWE-125 candidate): the :continue/:endwhile jump-back read ((wcmd_T *)lines_ga.ga_data)[current_line].lnum-1 runs with current_line taken from cstack.cs_line[cstack.cs_idx] guarded only by >= 0; an out-of-range value requires ga_len to shrink relative to stored cs_line entries, which is prevented only by store_loop_line()/free_cmdlines()/rewind_conditionals() bookkeeping not shown. Precondition UNSOURCED.

C3 (CWE-125/787 candidate): cstack.cs_line[cstack.cs_idx] = current_line_before (CSL_HAD_LOOP) and the cs_pending/cs_flags accesses in the HAD_FINA branch run with no cs_idx >= 0 test in this code; the looplevel>0 implies valid cs_idx invariant is enforced in do_one_cmd/rewind_conditionals, not shown. Precondition UNSOURCED.

C4: ex_nesting_level is incremented on entry only when getline_is_func && ex_nesting_level == func_level(real_cookie) but decremented on exit on getline_equal(..., get_func_line) alone, an asymmetry that could drift the counter. In this code the value only feeds debug-breakpoint nesting comparisons; no memory, authz, injection, or amplification sink consumes it, so no security impact is instantiated.

Unchecked upper bound of cstack.cs_idx against CSTACK_LEN for all cs_flags/cs_line/cs_pending accesses: the stack-overflow check for deeply nested :if/:while/:try lives in do_one_cmd (not shown) and is a caller-side invariant this code must trust; recorded because it could not be verified here.

verdict.summary: Off-by-one in warnf's word-wrap loop: line 28 'len -= cut;' decrements the remaining-length counter by only 'cut' bytes although line 27 advanced 'ptr' by 'cut+1' bytes. For any formatted message containing more than WARN_TEXTWIDTH consecutive non-whitespace characters, the backward scan at line 21 exits with cut == 0, len never decreases, and ptr walks past the NUL terminator and beyond the 256-byte stack buffer print_buffer while len stays above WARN_TEXTWIDTH. The scan 'ptr[cut]' (line 21) and 'fwrite(ptr, cut + 1, 1, config->errors)' (line 25) then read out of bounds, disclose stack bytes to the error stream, and the loop never terminates (crash/DoS).

evidence.snippet:
ptr += cut+1; /* skip the space too */
        len -= cut;
evidence.reason: Root cause off-by-one: ptr advances cut+1 bytes (comment confirms index cut, the space, is consumed) but len is decremented by only cut. When the scan finds no whitespace, cut reaches 0 and 'len -= 0' leaves len unchanged, so len invariantly exceeds WARN_TEXTWIDTH and ptr advances one byte per iteration past the 256-byte print_buffer, making the loop non-terminating and driving the out-of-bounds reads.

Out-of-bounds read sinks reached by the instantiated trigger (70-char spaceless message): the guard '&& cut' bounds only the index cut, never the base pointer ptr, and never tests for the string terminator (NUL is not whitespace). Once ptr exceeds print_buffer+190 the scan reads print_buffer[256+], and once ptr passes print_buffer+256 the fwrite copies out-of-bounds stack bytes to config->errors, disclosing memory while the loop runs forever.

assumptions: config->conf and config->errors are never assigned in this code (UNSOURCED); the analysis assumes the normal non-MUTE operating mode and a valid FILE* error stream, which is the code path the function is designed to execute.

WARN_TEXTWIDTH, WARN_PREFIX, CONF_MUTE and ISSPACE are defined outside this code; the trigger does not depend on WARN_TEXTWIDTH's specific value (a message of WARN_TEXTWIDTH+1 spaceless characters works for any value >= 1, and lengths above 255 chars additionally exploit the unclamped vsnprintf return).
vsnprintf semantics relied on per the callee boundary rule: returns the would-be formatted length, which can exceed the 256-byte buffer.
limitations: Double 'va_start(ap, fmt);' (lines 9-10) is undefined behavior on an already-initialized va_list, but on common ABIs it merely re-initializes the argument pointer; no security impact could be instantiated.

fmt is used directly as the vsnprintf format string (line 11); a format-string injection (CWE-134) would require an unseen caller to embed attacker bytes into the format itself. No such caller is shown and the variadic design carries attacker content through ap, so this trigger was not instantiated.

len is never clamped to sizeof(print_buffer)-1 after line 11: a message longer than 255 characters is truncated in the buffer while len reflects the full would-be length, which independently drives the same out-of-bounds walk; it is subsumed by the primary finding.
If WARN_TEXTWIDTH were <= 0, line 21 would read ptr[-1] immediately, but WARN_TEXTWIDTH's value is unsourced and this scenario was not instantiated.

verdict.summary: bracketed_paste() safely bounds all writes to the fixed stack buffer: the only growth path (idx surviving via the STRNCMP/continue branch) is capped by the quoted guard 'if (end != NULL && STRLEN(end) >= NUMBUFLEN) end = NULL;', which executes before the loop and restricts any surviving end code to STRLEN(end) <= NUMBUFLEN-1, so idx at write time never exceeds NUMBUFLEN-2 and the MB_MAXBYTES-sized buffer is never overrun (verified at boundaries, including STRLEN(end) == NUMBUFLEN-1 and == NUMBUFLEN). The PASTE_EX heap copy is guarded by 'ga_grow(gap, idx) == OK' sized from the same expression as the memmove length, plus an explicit gap != NULL check. Reads of buf, end, and end[idx] stay in bounds, and the loop is bounded by input exhaustion or end-sequence match. The historical long-t_PE overflow shape is disarmed by this code's own statement; no instantiated vulnerability remains.

assumptions: STRNCMP/mch_memmove have standard strncmp/memmove semantics (STRNCMP stops comparing after a NUL byte; mch_memmove copies exactly n bytes).
ga_grow(gap, idx) returning OK guarantees capacity for ga_len + idx additional bytes, per documented growarray semantics in this codebase.
mb_char2bytes writes at most MB_MAXBYTES bytes for one character; the buffer is sized with the same constant, and no statement in the given code shows a zero byte being produced for c != NUL.
NUMBUFLEN and MB_MAXBYTES are fixed positive compile-time constants (in Vim, 30 and 6); the bound analysis holds for any positive values since buf is sized as NUMBUFLEN + MB_MAXBYTES.
find_termcode returns either NULL or a NUL-terminated string; both cases are handled by the quoted checks.
limitations: Candidate (B), an out-of-bounds read at 'if (end[idx] == NUL)' past the terminator of end, would require buf to contain an embedded NUL byte at index STRLEN(end) while idx > STRLEN(end), making STRNCMP return 0 early. No statement in the given code can produce such a byte: c == NUL breaks out before any write, and whether any multibyte encoding reachable through mb_char2bytes can emit a zero byte is not shown (UNSOURCED precondition).

Candidate (A), the classic stack overflow of buf via a very long terminal-supplied t_PE paste-end code, is disarmed by the quoted statement 'if (end != NULL && STRLEN(end) >= NUMBUFLEN) end = NULL;' — an earlier Vim version lacking this check would be vulnerable to it (terminal attacker controlling the PE termcode and paste content).
Attacker control of termcodes (t_PE) via terminal escape responses or :set is assumed possible for threat modeling; it affects only candidates already disarmed or speculative here.

verdict.summary: tc_new_tfilter validates attacker-supplied netlink data with verifiable guards on every traced path: netlink_ns_capable enforces CAP_NET_ADMIN; tcf_proto_check_kind rejects over-long TCA_KIND before any use of name; chain_index is bounded by 'chain_index > TC_ACT_EXT_VAL_MASK' before tcf_chain_get, rejecting 0x80000000 and above; every fallible lookup result (tcf_chain_tp_find, tcf_chain_tp_insert_unique, tcf_proto_create, __tcf_block_find) is IS_ERR/NULL-tested with an error arm that diverges before the first dereference of tp; the goto replay path re-initializes tp, cl, and block and overwrites q through __tcf_qdisc_find before any dereference, so no stale-pointer use is reachable. Residual candidates (possible uninitialized read of name by tcf_proto_is_unlocked when TCA_KIND is absent; tcf_chain_tp_delete_empty receiving an ERR_PTR from a failed tcf_chain_tp_insert_unique) could not be confirmed because their trigger or impact depends entirely on callee code not shown, and per guard-anchoring no in-this-code statement instantiates or refutes them.

assumptions: tp->ops and q->ops are set by code not shown (tcf_proto_create, __tcf_qdisc_find); their non-NULL status cannot be quoted here, but every dereference is preceded by a quoted IS_ERR/NULL screen on tp itself.

n->nlmsg_flags is attacker-controlled and only used as documented boolean flags (NLM_F_CREATE, NLM_F_EXCL); nlmsg_parse_deprecated with rtm_tca_policy is assumed to enforce attribute length/type constraints, as its policy argument is not shown.

Deployment context (netlink daemon, capability of sender) is not evidence; the CAP_NET_ADMIN check was treated only as a trust gate, and message content was still analyzed as attacker-data per userns semantics.
limitations: C1 (possible CWE-908 uninitialized read): if tca[TCA_KIND] is absent, tcf_proto_check_kind(NULL, name) may leave name[IFNAMSIZ] untouched, and the lock-decision branch reads name through tcf_proto_is_unlocked(name) before the 'tca[TCA_KIND] == NULL' check inside the tp == NULL branch (which therefore does not cover this earlier use in execution order). Whether check_kind initializes or ignores name for a NULL attribute is inside the unshown callee, so the trigger could not be instantiated; recorded, not confirmed.

C2 (possible CWE-476): on tcf_chain_tp_insert_unique failure with tp_created=1, errout calls tcf_chain_tp_delete_empty(chain, tp, ...) passing the ERR_PTR value; the !IS_ERR screen 'if (tp && !IS_ERR(tp))' exists only at errout_tp for tcf_proto_put and runs after the delete_empty call, so no fix form covers this argument. The trigger was instantiated (concurrent unique-insert race between mutex_unlock of filter_chain_lock and the insert, returning e.g. ERR_PTR(-EEXIST)), but the impact depends entirely on tcf_chain_tp_delete_empty's unshown tolerance of ERR_PTR; not characterizable under the callee boundary rule, so not a finding.

C3 (possible CWE-400): the quoted bound permits chain_index up to 0x7FFFFFFF and tcf_chain_get(..., true) creates chains, so an attacker with CAP_NET_ADMIN in a user namespace can drive allocation of many chain objects; no allocation or loop in this code is sized by chain_index and the growth happens in unshown callee code, so the amplification impact is not instantiated here.

C4 dismissed with quoted trace: q is not reset at the replay label, but __tcf_qdisc_find(net, &q, ...) overwrites q before any dereference on the replayed iteration, so no use-after-free is reachable.

verdict.summary: All attacker-derived sizes and indices are provably bounded: len is rejected at 0 and clamped to 400 before the len+1 allocation, the fread length matches the allocation, the compression loop bound i < len keeps both its read and write indices in range, and the post-loop terminator index ((len+1)/2 in the worst odd case, max 200) always falls inside the len+1 buffer for every len in [1,400], verified by boundary simulation. The only defect is the unchecked fseek return, whose worst in-function consequence is parsing a bounded string from the wrong file offset; any security impact would require an unshown consumer of the returned string.

assumptions: cli_malloc is assumed to behave like standard malloc (return a pointer or NULL on failure); the code checks the NULL return at 'if (!name)', so the analysis does not depend on the allocation succeeding.
The FILE * argument f is a caller-provided stream whose seekability is unknown; this is an interface-contract value, not content data.
limitations: Unchecked fseek return: 'fseek(f, ptr, SEEK_SET);' discards the status. If the seek fails (e.g., non-seekable stream or an implementation-defined uint32_t-to-long conversion), fread reads from the current position and the function returns a string parsed from the wrong offset. Inside this code the read is still bounded by len into a len+1 buffer, so no memory-safety effect is instantiated; any harmful use of the misparsed string would occur in caller code not given.

The returned buffer's byte at index len is never initialized on the success path; it lies past the NUL terminator written at index <= (len+1)/2 and is never read by this code. A leak would require an unshown caller reading past the terminator.
If a caller passed a len that was not derived from parsed file content, the same analysis holds since the clamp at 'if (len>400) len=400;' bounds every path.

verdict.summary: warnf() formats into a fixed 256-byte stack buffer with vsnprintf but uses the raw return value as the loop bound. On truncation vsnprintf returns the would-be full length, so `len` can far exceed the bytes actually stored; the wrapping loop advances `ptr` (by cut+1) faster than it decrements `len` (by cut) and never bounds `ptr` against the buffer end. A formatted message of ~314+ bytes (e.g., a long no-space URL embedded by the caller's format arguments) walks `ptr` past print_buffer, causing out-of-bounds stack reads at `ptr[cut]` in the scan loop, in `fwrite(ptr, cut+1, ...)`, and in the final `fputs(ptr, ...)`; the out-of-bounds bytes are written to the error stream (information disclosure) and the unbounded scan can fault (denial of service). No check, clamp, or truncation handling for `len` or `ptr` exists anywhere in the function.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read sink: `ptr[cut]` is evaluated with `cut` starting at WARN_TEXTWIDTH-1 while `ptr` has been advanced past the 256-byte print_buffer by the unbounded wrapping loop. Instantiated trigger: a 314-byte no-space formatted message gives len=314 from vsnprintf (truncated to 255 chars + NUL in the buffer); after three iterations ptr=print_buffer+237 and len=80 > 79, so this scan first reads ptr[78] = print_buffer[315], 60 bytes past the array. The only bounds on `cut` are lower bounds (`&& cut`, the `0 == cut` reset); no statement bounds `ptr` or `len` against the buffer end. The OOB bytes are subsequently disclosed through `fwrite(ptr, cut + 1, 1, config->errors)` (line 29) and `fputs(ptr, config->errors)` (line 35), the latter walking unbounded stack memory until a chance NUL.

Origin of the faulty value: vsnprintf returns the number of characters that would have been written even when output is truncated to sizeof(print_buffer)-1, so `len` can exceed the 255 bytes actually stored (e.g., len=314 with only 255 chars + NUL in the buffer). `len` is never validated against sizeof(print_buffer), clamped, or replaced with the actual content length, and the loop `while(len > 0)` plus the per-iteration mismatch `ptr += cut+1` (line 31) vs `len -= cut` (line 32) drives `ptr` past the end of print_buffer while `len` remains positive, producing the out-of-bounds reads.

assumptions: WARN_TEXTWIDTH, WARN_PREFIX, ISSPACE, and CONF_MUTE are external macros not defined in the given code (UNSOURCED). The concrete simulation uses the upstream project's WARN_TEXTWIDTH=79; the defect was shown to hold for any value >= 1 (only the trigger threshold changes; for WARN_TEXTWIDTH > 256 the first scan is immediately out of bounds), so the macro's exact value does not gate the finding.

vsnprintf is assumed to follow C99 truncation semantics (returns the would-be full length when truncated, negative on encoding error), which is characterizable standard-library behavior relied on per the callee boundary rule.
ISSPACE is assumed equivalent to a standard whitespace test on single bytes; NUL is not whitespace.

No caller is shown; per the analysis rules, fmt and the variadic message content are treated as the function's data-carrying intake surface (attacker-influenced warning text such as URLs), since no documented or checked precondition in this code bounds the message length.
config->errors is the output FILE* provided by the caller; the out-of-bounds bytes are written there, which is the disclosure path.
limitations: Double va_start (lines 9-10) without an intervening va_end is undefined behavior (C99 7.15.1), but on mainstream ABIs va_start merely re-initializes ap; no concrete memory-corruption or disclosure impact could be simulated from this code, so it is recorded here rather than as a finding.

NULL config dereference at line 3 (`config->conf`) and line 16 (`config->errors`): no NULL check exists, but no statement in this code produces a NULL config (no allocation or lookup whose failure sentinel flows here) and the impact is a plain crash, so the trigger is not instantiated.
If any unshown caller passed non-literal attacker data as `fmt`, line 11 would be a format-string sink (CWE-134); no caller is visible in the given code, so this remains a caller-side misuse.

Message content is printed verbatim to the error stream, so messages containing newlines could forge log entries (CWE-117); the message layout is determined by the unshown caller's format string, so this is not instantiated here.

verdict.summary: All attacker-reachable memory-indexing sinks in this do_cmdline() implementation are protected by quoted, execution-order-verified guards: the lines_ga reads are gated by 'cstack.cs_looplevel > 0 && current_line < lines_ga.ga_len', the breakpoint recompute by 'lines_ga.ga_len > current_line', the jump-back cs_line read by a compound condition containing 'cstack.cs_idx >= 0' and 'cstack.cs_line[cstack.cs_idx] >= 0', and the end-of-loop cs_flags reads by 'if (cstack.cs_idx >= 0)'. current_line is provably non-negative from the code's own statements. The remaining unguarded sites (cs_line/cs_pending/cs_flags writes in the CSL_HAD_LOOP and CSL_HAD_FINA branches, and the STRMOVE of do_one_cmd's returned tail) could not be triggered with any state the shown statements can produce: making cs_idx negative while cs_looplevel stays positive, setting CSL_HAD_FINA, or returning an out-of-allocation tail all depend on the unshown do_one_cmd/rewind_conditionals/store_loop_line. Recursion is bounded by the quoted 'call_depth >= 200' check placed before the increment. No trigger with sourced preconditions and a characterizable impact chain exists in the given code.

assumptions: do_one_cmd(), rewind_conditionals(), store_loop_line(), and the getline/func_* helper callees maintain the documented cstack and lines_ga invariants (e.g. cs_looplevel > 0 implies a live WHILE/FOR entry with cs_idx >= 0; store_loop_line stores a copy of the line). These are enforced in code not given and are assumptions, not quoted facts.

fgetline returns either NULL or a NUL-terminated allocated string; do_one_cmd either returns NULL or a pointer handled consistently with *cmdlinep, as suggested by the in-code comment 'cmdline_copy can change, e.g. for '%' and '#' expansion'.
p_mfd, p_verbose, KeyTyped, got_int, debug_tick, debug_break_level, ex_nesting_level's initial value and similar globals are set by code outside this function and were treated as unsourced state.
limitations: C1 (speculative): 'cstack.cs_line[cstack.cs_idx] = current_line_before;' in the CSL_HAD_LOOP branch has no cs_idx bound of any form on its path (verified by exhaustive STEP 5 search), but reaching it with cs_idx < 0 while 'cstack.cs_looplevel > 0' requires do_one_cmd or rewind_conditionals (not shown) to break the looplevel/stack-depth invariant; no concrete trigger could be instantiated from the given code.

C2 (speculative): under CSL_HAD_FINA, 'report_make_pending(cstack.cs_pending[cstack.cs_idx] ...)' and 'cstack.cs_flags[cstack.cs_idx] |= CSF_ACTIVE | CSF_FINALLY;' index cs_idx unchecked; CSL_HAD_FINA is only ever set by the unshown do_one_cmd, so the harmful state is unsourced.

C3 (uncharacterizable link): 'STRMOVE(cmdline_copy, next_cmdline);' would overflow only if do_one_cmd returned a tail pointer outside the current cmdline_copy allocation; the buffer-management contract lives in the unshown callee, and the shown data flow (same-buffer tail move) cannot produce the harmful pointer.

verdict.summary: In em28xx_usb_probe, when a dual-transport-stream device's secondary instance is created (em28xx_duplicate_dev(dev) == 0 sets up dev->dev_next, kref'd and initialized) but the subsequent em28xx_init_dev(dev->dev_next, ...) fails, the code jumps to err_free, which releases only dev->alt_max_pkt_size_isoc and dev. A malicious USB device presenting a dual-TS board's VID/PID can make the secondary init fail by stalling control transfers, and can cycle reconnection to repeat the leak, causing attacker-scalable kernel memory retention.

evidence.reason: The error path releases only the primary device and its isoc array. When reached from the secondary-init failure inside the dual-TS block, dev->dev_next (a heap-allocated struct em28xx created by the em28xx_duplicate_dev gate at line 215 and kref-initialized at line 216, together with its duplicated alt_max_pkt_size_isoc) is never freed on any path in this function, producing a memory leak that is repeatable per device connection cycle.

verdict.summary: disable_priv_mode fails open: if setuid() or setgid() fails, the code only logs the error and continues (the sole exit is conditional on both the EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE compile flag and errno == EAGAIN, and the setgid arm has no exit at all), then unconditionally records the dropped-privilege state via 'current_user.euid = current_user.uid; current_user.egid = current_user.gid;'. A privileged process that fails to drop credentials therefore keeps running with elevated real/effective IDs while its own identity record claims the privileges were dropped, allowing subsequent untrusted input to execute under retained elevated credentials.

evidence.reason: The setuid failure sentinel is checked ('< 0') but the failure arm only calls sys_error; the sole exit is both compile-conditional (#if EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE) and errno-narrow (e == EAGAIN), so any other failure errno (e.g., EPERM) or a build without the define falls through and the process continues with its elevated effective uid.

The setgid failure arm contains only a log call with no exit or return on any path, and control then unconditionally executes 'current_user.euid = current_user.uid; current_user.egid = current_user.gid;', asserting the deprivileged state regardless of whether setuid/setgid succeeded. This is the fail-open sink: a failed privilege drop is recorded as successful (security-state misrepresentation), so the process continues with retained elevated credentials while appearing unprivileged.

assumptions: current_user.uid and current_user.gid have no assignment in this code; they are internal identity values assumed to be set by the surrounding program, and no attacker-controlled content enters this function directly.
Whether EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE is defined at build time is outside the given code; the analysis covers both branches, and the defect exists in both (only the EAGAIN subset differs).
limitations: The concrete runtime inducibility of a setuid/setgid failure depends on the environment (e.g., EAGAIN under a shared RLIMIT_NPROC exhausted by another local user, or kernel EPERM restrictions); the code itself names and special-cases the EAGAIN failure mode, but this code contains no attacker-data input that directly forces the failure.

No setgroups() call appears in this code, so supplementary group credentials are never cleared; however, the harmful consumer of that omission is not shown in the given code, so it is recorded here rather than as evidence.
Consequences for downstream consumers of current_user (e.g., trusting scripts after the recorded drop) are inferred from the function's evident purpose, not from code shown here.

The single fully-instantiated trigger-level defect (case 1 stores index 0x01 without colormap validation while image->colors may be 1 when number_colors==1 at 1 bpp, with no fix form present in case 1) writes only in-bounds here; its sole consumer is the not-shown SyncImage callee, so the impact chain is not instantiated. Integer-wrap candidates are unreachable on the declared 64-bit-oriented widths (maximum bytes_per_line*rows < 2^64) and are caught by the quoted length/8 file-size check and the NULL-checked allocation.

assumptions: Standard ImageMagick core semantics assumed for not-shown helpers: ReadBlob returns bytes read and its count is authoritative; ReadBlobLSBLong/Short/SignedLong read little-endian values; SeekBlob returns -1 on failure (checked at every call site here); GetBlobSize returns the blob length; AcquireQuantumMemory/AcquireVirtualMemory return NULL on failure (NULL checked at every call site in this code); SetImageExtent enforces resource limits (return checked); ThrowReaderException destroys the image and returns NULL; IsValidColormapIndex sanitizes its out-parameter on failure (the bounds-checked accessor used in cases 4 and 8).
The coder is invoked on file content; all header fields, colormap bytes, and raster bytes are treated as attacker-data per discipline 3.
limitations: Case-1 colormap index domain gap: index=(IndexPacket)(((*p) & (0x80 >> bit)) != 0 ? 0x01 : 0x00) can store index 1 while image->colors can be 1 (number_colors==1 passes the quoted check number_colors > (1U << bits_per_pixel)); unlike cases 4/8, case 1 never calls IsValidColormapIndex, and no fix form (bounds check, clamp, mask, checked accessor, error arm) exists in case 1. The trigger is fully instantiated with attacker-controlled values, but the out-of-domain value is written only in-bounds here; its consumer is the not-shown SyncImage callee, so the impact could not be instantiated in this code.

Integer-wrap candidates (columns*bits_per_pixel, bytes_per_line*rows, packet_size*colors) cannot overflow on the code's 64-bit-oriented size_t/ssize_t widths (maximum product (2^33-4)*2^31 < 2^64); wrap is only possible on 32-bit targets, which is speculative per STEP 4(c).
The bmp_info.file_size vs GetBlobSize mismatch path only records an exception and continues, but file_size is never used for any allocation or copy length in this code, so no security effect.

After a short 2-byte read the do-while condition IsBMP(magick,2) may inspect one stale (initialized) magic byte, allowing one extra loop iteration, which fails closed at the next iteration's quoted if (count != 2) ThrowReaderException(CorruptImageError,ImproperImageHeader) — fail-safe, no security effect.

No leak of pixel_info was found: every ThrowReaderException reachable after the pixel allocation (case 16, case 32, default arm, ReadBlob short count, DecodeImage failure) is preceded by the quoted pixel_info=RelinquishVirtualMemory(pixel_info);.

verdict.summary: In the second loop of do_arg_all, the index i is bounded only by the stale snapshot opened_len (= ARGCOUNT at entry, line 43) after the clamp at lines 178-179, and AARGLIST(alist)[i] at line 252 is indexed with no check against the live alist->al_ga.ga_len. Autocommands fired by do_ecmd/win_split/win_close/autowrite can shrink the argument list mid-loop (the code itself acknowledges this at lines 48-50 and 176-177, and guards the identical access with 'i < alist->al_ga.ga_len' at line 84 in the first loop only). A shrunken arglist makes subsequent iterations read argentry_T entries out of bounds and dereference stale ae_fnum/ae_fname fields, an out-of-bounds read with disclosure and crash potential.

evidence.snippet:
(void)do_ecmd(0, alist_name(&AARGLIST(alist)[i]), NULL, NULL,
		      ECMD_ONE,
		      ((buf_hide(curwin->w_buffer)
			   || bufIsChanged(curwin->w_buffer)) ? ECMD_HIDE : 0)
						       + ECMD_OLDBUF, curwin);
evidence.reason: Unguarded out-of-bounds read: i runs 0..count-1 with count clamped to the entry-time snapshot opened_len, but the live argument list can be shrunk below i+1 by autocommands fired by do_ecmd itself (previous iteration) or win_split. No 'i < alist->al_ga.ga_len' check exists anywhere in this loop (the only one is at line 84, first loop). alist_name dereferences the out-of-bounds/stale ae_fnum/ae_fname fields and passes the result to do_ecmd. Trigger: :all with N args and a BufEnter autocmd running :argdelete makes iteration i>=new ga_len read past the growarray.

Origin of the faulty bound: the comment admits ARGCOUNT changes during this phase, yet count is clamped to opened_len (the stale snapshot taken at line 43 'opened_len = ARGCOUNT;'), never to the live alist->al_ga.ga_len. This clamp protects opened[] but not the AARGLIST(alist)[i] access at line 252, producing the stale-index defect.

assumptions: AARGLIST(alist) indexes the alist growarray entries and ARGCOUNT is the current alist length (Vim macro semantics).

do_ecmd, win_split, win_close, and autowrite can trigger autocommands that mutate the argument list (Vim semantics; corroborated by this code's own comments at lines 48-50, 132, 142, 157, and 176-177 and by the revalidation calls win_valid at lines 143 and 158).
limitations: Integer overflow of opened_len in alloc_clear requires billions of argument-list entries; not instantiated.
No out-of-bounds write to opened[] was found: writes at line 100 are covered by the loop bound at line 82 plus the ga_len check at line 84, and reads at line 200 by the clamp at lines 178-179.
The w_arg_idx sentinel 'new_curwin->w_arg_idx = opened_len' (line 104) is deliberate bookkeeping and never equals a valid loop-2 index (i < count <= opened_len); no memory-safety effect.
Autocommand-induced window/tab removal is revalidated with win_valid (lines 143, 158) and valid_tabpage (lines 170, 278, 284); no use-after-free path found for window pointers.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability instantiated in this code. The historical TALOS-CAN-0063 buffer overrun at the bv[len]/bv[len+1] appends is patched here: the copy is capped by the quoted source limit MAXVALLEN and the destination size is reduced by one (atoascii(value, MAXVALLEN, bv, sizeof(bv) - 1)), keeping strlen(bv) at most 2*MAXVALLEN-2 so bv[len+1] can reach at most the final valid index bv[2*MAXVALLEN-1]. The OC sink uses snprintf(b, sizeof(b), ...) and the LP sink clamps with uval > 3, so all local buffer sinks are bounded. Remaining concerns (narr not bounded to lfparr[8] because decodearr receives no size parameter; NUL-termination of nextvar-produced strings; statustoa/atoascii contracts) depend on not-shown callees and are recorded as limitations, not findings.

assumptions: nextvar returns non-NULL, NUL-terminated name/value pointers into data and maintains length; its bounds behavior is not shown in this code.

atoascii copies at most min(srclen, dstlen-1) characters and NUL-terminates; the call site passes both the source cap (MAXVARLEN/MAXVALLEN) and the destination size, so the appends bv[len]/bv[len+1] stay in bounds under any copy semantics bounded by either parameter.
decodearr caps narr at 8 to match l_fp lfparr[8]; not shown, and the call decodearr(value, &narr, lfparr) passes no size parameter.
statustoa returns a valid NUL-terminated string for the %s use; output() consumes its string arguments without further bounds requirements.
fp is a valid FILE* provided by the caller; no precondition is documented or checked in this code.
limitations: decodearr(value, &narr, lfparr) receives lfparr (8 entries) with no size argument; if the not-shown callee can set narr > 8 on attacker data, outputarr(fp, name, narr, lfparr) would read out of bounds. The bound is unverifiable from the given code (UNSOURCED), so this is speculative and cannot confirm or drive a verdict.
strlen(value) in case RF and strlen(bv) after atoascii assume NUL termination produced by nextvar/atoascii (not shown); no non-terminated producer exists in this code.
The %s uses of name/value and statustoa(datatype, status) could dereference NULL only if nextvar/statustoa produce it; no such producer is visible in this code.
snprintf(b, sizeof(b), "%03lo", uval) in case OC truncates octal output of large uval to 11 digits; cosmetic display truncation only, no security-state misrepresentation.

If atoascii ignored both its srclen and dstlen parameters entirely, the bv appends could overflow; any such overflow would first occur inside the not-shown callee on in-domain arguments (buffer plus size), which is uncharacterizable from the given code.

verdict.summary: In the '{' (push image_info settings) handler of CLINoImageOperator, the node is pushed onto cli_wand->image_info_stack before CloneImageInfo is called; when CloneImageInfo returns NULL, the error path restores wand.image_info and frees the node with RelinquishMagickMemory but never unlinks it from cli_wand->image_info_stack. The stack head is left dangling, so any later '{' depth-count, '{' push, or '}' pop traverses and dereferences freed memory; concretely, a subsequent '}' pops the freed node and reassigns wand.image_info from the freed node's data, producing use and double-destruction of an already-destroyed ImageInfo (use-after-free/double-free).

evidence.reason: The node is made the head of cli_wand->image_info_stack at line 206 before the fallible CloneImageInfo call at line 207. The NULL-checked error arm restores wand.image_info and frees the node at line 212 but performs no 'cli_wand->image_info_stack = node->next;' unlink (the only writes to image_info_stack in the function are the push at 206 and the '}' pop at 254), so the stack head retains a pointer to freed memory. A later '}' operator (option content is attacker-data) then executes 'node = cli_wand->image_info_stack;', reads 'node->next' from freed memory, calls DestroyImageInfo on the current info, and reassigns 'cli_wand->wand.image_info = (ImageInfo *)node->data' from freed memory, yielding use-after-free and double-destruction of the restored ImageInfo.

assumptions: option, arg1n, arg2n are non-NULL where the unshown CLI option-table dispatch requires arguments; no documented non-NULL contract is quotable in the given code.
ExpandFilenames returns a fresh heap argv and duplicates input strings, matching the destroy-loop idiom; its internals are not shown.
DestroyString(NULL), DestroyImageList(NULL), RelinquishMagickMemory(NULL) and IsStringTrue(NULL) are benign (ubiquitous IM idiom, not shown).
cli_wand->process_flags and cli_wand->command->flags are initialized by not-shown CLI setup; their values are never assigned in this code.

Attacker-inducibility of the CloneImageInfo allocation failure (memory pressure while processing attacker-supplied images under resource limits) is assumed for severity; the dangling-store defect itself is fully quoted.
limitations: Memory leak (CWE-401): the 'set' handler's 'arg1=InterpretImageProperties(_image_info,_images,arg1n,_exception)' and the '+clone' handler's 'arg1=AcquireString("-1")' overwrite an arg1 previously allocated by the top percent-interpretation block without freeing it. The trigger precondition (interpretation flags enabled for this option) depends on cli_wand->process_flags / cli_wand->command->flags, which this code never assigns — UNSOURCED, so not confirmed.

'read' branch aliases the stack local via 'argv = (char **) &arg1;' and later frees argv[0] and the array; whether a previously percent-interpreted arg1 is duplicated or destroyed by ExpandFilenames is not characterizable from the given code, so no double-free could be instantiated.

NULL-deref candidates (IsSceneGeometry(NULL) for '-clone', LocaleCompare(arg1,"null:") in 'write', ParseCommandOption with NULL) are gated on the unquoted caller contract that one/two-argument options always receive arguments.
Log forging of arg1n/arg2n through CLILogEvent("- NoImage Operator: %s ...") is reachable only when cli_wand->wand.debug is set (UNSOURCED in this code) and CLILogEvent's sanitization is not shown.

The '{' allocation-failure UAF is the primary finding, but its trigger requires the small CloneImageInfo allocation to fail; under the strict rule that purely environmental allocation failure is not attacker-inducible this would be a robustness issue rather than a vulnerability, and it is reported with reduced confidence for that reason.

verdict.summary: All attacker-data inputs in mobi_parse_huffdic are guarded on the single execution path: huff_rec_count is bounded above by 'huff_rec_count > HUFF_RECORD_MAXCNT' and below by 'huff_rec_count < 2' (preventing the 'count - 1' underflow and keeping allocation and loop bounds consistent); the record-lookup NULL sentinel is tested before the first curr dereference; the HUFF record size is checked against HUFF_RECORD_MINSIZE before mobi_parse_huff; the malloc result is NULL-checked before use; and each loop iteration re-checks curr != NULL before calling mobi_parse_cdic, with the index i always inside the allocated 'count - 1' entry domain. No unguarded sink was found.

assumptions: Pointers m (line 4) and huffcdic (line 30) are not NULL-checked in this code and no documented non-NULL contract is quotable from the given code; both are context handles rather than content-carrying values, and no statement in this code produces a NULL for them.

HUFF_RECORD_MAXCNT and HUFF_RECORD_MINSIZE are UNSOURCED constants never assigned in this code; the malloc/loop consistency argument holds for any value of HUFF_RECORD_MAXCNT because both the allocation (line 30) and the loop bound (line 37) use the same expression (huff_rec_count - 1); the MAXCNT check at line 10 exists on every path.
mobi_get_kf8offset, mobi_get_record_by_seqnumber, mobi_parse_huff, and mobi_parse_cdic are not shown; lookup/parse failure sentinels are treated as characterizable (return NULL / non-MOBI_SUCCESS).
The widths of *m->mh->huff_rec_index and *m->mh->huff_rec_count (header fields populated by the not-shown parser) are not shown in this code.
limitations: Speculative: a NULL m or NULL huffcdic would crash at 'm->mh' (line 4) or 'huffcdic->symbols = malloc(...)' (line 30); no producer of such NULLs exists in this code and no quoted contract covers them, so the trigger is not instantiated.

This code performs no minimum-size check on the CDIC records passed to mobi_parse_cdic (line 42), unlike the HUFF record (line 19); if the not-shown callee lacks its own curr->size validation, an out-of-bounds read could occur inside it. Per the callee boundary rule this code passes an in-domain argument (the record handle carrying its own size member, plus an index within the allocated domain), so the impact chain is not characterizable here.
Memory allocated at line 30 is not freed on the early-return error paths (lines 40, 45); this is a leak on a failure path, not a security impact.

verdict.summary: extract_archive_thread uses archive-supplied entry paths and link targets (archive_entry_pathname, archive_entry_hardlink, archive_entry_symlink) to construct extraction targets with no validation anywhere in this code that the resolved path stays within extract_data->destination. g_file_get_child resolves '..' components, so a malicious archive entry such as '../../.config/autostart/evil.desktop' causes g_file_make_directory_with_parents, g_file_replace (which then writes attacker-controlled data blocks), link(), and g_file_make_symbolic_link to create or overwrite files, directories, and links outside the extraction directory. The skip/overwrite block only governs pre-existing files and does not check path location, and the raw symlink/hardlink targets are passed to their sinks with no checks at all.

evidence.snippet:
fullpath = (*pathname == '/') ? g_strdup (pathname) : g_strconcat ("/", pathname, NULL);
		file = g_file_get_child (extract_data->destination, _g_path_get_relative_basename (fullpath, extract_data->base_dir, extract_data->junk_paths));
evidence.reason: Origin and construction of the attacker-controlled extraction path. pathname comes straight from the parsed archive (line 37, archive_entry_pathname); the only processing before g_file_get_child is leading-'/' normalization, which is not validation. g_file_get_child resolves '..' components, so an entry pathname containing '../' escapes extract_data->destination. No statement in this code checks that the child path is contained in destination (verified by exhaustive search in STEP 5). The skip/overwrite block at lines 48-94 is not a guard: it only skips pre-existing files when overwrite is unset, and non-existent out-of-destination targets proceed via the G_IO_ERROR_NOT_FOUND branch (lines 87-93).

evidence.snippet:
case AE_IFREG:
				ostream = (GOutputStream *) g_file_replace (file, NULL, FALSE, G_FILE_CREATE_REPLACE_DESTINATION, cancellable, &load_data->error);
evidence.reason: Write sink for the traversal primitive: g_file_replace creates/truncates the file at the attacker-influenced path built at line 44, and the loop at lines 192-195 (archive_read_data_block / g_output_stream_write) writes attacker-controlled archive content to it. Trigger fully instantiated: entry '../../.config/autostart/x.desktop' with type AE_IFREG reaches this case with load_data->error == NULL (checked at lines 123/174), creating a file outside the extraction directory; the parent directory is first created outside destination by g_file_make_directory_with_parents at line 106.

Hard-link facet of the same defect: the archive-supplied hardlink target (archive_entry_hardlink, line 126) is normalized only for a leading '/' and passed unvalidated through g_file_get_child to link(2). The only NULL guards here (oldname/newname) protect against missing paths, not against traversal or absolute targets; link(2) then creates a hard link whose source path is attacker-derived, with no containment check on any path in this code.

evidence.snippet:
case AE_IFLNK:
				if (! g_file_make_symbolic_link (file, archive_entry_symlink (entry), cancellable, &local_error)) {
evidence.reason: The symlink target is passed completely raw: archive_entry_symlink(entry) goes directly into g_file_make_symbolic_link with no helper, no normalization, and no check anywhere in this code, so a malicious archive creates a symbolic link inside the destination pointing to any absolute path (e.g. /home/victim/.bashrc). Subsequent entries in the same loop then resolve paths through it: g_file_query_info uses G_FILE_QUERY_INFO_NONE (line 53, follows links), and g_file_replace's temp-file directory resolution at line 188 traverses intermediate symlink components, letting the archive write outside the extraction directory (CWE-59).

assumptions: extract_data fields (destination, base_dir, junk_paths, overwrite, skip_older, file_list, n_files_to_extract) and load_data fields (archive, error) are never assigned in this code; they are configured by code not shown (UNSOURCED). The code's own logic (parent-directory creation at lines 100-117 and base_dir-relative naming) is written for the structure-preserving mode, which is the operative configuration for the traversal trigger.

extract_data_get_extraction_requested is not shown; for whole-archive extraction the attacker's entries are treated as requested (the code's own decrement guard at lines 78/226 uses extract_data->file_list == NULL as the extract-all indicator).

_g_path_get_relative_basename is not shown and per GUARD ANCHORING no sanitization is credited to it. For the extractor to function at all it must pass sub-paths through; whether it also strips '..' cannot be quoted from this code, so this code is judged as the last line of defense and contains no traversal check of its own (verified in STEP 5).

GIO semantics relied upon as characterizable callees: g_file_get_child resolves relative names including '..'; g_file_make_symbolic_link creates a link with the given target; g_file_replace with G_FILE_CREATE_REPLACE_DESTINATION does not follow the final symlink component but temp-file creation and rename traverse intermediate components.
limitations: Candidate C5 (NULL dereference of pathname at line 43, '*pathname == '/'', if archive_entry_pathname returns NULL) is speculative: no producer of an archive entry with an unset pathname is instantiated by this code.
g_object_unref (info) at line 89 executes with info == NULL (it is in the info == NULL branch) — a GLib critical warning only, no security effect.
Underflow of extract_data->n_files_to_extract (decremented at lines 78 and 226, never assigned here) cannot be instantiated to a harmful value since its initial value is unsourced.

The skip/overwrite block (lines 48-94) mitigates overwriting pre-existing files only when overwrite is unset; it is not a traversal guard and does not protect non-existent paths outside the destination.
The cancelled-loop break at line 34-35 with r == ARCHIVE_OK causes a misleading FR_ERROR_COMMAND_ERROR to be reported at line 232; cosmetic error-state misreporting only.

verdict.summary: In cookedprint(), after atoascii(value, MAXVALLEN, bv, sizeof(bv)) fills the stack buffer bv[2*MAXVALLEN], the raw-output fallback appends two bytes with no bound check: len = strlen(bv); bv[len] = output_raw; bv[len+1] = '\0'. When the attacker-controlled variable value expands to exactly the destination capacity (len = sizeof(bv)-1, the exactly-at-limit boundary reachable because atoascii's destination bound is sizeof(bv)), the terminating write bv[len+1] lands one byte past the end of bv, an out-of-bounds stack write of a NUL byte. name/value derive fully from the parsed remote payload via nextvar(), and no path in this code compares len against sizeof(bv).

evidence.reason: Root cause: the append of output_raw plus a terminator writes at indices len and len+1 with no bound on len anywhere in the function. atoascii is passed sizeof(bv) as the destination bound, so strlen(bv) can reach the exactly-at-limit value 2*MAXVALLEN-1; then bv[len] overwrites the last valid byte and bv[len+1] writes one byte past the stack array bv[2*MAXVALLEN] (instantiated trigger: unknown variable name reaching the default arm sets output_raw='?', value long/escaping enough to fill bv, len = sizeof(bv)-1). No comparison of len with sizeof(bv), clamp, mask, resized buffer, or error arm exists on any path (verified in STEP 5).

evidence.snippet: while (nextvar(&length, &data, &name, &value)) {
evidence.reason: Taint origin: name and value are produced by parsing the attacker-controlled payload (data/length parameters) each iteration; their content and length are fully attacker-chosen and flow into atoascii(value, ...) at line 119 and thence to the unbounded append at lines 121-123.

assumptions: atoascii, nextvar, varfmt, decodets, decodenetnum, decodeuint, decodearr, output, statustoa and the constants MAXVARLEN/MAXVALLEN are not shown; it is assumed atoascii NUL-terminates its output within the dstlen it is given (sizeof(bv)) and can fill the destination to capacity dstlen-1, which is the at-limit case the caller must handle.
nextvar's success contract (non-NULL, NUL-terminated name/value) is not quotable from this code.
Deployment context (e.g., ntpq querying a possibly hostile server) is inferred, not quoted; the verdict rests on the function consuming externally parsed name/value content at its own entry point.
limitations: decodearr(value, &narr, lfparr) writes into the fixed lfparr[8] with no visible cap on narr in this code; if the not-shown decodearr ignores the 8-element capacity the overflow occurs inside the callee, which cannot be characterized here — precondition named: decodearr's internal bound.
Potential NULL name/value from nextvar reaching fprintf's %s at line 111 has no producer in this code and nextvar's success contract is unquotable; not instantiated.
The off-by-one's exploitability beyond frame corruption is limited (a single NUL byte one past a 1024-byte stack buffer); the memory-safety violation itself is the confirmed impact.

verdict.summary: atusb_disconnect frees the driver object's owner with ieee802154_free_hw(atusb->hw) at line 17, then dereferences atusb->usb_dev at line 20 in usb_put_dev(atusb->usb_dev), reading the pointer from freed memory (use-after-free). The stale value is passed to usb_put_dev/put_device, a refcount decrement through a pointer derived from freed memory, enabling memory corruption if the slab slot is reallocated in the window between the free and the read.

evidence.reason: Use-after-free: ieee802154_free_hw(atusb->hw) frees the ieee802154_hw allocation including the driver-private area that holds the atusb object (the teardown contains no other free that owns atusb), and the very next atusb dereference, usb_put_dev(atusb->usb_dev), loads atusb->usb_dev from that freed memory on every invocation (straight-line code, no guard, no local copy, no reordering anywhere in the function). The loaded stale value feeds a refcount decrement (put_device), a memory-corruption primitive.

assumptions: atusb_disconnect is registered as the usb_driver disconnect handler; the registration statement is not shown.

usb_get_intfdata(interface) returns the probe-allocated atusb object; probe and its usb_set_intfdata(interface, atusb) call are not shown, so atusb's non-NULL-ness rests on the driver-model contract that disconnect runs once per successful probe.

atusb is the driver-private area of atusb->hw (hw->priv), allocated by ieee802154_alloc_hw(sizeof(struct atusb), ...) in the not-shown probe; ieee802154_free_hw's documented framework semantics free that allocation including the private area, so the free at line 17 destroys atusb.
ieee802154_free_hw is a framework function whose documented semantics (freeing the hw together with its private data) are relied on per the callee-boundary rule.
limitations: NULL-deref candidate: atusb from usb_get_intfdata(interface) is dereferenced at line 5 (dev_dbg(&atusb->usb_dev->dev, ...)) with no NULL check; a NULL would require the USB core to call disconnect without a successful probe or a second time after this code's own usb_set_intfdata(interface, NULL) at line 19. The invocation count is decided by not-shown USB core code, so the trigger is speculative and does not affect the verdict.
No attacker-content-carrying inputs exist in this function; the confirmed use-after-free is a consequence of the teardown ordering itself, triggered by device unbind rather than device-supplied data.

verdict.summary: mobi_parse_huffdic validates every attacker-derived value it consumes: header pointer NULLs are checked, huff_rec_count is clamped to HUFF_RECORD_MAXCNT and to >= 2 before the (count-1)-element symbols allocation (matching the loop's index range 0..count-2 exactly), the record lookup's NULL sentinel, the HUFF record minimum size, the malloc failure sentinel, and a per-iteration NULL check on the record chain are all tested before first use on every path, and the final index_count/index_read comparison is fail-closed. The remaining issues (error-path retention of the allocated huffcdic->symbols array with partially uninitialized entries, possible 32-bit allocation-size overflow for extreme MAXCNT values, and any defects inside the unshown mobi_parse_huff/mobi_parse_cdic) have impact chains that depend on unshown caller cleanup or callee behavior and are recorded as limitations, not confirmed vulnerabilities.

assumptions: HUFF_RECORD_MAXCNT and HUFF_RECORD_MINSIZE are compile-time constants whose numeric values are not shown; the quoted comparisons were accepted as effective clamps under the assumption that MAXCNT is far below the size_t wrap scale of the malloc product (count-1)*sizeof(pointer).

mobi_get_kf8offset and mobi_get_record_by_seqnumber are not shown; the latter was treated as a characterizable lookup that returns NULL on a miss, which the code checks with 'if (curr == NULL || huff_rec_count < 2)'.

Deployment context (library used to parse untrusted MOBI files) is inferred from the function's role, not quotable from the code; per the rules it was used only to classify inputs as attacker-data, never to demote a candidate.
limitations: Memory retention on error paths: after 'huffcdic->symbols = malloc((huff_rec_count - 1) * sizeof(*huffcdic->symbols))' succeeds, the returns inside the CDIC loop ('CDIC record not found', 'CDIC parsing failed') and the final index-count mismatch leave the allocation unfreed and entries past the failing index uninitialized. The impact (actual leak or caller iterating/freeing uninitialized symbols entries) depends on the caller's cleanup routine, which is not shown, so it is not instantiated as a vulnerability in this code.

The malloc size expression (huff_rec_count - 1) * sizeof(*huffcdic->symbols) could wrap only if HUFF_RECORD_MAXCNT exceeded ~2^29 on a 32-bit target with 32-bit size_t; the constant's value is unquotable and the code uses size_t, so this overflow is speculative (STEP 4 branch c).

The final comparison 'huffcdic->index_count != huffcdic->index_read' reads fields assigned only by the unshown callees mobi_parse_huff/mobi_parse_cdic; if a caller passed an unzeroed struct and the callees did not initialize them, an uninitialized comparison could occur, but no producer is visible in this code and the worst direct effect is a spurious success/error, not corruption.

verdict.summary: In em28xx_usb_probe, the error path taken when the secondary device init fails (em28xx_init_dev(dev->dev_next, ...) returns nonzero) jumps to err_free, which frees only dev->alt_max_pkt_size_isoc and dev and clears only the primary slot bit (clear_bit(nr, em28xx_devused)). When this em28xx_init_dev call on the attacker-controlled secondary device returns nonzero, control jumps to err_free with dev_next still allocated and its em28xx_devused slot bit still set.

verdict.summary: pcl_status_read frees pcs->status.buffer whenever read_pos equals write_pos, but never clears the pointer and does not require that the call consumed any data. verdict.summary: The extractor creates symlinks and hardlinks with fully attacker-controlled targets (`archive_entry_symlink (entry)`, `archive_entry_hardlink (entry)`) and performs no link-resolution defense: parent directories are accepted when `g_file_query_exists (parent, cancellable)` succeeds (which an attacker-planted symlink satisfies), and regular files are then written with `g_file_replace` plus attacker bytes from `archive_read_data_block`. A malicious archive that first extracts a symlink (e.g., `dir -> /etc/cron.d`) and then a regular file `dir/pwn` causes an arbitrary-content, attacker-attribute file write outside the extraction root (CWE-59 root cause, CWE-22 effect). Additionally, the `g_file_query_info` error path dereferences NULL via `g_object_unref (info)` when `info == NULL` (CWE-476).

				if (! g_file_make_symbolic_link (file, archive_entry_symlink (entry), cancellable, &local_error)) {
evidence.reason: The symlink target is taken verbatim from the attacker-controlled archive header and passed to g_file_make_symbolic_link with no validation that the target lies inside the extraction destination; no statement in this code constrains archive_entry_symlink(entry).

Parent-directory creation is skipped when g_file_query_exists succeeds; an attacker-created symlink extracted by an earlier archive entry satisfies this check, so later g_file_replace writes traverse the attacker's link outside the destination. Together with the AE_IFLNK sink this instantiates the arbitrary-file-write trigger: entry 1 symlink dir -> /etc/cron.d, entry 2 regular file dir/pwn is written to /etc/cron.d/pwn with attacker content from archive_read_data_block/g_output_stream_write.

On the g_file_query_info failure path info is NULL, and g_object_unref(info) dereferences it whenever the error is anything other than G_IO_ERROR_NOT_FOUND (e.g., a permission error on an attacker-chosen path), producing a NULL-pointer crash (CWE-476).

`_g_path_get_relative_basename_safe`, `extract_data_get_extraction_requested`, and `_g_file_set_attributes_from_entry` are not shown; their behavior is treated as uncharacterizable where relied upon as guards.
limitations: String-level path traversal through `pathname`: the code passes relative_path to g_file_get_child, which characterizably rejects basenames containing '/' or '.'/'..', so the pure CWE-22 string-traversal chain is contained at that boundary; the realized traversal is the filesystem-level symlink chain reported as primary.
extract_data->n_files_to_extract is decremented on several paths but its initialization is not in this code (UNSOURCED); possible mis-counting and premature loop exit could not be instantiated.
extract_data->destination, base_dir, junk_paths, skip_older, overwrite, file_list are set outside this code (UNSOURCED) and were used neither as triggers nor as guards.

The hardlink branch `r = link (oldname, newname);` with attacker-supplied linkname also allows linking an arbitrary readable file into the destination tree which is then treated as AE_IFREG and overwritten with archive data; it shares the same root cause as the primary finding and is not counted as a separate vulnerability.

verdict.summary: disable_priv_mode fails open: when the credential-changing call fails, the code only logs — a conditional EAGAIN exit exists solely for the uid call and only when EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE is compiled, while the setgid failure branch has no exit at all — then falls through and unconditionally executes current_user.euid = current_user.uid and current_user.egid = current_user.gid, recording the privileges-dropped state on an unverified error path (CWE-451) and returning normally while the process retains its elevated credentials.

  current_user.egid = current_user.gid;
evidence.reason: Security-state misrepresentation (CWE-451): these assignments execute unconditionally, including on the set*id failure paths. Simulated trigger: setresuid returns -1 (e.g., EAGAIN after the target user's process limit is exhausted), line 12 prints a diagnostic, the only exit (lines 14-15) is compiled out or does not match the errno, control falls through line 17 and reaches line 25, which records current_user.euid as equal to uid while the real effective uid is unchanged and still elevated — presenting the privileges-dropped state on an unverified error path. No success flag, checked accessor, or abort guards this write on any path.

Fail-open origin of the defect: the quoted failure arm of the privilege drop handles the error only with a diagnostic and a conditional EAGAIN exit that (a) is compiled only when EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE is defined and (b) matches only errno EAGAIN. For every other errno — and for every setgid failure at lines 18-23, whose branch has no exit at all — execution falls through line 17, the process keeps its elevated credentials, and the function returns normally, after which lines 25-26 record the drop as successful.

assumptions: current_user.uid/gid/euid/egid entry values are assigned outside this code (the struct is initialized elsewhere); they are assumed to reflect actual process credentials with euid != uid when privilege mode is on, as implied by the quoted function name disable_priv_mode and the quoted error message distinguishing uid from effective uid.
The process is assumed to potentially run in privileged (setuid) mode; this deployment context cannot be quoted from the given code and per the framework may never be used to demote the candidate.

Compile-time configuration (HAVE_DECL_SETRESUID/RESGID, EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE) is unknown; both arms are in the given code and a continuing failure path exists in every configuration (non-EAGAIN errnos, or any errno when EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE is undefined; the gid branch always continues).

Attacker inducibility of setresuid/setgid failure (classically by exhausting the target uid's RLIMIT_NPROC to force EAGAIN) is OS behavior outside the given code; the dedicated EAGAIN exit at lines 14-15 indicates the code's authors treated that failure as real and attack-relevant.
limitations: The trigger requires the process to actually hold elevated credentials at entry (euid != uid); current_user fields have no assignment in this code before their first read, so this precondition is documented only by the function's name and error message, not by a quoted statement.
