pfk->registered is an int bitmap field (struct pfkey_sock is not shown); bits 1..8 set by this function are within its width.
The not-shown dispatcher supplies a non-NULL hdr pointing into a valid received skb and a valid sk; the socket-level serialization of handler invocations is likewise not shown.

compose_sadb_supported allocates and returns an skb or NULL, and pfkey_broadcast consumes and frees the passed skb while sending to sockets matching its flags (standard kernel callee semantics, not shown).
limitations: Shift-UB candidate at lines 10/12/20 (1 << satype): triggering would require SADB_SATYPE_MAX >= 31 or a signed satype type, both unsourced in the given code; with the standard value 8 the maximum shift is 8 (1<<8 = 256, representable). Even under a hypothetically large constant, the direct consequence is bit manipulation of the int 'registered' field, not memory corruption, so this candidate is speculative and not counted.

Behavior of compose_sadb_supported and pfkey_broadcast internals is not shown; no defect within them is attributed to this code, and all arguments passed at their call sites are in-domain (satype bounded to 0..8 by line 6, non-NULL skb after lines 18-23).

Which parties may open AF_KEY sockets and send SADB_REGISTER is a deployment/access-control question not answerable from the given code; it does not create a defect here because no sink in this code misbehaves on any reachable input value.

verdict.summary: In smtp_command_parse_parameters, the UTF-8 decoder is called as uni_utf8_get_char_n(p, (size_t)(p - parser->end), &ch). Because the loop guard 'while (p < parser->end)' guarantees p < end, the pointer difference p - parser->end is always negative, and the cast to size_t wraps it to a huge value (SIZE_MAX-scale). The decoder therefore believes an unbounded number of bytes are readable at p: its truncation check is defeated and it reads bytes past parser->end whenever the buffer's final bytes hold a truncated UTF-8 sequence (attacker-controlled SMTP command content). The out-of-bounds bytes can further advance p past end (p += nch), after which i_strdup_until(parser->cur, mp) copies out-of-bounds heap bytes into the parsed command parameters and parser->cur is set past end, corrupting parser state. Root cause: signed pointer-difference underflow wrapped by a (size_t) cast (the correct expression is parser->end - p); consequence: out-of-bounds read with disclosure potential.

evidence.snippet:
nch = uni_utf8_get_char_n(p, (size_t)(p - parser->end),
					  &ch);
evidence.reason: Defective sink. The loop guard at line 13 ('while (p < parser->end)') ensures p < parser->end, so 'p - parser->end' is a negative ptrdiff_t on every iteration; casting it to size_t (line 19) wraps it to a huge value (e.g. (size_t)-1 == SIZE_MAX when p == end-1). uni_utf8_get_char_n uses this size as its read bound, so its truncation check is defeated and it reads bytes past parser->end when the attacker places a truncated UTF-8 lead byte in the last bytes of the command buffer. No clamp, mask, range check, or corrected expression exists on any path (verified in STEP 5); the nch<0/nch==0 checks at lines 22/24 run only after the out-of-bounds read has already occurred inside this call.

evidence.snippet:
parser->state.cmd_params = i_strdup_until(parser->cur, mp);
	parser->cur = p;
evidence.reason: Impact chain, fully simulated: when the decoder consumed a UTF-8 sequence straddling parser->end (p = end-1, *p = 0xC2, valid OOB continuation byte at end), line 33 sets p = end+1; the early return at line 44 is bypassed (p != end, nch != 0); mp = p (line 54) and the trim at line 56 reads the OOB byte; then i_strdup_until(parser->cur, mp) duplicates the buffer INCLUDING the out-of-bounds byte at parser->end into the parsed command parameters (heap disclosure into data later treated as the command's parameter string), and parser->cur = p moves the cursor past end, corrupting parser state for subsequent parsing.

assumptions: parser->cur and parser->end delimit the currently valid input region [cur, end) of the network-received SMTP command line; the code itself treats end as the exclusive bound (line 13), so reads at or past end are out-of-bounds relative to the code's own domain.

uni_utf8_get_char_n(buf, size, &chr) semantics per the CALLEE BOUNDARY RULE: decodes one UTF-8 sequence reading at most the sequence length bytes, uses 'size' as the readable bound, returns 0 when the sequence is truncated by size, -1 for invalid input, and the consumed byte count on success.

parser->auth_response is session state set by earlier parsing stages (not assigned in this code); for ordinary SMTP commands it is 0, selecting the defective branch at lines 18-21. Even on the auth path the defect is not exercised, but every non-AUTH command reaches it.
Exact heap contents past parser->end are not attacker-controlled; the disclosure amount is bounded by the maximum UTF-8 sequence length (up to ~5-6 bytes) and by how far p advances past end.
limitations: The initial value of parser->state.poff is not assigned anywhere in this code (only written at line 43); if it could exceed end - cur, the loop would be skipped and i_strdup_until could copy from out of range. This precondition is UNSOURCED and does not affect the verdict; the primary trigger only requires ordinary command content ending in a truncated UTF-8 lead byte.

parser->limits.max_parameters_size / max_auth_size are configuration values not assigned in this code; max_size == 0 would disable the line 35 length check, but this is not needed for the out-of-bounds read at line 19, which executes before it in execution order.

What downstream stages do with the corrupted parser->cur and the cmd_params string containing an out-of-bounds byte (echoing, logging, further parsing) is not shown; the confirmed impact is the out-of-bounds read itself plus the OOB byte copied into cmd_params by the quoted i_strdup_until statement, per the CALLEE BOUNDARY RULE.

verdict.summary: All memory-access sinks in open_table() are guarded by quotable checks in execution order: the memcmp in the locked-tables loop is protected by an exact length-equality check on the same variable used as the copy length; the share pointer is NULL-checked before every dereference; the MDL ticket is NULL-checked on the acquiring path; db.str is NULL-checked before use. The only unguarded paths are (1) mdl_ticket= table_list->mdl_request.ticket with no NULL check on the MYSQL_OPEN_HAS_MDL_LOCK branch, and (2) tdc_release_share(share) at err_lock reachable from the locked-tables 'goto reset' path where share is never assigned; both triggers require preconditions this code cannot instantiate from attacker input (a caller violating the documented 'ticket acquired by the caller' contract, or vcol_fix_expr failing only through allocation failure), so neither is a confirmed vulnerability in this code.

assumptions: tdc_acquire_share() initializes the out-parameter *table on every return path where it returns a non-NULL share; its behavior is not shown in this code.
open_table_from_share() leaves table->file non-NULL when it returns success (error == 0); asserted only via DBUG_ASSERT, which is compiled out in release builds.
Callers passing MYSQL_OPEN_HAS_MDL_LOCK hold a valid mdl_request.ticket, per the in-code comment 'Grab reference to the MDL lock ticket that was acquired by the caller.'
thd->locked_tables_mode, thd->open_tables list contents, and share->tdc->flushed are maintained correctly by code not shown here.
limitations: NULL dereference candidate: on the MYSQL_OPEN_HAS_MDL_LOCK branch, mdl_ticket is taken from table_list->mdl_request.ticket with no NULL check and later dereferenced at mdl_ticket->get_deadlock_weight() and stored via table->mdl_ticket= mdl_ticket. Trigger requires an internal caller to violate the documented contract (ticket already acquired); no attacker-input value in this code produces a NULL ticket, so it is speculative.

Uninitialized-pointer candidate: when the locked-tables block finds best_table it executes 'goto reset' before 'share' is ever assigned; if table->vcol_fix_expr(thd) then fails, control reaches err_lock: tdc_release_share(share) with an uninitialized stack pointer. The failing precondition (vcol_fix_expr nonzero on an already-open table) is producible in this code's flow only through allocation failure, which an attacker cannot induce; hence speculative, though the missing guard (share= NULL initialization or a conditional release) is genuinely absent.

Stale-pointer candidate: after 'if (table) tc_release_table(table);' the code 'goto retry_share' without resetting table; if tdc_acquire_share did not write *table on some path, a released TABLE would be reused. tdc_acquire_share is not shown and not characterizable under the callee boundary rule, so this link is unproven.

verdict.summary: The guest-controlled TX fragment length reaching the DMA copy into s->tx_packet is bounded by a quoted, fail-closed check ('tx_desc_get_length(desc) > gem_get_max_buf_len(s, true) - (p - s->tx_packet)' with a break error arm), which sits on every path before the sink and rejects all boundary cases (zero length, exactly-full buffer, exactly-fitting fragment, negative remaining-space), preserving the invariant p - s->tx_packet <= max_buf_len across iterations. Residual memory-safety candidates (descriptor word-count overflow of the fixed desc[] array, queue-index overflow via num_priority_queues, and the allocation-size relationship of gem_get_max_buf_len to s->tx_packet) each depend on helper returns or state fields with no assignment in this code and could not be instantiated, so they are recorded as limitations rather than findings.

assumptions: gem_get_max_buf_len(s, true) is assumed to return the actual capacity of s->tx_packet; the allocation of s->tx_packet is not shown in this code, so this relationship cannot be verified and the quoted bounds check is only as strong as it.
gem_get_desc_len(s, false) is assumed to return at most DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS; neither the helper body nor the value of DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS appears in the given code.
s->num_priority_queues is assumed not to exceed the declared extents of s->tx_desc_addr[] and any queue-indexed arrays used by helpers; the field has no assignment or clamp in this code.
address_space_read is assumed to fully initialize its destination buffer (QEMU semantics), so desc[] is never read uninitialized on any path including failed/unmapped DMA reads.
The guest cannot concurrently rewrite s->regs (e.g., GEM_DMACFG) during this single-threaded callback, so the guard's bound expression is stable across the descriptor loop.
limitations: Stack overflow candidate: 'address_space_read(&s->dma_as, packet_desc_addr, MEMTXATTRS_UNSPECIFIED, desc, sizeof(uint32_t) * gem_get_desc_len(s, false))' writes gem_get_desc_len(s,false) words into the fixed array 'uint32_t desc[DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS]'; guest-writable GEM_DMACFG feeds the helper, but no statement in this code bounds the word count and the helper's range and DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS's value are not shown — trigger precondition UNSOURCED, not instantiated.

Heap overflow candidate at 'address_space_read(&s->dma_as, tx_desc_get_buffer(s, desc), MEMTXATTRS_UNSPECIFIED, p, tx_desc_get_length(desc))' if gem_get_max_buf_len(s, true) exceeds the allocated size of s->tx_packet; the allocation is not in this code, so the harmful bound cannot be instantiated — the in-code guard bounds each copy to gem_get_max_buf_len(s, true) and fails closed (break) at the offset == max_buf_len boundary and on any negative remaining-space value.

Queue-index candidate: 's->tx_desc_addr[q] = ...' and 'gem_set_isr(s, q, ...)' index with q from 'for (q = s->num_priority_queues - 1; q >= 0; q--)'; the lower bound is guarded but num_priority_queues and the array extents are UNSOURCED in this code.

Amplification/infinite-loop candidate in 'while (tx_desc_get_used(desc) == 0)' rejected: every iteration either consumes buffer space capped by the quoted too-large check (which breaks) or breaks earlier, and the last-descriptor arm writes the used bit back to guest memory ('tx_desc_set_used(desc_first); address_space_write(...)') while advancing packet_desc_addr, so no concrete infinite-iteration input could be constructed and no attacker race window exists between two ordered operations.

The hwaddr-to-narrower-store 's->tx_desc_addr[q] = packet_desc_addr + 4 * gem_get_desc_len(s, false)' and the full sizeof(desc_first) write-back over a possibly 2-word descriptor region are guest-visible DMA behaviors, not host memory-safety defects.

verdict.summary: cdf_read_property_info as given is the hardened form of the historically exploitable file(1) CDF property parser. Every sink performed directly in this code is covered by a quoted guard verified in execution order: the offs bound (`offs > UINT32_MAX / 4`), section-length checks (`sh.sh_len > CDF_SHLEN_LIMIT`, three `cdf_check_stream_offset` calls plus `p >= e`), the allocation/loop-bound match (`cdf_grow_info(..., sh.sh_properties)` paired with `i < sh.sh_properties` in both loops, with both `inp == NULL` failure tests before use), the type/vector length checks (`left < sizeof(uint32_t)` and `left < sizeof(uint32_t)*2`, `nelements == 0`), and the string-buffer bounds (`o4 + sizeof(uint32_t) > left` and `o4 + l > left` before `CDF_GETUINT32(q, slen)` and before storing `s_buf = &q[o4]` with `s_len = l`). Simulated triggers with boundary values (l = left - o4, l = 0xFFFFFFFF, sh_len = 0, sh_len = sizeof(sh), left = 4/8 exactly) are all rejected or stay in bounds. The only values whose extent is not validated in this code are the scalar `&q[o4]` copy arguments, whose bounds check resides in the unshown helper cdf_copy_info, plus the `*count <= *maxcount` invariant maintained by the caller; per the callee-boundary and guard-anchoring rules these are recorded as limitations/assumptions, not evidence, and no candidate with a fully instantiated trigger and quoted impact chain remains.

assumptions: cdf_check_stream_offset validates a pointer plus length against the stream bounds and returns -1 on violation; every conclusion about p, e, and shp lying inside sst_tab rests on this unshown helper, as does the meaning of the three quoted calls to it.
cdf_get_property_info_pos returns NULL when the property slot at index i does not fit in [p, e); this code quotes the NULL test before the pi_id read, but the extent guarantee itself is unshown.

cdf_grow_info reallocates *info to hold at least the previous *maxcount plus the passed count entries, enforces CDF_PROP_LIMIT internally, and returns NULL on failure; this code quotes both NULL tests but not the capacity arithmetic.

cdf_copy_info bounds-checks its source pointer plus size against the end pointer before copying (returning 0 on failure); the scalar-property reads at &q[o4] of 2/4/8 bytes are only guaranteed q+o4 <= e by this code's own checks (e.g. left == 4, o4 == 4 leaves q+4 == e), so their safety depends entirely on this unshown helper.

The invariant *count <= *maxcount holds on entry; `inp += *count` and the capacity of `inp[i]` writes past the first sh.sh_properties entries depend on it, and it is neither asserted nor assignable from the given code.

CDF_SHLEN_LIMIT and CDF_PROP_LIMIT are finite, sanitizing constants (their numeric values are unsourced here); the offs, sh_len, and sh_properties bounds all rely on them being small enough that the downstream size_t arithmetic cannot wrap.
CDF_GETUINT32(q, n) reads a 32-bit little-endian value at q + 4*n; CDF_TOLE4 is a byte-order conversion; DPRINTF is compiled out unless a debug macro is defined.
The function is invoked by same-module callers that maintain the info/count/maxcount state; no direct attacker call path is visible in the given code.
limitations: Scalar-property out-of-bounds read candidate: for a non-vector property with left == 4 and o4 == 4 (e.g. CDF_SIGNED32), this code passes &q[o4] == e with size 4 to cdf_copy_info without any quoted extent check of its own; whether an out-of-bounds read occurs depends entirely on the unshown cdf_copy_info, a link that is neither quoted nor a characterizable standard-library call, so per the callee-boundary rule this can be neither confirmed as a vulnerability nor verified as guarded.

Caller-state trigger: if *count exceeded the grown capacity on entry, `inp += *count` followed by `inp[i]` writes would be out of bounds; the precondition is UNSOURCED in this code (no assignment or assert establishes it), so it is not instantiated.

32-bit width behavior: on a platform where size_t is 32-bit, `o4 + l` in the string loop can wrap if left exceeds 4 GiB (a >4 GiB CDF stream), letting an out-of-range l pass; the code as written declares size_t and no 32-bit path is exercised, so this is speculative (STEP 4(c)).

Debug-only out-of-bounds read candidate: DPRINTF prints s_buf with %s, and s_buf is l verified in-stream bytes that are not guaranteed NUL-terminated; impact requires a debug build whose compilation flags are not shown, and the read cannot cross the stream end without first passing a NUL-free region still inside the stream.

verdict.summary: All attacker-controlled values (optlen and the copied sctp_authkey contents) are guarded on the single execution path to each sink: the copy length and allocation size are the same verbatim expression optlen; the downstream key-length consumer sctp_auth_set_key is preceded by an on-path bounds check 'if (authkey->sca_keylength > optlen - sizeof(struct sctp_authkey))' that, at the exact-fit boundary keylength == optlen - sizeof, keeps the key bytes precisely inside the optlen-byte allocation; a negative optlen, which slips past the unsigned first comparison, is caught because kmalloc of an impossible size returns NULL and 'if (!authkey) return -ENOMEM;' is quoted on the only forward path. No trigger for memory corruption, OOB access, injection, or bypass could be instantiated.

assumptions: The struct sock *sk and sctp_sk(sk)->ep are supplied by the kernel setsockopt framework and are treated as internal-trusted kernel objects; no validation of sk appears in this code.

struct sctp_authkey is assumed to be a header (assoc id plus u16 length fields, covered by sizeof(struct sctp_authkey)) followed by an in-struct key array, so that keylength bytes starting at offset sizeof(struct sctp_authkey) fit exactly within optlen when keylength == optlen - sizeof(struct sctp_authkey).
Standard allocation semantics are relied upon as characterizable: kmalloc of an unsatisfiable (huge) size returns NULL, which the quoted 'if (!authkey)' check handles.
limitations: asoc can legitimately be NULL (when sca_assoc_id is 0 or on a TCP-style socket) and is then passed to sctp_auth_set_key(sctp_sk(sk)->ep, asoc, authkey). Whether the not-shown callee dereferences asoc cannot be quoted or characterized from the given code, so no CWE-476 finding can be confirmed; the impact chain breaks at the callee boundary.

sctp_auth_enable is UNSOURCED in this snippet (no assignment here); its only use is a fail-closed -EACCES gate, so it cannot produce a fail-open condition, but its runtime value cannot be established from this code.

A negative optlen passes the int-vs-size_t comparison 'if (optlen <= sizeof(struct sctp_authkey))' (unsigned wrap in the comparison); this is harmless only because the subsequent kmalloc of the wrapped huge size fails and returns NULL, which is checked. A defense-in-depth explicit signedness check on optlen is absent, but no security impact is reachable.

verdict.summary: Within the given code, the only memory-write sinks are either guarded by a quoted, execution-order-verified, fail-closed length check (the fragment copy into s->tx_packet and all consumers of total_bytes, which provably equals p - s->tx_packet), use exact-size copies (desc_first with sizeof(desc_first)), or are sized by not-shown helpers whose return ranges cannot be bounded or instantiated from this code (gem_get_desc_len into desc[DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS]; gem_get_max_buf_len vs the unshown s->tx_packet allocation; num_priority_queues vs the unshown s->tx_desc_addr[] dimension). No trigger precondition for a harmful value can be sourced to a quoted statement, so no vulnerability is provable; the indeterminacies are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: s->tx_packet is allocated with capacity >= gem_get_max_buf_len(s, true); no allocation or size statement exists in the given code.
gem_get_desc_len(s, false) returns at most DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS; the helper body and the value of DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS are not in the given code, so this bound could not be quoted.

s->num_priority_queues is within the dimensions of s->tx_desc_addr[] and of the ISR/queue arrays used by gem_get_tx_desc_addr/gem_set_isr/gem_get_tx_queue_base_addr; no assignment or clamp exists in the given code.
address_space_read fills the destination buffer (or leaves it initialized) even when the guest-supplied DMA address is invalid; failure semantics are not shown.
tx_desc_get_used/length/buffer/last/wrap read only the descriptor words filled earlier in this function; helper bodies not shown.
DB_PRINT expands to a no-op or debug-only logging; the macro is not shown.
limitations: Candidate A (stack overflow of uint32_t desc[DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS] at the two address_space_read(..., desc, sizeof(uint32_t) * gem_get_desc_len(s, false)) sites): no in-code bound on gem_get_desc_len's return exists (verified by STEP 5 search over all fix forms), but the precondition 'GEM_DMACFG value maps to desc_len > DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS' is UNSOURCED because the mapping lives entirely in the not-shown helper; trigger not instantiated.

Candidate B (overflow of s->tx_packet at address_space_read(..., p, tx_desc_get_length(desc)) if gem_get_max_buf_len(s, true) exceeds the buffer capacity): the in-code check bounds writes by max_buf_len minus current offset and is fail-closed at the boundary, but the relation max_buf_len <= sizeof(s->tx_packet) is not shown; capacity is UNSOURCED.
Candidate C (out-of-bounds write s->tx_desc_addr[q] when s->num_priority_queues exceeds the array dimension): num_priority_queues has no assignment in this code; trigger UNSOURCED.

Candidate D (uninitialized read of desc in while (tx_desc_get_used(desc) == 0) if the descriptor DMA read fails or transfers zero words): depends on not-shown address_space_read failure semantics; even with garbage descriptor contents, all length-consuming sinks remain bounded by the quoted check, so no in-code corruption is instantiable.

verdict.summary: ha_maria::drop_table passes the attacker-influenced table path 'name' (a content-bearing parameter of a handler entry point) directly to the file-deletion call maria_delete_table_files(name, 1, MY_WME) with no validation on any path in this function: no bounds, NULL, emptiness, or canonicalization check, no clamp, mask, or error arm, and no failure-sentinel test. The only diagnostic statement, DBUG_ASSERT(file->s->temporary), concerns a different unsourced field, is compiled out in release builds, and never inspects 'name'. A path value containing out-of-directory components therefore reaches the deletion sink unmodified, enabling deletion of files outside the intended table directory (CWE-22).

evidence.snippet:
(void) ha_close();
  (void) maria_delete_table_files(name, 1, MY_WME);
evidence.reason: The attacker-data path 'name' is passed unvalidated to the file-deletion call maria_delete_table_files(name, 1, MY_WME). The instantiated trigger: name carries out-of-directory components (e.g. "../../otherdb/victim"), flows unmodified past the DBUG_ASSERT (which tests a different, unsourced field and is compiled out under NDEBUG) and past ha_close(), and reaches the deletion sink; no check, clamp, canonicalization, or error arm exists anywhere in the function, so files outside the intended table directory are deleted.

evidence.snippet: void ha_maria::drop_table(const char *name)
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: the untrusted, content-carrying path enters as the parameter of a non-static, exported handler method. No documented, asserted, or checked precondition on 'name' exists anywhere in this code, so its content is attacker-data per the handler-function rule and cannot be treated as an interface contract.

assumptions: maria_delete_table_files(name, log_file, flags) is the Aria engine framework function whose characterizable semantics are: delete the files that constitute the table identified by 'name'; per the CALLEE BOUNDARY RULE the call statement at line 5 is the defective statement.
DBUG_ASSERT follows standard assert semantics: compiled out under NDEBUG, so it enforces nothing in release builds and constrains 'file', never 'name'.

The concrete transport from attacker SQL identifiers to the 'name' value lives in the not-shown server layer; per the framework's handler-function rule the caller is untrusted and controls the content of 'name', and no statement in this code constrains it.
MY_WME is a mysys error-reporting flag constant and the literal 1 is the callee's flag argument; both are internal constants of this code.
limitations: Possible NULL dereference of 'file'/'file->s' at line 3 (DBUG_ASSERT(file->s->temporary)): 'file' has no assignment in this code (UNSOURCED), so file == NULL cannot be instantiated; additionally the deref is compiled out in release builds and is an abort (crash) at most in debug builds. Not a finding.

Ignored error returns: (void) ha_close(); and (void) maria_delete_table_files(name, 1, MY_WME); discard failures (fail-open drop). The downstream consequences (stale table files surviving a 'successful' drop, dictionary/filesystem divergence, later reuse of stale files) occur in server/filesystem behavior that is neither shown nor characterizable, so the impact is not instantiated in this code.

The DBUG_ASSERT enforces the temporary-table precondition only in debug builds; a non-temporary table reaching drop_table would be deleted with flag 1. Both the precondition (file->s->temporary == 0 at this point) and any distinct harm from flag 1 depend on unsourced state and not-shown callee semantics, so this trigger is speculative.
NUL-termination of 'name' is never verified (no length parameter, no check); any resulting overread would occur entirely inside the not-shown callee and is not instantiated in this code.

verdict.summary: The UTF-8 decode length is computed with reversed operands: inside the loop p < parser->end always holds, so (size_t)(p - parser->end) is a negative pointer difference that wraps to a near-SIZE_MAX value (SIZE_MAX when p = end-1). uni_utf8_get_char_n is therefore handed an effectively unbounded length and reads up to 3 bytes past the end of the received data whenever an attacker ends a command line with a truncated multibyte UTF-8 lead byte. p then overshoots parser->end by up to 3, and the trailing-space trim (*(mp-1)) and i_strdup_until copy bytes beyond the validated buffer region into cmd_params. Out-of-bounds heap read in a network-facing parser, triggerable by any SMTP client.

evidence.snippet:
nch = uni_utf8_get_char_n(p, (size_t)(p - parser->end),
				  &ch);
evidence.reason: Root cause: the max_len argument uses p - parser->end instead of parser->end - p. The loop guard 'while (p < parser->end)' guarantees p < end at this call, so the difference is always negative and the cast to size_t wraps it to >= 2^63 (SIZE_MAX at p = end-1), while the safe domain is [0, end - p). The length-bounded UTF-8 decoder, given this bogus bound, reads continuation bytes past parser->end when an attacker sends a command ending in a truncated multibyte lead byte (e.g., a final 0xF0 byte) - an out-of-bounds heap read (CWE-125) caused by the integer underflow/signed-to-unsigned wrap (CWE-191).

Downstream impact of the same defect: after 'p += nch' (line 31) with nch up to 4 for a lead byte at end-1, p = end+3 and mp inherits that overshoot. The only guard is 'mp > parser->cur'; there is no upper bound against parser->end, so the trim loop dereferences *(mp-1) at addresses end, end+1, end+2 - reading out-of-bounds bytes past the validated data region.

evidence.snippet: parser->state.cmd_params = i_strdup_until(parser->cur, mp);
evidence.reason: Continuation of the impact chain: mp can be up to end+3 because p overshot parser->end via the bogus decode length, so i_strdup_until copies up to 3 bytes beyond the received data (uninitialized heap content past the data end) into the command parameters string, provided the max_size check at line 33 passes. The primary out-of-bounds read at the decoder call (lines 19-20) occurs regardless of that check.

assumptions: parser->auth_response, parser->cur, parser->end and parser->limits.* have no assignment in the given code; they are set by the not-shown SMTP parser state machine. The attacker effectively selects auth_response == 0 by sending any ordinary (non-AUTH) SMTP command, which exercises the UTF-8 decode branch; the exact assignment statements are outside the given code.

The buffer [parser->cur, parser->end) holds incrementally received SMTP socket data whose content the attacker (the connecting client) fully controls, including the position of the data end relative to a multibyte UTF-8 lead byte; this function is the trust-boundary intake for those bytes.

Disclosure of the out-of-bounds bytes to the attacker depends on the not-shown consumers of parser->state.cmd_params; the out-of-bounds read itself is fully instantiated in this code.

verdict.summary: cp_create parses the externally supplied encoder option string and stores OPT_MAXRLVLS via atoi into the signed int tccp->maxrlvls, validating only the upper bound (`maxrlvls > JPC_MAXRLVLS`). A negative value (e.g., maxrlvls=-1) passes that check, and the later fill loop `for (rlvlno = 0; rlvlno < tccp->maxrlvls; ++rlvlno)` compares an unsigned uint_fast16_t against the negative int, converting it to ~2^32-1. The loop then writes tccp->prcwidthexpns[rlvlno] and tccp->prcheightexpns[rlvlno] far past the fixed arrays inside the jas_malloc-allocated jpc_enc_cp_t, producing an attacker-triggered out-of-bounds heap write (memory corruption). The `maxrlvls < 1` sanity check exists only after the loop, so it runs too late to prevent the overflow.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink. rlvlno is uint_fast16_t (unsigned) while tccp->maxrlvls is a signed int that can hold -1 from the parsed option string; the comparison converts -1 to at least 4294967295, so the loop writes prcwidthexpns/prcheightexpns at indices far beyond the fixed-size arrays inside the heap-allocated jpc_enc_cp_t (jas_malloc at line 28). Instantiated trigger: optstr containing "maxrlvls=-1" reaches this loop with maxrlvls = -1; the first out-of-bounds store happens once rlvlno passes the array end, and the corrupted heap is a direct consequence of executing line 287/288.

Origin of the tainted value and the missing guard. atoi of the attacker-supplied option value can return any negative int; the only validation on any path before the fill loop is the one-sided upper-bound test `maxrlvls > JPC_MAXRLVLS`, which is false for -1. The lower-bound check `if (cp->tccp.maxrlvls < 1)` (line 381) runs only after the loop at line 286 has already performed the out-of-bounds writes, so no guard on any execution path rejects the harmful value before the sink.

assumptions: optstr is treated as attacker-data: this function is the parser/intake point for the encoder option string (jas_tvparser_create/jas_tvparser_next over optstr); per the data-origin impact model the caller's privilege or deployment is not evidence.
uint_fast16_t is an unsigned type at least 16 bits wide (typically 32-bit), so the loop comparison rlvlno < (int)-1 converts the negative bound to a value of at least 4294967295.

The declared sizes of tccp->prcwidthexpns and prcheightexpns are not shown; the out-of-bounds conclusion instead rests on the loop's converted bound (>= 2^32 iterations) provably exceeding any fixed array inside a single jas_malloc'd struct.

jas_taginfo_nonull, jpc_floorlog2, ratestrtosize, and jpc_atoaf are characterized by their conventional JasPer semantics; jpc_floorlog2 returns 0 for inputs <= 1, bounding prcwidthexpn/prcheightexpn to 0..31.
limitations: numgbits: `atoi` (line 197) can return 0 or a negative value, and the only check is `cp->tccp.numgbits > 8` (line 387), so out-of-range values pass. Their actual harmful use is inside encoder code not given, so the impact chain is not characterizable here; the missing lower-bound check is noted but does not drive the verdict.

tilewidth/tileheight: negative atoi values wrap when stored into uint_fast32_t fields and pass the `!cp->tilewidth` checks (lines 296/301); corrupted geometry flows into numhtiles/numvtiles/numtiles (lines 318-322), but those are consumed by not-shown tile-iteration code, so no in-code memory sink is instantiated.

imgareatlx/imgareatly = -1 collides with the UINT_FAST32_MAX 'unset' sentinel (line 232) and is silently replaced by 0; other negative values wrap in the geometry arithmetic (lines 238, 246, 248-261) but produce no memory or injection sink within this code.

JPC_MAXRLVLS, the encopts/modetab/prgord tables, and the jpc_enc_tccp_t array declarations are UNSOURCED (not assigned or declared in the given code); they were used only to show the intended bound, not as trigger preconditions or guards.

verdict.summary: bmexec_trans consumes attacker-controlled text/size but every memory access reachable with only in-code-sourced values is guarded: the len==1 path tests the memchr_kwset sentinel (lines 15-16), the tail loop's advance/read is preceded each iteration by the quoted guard 'while (d <= ep - tp)' with ep = text + size (lines 70-74), and the memchr escape tests its NULL sentinel before reuse (lines 54-57). The remaining out-of-bounds-read candidates in the fast skip loop (lines 31-46) and the tail entry read (line 71) require delta-table entries whose per-iteration sum exceeds the 11*len slack; kwset->delta and kwset->mind are never assigned in this code (built by the not-shown kwsprep), so those triggers are unsourced and cannot be confirmed. Likewise the 12*len integer overflow needs a ~179MB unsourced mind value, and any infinite-loop or OOB behavior inside the not-shown bm_delta2_search is uncharacterizable.

assumptions: The U macro (used as U(tp[-1])) is assumed to be an unsigned-char cast, as in GNU grep; it is not shown in the given code.
memchr_kwset is assumed to behave like memchr with translation: return a pointer within [text, text+size) or NULL; the NULL sentinel is tested at line 55 before any use.
bm_delta2_search is a not-shown internal helper; its effect on the tp it receives by address, including whether it keeps tp <= ep and always makes progress on failure, is assumed but unquotable.
The deployment context of bmexec_trans (who supplies kwset and the searched buffer) is unknown and was not used to promote or demote any candidate.
The return type of the function is not visible in the given code (line 1 starts at the function name).
limitations: Fast-loop out-of-bounds read (lines 31-46): the loop condition 'tp <= ep' is checked only once per outer iteration, and up to 10 delta increments (each bounded only by the unsigned-char table width 0..255 from 'unsigned char const *d1') occur mid-iteration. For len >= 232 the quotable 0..255 bound keeps all reads in bounds, but for len < 232 safety requires that kwset->delta entries be small (the design invariant delta <= len implied by the comment 'Significance of 12: 1 (initial offset) + 10 (skip loop) + 1 (md2)'). kwset->delta is never assigned in this code, so the trigger precondition (large delta entries) is UNSOURCED and cannot be confirmed or refuted here.

Tail-entry read (line 71 'd = d1[U(tp[-1])]'): if the fast loop exits through its condition, tp can exceed ep by up to 10*255; whether tp can exceed text+size for len < 232 depends on the same UNSOURCED kwset->delta contents.

Signed overflow of '12 * len' and '11 * len' (lines 26, 28): requires kwset->mind near INT_MAX/12 (~179 million), a value never assigned in this code; line 11 'if (len > size)' additionally forces size >= len. UNSOURCED trigger.

Potential non-termination of the tail loop (lines 72-79) if bm_delta2_search returns 0 without advancing tp: depends entirely on the not-shown callee's behavior, which cannot be characterized under the callee boundary rule.

Any out-of-bounds access occurring inside bm_delta2_search (lines 63, 77) is outside the given code; the arguments passed (tp, ep, sp=target+len, len in [2, size]) are in the domain implied by the in-code bounds established in STEP 2.

verdict.summary: ha_maria::drop_table forwards the caller-supplied table path 'name' directly into the file-deletion routine maria_delete_table_files with no NULL check, length check, canonicalization, or confinement to the data directory anywhere in the function (the only test present, the debug-only DBUG_ASSERT, constrains 'file', not 'name'); a non-canonical path supplied by the caller of this non-static handler method therefore reaches the deletion primitive and unlinks files outside the intended directory.

evidence.reason: The attacker-controlled table path 'name' enters at line 1 as the sole parameter of this non-static handler method with no documented or asserted precondition, and flows unvalidated through the straight-line body into the file-deletion call at line 5: no NULL check, no length check, no canonicalization, and no data-directory confinement exists on any path (the DBUG_ASSERT at line 3 tests only 'file' and is compiled out in release builds). Per the callee boundary rule the call at line 5 is the defective statement: it hands an out-of-domain, attacker-derived path to the table-file deletion helper, which unlinks the files named from that path, deleting files outside the authorized directory.

assumptions: maria_delete_table_files(name, 1, MY_WME) is MariaDB's table-file deletion helper that unlinks the data/index files whose paths derive from 'name'; its body is not shown, so this behavior is characterized from the function's role/name per the callee boundary rule.
DBUG_ASSERT is a debug-time assertion compiled out in release builds; it enforces nothing at runtime in production and constrains only 'file', never 'name'.
ha_close() closes the handler's open table file; its return value is discarded and its failure semantics are not shown.
The caller of this virtual handler method was treated as untrusted for the content of 'name' per discipline 3; no assumption about caller-side sanitization was used.
limitations: C2: DBUG_ASSERT(!file || file->s->temporary) dereferences file->s after only a NULL check of file; a NULL file->s would crash debug builds (CWE-476 flavor), but 'file' and 'file->s' have no assignment in this code (UNSOURCED) and the assert is debug-only, so the trigger is not instantiated.

C3: the (void) discards of ha_close() and maria_delete_table_files() return values suppress error reporting (a failed drop is invisible to this void API), but no statement in this code consumes the failure state and the unshown caller's reaction cannot be characterized, so the impact chain breaks.

If the deployed MariaDB SQL layer only ever passes server-normalized, traversal-free table paths to this handler, the C1 trigger would not be instantiable in the real product; that upstream sanitization is not quotable from this code and therefore cannot demote the finding, but it is recorded as context.

verdict.summary: In hfsplus_find_cat, the bad-thread-record branch returns `err` after `if (err) return err;` has already guaranteed err == 0, so a detected-corrupt catalog thread record yields a success (0) return. An attacker mounting a crafted HFS+ image controls tmp.type (copied from disk by hfs_brec_read), so any record whose type is neither HFSPLUS_FOLDER_THREAD nor HFSPLUS_FILE_THREAD triggers the error branch, which prints an error and then presents the found/valid state to the caller — fail-open security-state misrepresentation. The historical name-length overflow in this function is guarded by the verified `> 255` check and is not the finding.

evidence.reason: Fail-open security-state misrepresentation: on the path where a corrupt thread record type is detected, the function returns `err`, which is provably 0 here because lines 10-11 already returned on any nonzero err. The attacker controls tmp.type via the disk record read at line 9 (e.g., type = 0x0001), enters the branch, prints an error, and returns success for an invalid record.

Origin of the faulty value: err is assigned only from hfs_brec_read, and this early return guarantees err == 0 on every path that reaches line 13, so the `return err;` inside the bad-type branch at line 16 can only return 0 (success), never an error code.

assumptions: fd and fd->search_key are assumed valid pointers supplied by kernel-internal callers; this code contains no NULL check and no documented contract, and no statement in this code can produce a NULL fd, so this remains an unquotable interface assumption rather than an instantiated trigger.

hfsplus_cat_build_key, hfsplus_cat_build_key_uni, and hfs_brec_read are treated per their HFS+ framework roles (key builders; btree record lookup that can fail, whose failure sentinel is tested at line 10 before tmp is first used at line 13).
sb is internal kernel state; HFSPLUS_SB(sb) parameters consumed by the key builder are set in unshown code.
limitations: The classic name-length overflow (u16 nodeName.length up to 65535 copied into the fixed 255-element key name array, CWE-120/787 pattern) is NOT present in this code: the guard `if (be16_to_cpu(tmp.thread.nodeName.length) > 255) { ... return -EIO; }` sits on the only path to the hfsplus_cat_build_key_uni call, was edge-tested at length 255 (in-bounds: copies indices 0..254), 256 (rejected), 0 (valid empty key), and 65535 (rejected), so the candidate is dismissed as guarded.

If the on-disk thread record is shorter than sizeof(hfsplus_cat_entry), the tail of the stack struct tmp (including nodeName.name[]) may be uninitialized and is then copied into search_key (CWE-457 pattern). This requires underfill semantics of the unshown internal hfs_brec_read and has no disclosure or corruption path inside this code, so it is not instantiated here.

The heap sizing of fd->search_key depends on tree->max_key_len from the disk B-tree header, allocated and validated in unshown code (hfs_find_init / btree load); any overflow arising from an undersized search_key buffer would be a defect in that unshown code, not in this snippet.
A NULL fd passed by a caller would crash at line 8 (fd->search_key dereference, CWE-476 pattern), but no caller is shown and no statement in this code produces NULL; trigger not instantiated.

The practical downstream consequences of the success-return-on-corrupt-record depend on unshown callers of hfsplus_find_cat; the confirmed impact is the fail-open misrepresentation itself, completed at the quoted return statement.

The user-data guard compares cin.file.user_length > GetBlobSize(image) (total file size) rather than the bytes remaining after ~712+ consumed bytes, so ReadBlob(image,GetStringInfoLength(profile),GetStringInfoDatum(profile)) can short-read; whether the allocated profile tail retains uninitialized heap depends on unshown BlobToStringInfo zeroing and on unshown consumers of the 'dpx:user.data' profile.

The ping path (if (image_info->ping != MagickFalse) { (void) CloseBlob(image); return(image); }) returns before the columns*rows/8 blob-size check and before SetImageExtent, delivering unvalidated columns/rows/depth to unshown ping callers.

verdict.summary: On the keyword-table parse failure path in GmfOpenMesh, the failure arm 'if(!ScaKwdTab(msh)) return(0);' returns without freeing the heap-allocated GmfMshSct (calloc at line 13) and without closing the open FILE handle on the attacker-controlled mesh file (fopen at line 92 or 122), unlike every other error path which longjmps to a cleanup handler that calls fclose and free. An attacker who supplies a mesh file with a valid header (valid endian tag, version 1-4, Dimension keyword, dimension 2 or 3) but a malformed or truncated keyword table triggers the leak once per file opened; an application processing attacker-supplied mesh files retains one struct plus one file descriptor per file, leading to unbounded memory and descriptor exhaustion (denial of service).

evidence.snippet:
if(!ScaKwdTab(msh))
         return(0);
evidence.reason: Root cause: the failure arm of the keyword-table parse returns 0 with no cleanup. Every other error path in the function raises longjmp to the handler at lines 19-36, which performs 'fclose(msh->hdl)' (line 25) and 'free(msh)' (line 34); this arm executes neither. Trigger fully simulated: an attacker-controlled .meshb file with cod=1, ver in 1..4, KwdCod=GmfDimension, dim=3 passes all quoted validations (lines 100, 105, 113, 149), then ScaKwdTab fails parsing the attacker-corrupted keyword table and returns its failure sentinel, which this very line tests. The mesh structure allocated at line 13 and the FILE opened at line 92 are both retained; the number of retained objects is bounded only by the count of attacker-supplied files.

if(!(msh->hdl = fopen(msh->FilNam, "rb")))
            longjmp(msh->err, -8);
evidence.reason: Origin of the leaked resource: the FILE handle on the attacker-influenced file path is opened here (and the leaked heap structure originates from 'msh = calloc(1, sizeof(GmfMshSct))' at line 13). Neither this handle nor the structure is released when ScaKwdTab subsequently fails at line 166 and the function returns 0 at line 167, so the open descriptor and the allocation are retained per failed open.

assumptions: Constants GmfStrSiz, WrdSiz, GmfRead, GmfWrite, GmfKwdFmt, OPEN_READ_FLAGS, OPEN_WRITE_FLAGS, OPEN_READ_MODE, OPEN_WRITE_MODE and the helpers ScaWrd, RecWrd, GetPos, ScaKwdTab, safe_fread, safe_fscanf are defined outside the given code; their values and behaviors, except the success/failure semantics of the parse helpers that this code itself tests, are not quotable here.

Preprocessor configuration (WITH_GMF_AIO, GMF_WINDOWS, GMFDEBUG) and the deployment context (which process calls this API and with what privilege) are unknown and were not used to promote or demote any candidate.
limitations: fscanf(msh->hdl, "%100s", str) at lines 127/140 writes up to 101 bytes into 'char str[GmfStrSiz]' (line 5). An overflow requires GmfStrSiz < 101; GmfStrSiz is UNSOURCED (no definition or assignment in this code), so this candidate could be neither confirmed nor refuted.
ScaWrd(msh, (unsigned char *)&msh->ver) and the analogous calls for KwdCod, dim, cod write WrdSiz bytes into 4-byte int fields; an overflow requires WrdSiz > 4, an UNSOURCED constant.

FilNam is dereferenced by strlen (line 39) and strcpy (line 42) with no NULL check; a NULL argument crashes the caller's process. The only party that can supply NULL is the same-process API caller, and no trust boundary across which NULL arrives is exhibited by any statement in this code, so the impact is not instantiated here.

PtrVer and PtrDim (varargs fetched at lines 70-73) are dereferenced at lines 152-153 with no NULL or validity check; the written values are bounded (ver 1-4, dim 2-3) by quoted guards, but a wild caller-supplied pointer would yield an arbitrary-address write of a small constant. The pointer originates from the same-privilege library caller with no quotable trust boundary, so this is a caller-contract defect rather than an instantiated vulnerability in this code.

A TOCTOU window exists between strlen(FilNam) at line 39 and strcpy at line 42 (two ordered operations with a possible interleave), but the mutating party would have to be a thread in the caller's own process modifying the caller's buffer; no such attacker is exhibited in this code.

ScaKwdTab's internal parsing of the attacker-controlled keyword table is not shown; any memory-corruption behavior inside that callee is outside the given code, and the confirmed finding here rests only on its characterizable success/failure return, which this code tests at line 166.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is instantiable in this code. The copy length is clamped to i->count and checked for zero; the buffer index is masked into the ring; the allocation loop is bounded by pipe_full; allocation failure is tested before use; and the partial-page fusion arithmetic (`left -= PAGE_SIZE - off` with `left <= 0`, and `buf->len = min_t(ssize_t, left, PAGE_SIZE)` with `left == 0`) is boundary-correct as written. pipe->max_usage ≤ pipe->ring_size (enforced in pipe resize/allocation code not shown), so pipe_full caps allocation within the live ring.

Candidate: `unsigned int p_mask = pipe->ring_size - 1;` wraps to 0xFFFFFFFF if pipe->ring_size == 0, making the masked bufs index unbounded — precondition UNSOURCED: no assignment to ring_size in this code.

Candidate: if pipe->max_usage exceeded pipe->ring_size (unsourced), pipe_full would not stop the loop before the masked slot aliases a live unconsumed buffer, corrupting pipe data.

Candidate: the off != 0 path writes `pipe->bufs[iter_head & p_mask]` without a pipe_full check; harmful only if data_start returns an iter_head with no allocated buffer, which no statement in this code can produce.

verdict.summary: This io_uring io_read implementation checks every callee failure sentinel before first use, nulls the iovec pointer after ownership handoff before any later free path, and its retry-loop arithmetic (io_size -= ret) cannot underflow under the characterizable read contract (a read never returns more than the iterator count, which equals io_size at first read, and ret <= 0 / ret == io_size are excluded by the quoted entry chain). The remaining candidates (io_size underflow if a read returned more than requested, UAF if a queued read retained the freed iovec, NULL deref of rw after setup, iovec leak on early returns, and completion accounting via unshown kiocb_done) all have preconditions that no statement in this code can produce or impact links that break at unshown, uncharacterizable callees, so none is instantiated.

assumptions: io_iter_do_read is a read(2)-style call that never returns more than the current iterator count; the given code's entry chain (ret <= 0 || ret == io_size) plus this contract is what keeps io_size -= ret from underflowing - no in-code check bounds ret against io_size before the first io_size -= ret.
rw_verify_area returns 0 or a negative errno; the code treats any nonzero as failure via if (unlikely(ret)), which is safe only under that contract.

io_setup_async_rw returning 0 implies req->async_data is allocated and non-NULL, and that it takes ownership of (or copies) the passed iovec; both guarantees are in the unshown callee, not quotable here.
A read returning -EIOCBQUEUED has taken full ownership of the kiocb and everything needed for completion, so kfree(iovec) after goto out_free is assumed safe.
kiocb_done reports the request result correctly, including any accumulated rw->bytes_done; its behavior is unshown.
io_read is a static internal function reached only from io_uring SQE issue paths; even so, all SQE-derived state was treated as attacker-data per discipline 3.
limitations: io_size -= ret underflow (CWE-191-style): trigger requires io_iter_do_read to return ret with 0 < ret != io_size and ret > io_size, which violates the read contract; no statement in this code can produce that value, so the precondition is UNSOURCED (produced only by an out-of-contract callee).

kfree(iovec) after ret == -EIOCBQUEUED could be a use-after-free only if the queued asynchronous read later dereferences the iovec-backed iterator; that retention is behavior of unshown code and cannot be characterized, so the impact link breaks.
rw = req->async_data dereference after a successful io_setup_async_rw could NULL-deref only if the callee returned 0 without allocating; that combination is unsourced in this code.

Heap iovec may leak on the return ret ?: -EAGAIN and return ret2 early-exit paths if the callee does not take ownership; whether it frees is unshown, and each leak is a bounded per-request allocation, not demonstrated unbounded retention.

The do-while retry loop exits to done: kiocb_done(kiocb, ret, ...) with ret holding only the last chunk while rw->bytes_done accumulates prior chunks; whether the completion result is misreported depends entirely on unshown kiocb_done, so no impact is instantiated here (and a wrong byte count alone is not a memory-safety, bypass, disclosure, or amplification impact).

verdict.summary: hfsplus_block_allocate has a page-crossing allocation defect: on the success path every kmap(page) is balanced by a kunmap(page), but on the path where the allocation reaches the found label with i == 32 (mask 0, whole word consumed) the function falls into *curr = cpu_to_be32(n) and set_page_dirty(page) without any kunmap for the mapping acquired at line 13, and at line 92 the return length *max is computed from (curr - pptr) * 32 + i - start where pptr still points at the page mapping from line 13 while curr was advanced to a mapping acquired later at line 79. Because the kunmap at line 75 already released the original mapping, the arithmetic at line 92 dereferences and performs pointer arithmetic on a mapping that is no longer pinned, and the dirty page is written back to disk via the stale mapping. A crafted hfsplus filesystem where the first free block leaves a zero-mask word causes unbounded memory corruption and on-disk bitmap corruption during block allocation, and the miscalculated *max misreports the allocation length to the caller, corrupting subsequent free-block accounting. Trigger is fully instantiated: an attacker supplies a filesystem whose allocation file causes the scan to find a word with a zero mask and a zero remainder, reaching the found label with i == 32, and the writeback at line 91 completes the corruption. This is a memory-corruption primitive reachable by mounting a malicious filesystem image.

evidence.reason: On the success path every kmap is balanced by a kunmap, but this writeback path executes *curr = cpu_to_be32(n) and set_page_dirty(page) while the original mapping acquired at line 13 has already been released by the kunmap at line 75; the subsequent arithmetic (curr - pptr) * 32 at line 92 uses a stale pptr from the released mapping, so the dirty page is written back through an unpinned mapping and the computed length is wrong. This is the instantiated trigger: an allocation file whose first free word consumes the entire mask reaches the found label with i == 32 and mask == 0, hitting this path directly.

The origin of the trigger: start is computed from a word found with mask possibly zero (i == 32), and the loop n |= mask; if (++i >= 32) break consumes the whole word, causing the later code to fall into the writeback path with an unbalanced kmap and a stale pptr; this is where the defective control flow leading to the stale-mapping writeback is produced.

assumptions: PAGE_CACHE_BITS, PAGE_CACHE_SIZE, kmap, kunmap, read_mapping_page, and set_page_dirty have their standard Linux semantics (page-sized bitmap windows mapped at kernel virtual addresses); this is characterizable library behavior relied on per the CALLEE BOUNDARY RULE.

size, offset and *max are caller-provided values of the allocation-file metadata consumed by this non-static exported entry point; per STEP 1 the caller is treated as untrusted and a caller-supplied len of 0 takes the early return at line 6, which is a contract question, not attacker-data dismissal, since the quote len = *max; if (!len) return size; enforces it in this code.
A subsequent kernel writeback of a page marked dirty through a stale mapping performs the disk write; this is characterizable standard page-cache behavior, not unshown code.
limitations: Exploitability beyond memory corruption and on-disk bitmap corruption (e.g., turning a stale-mapping write into a controlled out-of-bounds write of chosen content) depends on kernel memory layout not derivable from the given code; the corruption primitive itself is fully instantiated.

Candidate: in the do full u32s loop, if len shrinks below 32 exactly as curr reaches end, the loop can advance to a new page while len < 32 and never reach the last-label partial-word handling, causing *curr at line 89 to write the full 32-bit word n as if it were complete; triggering requires a specific (len, curr, end) coincidence across page boundaries that was not proven reachable from the quoted statements alone, so it is recorded here and does not affect the verdict.

Candidate: HFSPLUS_SB(sb).free_blocks -= *max at line 93 can underflow if *max exceeds the free-block count; no statement in this code bounds *max against free_blocks, but reaching an underflow requires an allocation-file size inconsistent with the volume's free-block count, a relationship this code does not establish or quote, so the trigger is not instantiated here.

verdict.summary: In php_wddx_pop_element, when a value end tag arrives while stack->top == 1 and the top entry has NULL data, the else arm sets stack->done = 1 but leaves stack->top unchanged and never clears stack->elements[stack->top-1] before efree(ent1). The freed entry remains referenced by the stack, so any subsequent end tag processed at top == 1 (re-entry through wddx_stack_top at line 21 and the !ent1->data read at line 23) or any sibling value merged into its parent (wddx_stack_top at line 61 followed by the ent2->type read at line 64) operates on freed memory, yielding a use-after-free read/write and a reachable double free (efree(ent1) executed twice on the same pointer), triggered solely by attacker-controlled WDDX packet content.

evidence.reason: Root cause: when stack->top == 1, the else arm performs only stack->done = 1 and then efree(ent1) without decrementing stack->top or clearing the stack slot, so the freed entry remains at stack->elements[stack->top-1] with top == 1. Instantiated trigger: a WDDX packet with a content-less root-level value element (e.g. <string></string> inside <data>) drives this arm and frees the entry; a following sibling value element (e.g. <string>x</string>) is then merged into that freed parent, or a repeated matching end tag re-enters the function at top == 1, causing the freed pointer to be dereferenced (UAF read at 'if (!ent1->data)' / 'ent2->type', UAF write via Z_STRVAL_P(ent1->data) = new_str, and a double free via the second efree(ent1)).

Consumption site of the dangling entry: after stack->top-- (line 60), wddx_stack_top returns the entry at elements[top-1], which is the entry freed at line 29 in the prior invocation; the immediately following reads of ent2->type and ent2->data are uses of freed memory, and the subsequent Z_TYPE_P(ent2->data)/HASH_OF(ent2->data)/zend_hash_next_index_insert chain operates on pointers derived from freed memory, giving attacker-controlled corruption when the packet author grooms the heap between the two end tags.

assumptions: php_wddx_push_element and the character-data handler (not shown) create one stack entry per value start tag and leave ent->data == NULL when no character data arrived; this is corroborated by the quoted branch 'if (!ent1->data)' whose existence proves NULL-data entries are a produced state, and by the harvest arm 'else { stack->done = 1; }' at lines 124-125 which deliberately keeps the top==1 entry alive for the caller.
wddx_stack_top peeks at elements[top-1] without modifying top; this is established by this code's own usage, which performs an explicit 'stack->top--' after the peek at lines 60-61 and 133-134.

The XML parser invokes this end-element callback for every closing tag whose name is one of the listed element names, in document order, within a single XML_Parse pass; stack->done is never consulted by this function or by the parser to stop processing.
limitations: php_base64_decode result new_str (line 37) is not NULL-checked before 'Z_STRVAL_P(ent1->data) = new_str;' (line 39); empty input yields new_str == NULL with new_len == 0, producing a string zval with a NULL value pointer. No use of that zval occurs inside this code and the downstream consumer of the deserialized value is not shown, so the impact is not instantiated here.
strlen(ent1->varname) at line 116 assumes the varname is NUL-terminated; its producer (the push handler copying the XML attribute) is not shown, so no overread can be proven from the given code.

Whether the not-shown caller php_wddx_unserialize also dereferences stack.elements[0] after done is set cannot be determined from the given code; it would only add further UAF consumption sites, not change the defect located here.

verdict.summary: uncompressEntry creates symlinks whose target is read verbatim from the archive entry with no validation (File::createSymbolicLink (targetFile, originalFilePath, true)); the only symlink-traversal guard (hasSymbolicPart) is gated on FollowSymlinks::no and is bypassed by the directory-entry early return. A malicious archive can plant a symlink to an arbitrary filesystem location and, in FollowSymlinks::yes mode, write attacker-controlled content to arbitrary files outside the target directory (symlink-based Zip Slip). Additionally, the caller-supplied index is used unchecked via entries.getUnchecked, giving an out-of-bounds read.

evidence.reason: The symlink target originalFilePath is read fully attacker-controlled from the archive entry stream and passed unvalidated to createSymbolicLink (only the syscall's failure is tested, not the target's location). The isAChildOf guard at line 16 constrains only the link's own location, never its target, so a zip entry flagged isSymbolicLink plants a symlink to an arbitrary path (e.g. /etc/cron.d) inside the extraction directory. Root cause: improper link resolution before the later file access (CWE-59) defeating the restricted-directory guarantee (CWE-22).

With followSymlinks == FollowSymlinks::yes the only symlink-traversal guard (line 36, 'if (followSymlinks == FollowSymlinks::no && hasSymbolicPart (...))') is skipped, and the line 16 isAChildOf check is lexical. Simulated trigger: entry 'd' (symlink, payload '/etc/cron.d') creates the link via line 47; entry 'd/pwn' passes the lexical child check, skips the guard at line 36, and FileOutputStream/out << *in write attacker-controlled content through the symlink to /etc/cron.d/pwn, an arbitrary file write outside the target directory. Every precondition is sourced: archive content is the attacker input at this code's surface, the yes-mode is a supported parameter value, and the symlink itself is planted by this code's line 47.

evidence.snippet:
if (entryPath.endsWithChar ('/') || entryPath.endsWithChar ('\\'))
        return targetFile.createDirectory(); // (entry is a directory, not a file)
evidence.reason: Execution-order bypass of the symlink guard: this early return executes createDirectory() BEFORE the hasSymbolicPart check at line 36, so even with FollowSymlinks::no a trailing-slash directory entry whose path traverses an archive-created symlink (e.g. entry 'ln' symlink to '/usr/local/share' followed by directory entry 'ln/x/') creates a directory outside the target directory. The guard exists (line 36) but is unreachable for this branch, exactly the guard-position-in-execution-order defect class.

evidence.snippet: auto* zei = entries.getUnchecked (index);
evidence.reason: The caller-supplied index is passed to entries.getUnchecked (a documented unchecked accessor) with no bounds check, clamp, assert, or size() comparison anywhere in this function. An out-of-range index (e.g. INT_MAX or -1) yields an out-of-bounds element pointer that is immediately dereferenced (zei->entry.filename at lines 6/8), producing an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125, index handling CWE-129), crash/DoS, and potential heap corruption from operating on a garbage String.

assumptions: zei->entry.filename / isSymbolicLink / fileTime are populated by the archive central-directory parser (not shown) and are treated as attacker-data per the parsed-file-content origin.
entries' population and sizing code is not shown; no guard in this code uses its size, so the unchecked-index finding does not depend on it.
hasSymbolicPart's implementation is not shown; its guarding effect in FollowSymlinks::no mode for file entries is assumed from the call at line 36.
File::isAChildOf/getChildFile are assumed lexical (no symlink resolution) per documented JUCE framework semantics; Array/OwnedArray::getUnchecked is documented as performing no bounds checking.

Sequential extraction of multiple archive entries (caller loop) is not shown; the impact chain relies on line 47 of this code planting the symlink itself (STEP 4(d) exception) and on the function's evident per-entry purpose.
Whether callers actually use FollowSymlinks::yes is deployment-dependent and was NOT used to demote; it is a supported parameter value shown by the branch at line 36.
limitations: TOCTOU between the line 16/36 checks and the line 52 open requires a concurrent local attacker with write access to targetDirectory interleaving between two operations of this code; the window is not exhibitable as ordered operations here, so it is speculative.

readEntireStreamAsString (line 44) retains the entire symlink-entry payload in memory; a highly compressible multi-GB entry can force OOM (CWE-400-style DoS). Trigger is instantiable but recorded as a secondary observation, not driving the verdict.

In FollowSymlinks::no mode, regular-file traversal through archive-created symlinks is blocked by line 36 assuming hasSymbolicPart detects the link; the residual no-mode escape is the directory-entry early return (evidence lines 19-20).
Attacker-controlled entry.fileTime applied via setCreationTime/setLastModificationTime/setLastAccessTime (lines 60-62) has no security effect (cosmetic).

verdict.summary: handle_returned_header runs sscanf(input, "%u\r\n", &limit) on the libcurl header buffer, which holds exactly size*nmemb bytes and is not NUL-terminated. When the auth backend returns the configured timelimit header with an empty or all-whitespace value, the '\r'/'\n' bytes terminating the line are consumed as whitespace by the %u conversion, so sscanf must read at least one byte (and unboundedly many more if adjacent heap bytes are digits) past the end of the delivered buffer, a heap out-of-bounds read; the value parsed from out-of-bounds memory is then stored into client->con->discon_time.

evidence.reason:
Root cause: sscanf parses input as a NUL-terminated C string, but the delivered data is length-delimited (len bytes, not NUL-terminated per libcurl's header callback contract). The line-18 check only verifies the last two delivered bytes are

" (len = timelimit_header_len + 2) passes the line-14 length guard, the line-18

evidence.reason: Taint origin: ptr is the header line content delivered by libcurl from the auth backend's HTTP response — untrusted network content of exactly size*nmemb bytes, not NUL-terminated — which this callback consumes directly as the parse input at line 21.

assumptions: libcurl's CURLOPT_HEADERFUNCTION delivers header data as exactly size*nmemb bytes without NUL termination (documented framework contract, characterizable per the callee boundary rule).

url->timelimit_header, url->timelimit_header_len, url->auth_header, url->auth_header_len, and url->errormsg are state fields assigned outside this function (configuration/initialization not shown); the confirmed finding additionally assumes the timelimit feature is configured (non-NULL) and that errormsg is an array so sizeof(url->errormsg) is its allocation bound.

Unchecked dereferences auth_user->client (line 3), client->auth (line 8), auth->state (line 9), client->con (line 22) have no NULL producer in the given code; the header-data pointer is registered by unshown setup code, so no attacker-triggerable NULL dereference is instantiated.

A degenerate configuration with auth_header non-NULL and auth_header_len == 0 would set client->authenticated = 1 for every header line (lines 11-12), but that precondition is an unsourced configuration value this code never assigns.

The icecast-auth-message memcpy block (lines 31-45) was edge-tested and found bounded: copy_len is clamped to sizeof(url->errormsg) (lines 35-37), the write never exceeds the array, and the maximum read offset is len-2 (in bounds) even at len=25 and at copy_len == sizeof(errormsg) — no overflow instantiated.

verdict.summary: In the xmit_failed error path of mcba_usb_start_xmit, the transmitted skb is freed twice. Line 50 'can_put_echo_skb(skb, priv->netdev, ctx->ndx, 0);' transfers ownership of skb to the CAN framework echo ring (the documented contract forbids the driver from freeing it afterward; the success path at line 56 performs no free, confirming consumption). When mcba_usb_xmit fails, line 59 'can_free_echo_skb(priv->netdev, ctx->ndx, NULL);' frees the stored skb, and line 61 'dev_kfree_skb(skb);' frees the same allocation a second time, producing a kernel double free (memory corruption) reachable whenever a USB transmit submission fails, e.g. device disconnect or ENOMEM. The memcpy at line 45 was analyzed and is guarded by can_dropped_invalid_skb at line 14, which bounds cf->len to 8 before every use.

evidence.reason: Double free of the transmitted skb. Ownership of skb was already transferred to the CAN echo ring at line 50; can_free_echo_skb() performs the single legitimate free of the stored skb at line 59, then dev_kfree_skb(skb) at line 61 frees the same allocation again. Trigger instantiated: local user transmits a valid CAN frame (valid dlc<=8 passes can_dropped_invalid_skb), mcba_usb_xmit returns nonzero (USB disconnect/ENOMEM) and the branch 'if (err) goto xmit_failed' executes both frees consecutively, yielding kernel slab memory corruption (CWE-415). No revalidation, refcount bump, or alternate error arm exists between the two frees on any path.

evidence.snippet: can_put_echo_skb(skb, priv->netdev, ctx->ndx, 0);
evidence.reason: Origin of the defect: this call hands the skb to the CAN framework (documented semantics: the skb is consumed and stored in the echo ring at ctx->ndx, and the driver must not free it afterward; the function returns at line 56 with no further free of skb on the success path). The stale local skb pointer is then freed again at lines 59 and 61 in the error path.

assumptions: The struct mcba_usb_msg_can definition (including the size of usb_msg.data and the values of MCBA_SIDL_EXID_MASK, MCBA_DLC_RTR_MASK) is not part of the given code; the memcpy bound analysis assumes the upstream header where data[] is 8 bytes, matching CAN_MAX_DLEN.

can_dropped_invalid_skb is treated per its documented CAN framework semantics: it rejects invalid classic CAN skbs (skb->len != CAN_MTU, cf->len > CAN_MAX_DLEN=8, invalid can_id bits) and its check at line 14 executes before every cf dereference, bounding usb_msg.dlc at the line 45 memcpy to [0,8].

can_put_echo_skb and can_free_echo_skb are treated per their documented framework ownership semantics: can_put_echo_skb consumes the skb (stores it in the echo ring for loopback) and can_free_echo_skb frees the stored skb; this contract is also corroborated by the success path returning at line 56 with no skb free.
ctx->ndx is produced by the not-shown mcba_usb_get_free_ctx and is assumed to lie within the echo ring bounds (the framework BUG_ON would otherwise fire).
limitations: The double-free trigger requires mcba_usb_xmit() to return nonzero; the callee body is not in the given code. Upstream it wraps usb_alloc_urb/usb_submit_urb, which fail on ENOMEM and on device disconnect (an ordinary user-inducible event during transmission), and the code's own branch 'if (err) goto xmit_failed' treats the error path as live.

A potential async lifetime defect exists at line 52: mcba_usb_xmit receives '&usb_msg', a stack object. If the not-shown callee assigned it as an asynchronous URB transfer_buffer, a stack use-after-free would result; the callee's behavior cannot be characterized from the given code, so this is recorded as a limitation rather than a finding.

The memcpy(usb_msg.data, cf->data, usb_msg.dlc) overflow candidate was dismissed: the length is bounded to at most 8 by the can_dropped_invalid_skb call quoted at line 14, which executes before the copy on every path, and the RTR flag OR into dlc occurs at line 48, after the copy. The dismissal additionally rests on the unshown header's data[8] width (recorded as an assumption).
